A mesh upgrade can instantly transform your home Wi-Fi network

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tired of Wi-Fi drops throughout your home? The best mesh Wi-Fi systems can eliminate internet dead zones and turn your house into a powerhouse for connectivity, no matter how far away devices are from a router. To prove it, we've done the testing to help you find the right mesh system.

At Tom's Guide, we put each mesh Wi-Fi system through real-world scenarios, from multi-story homes to outdoor use. This allows us to see how fast internet speeds are at multiple ranges, especially through objects and walls. So, if you've been struggling to get a strong Wi-Fi signal across your home, the mesh Wi-Fi systems we recommend will help you sort that problem out.

For the best mesh Wi-Fi system you can buy today, we recommend the MSI Roami BE Pro for reliable speeds and long-distance coverage. This Wi-Fi 7 mesh system will take you far for its price, but there are more options we've tested for homes.

Soon, you'll see more of the next standard of mesh Wi-Fi systems arrive with Wi-Fi 8. We've already tested the first Wi-Fi 8 router, but there's no need to rush to get this yet, as there aren't any consumer devices that can take advantage of it. In the meantime, we have even more mesh systems worth considering!

For the latest wireless connectivity, or to cover your home on a budget, this guide will help you find the best mesh Wi-Fi system for your needs, with in-depth reviews and test results. Let's dive in.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The MSI Roamii BE Pro isn't the fastest around, nor does it deliver the longest range, but it excels at speeds, distances and setup for half the price of other tri-band WiFi 7 routers. That's why it's the best mesh Wi-Fi system we recommend for most, especially if you're looking for an affordable way to upgrade to Wi-Fi 7.

The Roamii BE Pro immediately stands out for its real-world speed across a whole house, reaching 1.885 Gbps at 15 feet and still delivering 66.3 Mbps at a distant 90 feet. That kind of consistent performance means you won’t be left hunting for a signal in the farthest room.

In our testing, the Roamii BE Pro also excelled at mid-range distances, recording 815.2 Mbps at 50 feet — a result that puts it squarely among the fastest mesh systems we’ve seen.

We found it outpaces the TP-Link Deco BE23 at close range (1.885 Gbps vs. 1.449 Gbps), but its real advantage is balancing those speeds with broader coverage, a feat some rivals like the Netgear Orbi 870 only match at longer distances. That makes the Roamii BE Pro a better pick for anyone who wants both fast speeds and reliable whole-home coverage, not just one or the other.

See our speed measurements tested at different distances

During two weeks of everyday use, the Roamii BE Pro kept up without breaking a sweat. That includes streaming 4K video, downloading large files, gaming and emailing.

Plus, wired device fans get a trio of 2.5 Gbps LAN ports and a USB 3.0 port. It's just a shame that this isn't available in single or three-packs, meaning you'd have to buy another two-pack if you're looking to add more nodes. At least it isn't too pricey!

Setup is a breeze: after scanning the QR code, entering a network name and updating the firmware, I had both nodes running in just 15 minutes. If you want the quickest path to reliable, top-tier Wi-Fi 7 speeds without fuss, the Roamii BE Pro is the system to beat.

The TP-Link Deco BE23 shows that high-speed, Wi-Fi 7 connectivity in a mesh system doesn't have to cost you a premium. For as low as $180, you can get a set of three powerful mesh networking devices that offer up far-reaching connectivity with some absolutely amazing speeds.

Each of the BE23 units comes in a neat, discreet design that can be placed anywhere while hiding in plain sight, and you can set up a connection for the whole house easily with TP-Link’s Deco app. Plus, any of the units can be used as a host router. Once you're set up, you can take control of your connectivity and devices via the app, like integrating and controlling Tapo, Kasa, Philips Hue and Matter home automation devices.

Speed is the star of the show, especially for this mesh system's affordable price. In our testing, we saw highs of 1.449 Gbps at 15 feet, and still 150.1 Mbps as far away as 90 feet. Those numbers beat many routers we've tested, even though it understandably falls behind the likes of a tri-band system (like the TP-Link Deco BE63 with 1.821 Gbps at 15 feet away).

With a maximum range of 115 feet for each unit, this mesh system will take you far (quite literally, connectivity-wise). Now that's an excellent balance between price and performance.

What you won't get here are more advanced features, like the 6 GHz band (just 2.4GHz and 5GHz here) or a super-wide 320 MHz data channel, and there's only a pair of 2.5 Gbps networking ports without a USB port, which makes wired connections limited.

For an affordable way to keep your whole home connected with fantastic internet speeds, the price is right with the TP-Link Deco BE23. It may not be the fastest or the most advanced, but for value, it's hard to go wrong with this mesh setup.

The Netgear Orbi 870 is a powerful mesh Wi-Fi system that really excels at medium and long ranges, even outperforming its larger, more expensive older sibling.

Despite its more premium price, I really like the more cylindrical design with a cleaner overall look of the Orbi 870 and the rest of the company’s Wi-Fi 7-powered mesh kits. While you’ll often see it in white at online retailers, you can actually get an all-black version too, but only on Netgear’s site.

The Orbi 870 is a very reliable and feature-packed mesh Wi-Fi system that’s ideal for futureproofing your home network thanks to its slew of multi-gig ports, including a 10 Gbps input. In his testing, Brian saw speeds of 1.82 Gbps at close range (15 feet).

However, it was the Orbi 870’s mid- and long-range performance that impressed him the most. For instance, at 50 and 75 feet, this mesh Wi-Fi system had download speeds of over 600 Mbps, beating both the entry-level Orbi 770 and even the Orbi 970 at the top of Netgear’s mesh lineup.

Even at a distance of 90 feet from Brian’s test laptop, it was at just over 100 Mbps, while the Orbi 970 and even TP-Link’s Deco BE85 were under 50 Mbps. At launch, a two-pack cost $1,000 (though you can often find it cheaper now), so the Orbi 870 is certainly an investment, just like the rest of the devices in Netgear’s Orbi line.

However, if you have a large home you want to fill with a strong Wi-Fi signal and a top-tier multi-gig internet plan, it could definitely be worth it. Just keep in mind that you will need to set aside some extra cash if you want to secure your home network with it using Netgear’s Armor security package or want extended technical support, as only 90 days are included.

The Acer Predator Connect T7 is a mesh Wi-Fi system with a heavy focus on gamers. However, unlike my previous mesh router pick for gaming, the Asus ROG Rapture GT6, it’s a Wi-Fi 7-powered device with a much more subtle look.

Instead of RGB and lots of logos, the Predator Connect T7 features a taller, rectangular design in white or black, and at first glance, it looks quite similar to an Xbox Series X. There’s a splash of RGB lighting on the top, but this mesh kit has a sleeker and more restrained look that I think definitely works in its favor.

Just like with the best gaming routers, the Predator Connect T7 has a low-latency design that uses Intel’s Killer Prioritization engine for peak gaming performance. It also comes with free built-in security software and makes full use of all of Wi-Fi 7’s best features.

During testing, Brian saw download speeds of 1.9 Gbps at close range (15 feet) with good mid-range performance. While the Predator Connect T7 has a multi-gig input port, its wired Ethernet ports are limited to gigabit speeds, so plugging in one of the best gaming laptops won’t give you a significant speed boost over connecting via Wi-Fi.

The Acer Predator Connect T7 is one of the few mesh Wi-Fi systems specifically designed for gamers and if you want a mesh router that looks as slick as your gaming PC, it’s a big step up from the Asus ROG Rapture GT7 (which superseded the GT6 we used to recommend).

However, it is on the expensive side at $330 per device, and unlike other mesh kits, you won’t see any discounts at all when buying a multi-pack. Still, if you want gaming-level network performance with the added benefits of mesh and want something less flashy, the Predator Connect T7 is an excellent mesh Wi-Fi system and the only one for gamers with Wi-Fi 7 support so far.

The Eero Pro 7 is a smaller and sleeker mesh Wi-Fi system that’s incredibly simple to set up and use. Unlike Eero’s past mesh kits, which had a puck-shaped design, this one has a rounded rectangular shape and, at 7.1 x 5.8 x 2.6 inches, you won’t have any trouble finding a place for it and its satellites around your home.

After testing the larger, more powerful Eero Max 7 myself, I really like the Pro 7’s more compact design and the fact that it's significantly cheaper, too. The biggest selling point of the Pro 7 and Eero’s other mesh Wi-Fi systems is that even a home networking novice will have no trouble at all getting them up and running.

Setup and configuration are handled entirely through the very user-friendly Eero app. Besides how it looks, I really like the way that updates are downloaded and installed automatically, so your mesh Wi-Fi system is always running the latest software.

In his testing, Brian saw download speeds of 1.9 Gbps at close distances (15 feet), but the Pro 7 was equally impressive at mid-range distances with speeds just under a gigabit.

The Eero Pro 7 does cost a bit more than the competition, but nowhere close to what you’d pay for an Orbi mesh kit. As an Amazon company, Eero works great with your Alexa-powered and other smart home devices, and you can even use an Echo Dot as a mesh extender to add some extra range to your home network.

If you want a fast and capable Wi-Fi 7-powered mesh system that’s simple to set up and just works, the Eero Pro 7 is very easy to recommend, especially since it's a lot cheaper than the Max 7. The one downside is that you’re limited to just two Ethernet ports, but they are the faster 5 Gbps variety, which is great if you have a multi-gig internet plan.

The TP-Link Deco BE85 is a top-of-the-line mesh Wi-Fi system that was actually the first mesh router with Wi-Fi 7 support. It builds on the cylindrical design of the Deco XE75 with a more refined and polished look, but it packs in a ton of multi-gig and even a USB port.

As someone who upgraded to fiber internet, I love how it has its own SFP+ port, which lets you plug your fiber line directly in at the back instead of into a separate ONT box first. Even if you’re still using one of the best cable modems, though, the Deco BE85 is a powerful mesh Wi-Fi system that won’t disappoint when it comes to performance.

One thing that’s really convenient about this mesh kit and TP-Link’s other Deco devices is that they’re all identical out of the box and you can use any of them as your main router. The company’s Deco app also makes setup and configuration very easy, and in my experience, it’s on par with Eero’s app in terms of usability.

15 feet (Toms Guide): TP-Link Deco BE85 scores 1.736.

50 feet (Toms Guide): TP-Link Deco BE85 scores 790.4.

75 feet (Toms Guide): TP-Link Deco BE85 scores 179.2.

90 feet (Toms Guide): TP-Link Deco BE85 scores 42.6.

During testing, Brian saw download speeds of 1.73 Gbps at a close distance (15 feet) and good mid-range speeds, too. While this might seem a bit low for a premium mesh Wi-Fi system, Brian was one of the first people to get and review the Deco BE85. It's possible this has improved with firmware updates since its launch.

The Deco BE85 has come down in price since it launched, but it’s still expensive, even though this model does go on sale quite frequently. However, if you have a fast, multi-gig fiber internet plan and want top-notch Wi-Fi 7 performance, this mesh router is the only one I’ve seen yet with an SFP+ port on the back.

It’s worth noting that, just like with Eero, all TP-Link Deco devices are compatible with one another, so you could always mix and match or upgrade to a more powerful model later on if you need to.

The mesh Wi-Fi systems we've used all come with amazing speeds, and we've done the testing to show how fast a router is at short and long ranges. But you'll find some will perform better at various distances, even if one delivers the fastest speeds around.

As an example, the Acer Predator Connect T7 offers the fastest speeds at 15 feet, but it loses out to the likes of the TP-Link Deco BE23 and others at 90 feet. It comes down to what you prioritize: speed or range (or a balance of both!)

So, to compare each mesh Wi-Fi system across the range of distances we've tested, check out the versus table below to help you make the right choice for your home.

Select a mesh Wi-Fi system to compare internet speed at different distances (measured in Gbps and Mbps)

We test every mesh Wi-Fi system to measure performance and range, using Keysight IxChariot. Testing is done in a multi-story home with brick walls. When we test standard routers, we look at performance at a distance to provide real-world information about coverage and speeds. In addition to lab testing, we evaluate the ease of setup and features of each device, too.

We measure performance at a 15-foot distance without obstructions, so that we can gauge the maximum amount of data that a router can move. Higher throughput will serve you better in data-heavy uses, like streaming video, gaming, or connecting multiple users at once.

Range measures the furthest usable distance for a particular router. Longer ranges are better for larger homes, where rooms are spread out at a distance. We measure how much data a router can move at 15, 50, 75 and 90 feet, as well as the maximum coverage area of a mesh Wi-Fi system.

We also test how well each mesh Wi-Fi system transmits and receives signals through drywall, brick, concrete and even metal walls, and how each handles coverage in a two- or three-story home. They also go through additional testing to see how well each system does when sending a signal through the main router and through the included satellites.

Of course (and most importantly), we also consider what you really get for your money, considering which features are worthwhile and how any given product compares with other devices from competing manufacturers.

A lot of factors come into choosing the mesh Wi-Fi system that will suit your space, from the coverage you need to the speeds you demand — all for the right price. We've got just the tips to make your choice easier.

Wi-Fi 8 is currently still in the early stages of being supported on all devices, so you won't be able to take advantage of the new connectivity standard right now. Currently, no consumer devices support Wi-Fi 8 coverage, and we're not expecting to see support until sometime in 2027 or 2028.

We've reviewed the first Wi-Fi 8 router, the Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro, and are impressed by its incredible Wi-Fi speeds and range. However, we couldn't see its full potential since we're still waiting for Wi-Fi 8 hardware. We'll have to see how well mesh Wi-Fi systems with Wi-Fi 8 perform, too.

While Wi-Fi 8 isn't worth getting right now, it may be worth it to many looking to future-proof their homes once more devices adopt Wi-Fi 8. Besides, it's backwards compatible with Wi-Fi 7, Wi-Fi 6 and so on. We'll keep you updated in the meantime.

Yes, a mesh Wi-Fi system can go through walls. Because Wi-Fi uses radio waves, these waves can pass through solid materials like walls to connect to a device.

However, when Wi-Fi meets a wall, some of it goes through, some bounces off and some is absorbed. Because of this, the signal can be weaker, especially when more walls are in the way.

A mesh Wi-Fi system has an advantage in getting past this. Instead of using one router to get a signal, a mesh system uses multiple nodes placed throughout a home to bypass hard objects or walls in order to get an unobstructed signal. This means there are fewer barriers to getting a clear Wi-Fi signal.

The main downside of using a mesh Wi-Fi system is that it can be very expensive, especially compared to traditional Wi-Fi routers. These are only needed for those living in large homes or for anyone who needs Wi-Fi coverage over a long distance. For those in smaller spaces, this is overkill.

Since mesh systems come in a multi-pack of nodes, this bumps up the price, as these extra devices deliver a better range of coverage throughout a space compared to other routers.

Nodes also must be placed close enough to catch a strong signal, which can be tricky in a home with many rooms separated by concrete or brick walls. Plus, with this signal hopping between multiple nodes, there may be an increase in latency, which isn't ideal for competitive gameplay.

Otherwise, the best mesh Wi-Fi systems try to overcome these downsides, and these are still the best option to upgrade your home network wirelessly.

Mesh Wi-Fi systems come with nodes and are usually available in two-packs or three-packs, but deciding which one to get depends on the size of your home. If you live in a small or medium house, then a two-pack will usually do the trick. For large homes with more than three bedrooms or multiple stories, a three-pack is the better choice, as this will ensure that your Wi-Fi signal reaches every corner and even upstairs.

The great thing about mesh Wi-Fi systems, though, is that you can always start small and work up to something bigger. For instance, if you buy a two-pack and find that you’re still dealing with Wi-Fi dead zones in certain parts of your home, you can always add another node later to improve your coverage.

Plug-in Wi-Fi extenders aren’t nearly as advanced or as powerful as the nodes in a mesh Wi-Fi system. The other big problem with Wi-Fi extenders is that most of them create a separate network you have to manually switch to each time you want to use them. For instance, let’s say you put a Wi-Fi extender in your bedroom. Whenever you want to get online in that particular room, you’ll have to switch from your main Wi-Fi network to the extender, which gets annoying really fast.

On the other hand, with a mesh Wi-Fi system, the nodes are all part of your main network and no switching is required. As you move from one side of your house to the other, your mesh system automatically hands off your connection to whatever satellite you’re closest to, which ensures you have a strong signal and a good connection wherever you are in your home.

As someone who's been working from home for the past eight years, Anthony Spadafora has tried everything from Wi-Fi extenders to powerline adapters to get the most out of his home network, before finally upgrading to a mesh Wi-Fi system. Along the way, he's tested out loads of different routers and network configurations. Based on what he's learned, Anthony tries to highlight the critical role Wi-Fi routers play in our day-to-day lives and how a mesh network can help solve the most common connectivity issues like Wi-Fi dead spots.

With experience in testing, using and evaluating wireless data from before Wi-Fi was even a word, Brian Nadel has tried out and reviewed every major router available in his home networking lab. A LAN nerd, his philosophy is to use the router the way you would, testing networking gear for ease of setup, performance, security and above all for value. The result is peace of mind when it comes to choosing the right router.

#3117. Build a Personal Brand to Help Employers Find You

Routine posting leaves a trail of breadcrumbs for recruiters to discover

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!In one year, the number of developers working for themselves has more than doubled. Stack Overflow’s annual survey of more than 30,000 developers showed that freelancers and sole proprietors went from about four percent of respondents to ten percent.

You can read this as a polite way of saying, “I got laid off and I’m figuring it out.” But I don’t think the number can be ignored.

Whatever the case, it leads to the question I keep hearing from engineers right now: What can I do to stay employable? One tried and true answer is to build a personal brand.

Over the last six years, I grew my LinkedIn audience to 40,000 followers and YouTube channel to 10,000. I don’t think you should aim to be famous (unless you’re into that sort of thing) but I do think it’s worth exploring how to be discoverable online in 2027 if you want an advantage in the open market.

Strip away the follower counts and the AI-generated thought leadership, and a personal brand comes down to a simple question: Does the internet know who you are? When a hiring manager goes looking for someone who has your skills, do you show up?

You can think of this as search engine optimization for your employability. Recruiters have mostly consolidated around a single platform to find people: LinkedIn.

Those 40,000 followers and millions of impressions came with barely a viral post to my name. Nobody is begging me to do sponsorships. But I rarely have trouble finding work, and far more opportunities come to me than I go looking for. That has much less to do with fame than with being easy to find.

You don’t need 10,000 followers. You need a trail of breadcrumbs.

LinkedIn is notorious for being overrun with AI-generated posts. It’s become a running joke. That’s good news for you, because the bar to stand out is “sound like a human being.”

Write about what you actually achieved: a hairy bug you squashed, how your team handles deployments, why you picked some obscure library, the migration that went sideways at 2 a.m. Specifics are hard to fake and easy to trust. (But be careful not to post sensitive information.)

And post a picture of yourself once in a while. People connect with faces a lot faster than with walls of text.

Posts with an opinion tend to outperform tutorials, but you don’t have to dunk on anyone to have one. For instance, if you work on a tech stack people love to mock (VB, .NET, some ancient Java monolith held together with prayer), try something like “What people get wrong about .NET.”

You’ll attract a few trolls in the comments—free engagement, honestly—plus people who want an actual conversation. These comments can turn into actual connections and even… friends.

Posting twice a week is not a big ask. Pick a simple, repeatable format so you’re never staring at an empty text box: what you worked on, what broke, and what you learned. Even a post that gets 10 views leaves one more breadcrumb about who you are and what you know.

Over time, the people who comment become your network. And because so few engineers post about their work on LinkedIn, you can become a big fish in a small pond surprisingly fast.

The best audience is engineers one or two steps behind where you are now. Answer the questions you had a year ago. It helps them, it sharpens your own thinking, and every so often it turns into mentorship in both directions.

It also tells a future employer more about how you think than any résumé bullet ever could.

The engineers who grab the most opportunities are the ones employers can find. You don’t need to become an influencer to be one of them. You just need to leave enough breadcrumbs that the right person can follow them back to you.

To help researchers search through the millions of peer-review publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library, IEEE has released a custom AI suite optimized for STEM literature. The suit allows users to search with natural-language queries and provides overviews with reference links.

AI has made it easier to access information in different domains, but specialist knowledge and human judgement still serve an essential role. Today, an engineer’s core value comes from knowing how to ask the right questions—not from knowing everything.

#3116. Top Wall Street analysts recommend these 3 dividend stocks for higher returns

Dividend-paying stocks can enhance portfolio returns by providing a steady income stream to investors and the potential for capital appreciation. Several investors seek exposure to dividend stocks in a volatile backdrop to ensure stable income.

In this regard, recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks, backed by strong financials and cash flows to support consistent dividend payments.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Energy Transfer (ET) is a diversified midstream energy company with about 140,000 miles of pipelines and associated energy infrastructure in 44 states. The company made a quarterly cash distribution of 34 cents per common unit for the second quarter of 2026. At an annualized payment of $1.36 per common unit, ET offers a yield of 6.3%.

Recently, JPMorgan analyst Jeremy Tonet reiterated a buy rating on Energy Transfer stock and slightly raised his price target to $25 from $24. The analyst noted that the company delivered a strong Q2 beat across all key metrics.

Tonet highlighted that Energy Transfer raised its 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to $18.8 billion-$19.1 billion from $18.2 billion-$18.6 billion, reflecting robust base results and cost optimization. About the Hugh Brinson pipeline, Tonet noted Phase 1 (1.5 bcfd) reaching full capacity by September 1 and Phase II capacity (0.7 bcfd) going online by Q1 2027. "All in, we see ET well positioned to continue capitalizing on organic growth opportunities across the value chain," said Tonet.

Tonet ranks No. 922 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 9%. See Energy Transfer Financials on TipRanks.

This week's second dividend pick is independent oil and natural gas company Permian Resources (PR). The company declared a base dividend of $0.16 per share for the third quarter, payable on September 30, 2026. At an annualized dividend of $0.64 per share, PR offers a yield of about 2.7%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Permian Resources stock and increased his price target to $27 from $22, citing an improved outlook on oil production growth and operational efficiencies.

The 5-star analyst noted that while PR stock has outperformed its peers so far in 2026, he sees further upside. He added that the program has completed about $1.05 billion in bolt-on deals this year (as of August 5).

"We see the continued success of PR's ground game as constructive toward future inventory replenishment and increasing working interest over time," said Mehta.

The analyst also emphasized Permian Resources' solid track record of generating growth in free cash flow (FCF) per share. Mehta expects the company's free cash flow per share to grow at a 20% CAGR (compound annual growth rate) from 2025–2028.

Mehta ranks No. 401 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.8%. See Permian Resources Statistics on TipRanks.

Moving on to Sempra Energy (SRE), a utility holding company. Earlier this month, the company declared a quarterly dividend of $0.6575 per share, payable on October 15. At an annualized dividend of $2.63 per share, SRE stock offers a yield of about 3.1%.

Recently, Jefferies analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith upgraded SRE stock to Buy from Hold but slightly lowered the price target to $97 from $101. The 5-star analyst noted that Sempra stock is trading at a price/earnings multiple that is 14% below its electric peers due to concerns about Texas transmission capital expenditure and the failure of California legislation.

Smith noted that the derating of weaker California peers PG&E (PCG) and Edison International (EIX) is weighing on the sum-of-the-parts (SOTP) valuation but is becoming less relevant given their materially higher fire risk compared to Sempra Energy.

Furthermore, Smith expects Sempra Energy's Texas capex plan to stay in place despite the opposition to transmission and data centers, though delays to 765-kV projects are likely. While a full recovery for SRE stock will need a clearer outcome from the Texas legislative session, Smith believes that the stock may already be an early opportunity for patient investors.

"We are early on the upgrade but see limited downside at current levels as the market is pricing in little transmission upside," said Smith.

#3115. CAD images suggest iPhone 18e will have an odd new camera design

CAD images of the iPhone 18e, said to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd new design for the camera bump.

If accurate, it would represent a big change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau …

The iPhone 17e was launched in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same.

The current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.

The site doesn’t share the images, but says that the camera bump looks similar to that of the M5 iPad Pro, shown below.

It’s unclear what might have prompted the change of design, especially as the site’s Filipe Espósito says he’s also seen CAD models for the standard model iPhone 18 or the iPhone Air 2, neither of which adopt it.

Previous reports have suggested that the only spec change with the iPhone 18e over its predecessor will be performance improvements thanks to the A20 chip.

#3114. Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous

Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead

• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development

• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress

Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”

Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.

Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities.

AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”

Cal Newport is a computer science professor at Georgetown University where he is also a founding faculty member of the Center for Digital Ethics. He's the author of multiple bestselling books about human flourishing in a technological world and is the host of The Cal Newport Show podcast.

The issue at hand as I see it is the human intelligence behind the AI. The AI does not say to itself, attack this server and extract this information, that is the human and the AI makes them powerful. Asking a computer to decide what it wants to do today without it accessing an LLM will be very difficult. For it then to decide to destroy mankind, again, without an LLM that specifically helps it do that. Also, there is no stopping what will come from peoplekinds AI adventure. Rogue nations will pursue it.

It's an interesting thought. I think we can draw parallels to the development of nuclear weapons. Notable scientists expressed fears about what they were creating, however proceeded due to fears about what would happen if the other side completed first. However, this time, it is OpenAI vs Anthropic, with elements of competition from China thrown in. And this time, the incentives are arguably stronger as they are immensely more profitable. Hubris will always manifest in the creator of such transformative devices so that they believe only they can control it.

Concerns about AI are legitimate. These systems can be used to intensify surveillance, generate convincing disinformation, facilitate cyberattacks, and concentrate economic and political power. More capable systems may introduce additional risks, particularly when deployed without adequate testing or oversight.

We should not dismiss these dangers. But neither should we treat catastrophe as inevitable simply because a technology is powerful.

The answer to risk is not blind faith. It is serious evaluation, independent testing, appropriate safeguards, accountability, and governance proportionate to the potential harm. High-risk applications warrant greater scrutiny than routine uses.

#3113. You can now DM Meta’s Muse on Instagram to turn saves into plans

Meta's personal AI agent now takes requests in Instagram's inbox, starting with the posts you have saved.

Meta has added its Muse AI agent to Instagram direct messages, inviting users to send it a DM to turn saved posts into plans, such as a trip. Muse already worked in its own app, in WhatsApp and on Instagram profiles, and Meta says it does not read private messages unless users allow it, though Reuters reported staff found it reading encrypted chats.

Meta’s Muse AI agent can now be messaged in Instagram DMs, where it can turn posts users have saved into plans. Meta announced the change through Muse’s own Instagram account on Tuesday, using a long-planned trip as the example.

Muse launched in the US in September as an agent that books, buys and negotiates for users. It works in its own app and in WhatsApp, and later that month users could add it to their Instagram profiles.

The DM option puts Muse where the saved posts already sit. Meta has not said which countries get it. Beyond the US, Muse is live in Canada and has launched in Australia, and it reached the UK this week.

Yet Reuters reported last week that Meta staff found Muse reading encrypted messages. Meta called those isolated incidents.

Users can also make Muse ask before it sends messages or buys anything. In September, though, a YouTuber said Muse shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before asking him. Meta said it was looking into it.

#3112. iPhone Handoff: Here’s the latest on carrier availability and pricing

iPhone Handoff is a new feature in iOS 27 that lets you use the same phone number across two different iPhones. However, the feature requires carrier support, so it isn’t available to everyone. Here are the carriers that currently support iPhone Handoff and those that have promised support.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

With iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones. Your number automatically moves between the two phones, depending on which one you pick up. This includes calls, voicemail, messages, and Find My location.

Simply unlock whichever device you want to use and you’re ready to go. Other data synced with iCloud will automatically update across your devices. Third-party apps work across both devices, following each app’s own syncing behavior.

iPhone Handoff is available on iOS 27 and later. The phones must be connected to Wi-Fi, share the same Apple Account, use Messages in iCloud, and be signed into FaceTime and iMessage with the same Apple Account.

The biggest limiting factor of iPhone Handoff is that it requires carrier support. Currently, just three carriers support the feature:

What about carriers that are working on the feature? In the United States, Verizon has promised it “will support iPhone Handoff,” but it’s unclear when the feature will launch. Verizon says it will charge $10 per month for the service.

AT&T, meanwhile, has no plans to support iPhone Handoff. In a statement in September, the carrier said that its focus “remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” The carrier noted that there “could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” but that customers should use “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” instead.

No other carriers have promised support for iPhone Handoff, so it’s unclear how quickly the feature will expand around the world.

In my testing, iPhone Handoff works really well. I have it set up between my iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. I use the iPhone Duo 90% of the time, but when I do pick up my iPhone 18 Pro, my number instantly switches to it. There’s a cute animation that expands from the Dynamic Island, confirming that the number has moved.

Have you tried iPhone Handoff? Are you willing to pay extra for it? Let us know down in the comments.
