Silence the world around you with the best noise-canceling earbuds recommended by our audio experts

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

True silence when you're out and about is impossible — but you can get incredibly close with some of the best noise-canceling earbuds. Thanks to advances in active noise cancellation (ANC), they're great at keeping the noise of your commute at bay, and their in-ear design makes them super portable. But which should you buy?

At the moment, the best noise-canceling earbuds you can buy are the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. They've got the best ANC we've ever tested, and offer a comfortable fit so that you can wear them for long periods of time. There's little more we'd ask.

If they're over your budget or you need something you won't worry about losing as much, there's always the excellent CMF By Nothing Buds 2A. They don't cost anywhere near as much, but also offer great ANC and solid sound quality.

I maintain the site's buying guides for headphones, wireless earbuds, Bluetooth speakers, soundbars, and more. I have spent more than 20 years testing audio equipment for my own enjoyment, and was previously the Audio Editor here at Tom's Guide. There's nothing more I love than jamming out to my favorite tunes on audio equipment of different prices and sizes.

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 bring improvements to the formula across the board, in all but one key area. If you were to unbox your brand-new buds next to a pair of the old model, you'd be forgiven for wondering if you'd be shortchanged.

They look identical. All the way down to their eartip shape and silicone fitting wing, the QuietComfort Ultra Buds family is one that has a particular style that it has stuck with for a long time.

Pop them in your ears and you soon notice the difference. They've got even better ANC than the old model, with some of the most impressive noise canceling around. They block out everything — I took them on a long train journey, and found that all of the noise of my carriage was completely unnoticeable, even when not listening to music. It's like magic, as the orchestral sound swells and the noise disappears.

The transparency mode is very good as well, and it works well if you want to order your breakfast when you're going to work. The touch controls work well, and the charging case now contains a wireless charging coil so that you can more easily keep them fully charged.

Battery life is still not the best, though. Six hours with ANC on isn't quite up there, and four hours when you turn on 'immersive audio' is lackluster. It's not really worth turning the Immersive Audio setting on anyway.

It just thins out your music as it tries to distribute it around an artificially extended soundstage, and uses up an extra two hours of battery life. The soundstage is wide enough as it is, and the sound improved over the first model for some great audio as well.

They're still the best ANC buds you can get your hands on, and the Gen 2 just cemented their place in the annals of earbuds history. That ANC is just so good.

With the AirPods Pro 3, Apple was looking to unseat Bose's buds from the top of the list. Unfortunately for Apple, Bose released the refreshed Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 just before the latest AirPods hit shelves, but the AirPods Pro 3 are still a significant step up over their predecessors.

They've got sound to match the XM5, with a similarly natural sound profile and some extra juicy features that make them a whole lot more usable than the majority of the other options. They're a great jack of all trades and perfect for iPhone users.

The ANC is, Apple tells us, "2x as good as the AirPods Pro 2". In our testing, we've found that the ANC is, indeed, much better than the ANC of the previous models. It's better at blocking out sounds across the frequency spectrum, although it still focuses on the sounds you'll hear in your day-to-day life.

That means that bus journeys are more comfortable and office stays more tolerable. The transparency mode is natural-sounding as well and gives you more battery life.

There are some extra features on board the AirPods Pro 3. There's a heart rate monitor and Live Translation, although we found these to be novelty extras as opposed to 'reasons to buy.'

There are meaningful improvements in some other key areas, however. Fit is far better, and it seals very well in the ear to help the ANC. The battery life is excellent, with 2 hours more than the previous model, bringing them up to par with the Sony earbuds.

There are a couple of drawbacks. Android users won't like their less impressive features for their OS, but you were probably eyeing up the buds from Sony and Bose. There's still only one color option — white — and I've got AirPods that have died permanently gray after spending too much time in my black jeans pocket.

The AirPods Pro 3 are still an excellent pair of buds for iPhone users, however, and some of the best ANC buds around.

There are good budget buds, but there are very few as impressive as the CMF By Nothing Buds 2A. If you weren’t already aware, CMF is Nothing's most affordable product range, and the 2A sit at the bottom price rung of the brand's earbud lineup.

You might have thought that such a low price would mean low-quality ANC — but no, that’s far from the truth. The CMF Buds (sorry CMF, I’m not typing “by Nothing” every time) 2A are a budget revelation when it comes to keeping unwanted noise at bay.

We found that the sound of buses and other public transport was blocked very well by the buds, making sure that your commute is more comfortable. It’s adaptive as well, changing and shifting depending on the ambient noise levels.

Transparency mode was great when we wanted to order some lunch, with clear sound when we were chatting with the service staff. It’s not quite up there with the AirPods Pro 3 or the Sony WF-1000XM6, but then you could buy nearly ten pairs of these for the same price as either of those.

They’re comfortable too, with loads of fitting options in the box so that you can dial them in according to your specific fitting preferences. The battery life is solid with 35 hours on tap — that’s plenty to get you through a week's worth of work and commuting. Multi-point makes sure you can connect to different devices without the need to dip into the settings menu, and it works well.

They’re obviously not perfect — some compromises have been made to keep the price down. They feel a bit cheap, and there’s no auto-pause when you take them in and out of your ears. But again, when you consider the price, the few cons are very easy to forgive.

Sound is impressive, and there are loads of extra features in the Nothing X app like a customizable EQ. We love the CMF Buds 2A, and we think you will too once you’ve got the $30 wonders in your pocket — and you want to keep the noise of your busy 7:30 AM train at bay.

Sony has been trying to take the ANC fight to Bose since the latter released its finest, and sometimes Sony has come out on top. In this case, though, it’s the runner-up — but it's so close. There are still key reasons to pick up the WF-1000XM6 instead of the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2.

But about that ANC; it’s very good. We tested the buds in a range of different environments, from the office, a train, a busy city, and more. The noise cancellation kept out just about everything, and didn’t affect the sound of the music we were listening to.

It loses out to the QuietComfort in the smoothness of the delivery. That means that changes in environments are handled slightly more roughly than Boses pair, with a little noise leaking in before the algorithm takes notice. To be clear — it’s so close. If you don’t try both, you won’t notice. Side by side though, there is an edge to the Sony that’s not present in the Bose buds.

The sound, though, is better than Bose’s buds. There’s more delicacy up top, and they’re less low-end heavy. Sony’s tuning is more pleasing to our ears across a range of different genres, making them a better bet for the sound-quality-conscious. The AirPods Pro 3 sound even better, though.

They’re comfortable too, with a solid range of different tips for different ear shapes. The buds themselves a slightly strange shape, and the case is a dumb shape (it's covered with angles, so it’s less comfortable to fit in a pocket than the lovely smooth Bose and Apple options), but this is still a stylish and comfy pair of wireless earbuds.

Battery life is… fine. It’s unimproved from the previous model, the WF-1000XM5, with around 8 hours of use with ANC turned on. That’s more than the Bose buds and around the same as the AirPods Pro 3. Still, we’d like to see more battery life from flagship earbuds, considering how much you get with more budget buds.

So in the end, it all comes down to a couple of things. If you want the best noise canceling, buy the Bose earbuds. If you want something with great ANC that works with an iPhone, then get the AirPods Pro 3. If you want something that works well with everything, offers great ANC and excellent sound quality, then pick the Sony WF-1000XM6.

The Noble Fokus Amadeus bring a certain class to proceedings. They're covered in a very regal red colorway, and the buds themselves have a resin finish that makes them look almost like jewelry. And I love them.

They're super comfortable, especially if you use the flanged eartips. Those will also make your ANC better, and it was already really good. It blocked out the fan in my office, and makes bus journeys and train trips a whole lot more tolerable. It's not quite up there with the Bose ANC, but it does get close to the Sony XM series. That's impressive, especially given that Noble is a much smaller company.

The sound is the best bit, though. Slip them into your ears, and you're treated to the very best audio experience this side of $400. The highs are incredibly detailed, the mids are incredible, and the bass is impactful. They sound excellent — hence why they're on the list.

They lack some of the features of the competition, like the Spatial Audio of the AirPods and 360 reality audio you'll find on Sony buds, but they more than make up for it thanks to their incredible sound.

For audiophiles looking for their portable audio fix, the Noble Fokus Amadeus are the buds for you.

Fitness buds are a dime a dozen, with plenty of options available should you want to listen to music while you work out. The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the latest buds from Apple's subsidiary, and they also happen to be the best buds for fitness fanatics. They've got a useful fitting hook on each bud, and then heart rate monitors to make sure they stay in place.

The noise canceling, as you'd hope, is excellent. I found it perfect for most different settings, be that a quiet office or a bustling train. I'm not known for my exercise, however, so I spoke to someone who is — and what they thought of the noise canceling on board.

They took them for months of long running sessions and other fitness work, and found they blocked noise very well. Gyms silenced, annoying traffic brought to nothing. If you want to make sure your jogs, cycling, or even your swimming is distraction-free, then the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the buds for you.

I was also very impressed with the battery life of the buds. According to Beats, there are 10 hours of ANC on battery life out of the buds, and my testing proved that to be pretty much spot on. That extends to 45 hours when you put them back in the (very large) charging case, for some of the best battery life in the segment. It will depend on volume level and even genre, but expect good staying power.

Sound does trip up slightly. They've got plenty of detail and some fairly dynamic bass, but there's an unfortunate cut-off in the lower mids that takes some of the edge out of your music. For most people, it's not going to be a problem. But if you're picky about how your music sounds, you may be better off with a different pair of earbuds.

The heart rate monitor is useful if you want to track more of your fitness metrics, but we found that it wasn't the most accurate. Not a massive issue, but one worth noting.

In the end, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are a solid ANC option for everyone, but they're particularly good for those looking for a fitness companion.

Samsung’s buds have never topped best lists, but they’ve always had a space reserved. While they might not have the same “all things for all people” vibes as the Sony WF-1000XM6, the ultra-impressive noise canceling of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra, or the Apple user features of the AirPods line, there has been little better for users of Samsung’s phones than Samsung’s buds. They offer great performance at a slightly lower price and bring some exclusive features to the table, making them even better.

Noise-canceling-wise, you’re looking at performance that gets close to the AirPods and the Sony buds, just slotting in behind the QuietComfort Ultra. They do a great job of keeping noise at bay, as we discovered when we put them head-to-head with the Bose buds, and with music playing, you won’t find any horrible noises making their way through.

Transparency mode is similarly excellent, and doesn’t add the same robotic hue as cheaper buds. Perfect for when you need to speak to someone and don’t want to pop your earbuds out. In case you lose them. The algorithms that Samsung uses here are very good, and there are different levels you can access with the Samsung settings app and a separate Samsung earbuds application you can install.

Sound-wise, they’re very good as well, bringing plenty of bass and richness to the table. They’re a “big” sounding earbud, with plenty of depth. They’re similarly lovely in the mids department, making sure that music sounds great no matter the genre. Detail heads will miss out on some of the really high and clear stuff, but they’ll be better served by the buds from Sony. Either way, the sound is top-notch, even if it does focus on different parts of the frequency range.

Battery life is solid as a rock, although not quite as special as the likes of the Apple or Sony buds. Seven hours of staying power is plenty to get you through the work day, especially if you charge them in the case over your lunch break. The 30 hours of life in the case is actually better than the competition, which is always good, and makes sure they’re not going to need a wall outlet as often.

AI features are going to be useful for some and less so for others. Still, the likes of Interpreter and others are fun extras, even if you do have to have a Samsung device for them to work properly. If you’re looking for the perfect accompaniment to your S23 or newer, then the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are the way to go.

Wired earbuds are back, and there’s no bigger sign than Bose’s noise-canceling version of the format. It’s not the first time that Bose has made wired earbuds with ANC inside, but this version brings the latest algorithms to the table for excellent ANC performance paired with a reliable, tethered connection. They’re good to, although it seems that Bose is keeping some stuff back for either the more expensive wired option or to account for a lack of a dedicated power source for the mics and tech needed for ANC.

The ANC is good. Very good, in fact — we found that it blocked plenty of noise when walking down a street or working in a busy office. If you’ve not experienced the likes of the upper ANC echelons, these are going to be perfectly serviceable for everyday use. They’re just a little weaker than some of the other options on this list, with some higher sounds making their way through the barrier.

Transparency works well enough, making sure that you can hear what's going on the other side of the buds without all the extra noise around you. It does affect the sound of the buds slightly, however, so you’ll pay the price in sound quality when you’re ordering your McDonald's breakfast. The price you pay for a double sausage and egg McMuffin, one supposes.

The sound quality is a highlight of the Noise Canceling Wired Earbuds. The bass is less in your face than prior models, although it’s a lovely addition to the table. Similarly, high-range and lower-register mids sound great no matter the genre you’re listening to. It's a less in-your-face audio experience than previous Bose products, which is a nice change.

Then there’s the wire, which comes with both pros and cons. You don’t have to worry about battery life, for one. The power for the ANC is pulled straight from your phone or laptops battery, so your earbuds will only die when your listening device does. That’s good. You also get lossless audio thanks to the USB-C connection, and low-latency listening should you want to play games or watch movies and TV shows on the go without the sound getting behind what’s going on on-screen.

The bad thing? You’re tethered. Forget to unplug them or take them out when you stand up and you’ll send your phone flying across the floor or violently disconnect them from your laptop. You’ll need to get used to it, that’s for sure. But for under $100? It’s well worth the trade-off, if not only for effectively unlimited battery life.

We test a lot of noise-canceling earbuds, but not everything can make it into our buying guides. Whether that's down to better performance or stronger features from rival models in a particular category and price, some miss ranking in this list by the slightest of margins. With that in mind, these models are strong contenders and great alternative considerations.

Apple's new noise-canceling earbuds are here, and they land at a lower price than the previous model. We were impressed with the ANC this time around, although the battery life simply isn't good enough to kick it with the options above. Still, Apple users on a budget will find a lot to like here.

The ZE300 are Final’s lightest earbuds yet, and they’re perhaps some of the most comfortable buds out there right now. For less than $50, you’re getting excellent sound quality across many genres and highly effective ANC indoors, packaged into a pressure-relieving design with a comfortable fit.

A strong pair of cheap wireless noise-canceling earbuds, the EarFun Pro 3 deliver nearly 40 hours of listening (with their case), making them some of the longest-lasting among their peers like the Soundcore Liberty 4 NC. The ANC in the EarFun set is effective and the buds also support aptX Adaptive audio, and have a custom equalizer in its app. Our review also mentioned the good call quality and wireless charging.

Soundcore has finally joined the big leagues, although the Liberty 5 Pro Max aren't quite up there with the best yet. They sound good and offer some useful features, but we'd say you're still better off with the buds from Sony, Apple and Bose right now.

Read our full Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max review

We've judged the best noise-canceling earbuds on several factors: audio performance, battery life, Bluetooth range, call quality, comfort and fit, and the effectiveness of the noise cancellation. We also weigh special features, such as included apps, and how easy they are to use.

During the testing phase, our reviewers wear each pair of earbuds for 2 hours at a time throughout the course of a week, to test comfort over time.

ANC, meanwhile, is tested in both indoor and outdoor environments where ambient sounds are produced at high levels. This includes airplanes, city parks, convenience shops, offices, and public transportation. ANC earbuds programmed with transparency modes are also tested thoroughly to determine how well the listener can hear their surroundings.

For sound quality, we listen to many different sample tracks and span as many music genres as possible, including hip-hop, rock, jazz, classical and R&B, while evaluating volume, clarity, and fullness. Find out what we listen for during our testing process and how to get the best headphone sound for you.

And now that more streaming music services are offering high-resolution audio, be sure to read our audio codec FAQ for all you need to know.

Finally, we’ll rate noise-canceling earbuds on our five-point system, with 1 being the worst and 5 the best. If a pair is particularly excellent, with a robust range of qualities, we may award it an Editor's Choice badge.

The first item to check off the list when shopping for the best noise-canceling earbuds is their active noise cancellation performance, which shouldn’t be confused with passive noise cancellation. What are the differences?

1. Active vs. passive noise cancellation: ANC uses advanced circuitry and microphones to pick up noise signals and create inverse waves that cancel out these sonic disruptions, whereas PNC physically isolates high-pitched sounds through the headphone design and materials. Most headphones advertised with noise cancellation are categorized under ANC.

2. Battery life: Noise-canceling earbuds have a reputation for sucking up lots of power, so you’ll want a pair that holds a charge long enough to get you through a long business flight or weekly commutes. Noise-canceling wireless earbuds are usually rated for 4.5 to 8 hours, but with included charging cases the total possible playback time might be much more competitive.

Think about how long and how often you’d want to wear your earbuds for on lengthy trips. A longer “per charge” battery life is better, but if you only want some entertainment on short commutes then it not quite so important, as you’ll probably be storing the buds in their case more regularly.

3. Sound quality: ANC technology can compress sound and reduce dynamics, which may affect audio performance when turned on. In some cases, you’ll notice a background hiss when listening to music. However, the best noise-canceling earbuds limit these disruptions to deliver full, crisp sound.

4. Design: The look, build and feel of a pair of in-ear 'buds is massively important when selecting the best noise-canceling earbuds, so consider how they look and feel and whether the style is right for you. In our best noise-canceling headphones round up we mention that over-ear headphones tend to give the best noise cancellation, but some of the more recent wireless in-ear models are proving to be just as effective.

5. Pricing considerations: Obviously, price is a big consideration when looking for the best noise-canceling earbuds. Although there are always exceptions, big-name brands will typically command a bit extra, but generally speaking, the less you spend on a pair of headphones the greater the chance that sound and features will be compromised. Going for a budget option isn't always the best choice, as any money you save on your purchase won't do you much good if you're constantly needing to recharge your audio gear, or the sound quality is poor.

ANC explained: Active noise cancellation (ANC) models employ built-in mics to pick up ambient sounds around the wearer. An identical but inverted audio signal of the noise is played back to the listener through the headphones.

Listeners aren't aware of this happening of course, as the inverted (or out of phase) signal effectively 'cancels out' the noise of the surroundings for the headphone wearer. The process removes the external sounds, which results in a significant reduction in the level of background noise at the very least.

Given that it uses both more computational power and a bunch of microphones in order to work, ANC has an effect on your battery life. This often chops a couple of hours off, so they won't last quite as long. If you want to keep the battery going for longer then you'll want to keep the noise canceling turned off.

In most cases, noise-canceling earbuds are very effective at reducing ambient sounds. There are limits, though, and some designs are less effective at silencing certain types of sounds than others.

The process is fast but it can’t physically occur in real time, so active noise cancellation (ANC) works best with consistent low-frequency sounds as opposed to higher-pitched, inconsistent sounds like human speech.

Vehicle engines and droning air conditioners are easy to cancel out, but the shorter wavelength of high-frequency sounds, like a sudden blast from a car horn, makes it tougher for the ANC’s anti-noise waves to perfectly mask these bursts.

Even so, all sounds will be at least a little quieter when you’re wearing noise-canceling headphones, and many sounds can be completely silenced even on low-cost pairs or earbuds.

Terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring new challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. They also call for new testing methods for devices, satellites, and networks. This paper explains the technology step by step. It also shows how NTN is shaping unified terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks in 6G.

#3101. Top Wall Street analysts find these 3 stocks attractive as long-term investments

Investors have been grappling with stock market volatility, weighing elevated oil prices, persistent geopolitical tensions, the Federal Reserve's rate hike and a debate about AI safety. For all that, it helps to look beyond short-term noise and focus on stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors gain clarity, as these experts conduct in-depth research to pick stocks with attractive growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Enterprise software and cloud infrastructure company Oracle (ORCL) recently announced better-than-expected results for the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The quarter benefited from solid growth in cloud infrastructure revenue.

After hosting a series of investor meetings with Ken Bond, Oracle head of investor relations following Q1 earnings, Guggenheim analyst John DiFucci reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $400. Oracle remains a Guggenheim Best Idea, he said.

"We continue to believe ORCL is a decade stock, driven by the massive (and profitable) opportunity ahead for AI training and inferencing," said DiFucci. He also cited the traditional Public Cloud business and additional AI-enabled cloud database and cloud applications for his bullish stance. DiFucci expects all the factors to drive revenue and profit acceleration over the next few years.

While Oracle delivered 850 MW of data center capacity in Q1 FY27, Bond cautioned that Infrastructure as a Service revenue in any quarter depends more on the timing of when that capacity comes online, than on the headline MW number. DiFucci expects IaaS growth to stay strong, with full-year growth expected above Q1 FY27's 120% constant currency rate. Management expects total revenue growth to accelerate sequentially throughout fiscal 2027, as the faster-growing infrastructure business makes up a larger share of the mix.

DiFucci addressed concerns regarding customer concentration, saying OpenAI's share of total remaining performance obligations has dropped from 80% last June to about 50% now, and is expected to keep falling as new contracts are signed with new and existing customers.

DiFucci ranks No. 263 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 62% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17.5%. See Oracle Insider Trading Activity on TipRanks.

Space systems and launch services provider Rocket Lab (RKLB) was recently initiated as a buy with an $80 price target by Raymond James analyst Brian Gesuale.

"RKLB has assembled launch, spacecraft, components, payloads and optical communications, with Neutron and Iridium completing medium-lift and applications/spectrum in 2027," said Gesuale.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that with the completion of the Iridium acquisition, Rocket Lab will become the only vertically integrated space company with positive free cash flow (FCF). The deal will add a deployed constellation valued at more than $3 billion, globally coordinated L-band spectrum and about $500 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) and $300 million in free cash flow (FCF).

Gesuale highlighted RKLB's strong revenue and backlog growth and progress toward positive EBITDA and FCF in 2027/2028. Rocket Lab is moving from a heavy investment phase into monetization, with estimated revenue growth of 59% in 2026, the analyst said, noting that RKLB's backlog has more than doubled to almost $2.4 billion from $1.1 billion in Q3 2025.

Given strong growth projections, the analyst expects RKLB's gross margins to expand from about a 35% trough in 2027 to about 47% by 2030, while R&D spending is estimated to decline from ~35% of sales in 2026 to about 10% in 2028, creating substantial operating leverage as the platform matures.

Gesuale ranks No. 369 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17%. See Rocket Lab Statistics on TipRanks.

J.P. Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth recently upgraded Meta Platforms (META) to buy from hold and raised his price target to $820 from $640. Despite the year-to-date underperformance of META, the 5-star analyst still sees significant upside, as Meta is in the early stages of launching frontier models and AI-powered offerings beyond advertising, particularly the Muse AI agent and Meta Model API access.

"Frontier models are at the core of Meta's product and monetization pipeline over a multi-year period, and its path toward superintelligence," said Anmuth.

In the summer of 2025, Meta set a goal to rebuild its Meta Superintelligence Labs team and deliver frontier AI models within a year, the analyst said. The team appears to have met its goal, rapidly advancing from the rollout of Muse Spark 1.1 in July to Muse Spark 1.3, which is competitive with Claude and GPT models, Anmuth said.

Meanwhile, Meta's Watermelon product will expand opportunities in consumer products, business intelligence, and Family of Apps engagement, the analyst said. The product will enhance internal operations and overall efficiency, said Anmuth, who's confident of Meta's ability to bring consumer-driven AI products to its extensive user base of 4 billion and views its distribution network as a competitive advantage.

While Meta has focused on frontier models and AI product development, Anmuth also sees solid opportunity in its AI infrastructure capacity, which he believes will support future compute needs.

Anmuth ranks No. 832 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of about 9.40%. See Meta Platforms Financials on TipRanks.

After testing it at home, I now rate the Eight Sleep Pod 6 as one of the best smart beds you can buy. Its automatic temperature adjustment has been a game changer, and I think it's worth the investment in this year's Black Friday mattress sales if you often wake up because you feel too cold or too hot.

My full review is coming soon but here's everything you need to know about the Eight Sleep Pod 6, and why it will soon be added to our best mattresses guide.

The Eight Sleep Pod 6 is a sophisticated piece of sleep tech. So it's no big surprise that it comes with a high price tag. A queen has an MSRP of $2,899 in the US, while in the UK you can expect an RRP of £2,399 for a double at Eight Sleep.

But Eight Sleep sales do happen semi-regularly and right now one of the biggest deals we've seen in a while is underway. There's up to $400/£400 off the Pod itself, and as much as $700/£700 when you buy the base as well.

You're unlikely to see a bigger sale than this from Eight Sleep, meaning now is the time to buy.

Before you click 'add to cart', however, let's talk subscriptions. You need to pay for an Autopilot subscription to use Eight Sleep and that starts at $17/£17 per month.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Eight Sleep Pod 6 comes in two parts: a control tower and a cover... plus an app but no mattress. The cover is fitted with a series of water tubes (to heat and cool) and sensors (to track the temperature) which feed back to the control hub to keep your sleep climate even throughout the night.

There are two things worth calling out about the Eight Sleep Pod 6. First, the control tower. It's small and compact but it does still take up vital floorspace. However, it's also whisper quiet. Apart from the occasional jump scare when it starts calibrating itself during the working day, I'd hardly know it was there.

Second, the mattress cover. It doesn't have a huge impact on the feel of your bed but I can tell it's there. I'm sleeping on the Leesa Original mattress and with the Eight Sleep on, the surface has less 'sink'. That's not a deal breaker for me but if you love a bed that 'hugs' the body, the Eight Sleep might get in the way.

Temperature is an important signal to our circadian rhythms, as we naturally cool at night. Increased temperatures — whether through environment our physiological causes — can disrupt your sleep quality.

That's why active climate control is the main focus of the Eight Sleep Pod 6. Its raison d'être, if you will. The integrated water tubes are at work throughout the night to subtly adjust the temperature of the surface.

I'm not a regular hot sleeper but hormonal shifts mean a few times a month I can expect a stuffy morning. Since using the Eight Sleep, I haven't woken up sweaty once. I have on occasion felt my body temperature rise — but the Eight Sleep responds with a flood of cool.

Before bed, I've been enjoying the opposite. The Eight Sleep gently warms in the minutes leading up to my bedtime, so I climb into a cozy bed And I don't have to warm the entire house to do so — I've often found turning the thermostat up before bed results in overheating around 3 a.m.

The Eight Sleep provides a gentle ebb and flow. It warms around 10 p.m., cools as I fall asleep, maintains that cooler feel until the early hours, then gradually warms again so I wake up cozy. And if at any point my body temperature or the room diverts course, the Eight Sleep can adjust to bring me back to the baseline.

The Eight Sleep has a temperature range of 55°F/12°C to 110°F/43°C. I haven't pushed it to the extremes yet but I have gone outside my comfort zone to sample either end of the scale and I've noticed the a significant difference each time. This isn't the placebo effect; the Eight Sleep really is changing the feel of your mattress.

You control the Eight Sleep via the Autopilot app, which is where you set alarms, adjust temperature and view your sleep tracking data.

Overall, I've been impressed with the sleep tracking and how it's displayed in the app. Autopilot shines when it comes to data comparison, showing how your sleep is changing night by night. It's a good way to identify patterns and spot issues before they become major problems.

However, you don't have to use the app to control the Eight Sleep (ish). While the tracking and set up is all done via app, you can adjust the temperature in the night using a panel on the side of the cover. At 3 a.m. when your room is a touch chiller than you want but you don't want to cope with the glare of your smartphone, this is a real benefit.

✅ You regularly overheat at night: I've felt first-hand how the Eight Sleep reacts quickly to excess warmth with a sudden burst of cool. If night sweats are destroying your sleep quality, it could be a smart investment.

✅ You've been on the fence about Eight Sleep: You're unlikely to see a bigger sale than this anytime soon so if you've been looking for a push, consider this it.

✅ You want smart sleep tracking: The integrated sleep tracking is both accurate and helpful, using comparative data to identify trends. Like, say, oversleeping at the weekend means disrupted rest on the Monday. That's news you can use.

❌ You need a new mattress: The Pod 6 is a cover only, designed to fit over your existing bed. If you need a new mattress to stop your night sweats, try our best cooling mattress guide instead.

❌ You don't care about sleep tracking: The Orion Sleep System is a similar temperature control mattress cover but a sleep tracking subscription is optional. And with a queen now only $1,795 (was $2,395), it's cheaper overall (US only).

#3099. iOS 27 adds new Messages app setting I instantly started using

iOS 27 brought several new features to the Messages app, including a setting that’s long been a popular request: the ability to customize or turn off the audio button. Here’s how to use it.

With iOS 27, Apple fixed a lot of bugs and also granted many feature requests from over the years.

Siri AI is the biggest example of that, offering a big upgrade over the old Siri. But smaller changes in apps like Calendar, Mail, and Messages reflect this focus on wish fulfillment.

In Messages, there’s a new setting that I instantly starting using. It lets you turn off the audio button that normally lives on the right side of the text input field.

The audio button has been conveniently accessible there for years, but I never use it. I don’t think I’ve ever sent an audio message. Sometimes I use dictation, but that’s always available from the bottom-right of the keyboard.

Since I never need that button, the only time it gets pressed is by accident. And as I suspect a lot of users have encountered—including Justin Bieber—it’s very easy to hit by accident.

Thankfully, iOS 27 has the fix. To disable the audio button, follow these steps:

Even if you turn the audio button off, you can still send audio messages by hitting the + button to open your iMessage apps then selecting ‘Audio.’

If you prefer to keep the button active, you can alternately now select ‘Record Audio’ or ‘Start Dictation’ as its function. That way the button will always stay set to your preference instead of dynamically changing like it did before.

Will you disable the audio button in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

#3098. iPad Air vs iPad Pro: Which should you buy?

Apple’s iPad lineup is incredibly strong, and two standout options are the iPad Air and iPad Pro. If you’re trying to decide whether the iPad Pro is worth the extra cost this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

Bonus pick: The all-new iPad mini is up to $100 off for Black Friday as well.

Apple updated the iPad Air earlier this year, bringing the M4 chip for improved performance along with 12GB of RAM, up from 8GB in the previous generation.

The iPad Air is available in 11-inch and 13-inch screen sizes, and uses an LCD display with a 60Hz refresh rate. This means it doesn’t offer OLED or ProMotion, unlike the iPad Pro. It uses Touch ID for biometric authentication, supports the Magic Keyboard and Apple Pencil Pro, and offers the full iPadOS multitasking experience.

The iPad Air is available in four colors: blue, purple, starlight, and space gray. It starts at 128GB of storage and can be configured up to 1TB.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad money can buy. It’s powered by Apple’s M5 chip and offers many advantages over the iPad Air.

The biggest difference is the display technology. The iPad Pro is available in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes and uses Apple’s Ultra Retina XDR display with tandem OLED technology. This means it offers deeper blacks, better contrast, and higher brightness than the LCD screen found in the iPad Air.

The iPad Pro also supports ProMotion with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. This means scrolling, animations, Apple Pencil interactions, and more will be significantly smoother.

Contrary to what the naming implies, the iPad Pro is also noticeably thinner and lighter than the iPad Air. The 11-inch iPad Pro measures 5.3mm thick, while the 13-inch model is even thinner at 5.1mm.

The iPad Pro offers Face ID instead of Touch ID, Thunderbolt connectivity, a four-speaker audio system, and nano-texture display options with the higher-end configuration.

For most people, the iPad Air is the right choice. It delivers the entire iPad experience, excellent performance, and comes in four fun colors and two different screen sizes.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad you can buy, but it’s overkill for most people. Don’t get me wrong, I love my iPad Pro. If it’s in your holiday budget, it’s a fantastic choice. I can’t overstate how impressive the tandem OLED display is. It’s significantly better than the LCD screen on the iPad Air. It’s also great having Face ID in the iPad form factor.

The iPad Pro is slightly more tempting at its current sale price, with the mid-range 13-inch model at an impressive $350 off.

Still, both the iPad Air and iPad Pro run the same iPadOS experience, and that’s why I think the iPad Air is the better value for most people. What do you think? Let us know down in the comments.

Coros has launched the Vertix 4 as its new flagship smartwatch, and it’s a major upgrade over the Coros Vertix 2S with an AMOLED display, a more attractive design that has a built-in flashlight, and satellite maps.

I’ve been testing the Vertix 4 for five days, which isn’t nearly enough time to get through its extensive battery life, but I have been able to get some first impressions of the watch by doing four runs with it, comparing it directly to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro.

You’ll find my early likes and dislikes for the Coros Vertix 4 below, along with its price and specs. For those wondering why Coros went from 2S to 4, skipping a Vertix 3, it’s to bring the Vertix 4 into line with its other watches: the Coros Apex 4 and Coros Pace 4 Pro.

The Coros Vertix 4 launched on 24 November 2026 and will be available to order from 27 November. It costs $799 in the U.S. and £669 in the U.K., a $100/£70 price rise on the Vertix 2S.

It does come in significantly cheaper than the latest Garmin Fenix 9 line-up, though, which starts at $999. However, there are some rivals that come in cheaper than the Vertix 4, with the Suunto Vertical 2 titanium model, costing $699/£639, and older Garmin Fenix models appearing in sales — the Garmin Fenix 8 is $749 at Amazon right now, for example.

The Vertix has previously had a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display, and while that does have some advantages, most notably longer battery life, I much prefer the AMOLED display on the Vertix 4.

It’s a very big, bright screen and easier to read than the MIP display on the Vertix 2S in all conditions I find, even in bright sunlight.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The new satellite maps also look great on the display, and the battery life on the Vertix 4 is still very good.

While it would have been great for Coros to make the Vertix 4 available with both MIP and AMOLED options, as Garmin does with the Fenix, it’s perhaps not practical in production terms, and I do think AMOLED is the better option here, with the Apex 4 offering a MIP alternative in the Coros line-up.

Adventure watches are, by design, big and bold devices to strap to your wrist, but the Vertix 2S was a little too huge, and the Coros Vertix 4 is a much more enjoyable watch to wear all day.

It’s thinner and lighter than its predecessor while having a larger display, and doesn’t feel too bulky even on my slim wrist.

In the past, I think Coros watches could be accused of prioritizing substance over style, which is no bad thing, but it’s better to have both, and both of the brand’s 2026 launches — the Pace 4 Pro and now Vertix 4 — have been more attractive than past options.

Ever since Garmin added a built-in flashlight to the Fenix 7X, it’s been a feature that people have wanted in their smartwatch, and the Vertix 4 is the first Coros watch to get it.

Coros has swerved from the usual flashlight setup used by other brands, though, sticking its light on the side of the Vertix 4, between the digital dial and back button, as opposed to on the top as Garmin, Suunto and Amazfit do.

This has its advantages — the flashlight naturally focuses the way your arm is pointing, and you can switch the orientation of the buttons on the watch if you wear it on your right wrist.

I’m still on the fence about whether I prefer this or having the flashlight on top of the watch, but ultimately it’s a big addition to the Vertix line in general, and a very handy feature to have.

Another interesting new feature on the Vertix 4 is satellite maps, which you can download to the watch and use instead of the standard maps. This is a feature I’m testing in beta, with it expected to launch in early 2027.

The satellite maps look great on the AMOLED display, and at times, it's a bit clearer to see what’s around you using them, especially in the forest.

It was pretty quick and easy to get my local area onto the watch through the Coros app, though the satellite map files are larger than the standard, so you will want to be choosy with the areas you download to the watch.

While the standard maps on the watch work fine, having the satellite option is useful at times, and it differentiates the Vertix 4 from other brands since these maps are free.

The Vertix 2S offers incredible battery life — it lasted me 22 days on a charge and even outperformed the Garmin Enduro 2 on this front.

Given the switch to an AMOLED display, the fear would be that the Vertix 4 fell short on this front in comparison, but the listed stats are still very impressive for the watch.

Coros suggests it will last up to 30 days in watch mode, or 10 days with the screen always on, and it offers 48 hours of multi-band GPS tracking with the screen always on.

So far, the Vertix is on track to beat those estimates for me, although aided by the fact that I haven't used it for sleep tracking so far.

With the screen always on and running every day using the most accurate multi-band mode, it’s on track to last over 10 days.

All the Coros watches launched over the past couple of years have impressed me with their GPS accuracy, and that’s the case with the Vertix 4 so far as well.

I’ve been running with it and the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro, with both set to their most accurate mode, and checking the GPS tracks afterwards. The Vertix 4 tracks have been spot on and in line with the Fenix 9 Pro on pace and distance stats throughout the runs too.

Unlike GPS accuracy, the heart rate accuracy of the Vertix 4 has been a bit iffy in my early testing when comparing the readings to a chest strap.

In the Vertix 4’s defence, I’ve been testing it in cold weather, when optical sensors on watches do tend to be less accurate, but I’ve still been a little underwhelmed by the results.

On my easy runs, it’s mostly been pretty close to a chest strap, but on a hard progression run, the Vertix 4’s readings were too high throughout. Based on my early tests, you’d definitely be wise to pair a chest strap to the Vertix 4, at least in cold conditions.

The Vertix 4 is noticeably slimmer and lighter than past versions, but it’s still quite a big watch, and Coros does not offer any size options, something that Garmin does with the Fenix 9.

There are the Apex 4 and Pace 4 Pro as smaller alternatives in the Coros line-up, but if you want the flagship model, you have to accept that it only comes in one size, and it’s a biggie.

It doesn’t take long when testing a Coros watch to realize that they really make sports watches, not smartwatches.

The Vertix 4 can store music, but only files you drag and drop onto the watch; it doesn’t pair with streaming services. It also doesn’t offer NFC payments, and you can’t customize the watch face as much as on rivals.

Personally, I don’t miss these smart features much, but they are a selling point not only true smartwatches like the Apple Watch Ultra 4, but also Garmin watches, which combine great sports tracking with useful smarts.

Follow Tom's Guide on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our up-to-date news, analysis, and reviews in your feeds.

Nick Harris-Fry is an experienced health and fitness journalist, writing professionally since 2012. He spent nine years working on the Coach magazine and website before moving to the fitness team at Tom’s Guide in 2024. Nick is a keen runner and also the founder of YouTube channel The Run Testers, which specialises in reviewing running shoes, watches, headphones and other gear.

Nick ran his first marathon in 2016 and became obsessed with the sport. He now has PBs of 2hr 25min for the marathon and 15min 30sec for 5K. Nick is also a qualified Run Leader in the UK.

Nick is an established expert in the fitness area and along with writing for many publications, including Live Science, Expert Reviews, Wareable, Coach and Get Sweat Go, he has been quoted on The Guardian and The Independent.

#3096. 3 Unstoppable Stocks That Can Be Great Buys for Decades

Amazon, Microsoft, and Walmart are massive companies that are likely to continue to dominate their respective industries for years to come.

By David Jagielski, CPA – Nov 24, 2026 at 2:22PM EST

Stocks that are great long-term investments have solid underlying financials, and there's a great deal of predictability around their futures. What the recent Nvidia scandal has brought to light is the importance of investing in a business that may not be highly dependent on just a single person or the outlook for artificial intelligence (AI).

Three companies that look like unstoppable investments for the long term, regardless of what happens with AI, are Amazon (AMZN -1.21%), Microsoft (MSFT +0.74%), and Walmart (WMT +2.11%). Here's why they can make for excellent buy-and-forget investments.

Amazon's stock hasn't gotten much love over the past year. While it has generated decent 12% returns over the past 12 months, that pales in comparison to some of the gains tech stocks have accumulated over that stretch.

But for a company that's typically at the forefront of any tech innovation, its modest gains can actually be excellent news for investors who buy the stock today. While its financial results have been improving, its valuation hasn't taken off, and thus, it has become a much more attractive investment in the process.

The stock is currently trading at 23 times its expected future profits (based on analyst projections). That's a modest valuation for one of the leading tech companies in the world. It's developing robotaxis, its own AI chips, and deploying drones for delivery, among other opportunities it's pursuing. On top of all that is, of course, its massive e-commerce business.

To buy such a tremendous stock at a low valuation could prove to be a steal of a deal in the future.

Another tech giant that I like for the long haul is Microsoft. It's been a top name in tech for decades, and the reason I don't see that changing is because of how trusted and entrenched its software is within corporate environments. Businesses rely on Microsoft's Office software on a daily basis.

While there have been other options and there will continue to be more competition in the future, I think the reliability that its software offers and the trust it has built up over the years is what gives it a huge competitive advantage. And the company's investments in AI could also pay off significantly, with Microsoft's Office software now able to do much more, with its Copilot assistant helping create spreadsheets and documents in just minutes, potentially saving corporate clients hours each day.

Shares of Microsoft crashed earlier this year due to panic that AI would wreak havoc on software companies. I don't believe that will happen with Microsoft, and I am confident it'll be able to invest in AI effectively to add more value for its customers.

It's up less than 3% this year, and its forward earnings multiple of 24 is also not terribly high, especially for such a solid tech business.

Another business that I'm confident isn't going anywhere decades from now is Walmart. The big-box retailer seems intent on going toe-to-toe with Amazon, as it has ramped up delivery options over the years to also provide customers with day-to-day goods and necessities quickly in order to be more competitive with the tech company.

Walmart continually generates solid, stable growth, as consumers flock to its stores for all types of goods, making it arguably the ultimate one-stop shopping location due to its diverse mix of products. And with a heavy grocery business, it makes it easy for consumers to come in to buy essentials and also purchase other items while they're inside its stores.

The stock has done well this year, rising by around 19%, as investors have loaded up on it for the long-term safety and stability it offers. The only thing I don't like about the stock is that it's trading at a high valuation -- close to 40 times projected future earnings. However, that just means that returns may be limited in the near term. But that becomes a relatively minor issue if investors are prepared to hang on for decades.
