#3094. Fluence (FLNC) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record backlog meets Houston delays and penalties that hit profitability.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 2:24PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Fluence (FLNC +7.89%) reported fiscal 2026 results that were impacted by significant manufacturing and delivery delays, even as customer demand for its energy storage solutions reached record levels. Management announced a comprehensive transformation strategy to address these operational failures, focusing on four primary pillars: fulfilling customer commitments, enhancing financial and operational discipline, prioritizing profitable growth over volume, and strengthening cash generation. The company is currently working through a record backlog, with the U.S. market and data centers emerging as the primary drivers of growth. While production at the key Houston manufacturing facility has improved, management is prioritizing execution to stabilize margins and recycle working capital to avoid the need for external capital in fiscal 2027.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Fluence Energy Fourth Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I'd now like to hand the conference over to Chris Shelton, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Chris Shelton: Good morning, and welcome to Fluence Energy's Full Year Fiscal '26 Earnings Conference Call. With me today are Axel Meier, Interim Chief Executive Officer; Ricardo Roizen, Interim Chief Financial Officer; and Bernerd Da Santos, Chief Operating Officer. A copy of our earnings presentation, press release and supplementary metric sheet covering financial results, along with supporting statements and schedules, including reconciliations and disclosures regarding non-GAAP financial measures, are posted on the Investor Relations section of our website at www.fluenceenergy.com.

During the course of this call, Fluence management may make certain forward-looking statements regarding various matters related to our business, including, but not limited to, statements related to our future financial and operating performance, future market growth and related opportunities, anticipated growth and business strategy, liquidity and access to capital, expectations related to demand, customers and pipeline, order intake and contracted backlog, conversion of backlog into revenues, future results of operations, transformation strategy, management transition and potential benefits, our multiyear agreement with EVE Power, projected costs, beliefs, assumptions, prospects, plans and objectives of management and the timing of any of the foregoing.

Such statements are based upon current expectations and certain assumptions that are, therefore, subject to certain risks, uncertainties and other important factors, which could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings and press release for more information regarding these risks, uncertainties and important factors. You are cautioned not to place undue reliance on these forward-looking statements, which speak only as of today. Also, please note that the company undertakes no duty to update or revise forward-looking statements. This call will also reference non-GAAP measures that we view as important in assessing the performance of our business, including adjusted EBITDA, adjusted gross profit and adjusted gross profit margin.

A reconciliation of these non-GAAP measures to the most comparable GAAP measure is available on our earnings materials on the company's Investor Relations website. Following our prepared remarks, we will conduct a question-and-answer session with our team. As previously communicated in our press release on our management transition, we will not be providing 2027 guidance today. With that, I'm pleased to turn the call over to Axel beginning on Slide 4.

Axel Meier: Thank you, Chris, and welcome to everyone joining us on this call. I would like to start by reiterating that the recent management changes have proven experience in financial management, operational transformation, manufacturing and customer delivery as Fluence works to strengthen production systems and processes, improve execution and reinforce financial discipline. The management changes also reflect the continued strong support from our controlling shareholders, Siemens and AES, and their confidence in Fluence's potential and significant market opportunity. In terms of my own background, I have more than 3 decades of experience at Siemens, including senior leadership positions in communications, industry and infrastructure. Most recently, I served as the CFO of Siemens Smart Infrastructure.

In that role, I helped to shape the business into a strong and reliable performer, delivering 23 consecutive quarters of year-over-year profit margin expansion and disciplined cash conversion, while at the same time, significantly growing the business. I was one of the first members of the Fluence Board of Directors in 2020, and thus, I have a long history with the company and a deep understanding of its business. I continue to believe that Fluence is well positioned to succeed in this rapidly growing energy storage market.

As we noted in our recent press release, the Board is keenly focused on strengthening Fluence's ability to capitalize on its competitive capabilities, including our differentiated products and our record $9 billion (sic) [ $8.9 billion ] backlog as of the end of fiscal '26. Our transformation strategy is designed to deliver on commitments to customers and suppliers, improve financial and operational execution, prioritize profitable growth and strengthen cash generation. Bernerd will add more color today on what we mean by each of these objectives, but we are not yet in a position to provide details. However, we do expect to provide 2027 financial guidance on our first quarter call in February. Turning to Slide 5.

I'll review the highlights of our fourth quarter and full year results. We had order intake of $3.5 billion in quarter 4 2026, approximately 150% higher than our previous best of $1.4 billion just set last quarter. We ended the quarter with a backlog of $9 billion (sic) [ $8.9 billion ], representing 39% growth over the third quarter and 68% growth over the $5.3 billion at our last fiscal year's end. Total liquidity at quarter end was approximately $855 million, in line with our liquidity at the end of the third quarter.

These were key achievements in fiscal year 2026, but our overall performance did not result in the profitability required to create value for our shareholders, nor did we deliver on the commitments that we have made to our customers and suppliers. This new management team has committed to the transformation of our business expected to convert our backlog into profitable growth as measured by EBITDA. Now to Slide 6 for an update on market demand trends. We're continuing to see rapid growth in the energy storage market across our key customer segments. Increasing electrification and competitive pricing for storage relative to new generation and a growing number of applications for battery storage are driving this growth.

Developers view storage as a way to enhance project economics. Utilities see storage as a means of shaving peak demand and reinforcing voltage across the grid. Data centers see storage as a critical path to improving the quality and speed to power. Fluence is well positioned with respect to all of these customer segments, and we have been receiving interest from each of them as reflected in our strong order intake. Turning to Slide 7. As I noted earlier, quarter 4 2026 order intake was a record of $3.5 billion, accounting for more than half of the full year '26 of total $6.2 billion.

Following our revised guidance call in mid-September, we booked approximately 70% of our fourth quarter orders, reconfirming customer confidence in Fluence's capabilities. Our fourth quarter total also included $586 million of orders that were awarded by a hyperscaler as we discussed on our third quarter earnings call. We are seeing ongoing momentum in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 and expect it to continue in future quarters, driven by demand across power developers, utilities and data centers. We do have a healthy mix of both new and repeat customers and orders continue to be concentrated in our core markets, U.S., Europe and Australia. Please turn to Slide 8 as I discuss the growth of our backlog.

As I noted earlier, the strong order intake during the fourth quarter resulted in the growth of our backlog to $9 billion (sic) [ $8.9 billion ] at September 30. Approximately 1/3 of our backlog is expected to convert to revenues in each of the next 3 fiscal years. Our backlog continues to reflect the accelerated growth we are harnessing in the U.S., which accounted for approximately 70% of our total backlog, up from 58% in fiscal year 2025. From a customer segmentation standpoint, developers and power producers are the largest segment, followed by utilities and data centers, which account for 10% of our backlog today and represents our fastest-growing customer segment.

Turning to Slide 9 and the competitive advantages of our Smartstack products. From a product standpoint, Smartstack represents over half of our backlog, and we expect that percentage will grow further as we deliver the remainder of our older product lines. This represents a rapid adoption rate when considering that Smartstack was launched relatively recently. Although we have shared these points in the past, I think it's worth reiterating why we believe that our Smartstack product is gaining traction with customers so quickly: higher energy density, which reduces the size of the required area of footprint; modular design, which allows Smartstack units to be deployed in 5 parts, including our Smart Skid with 4 battery modules.

This enables customers to deploy Smartstack with a forklift instead of a crane; available with domestic content, allowing our customers to capture U.S. tax credit. Fluence's products have a strong track record of availability as validated by DNV with 99% fleet performance availability for large energy storage projects; fire safety testing and cybersecurity features, both of which are designed to give our customers confidence in our product; integrated hardware and operating system, which provides an improved ability to smooth load and carry out other functions. Smartstack is a result of the internal product development by Fluence, coupled with the strength of our suppliers.

Now I'd like to turn the call over to Ricardo Roizen, who will review our fiscal 2026 results in more detail and provide an update on liquidity, beginning on Slide 11.

Ricardo Roizen Gottlieb: Thank you, Axel. First, I'd like to share with you a bit of my background and experience that I'm bringing to Fluence at this critical time. I have worked at AES for 18 years, most recently serving as CFO of AES Andes. My experience gives me not only a familiarity with the energy generation industry, but also a deep understanding of the perspective of a long-term strategic shareholder and the importance of delivering sustainable value for all our shareholders. AES Andes has also been a customer of Fluence, so I am already familiar with the company and our products. Much of my background has centered on financial discipline, cash and working capital management, capital allocation and operational execution.

These areas are particularly relevant to Fluence as we focus on strengthening execution, improving margins and cash generation and positioning the company for sustainable profitable growth. Turning now to our fiscal 2026 results on Slide 12. Revenue for the fiscal fourth quarter was $744 million and for the full year, we generated revenues of $2.3 billion, with both periods coming in below our forecast, primarily driven by delays in project delivery due to production shortfalls at our contracted manufacturing facility in Houston. A key driver impacting our full year results was approximately $90 million of penalties associated with delayed deliveries. Adjusted EBITDA for the fourth quarter was negative $112 million and for the full year was negative $203 million.

These results were also impacted by $85 million, primarily due to cost overruns associated with equipment and manufacturing costs related to the delivery of new products, in addition to $25 million of increased sales and marketing expenses and R&D expense. While this performance is disappointing, our transformation strategy is structured to address this impact, as Bernerd will discuss shortly. Please turn to Slide 13 for an overview of our liquidity profile. We ended the year with total liquidity of $855 million, which includes $379 million in cash. This is consistent with our position at the end of the third quarter. During the fourth quarter, we built our inventory position to $970 million, more than double the year ago.

75% of this inventory is equipment and materials awaiting assembly into our finished products, some of which has already been delivered to customers from our Houston facility. The remaining inventory is finished product as of September 30. These materials are expected to fulfill customer delivery commitments that will then convert to revenue and cash in fiscal year 2027. Our intent is to recycle this working capital into new projects in our backlog, supporting our expectation for no external capital needs during fiscal year 2027. Our revolver is one of the credit facilities included in our total liquidity profile.

We are proactively working with our banks to address the EBITDA covenant in our revolving credit facility through an amendment and extension, which was also granted last year. At the same time, the issues we experienced at our new manufacturing facilities are being resolved and operational performance is improving. With that, I will turn the call over to Bernerd to cover our transformation strategy, beginning on Slide 15.

Bernerd Raymond Da Santos Avila: Thank you, Ricardo. In my prior position at AES, I was involved with the creation of Fluence, then the customer of Fluence. More recently, I was named to Fluence's Board. And on September 16, I became the company's Chief Operating Officer. I have spent my career driving transformation, performance and expansion across multiple businesses at AES, including as the Chief Executive Officer of their Clean Energy business. I would like to share with you the opportunity I see with Fluence and why I was motivated to take this role. As Axel discussed, battery storage has entered a period of accelerating growth. In my view, once-in-a-generation opportunity driven by falling prices and increasing applications.

Fluence is a leading participant in this industry with very competitive terms as reflected by our order intake and backlog. The challenge in front of us is to deliver on this backlog with execution that drives profitability. During my career, I have successfully faced and resolved execution issues similar to those that Fluence has been experiencing. And I am confident that these are solvable. These fixes must be made with urgency and discipline so we can reach our goals. Turning to Slide 16. Over the next 5 slides, I will outline our transformation strategy. We have 4 main pillars: delivering on our commitments to customers and suppliers, improving financial and operational execution, prioritizing profitable growth and strengthening cash generation.

I will address each of these in turn, beginning on Slide 17. First, delivering on our commitments to customers and suppliers. To realize the value of our $9 billion (sic) [ $8.9 billion ] backlog, our supply chain must supports the delivery of projects on time and on budget. To that end, we have been expanding manufacturing capacity at home and abroad. Production at our Houston facility, which was running approximately 3 units per day in early September, is now producing at 10 units per day over the past few weeks. Also, since the September call, we have welcomed customers at the Houston facility, so they can verify the progress we have made.

Across our suppliers, we now have production capacity of 25 gigawatt hours to serve our international and U.S. markets with a wide range of domestic content configurations, which supports our ability to deliver our 2027 and 2028 backlog. We expect further improvement in our facilities as well, which will position us to grow our backlog for 2028 and beyond. As we carry projects from 2026 to 2027, we are looking at the timing of expected production against our delivery commitments. In some cases, we will revisit timelines with customers who may have flexibility in order to mitigate potential penalties. In other cases, we will be discussing where contract pricing reflects the value of customization adjustments requested by the customers.

Second, improving financial and operational execution. We are working on putting systems and processes in place to enhance commercial, operational and financial discipline. For example, we are implementing a more robust pricing model with strong internal controls to help ensure a systematic approach to inputs and assumptions and our expected margins above this cost. We are also strengthening our integrated planning process across materials, production and delivery. This will help mitigate the potential for cost overruns such as those we experienced in the fiscal year 2026. Third, prioritizing profitable growth.

There are a few components to prioritizing customer segments and markets in order to most effectively allocate our resources: improving pricing discipline, particularly for customization adjustments, strengthening project execution to achieve gross margin and profit targets on a project-by-project basis, and reviewing and rightsizing our cost structure. Additionally, given the size of our backlog, over time, we expect to achieve economies of scale in cost of goods sold. The fourth pillar is to strengthen cash generation and avoid accessing capital markets. We will protect liquidity by looking at cash commitments and expenditures and recycling working capital into new projects. Longer term, we will generate positive cash flow by improving profitability.

With that, I will now turn the call back over to Axel for closing remarks on Slide 21.

Axel Meier: Thank you, Bernerd. In summary, we are focused on implementing our transformation strategy to deliver on commitments to customers and suppliers, improve financial and operational execution, prioritize profitable growth and strengthen cash generation. These fixes are being made with urgency and discipline so we can restore the confidence of our shareholders, lenders, customers, suppliers and employees. We look forward to sharing updates on our progress.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from George Gianarikas with CGF.

George Gianarikas: So maybe to start on the welding issues that impacted your U.S. ramp in the quarter. Can you update us on whether the equipment has been permanently retooled to eliminate manual workarounds and maybe a clear line of sight as to when the plant will reach full nameplate capacity and normalized unit costs?

Bernerd Raymond Da Santos Avila: Yes. George, nice to meet you by phone. Bernerd Da Santos here speaking to address your question. First, let me start saying that we are making steady progress in our manufacturing facility. And with relate to the output, we put a plan in place that support our backlog for 2027 and 2028, and the 10 units, 11 units per day that we have seen sustainable delivery in the last 2 weeks is in line with that plan. It is not yet at the maximum capacity plate -- plate capacity as you mentioned. So there are still areas of improvement that we can eliminate.

As we see the progressing and the trend that we're seeing right now, we see those improvements more likelihood to materialize in the near future, and that will open the possibility to moving a slot to 2027, but also to open a slot in 2028 additional. Related to our automation facilities, most of these issues or those -- most of these enhancements actually have been putting in place, and we see that they are in line with our plans, as I mentioned at the beginning. So again, making steady progress in the manufacture that gives me confidence that an opportunity in order to continue to improve as we move forward in the action plans that we put in place.

George Gianarikas: And maybe as a follow-up, you clearly had some very strong orders despite the supply chain hiccups. And I'd love to have some color on the recent commercial discussions you're having. How are customers weighing your product against the recent delivery track record? How much of your retention and growth is maybe driven by a scarcity of competition versus product quality?

Bernerd Raymond Da Santos Avila: Thank you, George. I think the way to look at this is looking at our backlog and looking at how was the order intake that we took in our end of the quarter after the announcement that the company made in the mid of September. So we continue to see a strength in our order intake. We continue to see strength in our backlog. And that honestly gives a comfort, but also support for the product that we have in place. And talking about the product, because I think those order intakes respond to the product itself.

It is a product that is -- will have a smaller footprint and will have a wide range in the U.S. market to fulfill domestic content. We can go all to the 100% and in any actually a ratio that is needed for our customer needs. So that's number one. Second is the availability. This is an availability product of 99% for large projects actually certified by DNV. And that is a great support to have. And the third is related to the footprint of the capacity due to the modularity and the density of the product. We have the Smartstack in the version of 7.5 and 10.

And we also have the Gridstack in the 2-megawatt hours and in the 5-megawatt hours version. So all the products converting into domestic content and serving depending on what is the customer needs. So those products, actually, as we fulfill multiple applications for our customers, we continue to see strong in the order intake.

The focus of our management team in this moment is in execution, is realize the commitment that we do with our customers, is realize the profitability that deserves to our shareholders, and it is elevating the execution to an excellent point in order to continue to perform and continue to have Fluence as a leader in the market in the United States, but also in other markets that we serve.

Operator: Our next question comes from Dylan Thomas Nassano with Wolfe Research.

Dylan Thomas Nassano: I was wondering if you could just expand a little more on how you are going about prioritizing new orders, just given the influx of new orders and keeping in mind the delayed projects you still have to execute on and the desire to avoid capital markets. I'm just curious, I mean, are you prioritizing by like margin or customer relationship? Any color there would be helpful.

Axel Meier: Dylan, this is Axel. Thanks for your question. In regards of orders and prioritization, we have said clearly that our aim is profitable growth, which clearly indicates that the margin conversion we're looking for has to be meaningful, first comment. The second comment is we are already looking at the situation of there is an accelerated market demand meeting a constrained capacity available. And in that regard, I think what we are observing is that the market is shifting more and more towards allocation. We're not there yet. But typically, with that said, it also drives into, okay, how do I allocate my capacity.

I have to say, I was last week attending RE+ in Las Vegas, which is a big renewable convention. And it basically reconfirms what I said about the market. But I also have to say I was really positively impressed or even excited to see the response we saw towards our portfolio. So in summary, I'd say we look clearly for profitable growth. We are looking for orders which underline this aim there, but we also honor the relationship we have with existing customers. That doesn't mean that we are not looking for a healthy mix of new customers and also existing customers.

Dylan Thomas Nassano: Got it. And then I guess two quick follow-ups on the previous topic, to what extent are you turning away any new business? And then just a follow-up on the changes to contract pricing. Can you just maybe tell us a little bit about what exactly is changing? How much of the backlog is fixed price? How much raw material price exposure do you have?

Axel Meier: Yes. Maybe I'll take the first part, and I would hand it over for the second part to Bernerd. So on the first part, I think we are turning away in a moment when we cannot provide the capacity needed to deliver to the needs of the customer. If you look into the situation right now, currently, the capacity is being utilized for the backlog in fiscal 2027. As Bernerd said before, if we continue to optimize manufacturing capacity, we might be able to open a few slots, but we would not engage in any kind of commitments and new orders if we cannot, at the same time, fulfill that we can make this product available.

So I'd say for 2027, the capacity we have is mostly utilized. At the same token, obviously, we are working on increasing capacity in the outer years. And based on what the customer is looking for at which point in time they want to have this product installed, we would basically take the order or not. Bernerd?

Bernerd Raymond Da Santos Avila: Yes. Thank you, Axel. Let me explain why we see that path in order that profitable growth and actually pursuing those markets, and that I will say with premium as we position ourselves as a value product in markets that appreciate value rather than just competing for the lower cost.

And so just to comment on that, of our objective and how we're pursuing: when we look at the actions that we're taking is, as we see our trending and progress in our facilities, not only the manufacturing Houston facility that is the main, but other facilities, we're looking at what our expect production slot opening and what is the delivery commitments that we have with our customers in order to actually peer in looking at that and move the slots in a way that makes a win-win situation between customers and Fluence.

We also are going to revisit some of the customization that we have made with customers for specific applications requested by them in order to actually look at time and look at price in the way that we actually maximize not only the profitability, more importantly, the delivery of the commitments to them. Other actions that we are covering is we are going to prioritize customer segments based on the value that they see in our products and based on the applications that we serve them. But as well, we're going to look at the markets. What are the specific markets that we actually can compete and attain that profitability.

But more important, to better allocate also our -- effectively our resources in those markets versus these 2 pieces is not only the market and price and the value, it's also the lean structure in cost in order to serve it. Improving price discipline, we talked about that, in order to have differentiation price for those customization adjustments that are required by our customers. Of course, strengthening the project execution to achieve that gross margin and profit target. And this is a project-by-project basis. We serve our customers. They have their project itself, and we need to fit our project timelines and schedules within their projects and work as one project mindset.

And we're going to review the rightsizing of our cost structure as well. And given the size of our backlog, and we pursue more economies of scale, and all of these actions should yield for a more profitable outcome. As I mentioned, we are making steady progress into that direction, and we see the path in order to achieve those objectives.

Operator: Our next question comes from Julien Patrick Dumoulin-Smith with Jefferies.

Julien Patrick Dumoulin-Smith: Maybe just to start with a macro question in the marketplace. What are we seeing on pricing? What are you all observing here just in as much as the competitive landscape seems to be changing in recent months and weeks? Where are ASPs trending? Obviously, you talk about profitable growth, but where is the marketplace evolving? It seems as if pricing is seeing an uptick of late. Can you speak to it and quantify a little bit what you're seeing out there and how that contributes to your confidence on this profitable growth strategy?

Axel Meier: Julien, this is Axel again. Yes, let's frame it this way. So the good news is we have an accelerated market growth. And I'd say while there have been traditionally utilities and developers driving this market growth, latest with the data centers adding to this market segment, we see that this is the fastest-growing market element, driving the overall market growth to an acceleration we have not seen before. Having said this, at the same token, the speed of having available capacity is being constrained, so which typically then obviously adds to the pricing quality.

Now what we do observe in the market is on a competitive landscape that some of the existing capacity has been reallocated into different market segments, up to upsetting customers. What we also see is that, in some cases, the prices have been raised in a double-digit percentage. So having seen this in the past in adjacent businesses I've been, I wouldn't be surprised to see that, overall, the price quality of the business we are in will go up, which then obviously is another lever for adding to our profitable growth story.

But at the same token, while we take this lever, we are focusing on the priorities we have given ourselves to be in a profitable growth situation even before this element. I hope it answers.

Julien Patrick Dumoulin-Smith: No, no, indeed. And then if I can zero in a little bit more about the operational progress, right? So you're at 10 units now. What is the target fully ramped production rate at Houston in the terms of units per day? And when would you expect to reach that, just to zero in a little bit more specifically about the operational metrics? And going forward, will you provide color on where you are in terms of those units, right, as a metric to kind of watch that progress?

And specifically, where are we on this automated welding dynamic, in as much as I think for a moment, there was manual welding on site with subcontractors, if you can speak to that transition?

Bernerd Raymond Da Santos Avila: Julien, Bernerd here. So let me sum it up in saying, as again, our AES Houston facility is doing steady progress and sustainable progress. The more important point that I want to highlight is, with the units performing in this moment at the plant, we can support and fulfill entirely our 2027 and 2028 backlog. The second point is any improvement that we made going forward is going to be steady and progressive because this is about execution discipline rather than changing the number. We already are at the level to fulfill and support our 2027. The next gate is improvements in order to open up more slot capacity. I will wait to see that come through.

And when I feel confident, then I will go back to the market and indicate what is really the size of that improvement and how we're going to address it in the future in our slots and aligned with our customers' schedules, as I mentioned, because our priority as well is to deliver to our -- to the commitments that we took with our customers. Related to the welding facility, the welding -- the automation is already in place. We continue to make improvements, and we are in the plan that we put in place back in September, performing at this moment.

And actually, yesterday morning, when I look at the manufacturing, we continue to see the improvement and could yield even to a better week this week despite Thanksgiving. But I want to hold to announce any numbers related to that because one particular day is not necessarily a trend. We need to see more days coming through in order to solidify that trend. Achieving all of these objectives, we continue with that steady progress.

And as I mentioned, I feel very confident that we're going to deliver our 2027, 2028 backlog with the levels that we're seeing today, and I am looking forward for the continuous improvement of the actions that we have taken as they have demonstrated to be the right actions yielding the right success. Our strong partnership with our manufacturing facilities around the world, and we're working together side by side in order to actually continue to pursue improvement now that we have achieved our objectives in the original plan.

Julien Patrick Dumoulin-Smith: Excellent. Just when do you get to the cash flow positive piece that you have on the slide here? Is there a specific target date?

Bernerd Raymond Da Santos Avila: Thank you. The affirmation that I'm going to do right now is we're going to get to positive cash flow. I will hold in order to actually say numbers at this moment as we indicated at the beginning of the call and in the press release, we're not providing guidance today. I appreciate the question, Julien, and hold tight, we will come back to you.

Operator: Our next question will come from Brian K. Lee with Goldman Sachs.

Brian K. Lee: I guess I remember a few years ago, maybe last cycle, Fluence found itself in a similar situation where you had some contracts/projects that maybe weren't priced correctly. And I think the decision -- I know this wasn't under your watch, but the decision at that time was to honor the contracts, not make the target margin and then kind of live to fight another day and not lose market share with those customers and then be able to continue to do business with them. It sounds like you guys might be taking a different approach here with the contract repricing approach.

So I'd be curious, what's changed today versus the last time you kind of went through this last time? I think it was really on the back of rising battery costs. But how much of the $9 billion (sic) [ $8.9 billion ] backlog is subject to contract repricing as you kind of go through this exercise of what's at your target margin, what needs to come up? And would you be willing to just walk away from business as opposed to just honor contracts the way you did last time around?

Axel Meier: Yes. Thank you, Brian, for your question. Let me say, we do honor the contracts we have closed, right? I mean the $8.9 billion in our backlog has been signed with a clear commitment, with a clear contractual language in place, and we will honor this. Now having said this, while this is the statement for existing backlog, every new order coming in, we will basically take into consideration what is the situation in the market, what is the available capacity, what is the situation on the supplier side, what makes up the pricing. And I think also what Bernerd said is what we will take into consideration is what we call value pricing.

So we say, okay, what is it that we bring to the table and what is the value basically realized on this one. We have had historically -- we have had in the past too much customization in there without any recognition on the price, which certainly we will address. But again, we do honor what we have in place for the $8.9 billion. So we will not move away from this one. But going forward, clearly, we take those new approaches.

Bernerd Raymond Da Santos Avila: I will complement Axel, indicating that there is more than one action that will yield to a profitable path here. And it's a different size of company, it's a different scalability and it's a different size of the backlog. All of those, as I mentioned, as we look at this and our progress is steady, will yield to economies of scale, focus on market and make right, effective allocation of our resources, look at our cost structure entirely. So there are more than one action than just at the customer side that Fluence today has as a lever in order to yield that work. So the name of the game here is execution and discipline in the execution.

So as we mentioned in our remarks, this is actions that we're taking with urgency, actions that we're taking more on discipline, and it is really focused on the execution that I will say in a very good team for the situation and the position that Fluence is today.

Brian K. Lee: Okay. Fair enough. And then maybe going back to George's earlier question, just on kind of customer sustainability and the feedback you're getting. If I just run the numbers, I guess, the $8.9 billion backlog and the shipments this quarter, I guess I'm getting to like a $200 million delta. Was there any debookings, or did you reprice anything in the backlog in the quarter? Because it does seem like there's like a $200 million delta from last quarter's backlog, if I just adjust for orders and deliveries.

Chris Shelton: Brian, it's Chris Shelton. Just trying to follow. Can you -- maybe we can take it offline if the math is involved on that. But I think we didn't have any debookings during the quarter, to confirm that. We talked in the prepared remarks about a little bit of a breakdown of the $8.9 billion, but...

Brian K. Lee: Yes, I can take that offline. No worries, Chris.

Operator: Our next question will come from Justin Lars Clare with ROTH Capital Partners.

Justin Lars Clare: So just wanted to start, in the 10-K here, it indicates about 37% of the $8.9 billion backlog is anticipated to convert to revenue in the next 12 months. It's about $3.3 billion. Just wondering, do you have additional capacity here that can support more orders for fiscal '27 delivery? And then if you could potentially share how you're thinking about the quarterly cadence of revenue recognition in fiscal '27? And then just lastly, would you be able to share beyond fiscal 2027, the cadence of expected revenue recognition? How much is scheduled for fiscal '28 recognition versus later years?

Chris Shelton: Justin, it's Chris Shelton. I appreciate you must have late night reading with the 10-K last night. I'm impressed. What we said -- so we're not giving guidance today. I'll jump in, so we can go through the K. What we did say, though, is we gave backlog breakdown by year in the prepared remarks. So approximately $3 billion is the backlog roll-off for '27 and then another 1/3, so approximately $3 billion would be for '28. Those are really the parameters we gave today. And we're not giving guidance. We'll do that at a future point. Does that answer the question?

Justin Lars Clare: Yes. No, that's helpful. Yes, I appreciate it. I guess then just on the profitability. So gross margin in the fiscal Q4 was negative 3.7%. Can you comment on expectations for margin recovery in fiscal '27? Do you anticipate any additional kind of project-related costs, onetime items, liquidated damages extending into fiscal '27? And then just wondering, like is the 10% to 15% adjusted gross margin range still the right level we should be thinking about longer term here?

Axel Meier: Justin, it's Axel. Let me frame it this way. So if I look into last fiscal year, in particular in quarter 4, I'd say there's three elements which yielded into the loss we were realizing. The one is we had this challenge on the ramp-up in our Houston facility, which prevented us from basically executing on the revenue with the lost margin associated with this, first comment. The second comment is if you don't deliver, you run the risk of liquidated damages. A big part of liquidated damages we saw in the last fiscal year were contributing based on this fact.

And the third one is cost overruns, where we, to some degree, underestimated new products, which we launched in the market. Now having said this, number one and number two are being addressed as we talk when it comes to safeguarding the capacity in our manufacturing environment. On the cost side, we are driving transformation. We are tightening the activities within the company, optimizing cost position there in order to realize the margin quality we also have booked. And then lastly, on your question, is 10% to 15% the right frame? Yes, it is. But I think the issue is more -- it's not the short term. It's something which we are basically aiming for.

And I know everyone is anxious when we are laying out the guidance and how the years after will look like. So we reconfirm we will come back to you for fiscal '27 after the quarter 1 call or in the quarter 1 call. And we also have agreed in the management team that in the second half of the fiscal year, we go in depth with you with the capital markets and give you a view on the outer years.

Operator: Our next question comes from Davis Sunderland with Baird.

Davis Sunderland: Most of my questions on backlog have been covered. Maybe just one other thing to pick on there. Is there any color you can give as to the percentage of backlog or maybe the amount of backlog that is specifically domestic content tied to that Houston facility? And then I have one follow-up.

Chris Shelton: Davis, Chris Shelton. So domestic content from the Houston facility is the question. Could you just restate it maybe?

Davis Sunderland: Yes. Just trying to get a sense for how much of the backlog is planned capacity or was planned capacity to come out of that facility?

Chris Shelton: Got it. Yes. So we haven't broken down -- broken our capacity build by facility yet. I think what we've said -- what we're experiencing is particularly in the U.S., but also globally, we've got customers that are interested in either domestic content or imported solutions. So that's -- we can serve the U.S. market from -- Bernerd would have something to add on the capacity we're seeing.

Bernerd Raymond Da Santos Avila: Yes. I think when we look at the capacity, there are two things here. If we look at our backlog, our backlog has moved from being more in the 50-50 U.S. and international. Actually, when you look at 2024, probably was actually 60% international, 40% U.S. and has been in the 50-50, and now it's actually switching to be more weighted to the U.S. market than the international market. I need, for top of my mind in this moment, I think we are in the 60% in 2027 and growing in 2028 when we look at the market. If you look at the capacity, we have a wide range of our supply chain.

So when you look at the product Gridstack Pro 2000 and Gridstack Pro 5000, those are deliveries from the United States, and mostly those are products for domestic content and for the U.S. market. When you look at the Smartstack, that is really what is heavy in our backlog that you are looking, is that modularity. We can go in threshold that go as low -- we can do 0. That is the easy path to go. But we can go in any threshold that go up to 25% all the way to 100%, depending on what is the request, the customer needs in order that they can hit the ITC.

So more than the specific number of our supply chain to satisfy the U.S. market, what I will say is the flexibility of our supply chain in the way that has been structured our product, the Smartstack, in order to serve a wide range of domestic content all the way through 100%. So if you look at all of that, we sum it up probably 60% for 2027 at this point and growing due to that flexibility. Again, the acceptance of the product has been great in the market. And again, one more time, our focus is on execution.

As we open up a slot, we're going to have more capacity to bring in, and that will be more order intake and further expansion we can discuss when we enter more in date in 2027.

Davis Sunderland: That's super helpful. Maybe just one other, and it's a good segue from your last comment. Just in thinking about the order intake and the conversations you guys are having with customers, has there been anyone coming to the table who maybe previously wanted domestic content, but due to just tightness in the market or timing or whatever the reason may be, is now opting for internationally produced cells or internationally produced capacity just to get it as soon as possible? Or is there still, I guess, the preference for domestic content? And I'll leave it there.

Bernerd Raymond Da Santos Avila: No, thank you. I only will say I confirm the comment. Yes, there are customers that are looking at any range of what is called domestic content or what we call U.S. market nondomestic.

Operator: Our next question comes from Ameet Ishwar Thakkar with BMO Capital Markets.

Ameet Ishwar Thakkar: Maybe just one quick one. I think Ricardo was pretty clear that your plan doesn't involve any external capital at this point. But just is that contingent on kind of amending the revolver? I think your leverage test ratio goes to 3.5x in the beginning of 2027. Just any color there, I'd appreciate it. And if you could give us any color on kind of what drove kind of the incremental $174 million of additional nonrefundable deposits for '27 as well.

Ricardo Roizen Gottlieb: Sure. So if we step back, I would say, today, we have a strong liquidity position similar to the previous quarter. Total with all the facilities, we have $855 million. In addition to that, we have built up inventory to $970 million. So what I can tell you today is that as production improves, as Bernerd mentioned, we will be converting that inventory in cash. And we will show the improvement in the liquidity as we move forward. So we are in a solid position today. In terms of the revolver, the revolver is important. The revolver today is not drawn. It's only used for letter of credit.

And what we are doing today is that we are talking with our banks, which are relationship banks, to anticipate any potential issue to amend and extend that facility with time not to have any problem.

Operator: That concludes today's question-and-answer session. I'd like to turn the call back to Chris Shelton for closing remarks.

Chris Shelton: Thanks, everyone, for the time this morning. And please don't hesitate to reach out to me for any follow-up questions you have. I know we had a couple on the call or any others that are top of mind as you go through our disclosures. Thank you, and have a good day.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

Looking for something new to watch this weekend? Don't just sit around in a turkey haze when you can wake up your senses with the pulse-pounding thrillers newly available on Prime Video. Each week, I comb through the streaming service's latest additions to hunt down the suspenseful picks actually worth carving out time for.

November's new-arrivals shelf is still buried under holiday movies, so I dug through the tinsel to find three standout thrillers for your queue. I'll grant that one leans a little more action than pure suspense — an '80s hostage-rescue caper starring Chuck "Walker, Texas Ranger" Norris — but it packs more than enough tension to earn its spot alongside a razor-sharp Cold War mind-bender and a blood-soaked modern thriller about a rogue CIA assassin.

All three are well worth adding to your watchlist before the leftovers run out. Let's get into the three new-to-Prime Video thrillers I'd recommend streaming this week. You'll be glad you didn't just eat and sleep over Thanksgiving weekend.

If you only stream one of my picks this week, make it this one. More than sixty years later, John Frankenheimer's "The Manchurian Candidate" is still one of the best political thrillers, and it feels surprisingly fresh. Frank Sinatra gives one of his finest screen performances as Major Bennett Marco, but it's Angela Lansbury who makes one of cinema's most monstrous mothers years ahead of her turn in "Murder, She Wrote."

During the Korean War, a U.S. Army platoon is captured and brainwashed by Communists, and Sergeant Raymond Shaw (Laurence Harvey) comes home a decorated war hero. He has no memory that he's been reprogrammed as a sleeper assassin, triggered by the sight of a particular playing card. Marco (Sinatra), plagued by the same recurring nightmare as the other survivors, starts investigating, and the conspiracy leads straight to Shaw's domineering mother (Lansbury) and her senator husband (James Gregory) as the culprits.

Watch "The Manchurian Candidate" on Prime Video now

I'm not going to sugarcoat it: "Delta Force" is prime cheese, the kind of action thriller where Chuck Norris mows down terrorists from a rocket-launching motorcycle. It's got an absurd bench of old-school talent, led by Lee Marvin in his final film role as the gravel-voiced Colonel Nick Alexander, and it'll keep you on the edge of your seat.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Loosely inspired by the 1985 hijacking of TWA Flight 847, the film follows an elite U.S. commando unit sent in after Lebanese militants seize a passenger jet and reroute it to Beirut. Norris plays Major Scott McCoy, who's pulled back into service to rescue the hostages. If you want to check out a gem with plenty of explosions and unexpected twists, this is one of the best in Norris's early catalogue.

Not to be confused with the Vince Vaughn–Owen Wilson comedy, this 2026 "Internship" is an R-rated action thriller with a nasty streak. It follows a CIA-trained killer, raised from childhood in a secret program that recruited kids under the cover of an "internship," who sets out to burn the agency down.

Lizzy Greene takes the lead role as Renee, the assassin who rallies her fellow "interns" into a bloody uprising against the organization that stole their childhoods, forcing the CIA to answer with equally lethal force. Megan Boone ("The Blacklist") and Sullivan Stapleton ("Blindspot") round out the ensemble.

#3091. Things 3.25 update brings new touch features to the MacBook Pro

Cultured Code is bringing swipe gestures to Things on Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro. Version 3.25 builds on the task manager’s basic touch support so you can schedule a to-do with a swipe or select several tasks with two fingers and drag them all at once.

Say you’re going through your Today list and want to put something off until tomorrow. Swipe right on the to-do to open the date picker. Open it by touch and you’ll see taller rows that make dates easier to tap. Custom menus get the same treatment.

Swiping left selects a to-do. Swipe left again to deselect it. For a longer list, swipe up or down with two fingers to select several items at once. Then touch and hold any selected item to pick up the whole group, even if some of those tasks are offscreen. You can also drag individual to-dos and headings.

A single tap selects a to-do, and a second tap expands it. Double-tapping works too. Inside a to-do, checklist items are easier to reorder by touch. You can also cancel a to-do or checklist item by pressing and holding its checkbox.

Cultured Code has also made the sidebar easier to resize with a finger and given buttons throughout the Mac app larger tap targets.

The update follows Siri AI and Spotlight integration in Things 3.24 and more flexible scheduling for repeating to-dos in Things 3.23. You can find Things for Mac on the Mac App Store.

#3090. Leaks say Apple has four special edition products launching next week in red

Apple has had a busy fall for new products, but leaks indicate next week will bring another launch, with special edition Product(RED) versions of AirPods Max 2, HomePod mini 2, and more coming.

Earlier this week Mark Gurman at Bloomberg reported that Apple is preparing to continue its Product(RED) partnership with two special edition products: AirPods Max 2 (now only $419) and HomePod mini 2.

The launch is expected for Tuesday, December 1, which is World AIDS Day.

In follow-up posts, Gurman says there are red versions of the Apple Watch Sport Band and Wrist Strap for AirPods and iPhone coming too. He also said Apple Stores have already begun receiving “lots of inventory.”

So we’re expecting at least four Product(RED) debuts on December 1:

The Black Friday deals have arrived, and although it's only Tuesday, there are already plenty of great discounts on the best action cameras, 360 cameras and vlogging cameras.

I'm Pete, reviews editor here at Tom's Guide and the man in charge of our camera coverage. I test all action and 360 cameras, so I have to keep an eye on pricing throughout the year. This is usually the best time of the year to pick up a deal on action cameras and other gear. After all, it's never too early to start planning out your content for next year!

My favorite deal so far is on, well, my favorite action camera. The DJI Osmo Action 6 is the best action camera around, and is now $70 off at Amazon. This is the latest DJI flagship, so it's the first time I've seen this camera discounted in the U.S., and $70 is nothing to sniff at.

The biggest discount, and arguably best deal around right now, is on the GoPro MAX2 360 camera, which is down 45% from its $499 MSRP to just $274 at Amazon. Crazy value, in all honesty. But there's plenty more where that came from, including vlogging cameras like the DJI Osmo Pocket 3 at its lowest ever U.S. price of $373 at Amazon.

I'm only including deals that are actually good. I'm discounting any products (ahem, Insta360 X3, ahem) whose prices have been deliberately hiked before the sales events to make it look like a good deal. Read on for genuinely good savings!

Don't be fooled by the $299 MSRP — this camera usually sits around the $220. However, at $179, the DJI Osmo Action 4 still just hit its lowest price in the U.S., so there's never been a better time to pick up this little camera. It might be a couple of years old, but if you need professional-looking 4K video for YouTube, it's still plenty capable enough.

I'm shocked at this one. The GoPro MAX2 is the latest 360 camera from GoPro and a serious contender against the Insta360 X5 and X6, and Osmo 360 II. The fact it's second place in price order on this list is therefore pretty wild. If you want the flexibility of 8K 360 footage, I'm pretty sure this deal right here is the cheapest way there's ever been to get that.

The X4 Air is the revamped X4 — the first 8K 360 camera. The X4 Air packs some choice updates, namely to its audio (featuring the X5's wind guard) and stripped down weight. It's dropped to $299 before, but never lower, and tends to sit at the $399 MSRP outside of sales events. This is already a good deal, but I'd maybe wait to see if it drops a little further as Black Friday itself approaches.

DJI has faced an uphill struggle in the U.S. recently, thanks to its ongoing feud with the government and trade tariffs affecting its pricing. As such, the newer Pocket 4 models are borderline outrageously priced in the U.S. The DJI Osmo Pocket 3 is still a brilliant choice for content creators though, offering 4K gimbal-stabilized video. This is actually the lowest we've seen it drop (the previous low being $378).

The DJI Osmo Action 6 is the latest and greatest flagship action camera. It's my top pick for action cameras generally, and it's the camera I use personally. It offers the best blend of high-res capture, stabilization, battery life and waterproofing. I gave the Insta360 X5 our full five stars when I reviewed it in 2025. And it was well deserved. This isn't a huge discount, which is to be expected given how new this camera is, but it's still the lowest price we've yet seen the X6 drop.

#3088. CarPlay Ultra coming to these cars, according to Apple

Last year, Apple officially announced CarPlay Ultra, the next-generation version of CarPlay that it first teased way back at WWDC 2022.

CarPlay Ultra first launched for Aston Martin owners in the United States and Canada. What about other automakers? Here’s what we know.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

Updated November 24, 2026: Latest on Hyundai, more.

In December 2023, Apple said that Porsche and Aston Martin would be the first automakers to support next-generation CarPlay starting in 2024. That deadline came and went, and Apple confirmed in January that next-gen CarPlay had been delayed but was still in development.

Apple doesn’t offer a timeline on when CarPlay Ultra will actually be available through any other brand beyond Aston Martin. The company also does not have a dedicated list of automakers that have signed on to support CarPlay Ultra listed on its website.

When Apple announced the next-generation version of CarPlay at WWDC 2022, however, it stated that several brands had committed to supporting the platform. In May of last year, Apple touted that three new partners had signed on: Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis.

However, several brands have also dropped their plans to support CarPlay Ultra. Mercedes-Benz was originally on Apple’s list, but abandoned its plans to support next-generation CarPlay in 2024. According to the Financial Times, Audi, Volvo, Polestar, and Renault have also decided against supporting CarPlay Ultra, despite originally being touted as partners by Apple.

With all of that said, here is the full list of automakers who plan to eventually support CarPlay Ultra, as of April 2026.

What do we know beyond this list? Not a whole lot. Interestingly, Top Gear reported that the Hyundai IONIQ 3 EV would support CarPlay Ultra. Hyundai announced the IONIQ 3 in April, but has not commented on whether the vehicle will support CarPlay Ultra as rumors suggested.

Mark Gurman at Bloomberg has also reported CarPlay Ultra will launch for “least one major new Hyundai/Kia model in the second half of this year.”

While Apple has touted Ford as a partner for CarPlay Ultra, the automaker recently signaled it’s not too impressed with the first version of a platform.

In a recent interview, Ford CEO Jim Farley was asked whether the company is “considering” CarPlay Ultra support. Here’s what he said:

“We are. We don’t like the execution in round 1 of Ultra, but we’re very committed to Apple. I’ve talked to Tim many times about this.”

It’s better than a flat “no,” but perhaps not the enthusiasm Ford drivers might have hoped to hear.

The question at this point is whether any other automakers have ditched CarPlay Ultra. Ideally, Apple will provide a full list sooner rather than later, but in the meantime, this is the only information we have.

Learn more about everything new with CarPlay Ultra in our dedicated coverage.

#3087. With Jensen Huang Back as CEO, Is It More Likely That Nvidia Will Rebound to $243.37 or Plummet to $100?

Nvidia stock is dirt cheap, but there are serious risks to the investment thesis.

By Daniel Foelber – Nov 24, 2026 at 2:29PM EST

Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%) was in free fall. As of market close on Nov. 20, the stock was down 42% in one month in response to CEO Jensen Huang sending an email to employees saying he was unfaithful to his wife, and news of additional reported affairs, one of which was allegedly with Alice Huang, who is being investigated by U.S. officials for being a Chinese spy. Nvidia is restricted from selling its high-end products in China. If Huang was involved in getting chips to China through backdoor channels, such as Singapore markets, that could have major repercussions for Nvidia.

Over just four days, Huang went from being one of the longest-tenured CEOs in Silicon Valley to resigning. On Nvidia's Nov. 17 earnings call, Nvidia said it had no intention of reinstating Huang as CEO. He had not been charged with any crime.

On Nov. 23, everything changed. Nvidia published a press release before the market opened, announcing Huang's reinstatement following a unanimous vote by the board. In the press release, Nvidia said that "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."

Nvidia closed at $165.05 per share on Nov. 23, up 31.5% and marking the largest single-day market cap gain by any company in history.

Here's the case for why the growth stock could rebound past its prior all-time high of $243.37 per share, or fall further to $100 a share.

The simplest reason Nvidia stock deserves to blow past its previous all-time high is that the company's results are nothing short of exceptional. Nvidia's Nov. 17 earnings report for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 featured blowout numbers, including $115.8 billion in revenue -- a 103% increase from a year ago. Nvidia has unbelievable pricing power, with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) gross margin of 74.8%.

Nvidia continues to prove the doubters wrong by growing its top line rapidly despite its size. Part of the reason is that its key customers, hyperscalers and leading artificial intelligence (AI) companies, continue to ramp spending to accelerate compute capacity.

Nvidia also has a long runway for growth because it just began shipping products under its Vera Rubin platform in August. On the Nov. 17 earnings call, Nvidia said that Rubin generated nearly $20 billion in first-quarter production shipments compared to $107.6 billion in total data center revenue. With Rubin orders piling up, Nvidia expects fiscal 2028 revenue to be 75% higher than fiscal 2027.

That kind of growth rate, paired with Nvidia's high margins, should allow Nvidia to surpass Alphabet (GOOG -1.05%) (GOOGL -1.08%) as the world's most profitable company within the next year.

Because Nvidia's earnings are growing quickly and its stock price has fallen, Nvidia's valuation has gone from compelling to dirt cheap. The semiconductor stock now trades at just 17.7 times trailing 12-month earnings -- which is hard to fathom for an industry-leading high-margin company growing at a breakneck rate. And it's worth mentioning that Nvidia was already cheap even before the Huang drama unfolded.

Based on Nvidia's growth rate and market positioning, Nvidia is arguably worth more than double what it costs today. Especially when slower-growing tech stocks like Microsoft (MSFT +0.74%) are priced at 25.7 times earnings.

Nvidia's sell-off is a painful but timely lesson on why the market cares more about where a company could be headed than where it has been. The reason Nvidia sold off had nothing to do with its results or next fiscal year's guidance. Rather, it was due to fears of a potential slowdown in artificial intelligence spending, paired with the fallout from Huang's abrupt exit.

As mentioned, Nvidia was already cheap even before Huang resigned because some investors were concerned that hyperscalers would eventually pull back on AI infrastructure spending to give their cash flows time to recover. After all, Alphabet, Amazon (AMZN -1.21%), and Meta Platforms (META -1.30%) went from cash cows to generating negative free cash flow due to record capital expenditures. Even so, Nvidia was well prepared to endure a slowdown.

Nvidia's rack-scale Vera Rubin offering for AI data centers consists of more than just graphics processing units; it also includes central processing units and interconnects. Controlling a larger share of the data center market makes Nvidia less dependent on one-off chip sales. It is well positioned to capture recurring revenue as customers upgrade their hardware to the latest tech. And Nvidia's CUDA computing platform plays an integral role in GPU programming.

Nvidia was also working to diversify its customer base beyond hyperscalers by partnering with financial institutions to make compute more accessible for enterprises and AI start-ups. A $500 billion AI infrastructure financing plan announced between Nvidia and six financial institutions would effectively turn AI infrastructure into an investable asset class, with Nvidia's hardware and ecosystem at the center.

So even if there were a slowdown in AI spending, Nvidia's growing addressable market in data centers, paired with its expanding customer base, would provide a wide moat.

Without Huang, much of Nvidia's moat was called into question. There was a very real chance the $500 billion financing deal would fall through, as no firm contracts were signed, only memorandums of understanding. But with Huang back in the driver's seat, these mega deals look a lot more likely to stay intact.

Another concern had been Nvidia's margins. A major differentiating factor for Nvidia has been its pricing power. Huang had been adamant about not giving out deals or discounts based on the competition. Rather, his mission was to deliver the most cost-effective and efficient compute, which would naturally command a high price because it would pay off for customers in the long run. If Nvidia hired new management that focused on the short term by maximizing sales, some of its pricing power may have eroded.

Nvidia's growth rate has been heavily dependent on massive leaps in its architectures. Vera Rubin was a monumental leap from Blackwell, which was a massive jump from Hopper. Because progress has been swift and substantial, it's in the best interests of Nvidia's customers to pay a premium for the latest tech. If the architecture after Rubin doesn't deliver a large enough performance jump, it could drastically lower Nvidia's growth rate.

Plus, there are intense internal challenges at Nvidia, including the fact that Huang positioned the company with a flat organizational structure in which dozens of leaders reported directly to him. Without Nvidia's flexibility and Huang's leadership, the company would risk moving more slowly and losing valuable talent, especially if its stock price remains depressed, which reduces the appeal of stock-based compensation.

With Huang back as CEO, some investors may wonder why these risks are worth discussing at all. But in just a week and a half, Huang resigned and was then brought back despite the board saying they wouldn't even consider him on the Nov. 17 earnings call.

Huang's role as CEO is less secure than in the past. And with no succession plan, Nvidia still faces a very real key-person risk that should be top of mind for investors. There's also the risk that external and internal investigations uncover facts that force Nvidia to push Huang out yet again. Until these investigations provide conclusive evidence, investors can't rule out these risks, especially given the severity they impose on the long-term investment thesis.

I don't think Nvidia will reach $100, but I see a long road ahead before Nvidia can make all-time highs.

For now, I think Nvidia stock is worth holding, but it's not the screaming buy its valuation implies. With ongoing investigations and a slew of governance concerns, Nvidia's investment thesis remains damaged, but it is no longer broken.

#3081. Is Microsoft the Best Big Tech Stock to Buy Now?

Microsoft's positive cash flow is a big deal for the market.

By Keithen Drury – Nov 24, 2026 at 2:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Microsoft ›

There has been a lot of talk surrounding Nvidia over the past few days, and rightfully so, amid serious allegations at the CEO level and potential company misconduct in the getting around U.S. export controls. Other companies have also been in the news such as Anthropic (ANT -6.54%) and its blockbuster initial public offering.

However, one that has flown under the radar is Microsoft (MSFT +0.74%). When the market has a bearish mindset, staying under the radar as a company is normally a good idea, but a company can only keep so much of a low profile when it's the second-largest in the world by market capitalization.

But is Microsoft a good buy today? Or should the market be worried about it too? After all, it hit a fresh all-time high just days ago.

The best companies to compare Microsoft to are Alphabet (GOOG -1.05%) (GOOGL -1.08%) and Amazon (AMZN -1.21%). These two may not seem like great comparisons on the surface, but they are all approaching AI in a similar manner: Investing in outside companies and building out computing power. All three of these companies have significant investments in AI labs to give them exposure to the companies pioneering AI technology.

While Alphabet and Amazon own a massive amount of Anthropic (about 30% combined), Microsoft owns nearly the same amount of OpenAI, its primary competitor. While OpenAI isn't public yet, it will likely become so in the near future, and is likely keeping an eye on how successful Anthropic is on the public markets. So, Microsoft's payday for its OpenAI investment will need to wait, which may not be a bad thing.

The other area these three compete heavily in is cloud computing. AI firms don't have the resources to build out an extensive data center network to power their workloads. So, they choose to rent it from providers like Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Google Cloud. All three companies have seen their backlog explode from massive AI computing demand, and the backlog totals are in the hundreds of billions for each company. As a result, each company is spending heavily to build out its computing capacity.

However, Microsoft is being less aggressive, which the market respects. This year, both Amazon and Alphabet plan to spend at least $200 billion on data center capital expenditures. Microsoft only plans to spend $170 billion. While this may sound like it's falling behind, the reality is that Microsoft isn't stretching itself thin.

MSFT Free Cash Flow (Quarterly) data by YCharts

Microsoft has maintained strong free cash flow, meaning that it's still sending cash to the bottom line. Amazon and Alphabet have dipped into negative territory, meaning they are either burning through cash reserves to fund operations or taking out loans. Both of these two activities aren't favorable in the market's eyes. This could lead to Microsoft being viewed more favorably, but it could cost it some market share in the end if it isn't aggressive enough.

The market normally takes a short-term view for situations like this, which is why Microsoft's stock is viewed favorably. But does that make it a smart buy now?

Microsoft is already in its fiscal 2027, ending June 30. So comparing forward earnings price tags is a bit difficult to its peers. But at 25 times forward earnings, Microsoft is neither expensive nor cheap.

Amazon is nearly in line with Microsoft's valuation at 24.5 times fiscal 2027 earnings estimates, but Alphabet is far cheaper at 18 times next year's earnings.

GOOG PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

That's a big mismatch, and could point to Alphabet being a smarter buy than Microsoft, especially if it can steal some of its cloud computing market share.

Microsoft is staying conservative in its spending. We'll see if it costs them, but as of right now, I'd say Microsoft is an OK stock to buy. It will likely beat the market, but won't do it by much due to its current price tag.

#3080. Skip the knockoffs: Real PITAKA aramid fiber cases start at $18.99 this Black Friday

Scroll through Amazon for five minutes and you’ll find dozens of $10–20 cases that look, through a thumbnail, almost identical to $50+ aramid fiber ones. Same dark weave, same slim profile, same pitch.

Once you actually snap one onto a phone, the differences are obvious. You handle your phone for hours every day, so rough seams around the charging port, awkward cutouts, low-quality materials will make you regret your purchase instantly. With PITAKA’s Black Friday sale taking up to 30% off selected cases, it’s worth breaking down what actually separates a real aramid case from a cheap lookalike, why you should spent the extra money on PITAKA’s high-quality cases.

Plenty of budget cases get the woven look by printing a pattern onto plain plastic. If you’re looking for that style, go for it, but it won’t behave like woven aramid fiber, which lets a case stay rigid and thin without adding much weight.

Even genuine aramid cases aren’t all made the same way. The weave, resin, thickness, and surface finish all change how a case feels in use. PITAKA uses woven aramid fiber in two main weights: 600D and 1500D. Those numbers measure yarn density; the finer 600D weave feels a bit smoother and produces a slightly thinner shell than 1500D. Whatever case you choose, look past the word “premium” and check whether the maker actually spells out what the case is made of.

Most aramid cases stick to plain black and gray. PITAKA’s Fusion Weaving method blends colored fibers and multiple weave styles directly into the shell instead of printing a graphic on the outside. PITAKA says the process requires tight control over fabric tension and how fibers cross between layers. In practice, it means you can pick something colorful like the Sunset colorway without giving up the feel of woven fiber, or stick with classic Black & Grey if you prefer a quieter look.

Online listings spend almost all their time showing off the back of a case, even though your fingers spend just as much time on the sides, buttons, and bottom edge. An awkward camera cutout makes quick shots annoying, a tight port opening fights bulkier charging cables, and sharp edges dig into your hand on a long call.

Rather than selling one shell in ten colors, PITAKA splits its lineup into three builds:

If you use a magnetic charger, wallet, or grip, how the magnets are built into the case matters just as much as the outer material. Sticking a separate magnet ring inside a shell usually adds extra layers and thickness.

PITAKA’s Amber Magnet Film process bonds coated magnets directly with the aramid fiber and resin under heat and pressure. That keeps the magnets enclosed without bulking up the case, which is the kind of detail you won’t spot in a photo but will notice in your pocket.

Spending more on a case doesn’t guarantee it’s better, and plenty of $20 cases are completely fine. Genuine aramid fiber by itself doesn’t guarantee better drop protection either. A thin shell like Edge is made for people who hate bulky cases. If drop protection is your main concern, look at a cushioned option like Cairn or Summa, and compare actual edge coverage and model-specific testing instead of judging by price or material alone.

What you’re really paying for with a higher-end aramid case is how it feels and fits every time you pick up your phone.

If you already want a thinner, better-finished case, Black Friday takes some of the sting out of the price. PITAKA’s Amazon offers run November 19–30, with discounts varying by device and colorway:

Buying directly from the PITAKA official website? Code PTKPR12 takes an extra 5% off from November 10 through December 31. It’s separate from the Amazon sale, so double-check eligible products and your final total at checkout.
