#2998. Micron vs. Sandisk: Which AI Memory Stock Is the Better Buy?

Both of these AI memory stocks still have triple-digit returns in 2026 despite selloffs since this summer.

By Dave Kovaleski – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:05PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Micron Technology ›

It has been a wild ride in 2026 for two leading memory chip stocks, Micron (MU -11.01%) and Sandisk (SNDK -11.13%).

Both are among Wall Street’s best performers year to date, but their paths to those returns have been extremely volatile.

At its 2026 closing high of $1,213 per share on June 25, Micron was up about 326% year to date. At its split-adjusted closing peak of $291 per share on June 22, Sandisk was up 870%.

Since then, Sandisk has lost 68% of its value, falling to $91 per share. But it's still up 209% from $30 per share at the start of the year. Micron had fallen 51% to $594 per share on Nov. 20, but bounced back on Nov. 23, climbing to $717 per share. It's still up 147% from $285 per share at the start of the year.

So, if you’ve owned shares since before this summer, you're still probably happy with the returns, despite the wild swings. But heading into 2027, which of the two is the better buy?

Both Sandisk and Micron have benefited from the current memory and storage supercycle, which was brought on by the fast advance of artificial intelligence computing. Demand for AI memory and storage has been magnified by the massive amount of AI infrastructure being built by hyperscalers, neoclouds, and others, and, in turn, chipmakers such as Nvidia, Intel, and Advanced Micro Devices.

The demand for chips that can provide quickly accessible memory and storage for the data AI requires and creates has boomed as a result. Because memory chips are essentially a commodity, the companies that manufacture them try to avoid overbuilding their production capacity. In the wake of the rapid surge in demand, they now can't keep up. This has given Micron, Sandisk, and their peers incredible pricing power and huge backlogs of orders.

While Micron and Sandisk have products that do directly compete with each other, their respective cash cow products are in separate areas. Micron's main product is high bandwidth memory (HBM) chips for AI data centers that can provide fast memory for AI processing. It is mostly sold out of HBM through 2027. Sandisk's main products are NAND and solid-state storage drives, which provide long-term data storage for AI computing.

Both memory giants also have long-term contracts with major hyperscalers and customers with commitments through at least 2030.

Sandisk just underwent an 8-for-1 stock split on Nov. 20, which brought its previously lofty share price down to a more accessible $91 per share.

Though both of these stocks have dropped so sharply over the past few months, that was mostly due to factors beyond their business performance. Many investors took profits when the stocks were higher. They were also brought down by broader concerns about whether the enormous levels of spending on AI infrastructure will deliver the return on investment that the bulls promise. The downtrend was likely exacerbated by the U.S. midterm elections, in which voters in many locales made it clear that they want stricter regulatory and government controls around data center development. This has led to concerns that hyperscalers might negotiate down or out of their long-term chip deals.

The Jensen Huang Nvidia situation did not help AI stocks either, although he was just reinstated as CEO on Monday, so we'll see where that leads.

The fact remains that both Sandisk and Micron are vital suppliers in the AI boom, and even if there are more controls on where data centers can go and a greater level of concern for their environmental impact, that won't eliminate the need for AI processing and storage.

Also, both of these stocks are dirt cheap, made even cheaper by the recent sell-off. This is a testament to their massive earnings power. Micron is trading at just 3.4 times 1-year forward earnings. Sandisk is even cheaper with a 1-year forward P/E of 2.5. And both have minuscule 1-year forward price/earnings-to-growth ratios of about 0.05.

I own shares of Micron and will add more at this low valuation, but Sandisk is also a screaming buy.

#2997. The Best Foldable Phones to Give This Holiday Season

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

For the tech enthusiast in your life, a foldable phone could be an interesting alternative to a traditional smartphone. We've rounded up our top picks, from book-style designs to flip phones.

If you’re shopping for someone this holiday season who deserves something a little more special — and you’ve got the budget to spare — a foldable phone can be a unique and practical gift that your loved one will use long after the holidays are over.

After reviewing our fair share of foldable phones, we’ve narrowed down our top three picks for the holidays and the perfect person on your list for each one. Who knows, you might end up caving in and treating yourself to a brand-new device? (You’ve been warned.)

For more mobile gift ideas, from budget-friendly smartphones to wearable devices, be sure to check out the video below.

The iPhone Duo is far from the first foldable phone, but as Apple’s debut into the market, it’s generated plenty of buzz. The Duo’s superpower is its ability to integrate hardware and software, creating a seamless experience across both displays.

The compact, 5.4-inch cover screen is great for sending texts and emails and checking notifications. The more expansive 7.6-inch inner display is ideal for multitasking, watching movies and working. It feels like using a smaller version of an iPad Mini that you can just fold up and toss in your pocket or bag.

The Duo is a great gift for someone who’s said they want a foldable phone, but refused to get one of the long-standing Android options already on the market. At last, Apple has its own offering that lets you stick with iOS. It’s a handy pick for people who often work on their phones and don’t always want to lug around a laptop. It’s also good for anyone who watches a lot of movies and TV shows on their mobile device. Plus, as a phone-tablet hybrid, it’s just fun to use.

The iPhone Duo isn’t perfect. It doesn’t support Face ID, but Apple did recently add an option to unlock the phone using the front camera. This isn’t as secure as Face ID, so you’ll still need to use Touch ID or a passcode for more sensitive functions like using Apple Pay or accessing passwords, and after around 45 minutes of inactivity.

The Duo’s cameras also aren’t as advanced as what you’ll get with the iPhone 18 Pro models, which have larger main-camera sensors and more advanced optical zoom capabilities. There’s also no telephoto camera on the Duo. Still, most people will be happy with the Duo’s 48-megapixel wide and ultrawide rear cameras, as well as the 12-megapixel selfie camera on the cover screen. The FaceTime camera on the inner display is best suited for video calls rather than snapping quality photos.

Multitasking on the Duo is seamless, but it’s not as flexible as it is on other foldable phones. You can only have two apps open side by side, and you can’t readjust them.

Perhaps the biggest downside is the price. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256GB of storage. That’s why it’s a good idea to keep an eye out for any deals that can help lower the price.

For the Android-lover in your life, there’s no better foldable pick than Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8. Like the iPhone Duo, this phone has a passport-size design. (Technically, Samsung beat Apple to the punch, but let’s refrain from the “Who Did It First?” game for now.)

The Z Fold 8 has a 5.5-inch cover screen and a 7.6-inch inner display that’s great for watching videos, working and multitasking with up to three apps, which you can resize to your liking.

It’s also very thin, measuring 9.7mm thick when folded and 4.5mm thick when unfolded. That means it feels similar in thickness to a standard nonfolding phone, even when it’s closed. The Z Fold 8 fits squarely in a palm and easily slides into a pocket – tiny women’s pockets included.

Like the iPhone Duo, the Z Fold 8 doesn’t have a telephoto camera. But the 50-megapixel wide and ultrawide cameras on the back and the 10-megapixel selfie cameras do a solid job.

The Z Fold 8 is also priced on the higher end, starting at $1,900 for 256GB. But its compact, sleek design and versatility help to make up for that sticker shock. Again, it’s a good idea to look out for any deals, especially around the holidays.

Some people prefer flip phones for their nostalgic designs and compact size. Motorola has plenty to choose from, but the best and most affordable pick for most people is the baseline 2026 Razr.

The phone features a classic clamshell design and a spacious 3.6-inch cover screen, making it easy to check notifications, reply to texts, control music or follow navigation without opening the phone. The 6.9-inch inner display feels like using an average nonfolding phone, even if the screen is a little narrower and taller.

For most people, the Razr’s 50-megapixel wide and ultrawide cameras and 32-megapixel selfie camera on the inner display will do the trick. There’s no room for a telephoto camera, but the Razr pulls its weight for more casual photography.

The Razr’s processor isn’t as powerful as what you’ll get on the pricier Razr Plus and Razr Ultra, but as long as you’re not playing intensive games all day, you probably won’t notice the difference.

The Razr’s $800 starting price is significantly lower than the cost of book-style folding devices like the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8. The Razr could be a more appealing option for someone who doesn’t need a phone-tablet hybrid but just wants a phone that’s fun to use and taps into the nostalgia of the original Motorola Razr.

No matter which phone you choose, your lucky recipient will enjoy the holiday spirit long after the season has passed, all while making quite the statement.

#2995. Uber, Nuro and Lucid Begin Fully Driverless Testing With Their Luxury Robotaxi

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The Lucid Gravity robotaxi is one step closer to a commercial launch.

Nearly a year after showcasing their “luxurious” robotaxi at CES, Uber, Nuro and Lucid have started fully driverless testing on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area, the companies said Tuesday.

The partnership, announced in July 2025, combines Uber’s ride-hailing platform, Nuro’s self-driving technology and Lucid’s electric vehicles. Autonomous rides take place aboard the Lucid Gravity robotaxi, which I had the opportunity to see first at a CES showcase in January (in the form of a “production intent design”), and then on the road this summer, with a safety driver behind the wheel.

Now, the partnership is ready to take its next big step, beginning with employee rides “soon,” the companies said. They plan to launch commercial robotaxi operations in the first quarter of 2027 in the San Francisco Bay Area, before expanding to Houston later next year. Lucid will begin manufacturing the first vehicles designed specifically for the commercial launch fleet “in the coming weeks.” Uber plans to deploy around 35,000 Lucid vehicles equipped with the Nuro Driver in the coming years in “dozens” of cities.

“Removing the safety operator from behind the wheel is an important milestone in our partnership with Nuro and Lucid, and a testament to all three partners’ focus on executing against our shared roadmap,” Samarth Kejriwal, Uber’s global head of autonomous mobility, said in a statement. “As we prepare for our first driverless passenger rides in the coming months, we’ll be working closely together to refine our operations, infrastructure and the in-cabin experience to ensure a safer, more comfortable ride.”

Nuro says it’s been conducting “round-the-clock autonomous testing of the Lucid Gravity robotaxi on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area and Houston” since December 2025, with a safety driver in the vehicle who can take over if needed.

In May, Nuro received a California Public Utilities Commission Drivered Pilot Permit, giving the company the green light to conduct pilot testing for an autonomous passenger service with a safety driver. Nuro also received a California Department of Motor Vehicles Driverless Testing Permit in April, allowing it to test self-driving vehicles without a safety driver.

Uber’s partnership with Nuro and Lucid is just one of dozens it has with other AV companies, including Waymo, Zoox, Avride, Wayve and May Mobility. Adding driverless options to an app that’s likely already on someone’s phone could increase their chances of giving the experience a try — despite the trepidation many people have about self-driving vehicles.

The Lucid Gravity robotaxi can seat up to six passengers, unlike rides from Waymo and Zoox that seat up to four. It has plenty of legroom and ample space for luggage in the back. The vehicle’s sensor suite is equipped with cameras, lidar sensors and radars for autonomous navigation.

It’s been a big year for autonomous vehicles, and it appears 2027 will be no different. The rapid expansion of AVs comes amid heightened scrutiny. Last week, the California DMV banned Waymo’s robotaxis from state freeways after a series of high-profile incidents — after which Waymo paused all of its freeway rides. Waymo, the largest player in the AV space, has been involved in a number of other safety incidents as it expands to more cities. Over the years, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has launched investigations into other AV companies, including Zoox and Tesla.

It’s against this landscape — and the full-speed-ahead race toward autonomy — that Nuro, Uber and Lucid will soon publicly debut their own robotaxi.

#2994. Cmb.Tech (CMBT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Strong tanker rates and asset sales shaped the quarter, with ammonia ambitions in focus.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:08PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Cmb.Tech (CMBT +4.22%) reported a quarter of elevated profitability driven by record tanker spot rates and strategic asset sales. Management focused on the transition toward ammonia-powered shipping while maintaining a diversified fleet across dry bulk, container, and offshore energy segments. The company stated its intention to prioritize balance sheet deleveraging and consistent dividend distributions as its heavy capital expenditure cycle approaches completion. Strategic initiatives highlighted during the call included the operational debut of the world's first ammonia-powered iron ore carrier and the expansion of bauxite trade demand.

Alexander Saverys: Good afternoon, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Cmb.Tech's earnings conference call for the third quarter of 2026. My name is Alexander Saverys. I'm joined by my colleagues, Ludovic Saverys, Joris Daman and Enya Derkinderen. I will hand the floor to our CFO, Ludovic, for the financials and the highlights.

Ludovic Saverys: Thanks, Alex, and good afternoon, good morning, everybody. We will start with an overview of the company again. We're a leading diversified maritime group. We have roughly $12 billion worth of maritime assets. On the bottom, you can see that we have roughly more than half exposure on dry bulk, still meaningful exposure on crude tankers with $3 billion and then small divisions, which are containers, chemical tankers and offshore energy.

If we zoom in into the results of the third quarter, we made a profit of $374 million, which included a capital gain of the sale of 2 vessels of roughly $100 million, which is the third quarter in a row that we match those net profit numbers, which we're very proud of. On the EBITDA side, it is also the third quarter that we have an EBITDA above $550 million. The liquidity of the company stands at $561 million. The Board has proposed to pay a dividend of $0.65, which we'll discuss later on. I'm happy to say that our equity on total assets has shot up in the last quarter to 58%. Again, the highlights.

Financially, in our company, we continue to delever the balance sheet. We continue to pay dividends and strengthen the balance sheet. It is driven by strong operations from our various shipping divisions, but as well a well-timed S&P, so sales and purchase, which is part of our business strategy. If I zoom in on the elements we haven't covered, our contract backlog still sits at $3.1 billion. We added a new building on the MPASV, which is the energy -- the offshore energy division with a delivery in 2029.

Our distribution of $0.65, which is roughly 50% of our net profits, including capital gains will be, again, paid in a different portion, an interim dividend of $0.21, which will be subject to withholding tax. And happy to say that we've been able to use $0.44, so roughly more than 2/3 will be paid without withholding tax. We took delivery of 4 newbuildings, Alex will go through the various ones later in the company, but one Newcastlemax Mineral Europa, which is a fantastic ship, the CSOV Windcat Antwerpen and 2 CTVs. On the right side, you can see that we have continued to capitalize on the very high values, asset values in tankers.

In Q3, we sold 2 Suezmaxes with a capital gain of $100 million, and in Q4 -- and sorry, Q3 was it, in Q4, we have locked in already roughly $190 million of capital gains on the sale of the Donoussa, the Bristol and Stella, which are Suezmaxes. If we look on the slides, what we try to show here, if you take any 15-year-old ship throughout the last 10 years, you can see that a VLCC was worth $46 million whereas today, the market is $165 million. That's a whopping more than 250% increase on the 10-year average. And we've shown this for the varied asset classes that we are operating in.

It's fair to say that on tankers, these are exceptional times, which we've been able to use to sell 9 VLCCs and 5 Suezmaxes within the year for over $670 million of combined capital gains. The operational free cash flow from the company is very strong. On this slide, we've shown what 2027 would look like. If on the bottom right, if you look on the green spot rates for our ships. As an example, the VLCCs at $122,000. Suezmax is at $77,000 and so for and so on. We would generate $722 million of free cash flow.

This is after the CapEx being paid, which gives us plenty of cash to be used to further pay dividends, invest in further newbuildings or delever the balance sheet. If one would -- and 10% on the spot rate or 20%, you can see that we get to roughly $900 million of free cash flow in a plus 10% scenario and more than $1 billion if we add 20% to the spot rates. The CapEx program, which, I would say, 2 years ago, stood over $3 billion today and the month of October is $840 million. This will reduce, as you can see, per quarter, roughly to $660 million by the end of the year.

And then next year, which is 2027, the last year of heavy CapEx payments of roughly $400 million in 2027. All that CapEx has been funded. There's $320 million for '27, for instance, that has been funded by committed financing at very attractive margins, and there is $80 million that we will use from operational cash flow or sale of assets. That comes to the end of my financial presentation. I'll hand the floor to Alex for a market update.

Alexander Saverys: Thank you very much. I want to give you a market update of the 5 segments in which we operate. As always, an overview sheet of where we stand on supply/demand in all the different segments we operate in. Starting with dry bulk. We see green numbers on the demand side in tonne-mile iron ore, bauxite, grains and coal, so very supportive demand side environment, specifically on the tonne-mile. Order book to fleet. As in every segment, the order book has grown, be it that in dry bulk, it is still at relatively low historical levels. We are at 19% order book-to-fleet in Capes, 14% in Panamaxes. The fleet has grown this year.

Capes have grown by about 2.5%, Panamaxes by close to 6%. That growth will accelerate in Capes, will slow down a little bit in Panamaxes. But we see a fleet growth next year of 5.5% to 6%, for instance, in Capesizes. It is aging. That is a general topic in all shipping segments. There's very little scrapping going on because all markets have been good to very good. But as you can see, close to half of the Capes is nearing the age of 15 years or older, 1/3 of the Panamaxes, which gives us a lot of scrapping potential going forward. All in all, we believe that the balance on dry bulk is positive.

Tankers, we will zoom in, in a minute on the wonderful world of tankers this year and specifically in the third quarter. It's a very mixed scene when you look at the headline numbers, and for instance, on tonne-mile, you can see that we actually have a reduction in tonne-mile. On the contrary, the tonne-days have added a lot of inefficiencies to it. So the actual demand was much, much higher on face value, but I'll speak about that in a minute. For next year, we see a demand forecasted a tonne-mile of plus 7%, so very radical numbers there. When we look at the oil demand, there was a reduction this year of about 2.5 million barrels per day.

The IEA is expecting that to rebound next year with plus 2 million barrels. The order book on tankers, we should talk about that. It is the reason why we are in the medium term turning cautious on that market, it has grown tremendously. We are now at 33% for Vs and 30% for Suezmaxes. The fleet growth on VLCCs and Suezmaxes is accelerating. This year, we're going to add 4% of capacity in Vs, 7% on Suezmaxes, but next year, both will go up by 7% and 9%, respectively. The fleet is aging. As I said, like in all segments, 20% of VLCCs and 20% of Suezmaxes are 20 years or older.

But all in all, even though the current market is definitely positive, very positive even with the big order book coming, we want to sound a word of caution. Containers have been surprising to the upside this year. Demand in TEU-mile has held up very well. We see that the order book has continued to grow. We are now at 44% of all the sizes, order book to fleet. The Red Sea rerouting has gone down a bit, so more vessels are passing through the Red Sea. This year's fleet growth was around 5%. Next year, we think that will go to close to 10%. We have been cautious on containers for a while.

As you know, we don't have any spot exposure, but in general, that market eventually should correct even though 2026 and 2025 has definitely surprised to the upside thanks to all the inefficiencies. On the chemical tankers, the order book is bothering us a little bit. We are standing at 24% of order book to fleet. This year, a big growth, 8% of extra capacity coming on stream, another 8% expected next year. When we look at the tonne-mile growth, we see that there has been a reduction expecting to rebound next year.

Chemical tanker market, of course, closely linked to the product tanker markets, so we are seeing some of the same dynamics that we have seen in the product tanker market. But all in all, on the balance, we are a little bit cautious on chemicals and then ending with the offshore energy. Expected capacity on offshore wind by 2035 should triple. That bodes very well for everything that is offshore supply and offshore wind vessels. The order book for CSOV vessels stands at 31 units. We believe that can be absorbed by all the new projects coming on stream in the following years and the same goes for the CTVs.

On offshore energy, we are positive, not only for the wind, but also for demand on oil and gas. Let's zoom in on a couple of hot topics in our segments. On the dry bulk, the fleet on the water, 41 Newcs, 37 Capes and 30 Kamsarmaxes and Panamaxes. In Q3, we achieved rates of $43,000 for the Newcs, $35,000 for the Capes and $20,000 for the Panamaxes. Very good profit-making rates. It was a good quarter. Definitely, the month of September was particularly strong in Capesizes. Different indicators, some negative, some positive. But in balance, the dry bulk market is very healthy from a supply-demand point of view.

The order book, as already mentioned, stands at the lowest of all the other segments is, of course, has increased since the beginning of the year. For the time being, we believe this is manageable. When we look at the dry bulk market, we need to make a distinction between the volume growth. Overall, year-to-date, we've added 50 million tonnes of volume to the dry bulk market, but also on the tonne-mile growth. The volume that has been moved has actually come from further away, and so the tonne-mile growth has been more important than the volume growth. That goes both for the Capesize typical commodities like bauxite, iron ore and a little bit of coal.

As for the Panamax commodities, coal, grain, a little bit of iron ore and a little bit of bauxite. I'm very lucky to have a fantastic colleague, Joris Daman, sitting in this room who every time highlights a hot topic in our different markets. We have already spoken to you about the Simandou iron ore capacity coming on stream and what the impact could be on Capes. Today, we want to zoom in a little bit on Guinea's bauxite loadings. We have some very interesting data to share with you on the following slides.

The first slide here shows you the export of bauxite and the import of bauxite, and the takeaways there are that about 3/4 of exported bauxite on ships is coming out of Guinea. On the import side, close to 90% of the import goes to China, so China and Guinea are crucial for that trade. When you look at the export volume growth over the last 3, 4 years. You can see that we are having a double digit -- actually mid-double-digit numbers and growth quarter after quarter, so we see that these volumes are really increasing year after year. And what is driving it?

Now there's a lot of different drivers, but what we wanted to do today is zoom in specifically on new energy vehicles, like electric cars, electric trucks or alternative energy trucks. What we see is that between 2018 and last year in 2025, the content of aluminum has increased in these type of vehicles, and it's expected to increase further until 2030 and beyond. But the first point here is what we're making is that the aluminum intensity in these new vehicles is increasing. At the same time, the new energy vehicles are growing 70% of passenger cars and 40% of commercial vehicles by 2030 should be new energy vehicles or electric vehicles.

That will add 8 million tons of aluminum demand, so only that specific segment that needs aluminum. As we get into bauxite, it means an extra demand of more than 20 million tons, and most of that extra demand will have to be imported to China. Of course, I have to put a little disclaimer here. Alexander Saverys: Yes. Frode, so a couple of things on selling tankers. You see it in the profit numbers, but also strategically we want to remain invested in crude oil tankers. The question then is how do we benefit from the market in the most optimal way? Frode Morkedal: Okay. That makes sense. I guess, how do you see capital allocation, let's say, priorities in 2027, right? Ludovic Saverys: I'll take that one, Alex. I think we've come a long way because as Alex mentioned, we're selling some assets, but I think we've invested dramatically in the last 3 years, often with the leverage buyouts. And so first, it was important as management and the Board to be able to quickly absorb those leverage buyouts, which I think we've successfully done. The newbuild program was important to us to have modern ships, fuel efficient ships at a inexpensive price when we order them. And now they're all delivering in the hot markets. So on that side, we've decided to reinstate the dividend because we could.

The operational cash flow was good enough, I think, the third quarter in a row to pay dividends, and we're going to continue to do that at what we see. Nevertheless, we still have, at the end of the year, $4.4 billion in debt, still $600 million plus in newbuilds on to continue to delever. And so for now, we continue to do dividends, delever and continue the CapEx. Ludovic Saverys: Yes. For the moment, yes.

Kristoffer Skeie: Yes. Understood, loud and clear. And on that note, you talked about potential acquisition or growth opportunities. Obviously, you're most bullish on dry bulk. Enya Derkinderen: The next person is Climent Molins.

Climent Molins: You made a compelling case for the rising share of EVs leading to higher bauxite demand going forward. But I wanted to ask about iron ore. Demand has been somewhat muted recently in China, and to what extent do you expect the lower price environment to lead to lower domestic production? Alexander Saverys: Yes. Thank you, Climent. So on iron ore, indeed, volumes have been underwhelming. Our demand has not been as high as what people might expect. I think what you need to look at is the domestic Chinese production is coming off. Iron ore prices have corrected as well a little bit, so expensive iron ore is being priced out of the market and is being replaced in general by longer haul iron ore. Simandou is a good example, but there are, of course, others, Vale in Brazil is expanding its capacity as well a little bit. We need to look at the headline number of the total iron ore produced and consumed every year but also where it's coming from.

And on the tonne-mile side, definitely, it's been supportive even though the volume has not really grown. The demand drivers for iron ore, you know that in the past, everybody was always focused on Chinese real estate. As you know, that is still a very difficult environment. We believe that China has a lot of external export potential on steel and that there are still enough projects that are supporting the steel consumption and hence steel production in China.

Climent Molins: Makes sense. I also wanted to follow up on Frode's capital allocation question. You've made a clear case for continued dividends. But at what point do you shift towards share repurchases given your discounted valuation?

Ludovic Saverys: That's a good question, Climent. Share buybacks are part of the distribution to shareholders. That's full stop. I think everybody knows it. The success of sustained share buybacks just in looking at shipping companies haven't always been a success. For now, we prefer delevering and dividends with strong cash flow that we have. I think we have come a long way to have a nice liquid stock. And at this stage and moment in time, I think we prefer indeed to have dividends and freeing up the capacity on the balance sheet to look at opportunities.

Climent Molins: All right. I mean the repurchases you did after the initial merger were outstanding, especially in hindsight, but we'll see. And then final question for me. Could you talk a bit about the logistics involved in bunkering the Mineral Europa with ammonia? Do you see any opportunities to invest further in that supply chain, given the increased visibility you now have?

Alexander Saverys: Yes. So you know we bought 25% in a Chinese ammonia logistics company called Andefu, the logistics to bring the ammonia to our ships, simply said is we transport the ammonia from the factory who our ammonia terminal today, it's in Nanjing. We then bring our bunker barge alongside the terminal. It loads the green ammonia, sails alongside the Yangtze River to Zhoushan, where there is a bunkering location dedicated for ammonia bunkering where our iron ore carriers refuel with ammonia. Now in the future, you talk about extra investments.

We will continue to support our partner in China to build further infrastructure, whether it is on pipelines, for instance, instead of trucking the ammonia, putting it through a pipeline, whether it is in a terminal to store the ammonia, or whether it is to develop further bunker barges because, of course, today, there's only one ammonia bunker barge in the world. Some are being built, but we will, of course, need a lot more to cater for the logistics.

The last point I want to say about that, why are we so adamant that the price of green ammonia on both of our vessels will fall, not only because we believe that the price of producing green ammonia will fall in the next couple of years, but also because we believe that the logistics of bringing the ammonia on board of our ship will go down tremendously. Today, it's still very expensive because we are moving this ammonia in trucks, having to pump it into a terminal, onto a bunker barge and onto our ship.

We believe that we will make this whole system much more efficient in the next couple of years, which will contribute a much lower price of green ammonia on board of our vessels. And I've already said this publicly, latest by 2030, we are expecting diesel parity on green ammonia.

Climent Molins: Well, we'll be on the lookout.

Enya Derkinderen: And we move on to August Klemp.

August Klemp: Two questions. First, the multipurpose support vessel that you took the option for here. Can you talk a bit about how many more options you have when they expire and kind of your thinking around that right now?

Alexander Saverys: Yes. So we signed an initial deal for one ship with 5 options, so we declared the second -- so the first option, so the second ship, we have another 4. And that is all declarable pretty flexibly into next year so we have quite a lot of time to declare. I haven't highlighted the reason why we lifted that option. I mean, first, we cannot disclose the price, but for us, the price was very attractive. The delivery was attractive. We were talking beginning 2029, and it is an asset type, which builds on our existing series of CSOV, it's just bigger. It's 190 passengers versus 150 and 120.

So it gives us the flexibility to operate in oil and gas and in the much larger wind farms, even better than our existing fleet.

August Klemp: Okay. And then the second one, you talked a bit about potentially selling some of the older tanker vessels, but that Euronav, of course, will still remain a core part of the business, so you will obviously then keep quite a lot of modern tankers as well. How are you thinking about time charter opportunities you're seeing right now? Or what are you seeing right now? What can you do and for how long and all that stuff?

Alexander Saverys: Short answer, we haven't seen any time charter opportunity that would have convinced us not to take the incredible spot rates that we have seen over the summer. That's the short answer. Do we continuously look at chartering out and finding some good time charters? Yes, we do. And actually, we have signed some time charters this year. But right now, right now, the balance is either being operating on the spot market or for the older vessels, the much older vessels, trying to sell them.

Enya Derkinderen: Then next, we have Jeffrey De Wolf.

Jeffrey De Wolf: I just have 2 questions. The first one is about the Mineral Europa. So I was wondering if there are any plans to have the emission data independently verified to further boost the capability of the ammonia play.

Alexander Saverys: Yes. So again, short answer, yes. And we have the emission data, first of all, verified on board of the vessel. But we also have the carbon content data being verified by the likes of BV, DNV, Lloyd's Register and other certification and classification societies on the production itself, including the whole transportation and CO2 emissions during transportation. It's early days, Jeffrey. So as and when we can share some more data, we will definitely do so. But yes, we are independently verifying both the emissions on board of the ship and the carbon content of the fuel, basically well-to-wake, so bringing it to the ship and then consuming it on board.

Jeffrey De Wolf: Any expectation regarding the timing? Or it's not possible to say?

Alexander Saverys: Well, it's not possible to say. Look, we are -- we just finalized our first round trip to Australia where we have been testing all the modes, switching back to diesel, back to ammonia back to diesel again. So once we will have more vessels coming because, of course, this -- in the next couple of months, more ships delivering, we'll have a more comprehensive data set. And I want to make sure the data is correct before we share it.

Jeffrey De Wolf: Sure. The second question is a bit generic. It's regarding the IMO meetings, if you can give an update or updated expectations of the outcome.

Alexander Saverys: I cannot, unfortunately, give you an update because I'm not there. I can tell you what I hope and what I think is going to happen. Let me first start with something I've mentioned to many people before. For us, a decision in the IMO to put limitations on CO2 emissions would definitely be a positive. We're not going to lie about it. This will definitely boost our strategy and create extra momentum for what we are doing.

This being said, we took the decision to invest in ammonia ships without having to wait for the IMO or without counting on the IMO, so we believe that even without an IMO regulation, there is still a very good business case to have green ammonia onboard of our ships, to have the optionality to burn either diesel or ammonia. Now what I think will happen, and this will be no surprise, and I think you will probably agree with me is that we will see the same dynamics as we saw at COP being that the United States, together with some fossil fuel producing countries, will try everything to block a compromise, a decision or a solution.

I'm of course, very hopeful that it will be the contrary, but I think we have to be realistic. Now this being said, I do not think that a failure of finding a compromise or a solution at the IMO this year means that the whole debate about decarbonizing shipping is gone. It might mean that a compromise on an international level is being pushed forward, but it will mean that regional schemes will come more into play. Now clearly, from my point of view, I'd rather have one international regulation than having a European one, an Australian one, Chinese one, a U.K. one, an African one.

The second best is that other countries are taking up the slack and basically deciding, okay, something needs to happen, let's go. I mean you saw the initiative recently by some African countries. You know that Australia is talking about it, the Chinese are looking into it. We have the U.K. that is very close to making a deal. So I think that the momentum is still there, unfortunately, not enough at the international level.

Jeffrey De Wolf: How do you see this domino effect taking place because some parts of the chain will go first? You see a tipping point happening somewhere in the future where the rest of the chain will have to follow?

Alexander Saverys: The biggest tipping point will be the price of ammonia. If -- or an alternative fuel, but I think ammonia will win the day in terms of pricing compared to methanol, LNG or the others. That, of course, is the biggest tipping point because once ammonia becomes not only green, but also cheaper than diesel then it's game, set and match. I think what we are seeing today is that a lot of countries understand that it is possible to put a CO2 tax on shipping because Europe has done it with EU ETS and the FuelEU Maritime. On top of that, to be very blunt and put it on the table, it's bringing extra cash to the government.

It's a huge revenue. I mean, it's billions and billions here in Europe. And I think some of the African countries, I think it's 6 of them now that have decided to implement the $17 per tonne of CO2 tax, realize that this actually is also a driver for their own development. So I think you will see that debate continuing because governments need money, don't they?

Jeffrey De Wolf: Yes, all governments, yes.

Enya Derkinderen: We received a few questions in the Q&A section, so I will go through them one by one. So the first one is there a commercial advantage currently to ammonia bunkering?

Alexander Saverys: Today, no, because it is more expensive than diesel bunkering. But as I said before, we think that the price, not only of the ammonia, but also the logistics, including the bunkering will fall in the years to come.

Enya Derkinderen: And the next question, why did charter hire expense increase in Q3? To what extent will it be ongoing when you guide on next quarter bookings, do you include any TCEs?

Alexander Saverys: It's a good question, and we received it from several people. This summer or the beginning of the year, we had concluded beginning of the year some very short-term COAs, and we decided to put our COA cargoes on charter in tonnage and not on our own vessels, purely because of positioning and TCE revenues was better to put it on charter tonnage and not put it on our ships, so it's a little bit of a technicality. Can I exclude that we will not continue to do TCEs in the next quarters? No, because we've always taken some short-term COAs but this is normally not a recurring expense.

Ludovic Saverys: And to clarify, it's not that we took a position on long-term time charter in ships on the company or we would have mentioned them. TCE expenses should match definitely, of course, the increased freight revenue that we get. And you could also see that in our Q3 figures compared to Q2, we had a much higher revenue eventually for the same bottom line with some capital gains differences, but that is definitely one of the explanations.

Enya Derkinderen: And next question, in regards to the green ammonia project in Namibia. What is the project status and what are the next steps?

Alexander Saverys: Not a lot has changed since the previous quarter. We are still finalizing all our plans for the ammonia terminals, so the first investment. And on the ammonia production, we are still in the FEED study, so that is still something that is only going to be finalized next year. So not a lot to announce on Namibia, but as soon as we are in a position to confirm the decision to build the ammonia terminal, we will definitely inform you.

Enya Derkinderen: We have 2 more questions, but I see that we have someone who wants to ask a live question, so I will first give the floor to Odin Einarsen.

Odin Einarsen: I'm just trying to wrap my head around a bit of the demand story in China because, obviously, you're seeing that imports are up, but you're seeing steel output down and that currently a few percentages of the mills are profitable. So I'm just trying to understand what you guys see for the rest of the year and '27 on China.

Alexander Saverys: Well, what we see on the spot market is that the iron ore to China has not been as impressive as what we would want, but there's still a lot of iron ore going there. What we see for next year, this is what we'll read from analysts and what people are forecasting. In terms of the steel production, as I said, I think when you look at steel production in China, you always need to look at what they need locally for their own economy and what they are exporting and using in other countries.

The figures that have been one to follow is how much of the domestic iron ore in China is being produced and being replaced by imported iron ore.

Enya Derkinderen: The next question, Q&A. It's a rather lengthy one. Rolling out the ammonia bunkering chain will be capital intensive. Currently, you are mainly looking at China. How do you see the future for further global expansion of ammonia bunkering along transport routes? Is there a possibility to collaborate with, for example, Vopak Air Liquide, whose ships are already located along the worldwide trade routes? Will Walvis Bay become a bunkering station on the U.S.A.-China or EU-China route?

Alexander Saverys: So it will be capital incentive, yes, but that doesn't mean that Cmb.Tech will have to bear all the capital costs because indeed, some of the names that you mentioned in your question are companies that have a vested interest to develop the infrastructure, to develop the bunkering possibilities. We've always said that on ammonia fuel, some things we will do ourselves to kickstart, to make sure that it happens. But we will always work together with third-party producers, always work with third-party logistics providers. So the answer to your question is yes on every subsegment. And will Walvis Bay 1 day become a bunkering hub? We truly hope so. That is an ambition that we have.

Enya Derkinderen: And next question, can you say more about ammonia propulsion program? You mentioned up to 18 bunkers. Are these including the ammonia-ready ships announced in relation to the Fortescue charter? Or is it only ships delivered ex yard with ammonia DF engines installed?

Alexander Saverys: So it's 10 ships that are being delivered with the ammonia engine on board, it's 8 ships that we will retrofit, it's one container vessel and it's 2 chemical tankers.

Enya Derkinderen: And then the last question. It's an add-on question on capital allocation. You understand the current preference is for dividends, but what would be the criteria to go for buybacks? Is your current free float and elements in the decision?

Ludovic Saverys: I think the long and the short could be, it's part of the equation on share buybacks. We have a nice free float now. Our liquidity and share is important to us to give the opportunity for people to get in and out. I think share buybacks has to be seen over a long period of time, not just a momentum, and we have a capital market story to tell. It takes some quarters to go from a pure play tanker to a diversified company paying dividends, having little CapEx and being set up for the next potential investment program, whether it's M&A or newbuilds.

So today, it does not favor -- we don't favor share buybacks this quarter, but this is something that we analyze every 90 days.

Enya Derkinderen: Thank you. I think this concludes the Q&A session. Back to you.

Alexander Saverys: Yes. Thank you very much, Enya, and thank you, all of you for joining us in this call. Thanks for all the questions. And as we said, if you have follow-up questions, don't hesitate to reach out to us, and we will see you next time. Bye-bye.

#2993. This hidden iOS 27 feature ensures you’ll never sleep through an alarm again

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Say goodbye to accidentally silencing your alarms.

A lesser-known iOS 27 feature includes a new alarm volume setting that gives alarms, timers, and ringtones independent volume control. You can adjust the volume settings for alarms and timers independently of your phone’s alerts and system sounds, so you don’t miss an alarm after lowering your ringtone volume.

Also: Apple reveals daily limits on your Siri AI use – here’s how much you’ll have to pay

There have been ways to adjust the iPhone alarm volume for a few years, but there’s an important distinction between what the new feature entails and what those methods involve.

Previously, you could adjust your Sleep Schedule alarms to always go off at a specific volume, regardless of the iPhone’s shared volume. Sleep Schedule alarms have a dedicated volume slider that you can set and adjust as needed, all configured within the Sleep focus. The new feature, however, lets you set an independent volume for all alarms and timers, not just those in the Sleep Schedule.

Alarms, Timers, Alerts, and System Sounds are set to match your ringtone volume by default, but you can turn them off in the Sounds and Haptics setting.

Also: 5 new Apple Health features you should try in iOS 27.3 – if your phone qualifies

Once you disable the option to match your alarm volume to your ringtone’s volume, you can set your volume for upcoming alarms. With this feature, you can maximize your alarm volume without affecting the volume of incoming calls and notifications.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

There’s something to play whether you’re into science fiction, horror or other genres.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is out now, and while it might be one of the most anticipated game releases of the year, not everyone likes the series or is interested in it. If you want to play something more fantastical, Xbox Game Pass has you covered with High on Life 2, Hela: Of Mice and Magic and more soon.

Xbox Game Pass, a CNET Editors’ Choice award winner, offers a wide selection of games you can play on your Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One and PC or mobile device for as little as $10 per month. With a higher-tier Game Pass Ultimate subscription ($23 per month), you can access hundreds of titles, including new ones on release day.

Here’s everything Microsoft is adding to Xbox Game Pass soon.

New to Game Pass Premium. Previously added to Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass.

This sequel to the 2022 first-person shooter High on Life has players once again traveling throughout space and taking down bad guys with the help of an arsenal of talking guns. The game comes from Squanch Games, which was founded by a co-creator of the Rick and Morty series, so expect some raunchy humor and antics.

This prequel to the Outlast series retains the horror of the other games and adds a Cold War-era twist. You’ve been abducted and are subjected to medical and psychological experiments. To survive, you have to fight and evade other test subjects in a massive facility run by the shady Murkoff Corporation.

You’ve seen mice, right? Small, cute creatures that scamper around and are sometimes kept as pets? Well, in this co-op game, you get to see the world through the eyes of one of those critters. You’ll solve puzzles, explore landscapes inspired by Northern Sweden and take in a heartwarming story told via fuzzy friends.

While Microsoft is adding several games to Game Pass, it’s also removing eight others on Nov. 30. So you still have some time to complete your main campaign or any side quests before you’ll have to buy these games separately.

For more, read our Xbox Game Pass review and learn about other titles you can play on the service. You can also check out our recent review of the Xbox Nano Controller.

#2991. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Global stock markets remain volatile amid persistent geopolitical tensions and concerns about the sustainability of AI trade. Given this backdrop, investors seeking steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

Tracking recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick attractive stocks, as these experts assess a company's ability to pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is a dividend king. The company has increased its dividend for 39 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share (annualized dividend of $7.12 per share), CVX offers a yield of 3.14%. Chevron will announce its third-quarter results on October 30.

In an earnings preview note on U.S. oil majors, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Chevron with a price target of $241. The analyst is focused on the company's international growth prospects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Specifically, Mehta highlighted management's commentary on solid execution in Venezuela, with gross production expected to more than double to nearly 600 kbd (kilo barrels per day) by 2031 via three joint ventures. He also noted a recent oil and gas condensate discovery in offshore Angola and is awaiting commercial updates on the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah projects in Iraq.

Furthermore, Mehta expects CVX to report improved productivity and capital efficiency across domestic shale assets. He expects the improvement mainly in the Permian Basin, where Chevron projects advanced chemical treatments to drive about a 10% recovery uplift in new wells and bring down capital spend per barrel by about 25% year-over-year. Overall, Mehta expects Chevron to report Q3 2026 EPS of $4.95, above the consensus of $4.89.

"While unfavorable timing effects and volatile commodity prices may present quarterly earnings headwinds, we highlight healthy U.S. refining margins and strong asset utilization as partial offsets," said Mehta.

Mehta ranks No. 381 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Chevron KPIs on TipRanks.

Kinetik Holdings (KNTK) is a fully integrated, pure-play, midstream company operating in the Delaware Basin. Earlier this month, the company declared a dividend of $0.81 per share, payable on October 30, 2026. With an annualized dividend of $3.24 per share, KNTK offers a yield of 5.82%. Kinetik will announce its Q3 earnings on November 4, with a conference call scheduled the next day.

Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, Goldman Sachs analyst John Mackay reiterated a buy rating on Kinetik stock and slightly raised his price target to $58 from $57. He expects the company to report Q3 2026 EBITDA of $279 million, higher than the Street's expectation of $270 million but lower than the second quarter's EBITDA of $281 million.

The 5-star analyst expects Kinetik's Q3 performance to gain from higher gas volumes after notable curtailments in the second quarter. Mackay also expects the quarter to benefit from higher production and steady commodity margins, even though some lower-margin contracts and weaker Waha spread marketing gains could weigh on results.

Overall, Mackay increased his Q3 2026 estimates to reflect higher volumes, driven by rapid Permian egress pipeline commissioning, stronger throughput at Kings Landing I, and higher M2M commodity prices, offset by increased costs.

"As natural gas takeaway constraints ease across the Permian, investor focus centers on KNTK's YE26 volume trajectory and durability of its multi-year growth," said Mackay.

Mackay ranks No. 569 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.9%. See Kinetik's Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Moving to Crescent Energy (CRGY), an exploration and production company with activities focused in the Eagle Ford, Permian, and Uinta Basins. With a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share (annualized dividend of $0.48 per share), CRGY's dividend yield stands at 3.56%. Earlier this month, Crescent announced an agreement to acquire Eagle Ford assets from Devon Energy (DVN).

Heading into Q3 earnings on Nov. 2, Evercore analyst Stephen Richardson reiterated a buy rating on Crescent stock and slightly lowered the price target to $17 from $18, citing dilution from new shares.

"CRGY's recent acquisition of DVN's Eagle Ford assets marks a strategic, growth-oriented move, potentially enhancing cash flow performance," said Richardson.

The 5-star analyst noted that the acquisition of the Eagle Ford assets at a net purchase price of $3.85 billion will add about 68 MBoe/d of net production and over 600 net Tier 1 locations. Richardson added that a solid track record of synergies from past deals in the Eagle Ford region increases confidence about Crescent achieving efficiencies with this deal.

Additionally, Richardson noted that the financial implications of the acquisition seem impressive, with a projected increase in cash flow per share of about 9% for 2027 to 2029.

The analyst believes that Crescent is not just expanding its business through acquisitions but positioning itself as a more durable company, regardless of market conditions.

Richardson ranks No. 478 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Crescent Energy Statistics on TipRanks.

#2990. Kingsoft (KC) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Revenue jumped 40% on AI cloud demand, yet the bottom line slipped into a loss.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:12PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Kingsoft (KC +3.33%) reported its fastest revenue growth in five years, reaching RMB 3.48 billion in the third quarter as AI cloud services became the primary driver of top-line performance. Management stated that AI cloud gross billings now account for 61% of public cloud revenue, reflecting a shift toward intelligent computing and high-concurrency inference demand. The company reported record adjusted operating margins while executing a significant capital expenditure program to expand domestic computing resources. CFO Yi Li indicated that operating cash flow and customer prepayments covered nearly 100% of the quarter's cash capital expenditures, supporting the company's disciplined capital allocation framework.

Operator: Good day, ladies and gentlemen, and thank you for standing by for the Kingsoft Cloud Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note that today's call is being recorded. I will now turn the call over to Mr. Jacky Zuo, Senior Director of Capital Markets at Kingsoft Cloud. Jacky, please go ahead.

Jacky Zuo: Thank you, operator. Hello, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Kingsoft Cloud's Third Quarter 2026 earnings release was issued earlier today and is available on our IR website and through our PR Newswire. For today's conference call, our CEO, Mr. Tao Zou, will discuss our business performance and key developments. And then our CFO, Ms. Yi Li, will do a review of our financial results. Management will then take your questions. Consecutive interpretation will be provided for convenience and reference only. In the event of any discrepancy, management's statements in the original language will prevail. Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's call contains forward-looking statements made under safe harbor provisions of the U.S.

Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These statements involve risks and uncertainties, and actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by the forward-looking statements. Additional information concerning factors that could cause actual results to differ materially is included in the company's filings with the U.S. SEC. The company undertakes no obligation to update any forward-looking statements, except as required by the applicable law. Unless otherwise stated, all financial figures discussed on today's call are denominated in RMB. With that, it is my pleasure to turn the call over to our Chairman and CEO, Mr. Zou. Mr. Zou, please go ahead.

Tao Zou: Interpreted Hello, everyone, and welcome to Kingsoft Cloud's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. I'm Tao Zou, CEO of Kingsoft Cloud. Over the past quarter, we saw the AI industry enter a new phase, moving from rapid advances in capabilities to widespread application. This further validates our long-held vision of bringing AI to every industry. 4 years after the GPT moment in late 2022, the interplay of technological change, market supply and demand and regulation in AI and intelligent computing has become more complex. But short-term fluctuations do not change the industry's long-term potential. We continue to see a thriving and rapidly evolving open source model ecosystem, fast-growing inference demand and lower barriers to AI adoption for enterprises and individuals.

Beyond AI coding, agent applications such as AI office tools and personal assistants are moving from proof of concept towards massive adoption. FDE solutions are also gaining broad interest and recognition among enterprise customers. These developments reinforce our confidence and commitment to the AI cloud market over the long term. This quarter, Kingsoft Cloud remains committed to high-quality sustainable growth. We advanced our intelligent computing, general purpose computing, model as a Service inference and FDE businesses together, translating strong AI demand into solid growth in both revenue and profit. We delivered encouraging results in the third quarter. First, revenue continued to grow rapidly. Total revenue reached RMB 3.48 billion, up 40% year-over-year, our fastest growth in the past 5 years.

Second, AI cloud continued to be the strong growth driver. AI cloud gross billings reached RMB 1.68 billion, up 115% year-over-year and accounted for 61% of our public cloud revenue. Third, profitability continued to improve. Adjusted operating profit margin reached 4.4%, up 3.8 percentage points year-over-year. We continue to improve profitability while maintaining strong revenue growth. Now let me walk you through our business progress in the third quarter of 2026. In public cloud, revenue reached RMB 2.76 billion, up 57% year-over-year. We continue to pursue growth both within and beyond our ecosystem, satisfying sustained and strong demand for AI cloud services while improving business quality and mix.

First, within our ecosystem, we continue to execute our connected transaction framework agreements as planned. Revenue from the Xiaomi and Kingsoft ecosystem reached RMB 920 million, up 33% year-over-year and accounting for 26% of total revenue. AI cloud gross billings from ecosystem customers grew 105% year-over-year. As a key AI cloud service provider, we support Xiaomi's expansion of AI across its human, car and home ecosystem. We also provide MaaS services for WPS Comate, a core AI product of Kingsoft Office, supporting the deployment of AI capabilities in office applications. Second, beyond our ecosystem, we continue to capture demand from independent third-party customers. AI cloud gross billings from non ecosystem customers grew 120% year-over-year.

We supported key customers' model training and high-concurrency inference needs while actively repricing expiring contracts and on-demand contracts. Our strong industry reputation, full-stack product capabilities and differentiated position as a neutral cloud provider continue to help us expand our customer base. Our AI cloud business now serves leading customers across Internet platforms, Frontier AI Labs, embedded AI, autonomous driving, AI for science, fintech, gaming and online video platforms. This further strengthens our customer mix and industry diversification. Third, in MaaS inference, we continue to improve inference efficiency and utilization within our limited pool of owned computing resources. Our MaaS business remained stable this quarter.

StarFlow now supports more than 160 models and serves over 300 customers, further expanding the range of MaaS use cases. On October 20, 2026, DeepSeek fully open-sourced DeepInfer, its internal inference framework, and we responded quickly. In November, daily token usage on our MaaS platform reached more than 3x of the daily average token usage in December. In Enterprise Cloud, revenue reached RMB 720 million. We believe AI can transform every industry and all these AI applications will ultimately need to run on a cloud platform. Our focus is to deepen our understanding of each industry and conduct FDE projects that generate recurring operating revenue.

We remain open to a broad range of open source and industry-specific models without being tied to any single underlying model. We use ontology modeling to turn business objects, relationships, rules and knowledge into business semantics that can be processed and traced. Through our FDE approach, we work on site with customers to identify use cases, define problems, build rapid prototypes, validate solutions and turn the results into reusable assets and products. The specialized agent workbench provides a single entry point for digital employees in core roles for our customers, bringing AI into business workflows. Long-term operational contracts and token revenue sharing provides sustainable cash flow for us. Our enterprise cloud FDE and operations strategy gained further validation in Q3.

In digital health, we continue to advance the clinical research agent generation platform project at Wuhan Union Hospital, supporting intelligent services across the full life cycle of new drug clinical trials. The platform manages 6 categories of knowledge bases and 20 million outpatient records, supporting 66 agents and over 200 skills. In medical imaging cloud, we have spent 6 years validating an AI plus operations business model with deployments in Jiangsu, Chongqing, Hubei and Gansu. We have expanded from cloud services for digital imaging into health care value-added services and data assets operations. This year, our project in Gansu won first prize in the National Finals of the Smart Medical Insurance Competition.

In financial services, we won a corporate credit ontology modeling consulting project with Bank of Shanghai, creating a model case covering the full corporate credit workflow. In public services, we developed agents for Zhuhai covering end-to-end government and enterprise office workflows, helping frontline staff improve overall office productivity by more than 30%. In products and technology, we continue to strengthen our capabilities for training and inference in the AI agent era. This quarter, we further developed a 3-layer product portfolio covering model training, model services and agent hosting through our Xinghong training and inference platform, StarFlow model platform and AgentKit platform, respectively. We continue to upgrade our full-stack capabilities.

StarFlow added intelligent model routing and batch inference APIs, reducing the cost of integrating and switching between models while improving throughput for several core models by up to 140%. We also launched AgentKit Studio, a visual development and runtime workbench supporting device cloud coordination and multi-agent collaboration. We strengthened integration between AgentKit and StarFlow across knowledge bases, persistent memory and model services. Our open approach at both the model and harness architecture layers help enterprise customers focus on creating business value. At the same time, we continue to expand our domestic computing resources with the supply chain partners.

We completed testing and integration with the next-generation products from mainstream domestic chip providers, further strengthening the independence and control of our cloud infrastructure and setting a solid foundation for sustainable growth. Looking ahead, competition in AI cloud services will depend on the visibility of customer demand, reliable service delivery and sustainable returns on capital, rather than investment scale alone. Kingsoft Cloud will continue to plan capital expenditure expansion prudently based on customer orders and improved monetization through flexible computing services, MaaS inferences and FDE businesses. We aim to reward our shareholders' long-standing support with stronger cash generation capability and profitability. With that, I will hand the call over to our CFO, Ms.

#2989. I gave Gemini access to my Wallet, and it immediately started saving me money

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Gemini gave me a little tough love and told me what I needed to hear about my finances.

Google has added Wallet integration to Personal Intelligence in AI Mode, letting you learn about your spending habits, plan a budget, maximize credit card rewards, and more with a simple Search.

Starting today, Google announced, Personal Intelligence for Search is expanding to more apps, including Wallet and Drive. Google can’t move or manage any money, but it can give you tailored, personalized search results about your finances, like showing where you spend the most, identifying recurring subscriptions you might not be aware of, and suggesting which credit card might be best to use for travel. All you have to do is ask in a search.

Also: I tried Personal Intelligence in Android Auto – and it knew exactly where I wanted to go

This feature comes just over a week after Google introduced Personal Intelligence to Wallet.

To turn on the feature, go to https://gemini.google.com. Once you’re there, click on the Settings gear icon, and then “Personal Intelligence.” Choose “Connected Apps,” and you’ll see all available apps. When you choose Wallet, you might need to log in to your bank account to access it fully.

Once your Wallet is connected, it takes a few minutes to fully sync. Once it’s finished, you can ask questions through AI mode in Search.

I decided to give it a try for myself, starting off with a simple query: “Based on my spending, what’s a quick way I can save money?” I could have told you one of the primary culprits, but Google happily responded with what I already knew: far too much of my money goes to fast food and coffee.

“You frequently grab quick-service meals,” the response said, pointing out several fast food places that I do indeed frequent, “and specialty coffees throughout the week.” If I just cut that down to two meals and two coffees a week, Gemini explained, I’d save about $30 a week, or $1,500 a year.

Also: This powerful Gemini setting made my AI results way more personal and accurate

When I asked it to find recurring subscriptions, Gemini noted that I had several monthly charges. What I didn’t ask for, but it did, was to break down those subscriptions into an easy-to-see chart, complete with the name, price, category, the card it’s being charged to, and the timeframe it usually comes out. Gemini even offered a few free alternatives to services I was paying for.

Since Gemini also knows what cards are linked to your Wallet, it’s able to offer advice there, too. I’m planning a trip to New York City, so I asked which cards might be best to use for the hotels and airfare. Gemini was able to analyze my card benefits, considering things like rewards and built-in travel insurance, and make a recommendation.

Also: Slow Android phone? How to speed it back up in 4 easy steps

While Gemini Personal Intelligence can access your Gmail to learn more about your spending, it can’t access your bank account. The only information it knows about your finances and spending comes from receipts in your inbox or from your Wallet transaction history. I do use Wallet often (mostly when ordering through online apps), but it’s not quite my go-to option when I’m in a store. Given how useful this feature can be, though, I might just start using Wallet more to give it more information to work with.
