#2988. CNET Survey: $75 Billion in Packages Could Be at Risk of Holiday Porch Theft

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

US adults have an average package value of $276.24, yet one-fifth don't use security devices due to costs.

Big holiday sales, like Black Friday and Cyber Monday, are here, but before you click ‘buy,’ make sure you have a plan to protect your package from porch pirates.

CNET’s annual package theft survey polls US adults about their experiences with porch pirates and how they try to prevent thefts. This year, the average package value is $276.24, and 28% of US adults have had a package stolen, know someone who has or caught an attempted theft within the past year. Yet 20% of US adults don’t use security devices due to hardware costs or monthly subscription fees.

But leaving your packages up for grabs could be a big risk — especially when thieves know holiday gifts are being delivered. On the other hand, some bad actors don’t seem to mind being caught in the act on home security cameras, so are they really enough to deter bad actors? And what more can you do to protect your deliveries?

CNET’s findings show that some US adults have dealt with porch theft firsthand: 8% had packages meant for themselves or their households stolen within the past year, and 5% had a delivered gift stolen. Very few (1%) caught a theft in the act on a video doorbell or security camera.

Meanwhile, many US adults know someone who fell victim to package theft — 13% know a neighbor or community member who had a package stolen within the past year, and 12% know someone who doesn’t live in their community who has.

“Close to a third of our respondents are personally acquainted with package theft, which is still a high number compared to other issues like break-ins,” said CNET’s senior home security editor, Tyler Lacoma. “Thieves generally look for crimes of opportunity, and few things are easier than a package left on a doorstep, especially if nobody is home.”

Surprisingly, most US adults (72%) haven’t experienced package theft or know anyone who has.

Even though the percentages above may seem low, Lacoma said that package theft typically increases during the holidays when thieves know more deliveries are likely, and new porch theft tactics are always on the horizon.

There are reports of thieves trying Wi-Fi jamming to disable live security camera footage while they steal packages. And findings show that some are installing spy cams in high-value neighborhoods to learn your home’s layout and habits to take your packages shortly after they’re delivered. In recent years, pirates have even tracked shipping labels for high-value tech, like iPhones, to steal the package within minutes of arrival.

So while the majority of US adults haven’t fallen victim, that shouldn’t be a sign to shrug off the concern or relax your home security measures. Instead, now’s the time to plan how to safely store your packages if they’re delivered while you’re away.

Online shopping and deliveries to your door can be a convenient way to check off holiday wish lists, but the average package value this holiday season is less than last year. CNET found that US adults plan to have an average of $276.24 in holiday packages delivered during this holiday season. That’s $23.82 less than last year’s average of $300.06.

By generation, Millennials also have a lower estimated average package value than last year, with an average of $227.25, compared to their 2025 package value of $307.47 — an $80.22 difference, while Gen Z’s package value is only about $7 less than last year. But any package’s value is still worth taking precautions to help prevent it from being stolen.

Lacoma has thoughts on why that might be. In short, lower spending could mean fewer packages.

“I wonder if people have also simply gotten fewer packages in general this year due to tariffs, inflation and tech prices. That could pull these numbers down,” said Lacoma. But there’s a high chance that could be the case considering CNET’s 2026 annual holiday survey, which found that US adult tech spending is down to $808 — which is $123 less than last year’s average of $931.

Thieves may not always know what’s in boxes they’re stealing but they’re willing to take a chance. We asked US adults which items were stolen in package thefts in the past year to give you a sense of what’s at risk.

Among the items stolen, apparel and accessories were the most common goods stolen (40%). That’s followed by toys and games (23%). Then there are everyday home basics, like decor, cookware and small appliances (19%).

But personal tech devices and accessories are still among the items stolen. Small accessories like phone chargers and cases are most common (16%) among tech-related packages stolen. They are followed by audio gadgets like headphones and Bluetooth speakers, along with streaming devices and soundbars (11%, respectively).

Still, more costly tech like gaming consoles (10%), computers and laptops (9%) and smart home devices (6%) are among devices stolen.

You shouldn’t leave your packages up to chance. That’s why Lacoma recommends a few safer options to ensure your packages are stored securely after they’re delivered, even beyond keeping an eye on your doorbell or security camera. Instead, keep your packages out of sight with tactics like a delivery box with a code or key or ask for an in-garage delivery.

“Delivery boxes have reached a new level of popularity in recent years as an effective way to stop porch pirates completely. However, Amazon’s Key service that delivers to your garage is an alternative,” said Lacoma. “Either way, you’ll need to trust delivery people to handle your shipments, unless you want to arrange for pickup at a nearby shipping center, which some people like to combine with other holiday errands.”

If you don’t want to install a new security feature, try scheduling your packages to arrive when you know you’re home, requiring a signature from someone you trust or changing your delivery location to a pickup spot, like UPS’ Hold for Pick-Up locations or Amazon Lockers.

Home surveillance, like outdoor security cameras and video doorbells, can deter package thieves who don’t want to risk getting caught on camera. But US adults have mixed feelings about their effectiveness in protecting against package theft.

“Fortunately, the right home security picks can solve both these problems,” said Lacoma. “Brands like Tapo, Eufy, Aqara and even Google Nest offer package detection and alerts for free, so you don’t have to worry about extra fees.”

If you’re looking for a camera that’s off-the-grid, consider the Arlo Go 2. It’s an LTE camera, so it uses a cellular data connection instead of Wi-Fi. It still finds a signal, supports app operation and live video viewing. If you’re looking for a power-over-Ethernet camera that uses a cable connection, the Reolink Duo 3 is a good choice.

Among all US adults, only 14% have security devices with a monthly subscription that lets them save or playback video. By comparison, 12% have security devices but no subscription.

Those percentages could be low for a few reasons, including the overall perception of how helpful surveillance and security really are against porch theft. Eleven percent of US adults don’t think security devices deter porch thefts. It’s a valid concern since 4% fell victim to package theft or an attempted theft despite having security devices. And some US adults (9%) use security devices to get proof of a theft after the fact — not to prevent it.

But that doesn’t mean you should ignore the possibility of package theft — especially during the holidays. Even if you don’t want to install cameras or new security devices, make a plan to protect your packages and avoid the headache of package theft over the holidays.

“Remember, the simple presence of a security camera is enough to make many thieves look elsewhere – interviews have confirmed it,” said Lacoma. “And with today’s phone alerts about package detection, you can usually check on a package only seconds after it appears, or bring up footage if it unexpectedly vanishes, letting you take action fast. New practices like delivery boxes or in-garage delivery help address risks in concrete ways, too.”

CNET commissioned YouGov Plc to conduct the survey. All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,016 adults. Fieldwork was undertaken between Oct. 23–27, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus).

The $75 billion figure was calculated by multiplying the average value of deliveries each US adult expects to receive by the 2025 US population of adults ages 18 and over calculated by the US Census Bureau.

#2986. Bambu Lab’s New P3C 3D Printer Brings Advanced Features to the Mainstream

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Now everyday hobbyists have access to some of the latest tech without breaking the bank.

On Tuesday, Bambu Lab took the wraps off its third-generation 3D printer, the P3C. It brings to the mainstream the company’s “tool changer” technology, which was previously reserved for higher-end, flagship models like the $2,500 H3C. Given the P3C costs less than half the bigger model, it might be the perfect gift to get your favorite 3D printing hobbyist for Black Friday.

The big deal here is the introduction of the Swaptek 7-tool changer, which allows you to switch to a different color or material in just 6 seconds, preventing you from having to stop and clean the nozzle every time. The technology produces significantly less waste and allows you to create faster prints.

The tool changer technology also allows you to mix different materials with less of a fuss, so you can use a typical rigid plastic and something like a flexible rubber in a single pass without stopping. It can switch between different nozzle sizes in one job. You can switch between  0.2 mm, 0.4 mm, 0.6 mm and 0.8 mm midprint.

The P3C ships with an integrated sealed AMS 3P filament management system that can store up to seven spools, each of which is on an independent feed path to the printer. You can also connect up to four external AMS units, supporting up to 22 colors.

The P3C is more than just a 3D printer. The Swaptek system supports interchangeable craft tools, letting you cut, draw or emboss on materials.

Bambu Lab also included a few features that make the P3C more approachable to newcomers. The P3C provides full-auto calibration, automatically aligning nozzle offsets and multi-tool heads so you don’t have to do it yourself. There’s also a built-in AI monitoring system that can detect issues like nozzle clogs and purge-bin jams early on. A new health management system will no longer spit out vague or obscure errors when something goes wrong. Instead, the new system will explain the issue in plain language and provide step-by-step troubleshooting right on the screen.

CNET’s 3D printing expert, James Bricknell, hasn’t been able to test Bambu Labs’ latest model yet but is excited about it. “While the P3C didn’t arrive in time for a hands-on, it’s built with the same design language and hardware support as the recently released H3C. If it is anywhere near as good, and I think that’s likely, it’ll be at the top of any serious 3D printing enthusiast’s wish list.”

The P3C 3D printer AMS combo is available now worldwide for $1,149. The combo includes the printer, AMS 3P as well as 5 0.4mm standard PrintTools. Two slots are left open for you to customize. This combo option comes with virtually everything you need to get started printing your works of art and more.

#2985. Shoe Station (SHOE) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management is reversing store rebannering after a sharp traffic-driven sales slump.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:12PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Shoe Station (SHOE -18.39%) reported revisions to its retail operations following a quarter where comparable store sales declined 5.1%. Management reported that the company will reverse previous rebannering efforts by returning 27 locations to the Rogan's banner and approximately 75% of other rebannered stores to the Shoe Carnival name. The company stated that it will also invest $4 million to revert 74 stores to their original angled floor layouts to address customer feedback regarding shoppability. Despite these challenges, management reported that early fourth quarter traffic and sales have improved as seasonal weather drove demand for boots.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to Shoe Station Group's Third Quarter Fiscal 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Today's conference call is being recorded and is also being broadcast via webcast. Any unauthorized reproduction or rebroadcast of any portion of this call is expressly prohibited. Management's remarks today contain forward-looking statements that involve a number of risks and uncertainties that could cause the company's actual results to be materially different from those projected in such statements. Forward-looking statements should also be considered in conjunction with the discussion of risk factors included in the company's SEC filings and today's earnings press release. Investors are cautioned not to place undue reliance on these forward-looking statements, which speak only as of today's date.

The company undertakes no obligation to update or revise the forward-looking statements discussed on today's conference call or contained in today's earnings press release to reflect future events or developments, except as required by law. Management's remarks today will also reference certain non-GAAP financial measures. Reconciliations of those measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are included in today's earnings press release. I will now turn the conference over to Mr. Cliff Sifford, Interim President and Chief Executive Officer of Shoe Station Group for opening remarks. Mr. Sifford, you may begin.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today. With me on the call are Kerry Jackson, our Chief Financial Officer; Tanya E. Gordon, our Chief Merchandising Officer; and Marc Chilton, our Chief Operating Officer. Tanya and Marc are both available to take your questions during the Q&A portion of the call. Our third quarter results were below the expectations we shared with you in September. This morning, I will cover what happened in the quarter, what our customers are telling us and the work we have completed and still have ahead of us across our three groups of stores, Shoe Carnival, Shoe Station and our Rogan's stores, which have been rebannered to Shoe Station at Rogan's.

That includes two strategic decisions we have made about our rebannered stores, which I will describe in detail. Kerry will then take you through the financials and our updated outlook. Comparable store sales declined 5.1% in the quarter, and the quarter had two distinct parts. In fiscal August, during back-to-school, comparable store sales declined 2.7%, a meaningful improvement from the second quarter. When we spoke in September, we expected the third quarter to be approximately flat depending on when the weather turned. Unfortunately, once the need for back-to-school shoes dissipated, a combination of macroeconomic issues, including higher gas prices and warmer-than-expected weather across all regions combined to once again reduce the traffic in our stores.

In addition to that, our own advertising was lighter in September and October than a year ago because we weighted our second half spending toward the holiday season. As a result, our comparable store sales declined approximately 7% each month. E-commerce growth moderated significantly from the second quarter. The softness was broad-based as we experienced this across all banners, and the footwear marketplace remained highly promotional throughout the quarter. In early November, as fuel prices begin to drop, we began to see an improvement in our store traffic and as traffic improved, sales also improved. More on that later. The pattern underlying our sales results is consistent with what we described last quarter.

Store conversion improved again by almost a full point for the company with improvement in all banners. Customers who came into our stores bought. What declined was traffic. Traffic was weakest in our rebannered stores, and that fact is the starting point for the decisions I will describe in a few minutes. Since August, our new Chief Marketing Officer, Tracy Dick and her team have been studying how customers view our two largest banners, Shoe Station and Shoe Carnival. That work combined formal customer research with direct feedback from our store managers who hear from customers every day. I'll come back to what we learned.

Let me turn to the product because the category results show where the assortment work is taking hold and where we still have work to do. Adult athletic, our largest business at roughly 38% of sales, declined low single digits for the quarter. Men's athletic increased low single digits with running up mid-single digits and basketball up high single digits. Women's athletic declined high single digits with running down mid-single digits and the fashion athletic styles down considerably more. Women's nonathletic declined high single digits. Within that, due to the very warm September and October, sandals increased mid-single digits and casuals were approximately flat, while women's sport casuals were down double digit and accounted for most of the decrease.

Men's nonathletic declined mid-single digits with casuals down double digits and work boots up low single digits. Children's shoes declined mid-single digits. Children's nonathletic was flat, which is progress in a business we intend to own, while children's athletic declined high single digits once back-to-school ended. Boots are the category I ask you to watch. For the full quarter, boots were down low single digits and the trend improved as the season opened. In October, women's boots were approximately flat on a comparable sales basis with average unit retails up high single digits and improved margins.

As a peek into the first few weeks of the fourth quarter, once the weather turned seasonal, women's boots have produced a comparable store increase in the teens. Men's boots increased low single digits in October, led by work boots, which increased high single digits. Customers are responding to newer, better product at higher prices with less promotion. That is what we expected from this assortment and is the most important metric we have going into the fourth quarter. When I returned in February, we set out to address the business store group by store group. It is useful to describe where we stand the same way. The first group is our Shoe Carnival stores.

These stores needed assortments localized to the customer who shops them. This includes the moderate price points that Shoe Carnival shopper expects from us. We also needed to reengage those customers with in-store promotions along with our iconic Spin 'n Win Wheel. These elements are part of what has made Shoe Carnival a fun place to shop, a family tradition and a great shopping experience. That work has been accomplished. What remains is letting the customer know and that is the purpose of our intensified advertising in the fourth quarter, which is designed to drive traffic and invite customers to experience the brand again.

The second group is our Shoe Station stores, which have always been Shoe Station, the 21 stores we acquired and the 12 new stores we have opened. The needs were similar, localized assortment and brand-specific promotions. While much has been accomplished here as well, we still have work to do to further differentiate the Shoe Station assortment and shopping experience from Shoe Carnival, and that work continues. The corrective action plan is in place, and our fourth quarter marketing is designed to drive traffic and invite customers to experience the brand again. The third group is our rebannered stores, and this is where we have reached a different conclusion. We listen to our customers and our store managers.

And as we said on our last call, we analyzed the customer demographics of each rebannered store. We conducted focus groups in many of our large markets. What we learned is clear. Our strategy to merchandise each store based on the customer who shops there is the correct one. The localization of our assortments continue. And in most cases, the right assortment for that customer looks like a Shoe Carnival assortment inside a Shoe Station store. Customers in our focus groups also told us they see the rebanner store as a Shoe Carnival store with a new name. The Shoe Station banner needs to be perceived as an elevated store with an elevated assortment.

And in many of these locations, the demographics and the cotenancy do not support that. Customers also told us that the new store layout is harder to shop. The Shoe Station format uses straight-line shelving, what we call flow. When customers walk in, they see a wall of shoes that limits their view of the product further back in the store. Our loyal customers could not easily find what they came for and new customers could not see the full breadth of the assortment. Based on that, we have made two decisions.

First, during the fourth quarter, we plan to return to shelving in 74 rebannered stores to their original angled aisle layout and reflow the product to make the shopping experience easier and more natural. We have already tested this in two stores. And in both, we have seen favorable customer comments along with improved conversion and sales. We expect this work to cost approximately $4 million and to be completed in the fourth quarter. Second, we plan to return rebannered stores to the original banner where the demographics and cotenancy align with that banner. We currently operate 131 rebannered stores. Of those, 27 are Shoe Station at Rogan's locations, and they will return to operating solely under the Rogan's name.

We are evaluating the remaining 104 stores now and will determine the exact number over the next few weeks. We currently estimate that 75% or more of them will return to the Shoe Carnival banner. Because of the time needed for permits and new signs, we expect these changes to take place in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. Let me explain why we believe this is the right course. Many of these stores are in markets where decades of advertising and operating have built brand awareness and loyalty to both Shoe Carnival and Rogan's. In addition, we believe the Shoe Station name is the banner that offers us the best opportunity for long-term growth.

We believe the clear delineation of the two banners allow us to grow both Shoe Station and Shoe Carnival. Shoe Station is the better branded shoe in an accessory business, and Shoe Carnival is a moderate-priced footwear store for the entire family. Rogan's remains an important banner that services the blue-collar worker through its stores and trucks. Shoe Station growth is expected to come from new stores located in higher-income demographic areas of the cities we already serve under the Shoe Carnival banner and new cities where we have not yet opened a Shoe Carnival store. For that strategy to succeed, we cannot continue to operate Shoe Station stores in Shoe Carnival type centers or with Shoe Carnival product assortments.

We entered the holiday season with the strongest boot assortment we have offered in years, localized product in our stores, intensified advertising and comparisons that ease as the quarter progresses. We expect the promotional environment to continue, and our guidance does not assume that it improves. With that, I'll turn the call over to Kerry to review the financials and our updated outlook. Kerry?

W. Kerry Jackson: Thank you, Cliff, and good morning, everyone. Our third quarter results were below the expectations underlying the guidance we provided in September on lower sales and lower gross profit margin, and they include a noncash goodwill impairment charge. This morning, I will review the balance sheet, the quarter, our year-to-date results and our updated fiscal 2026 guidance, which we have lowered. I will start with the balance sheet. We ended the quarter with $116 million in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities, an increase of $8.4 million compared to the end of the third quarter last year. We recently renewed our $100 million credit facility for an additional five years, and we have no borrowings under it.

During the quarter, we paid our 58th consecutive quarterly dividend and repurchased approximately $10 million of our common stock. Year-to-date, we have returned approximately $31 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. Inventory ended the quarter at $421.1 million, down $14.2 million or 3.3% from last year, with inventory per store down 1.4%. We remain on plan for a reduction of approximately $50 million in inventory by fiscal year-end. Net sales in the third quarter were $280.0 million compared to $297.2 million last year, a decline of 5.8%. Comparable store sales declined 5.1%. By month, comparable store sales declined 2.7% in fiscal August and approximately 7% in each of fiscal September and October.

By banner, Shoe Carnival net sales were $180.3 million, representing 64% of total net sales and declined 4.7% with comparable store sales down 3.7%. Shoe Station net sales were $99.3 million or 36% of the total and declined 7.7% with comparable store sales down 7.6%. Comparable e-commerce sales increased 2.1% compared to the growth of 18.8% in the second quarter. Part of that slowdown reflects stronger prior year comparisons and e-commerce softened in September along with our stores. Gross profit margin in the third quarter was 31.9%, a decrease of 570 basis points from last year.

Merchandise margin decreased 480 basis points and buying, distribution and occupancy costs reduced gross profit margin by 90 basis points, primarily from deleverage on the lower sales base. The drivers of the merchandise margin decline are the same three we described last quarter. First, the third quarter of last year included a temporary benefit from raising retail prices ahead of tariff-related cost increases, which did not repeat. Second, we priced competitively in a promotional marketplace. And third, we continued to liquidate aged and excess inventory. The rate of decline moderated from the second quarter when merchandise margin decreased 630 basis points.

One additional item, we received approximately $660,000 of tariff refunds during the third quarter, which were recorded as a reduction in cost of sales. SG&A in the third quarter was $87.0 million, a decrease of $6.2 million from last year, driven by lower selling costs, including advertising and other rebanner-related expenses as well as lower performance-based compensation. As a percentage of net sales, SG&A was 31.1% compared to 31.3% last year. On advertising, our spending in the third quarter was below last year. Our second half advertising is weighted toward the holiday season, and we expect fourth quarter advertising to be above last year.

We recorded a noncash goodwill impairment charge of $18.0 million in the quarter, which represents all the goodwill on our balance sheet. The charge reflects our recent financial performance and updated expectations for the business. It is presented on a separate line of the income statement and is not included in SG&A. It is a noncash and does not affect our cash flow or liquidity. We also tested our Shoe Station and Rogan's trade names and concluded that neither was impaired. We recorded an income tax benefit of $2.1 million in the quarter, and the effective tax rate was 14.6% compared to 25.5% in the prior year quarter.

The GAAP net loss for the quarter was $12.3 million or $0.46 per diluted share compared to net income of $14.6 million or $0.53 per diluted share last year. Excluding the goodwill impairment charge, non-GAAP adjusted net income was $1.3 million and non-GAAP adjusted EPS was $0.05. Through the first 9 months, net sales were $835.0 million, down 5.2% with comparable store sales down 4.8%. The GAAP net loss year-to-date was $11.7 million or $0.43 per diluted share. Excluding the first quarter charges related to the CEO transition and our strategic review and the third quarter goodwill impairment charge, non-GAAP adjusted net income was $13.8 million. Adjusted EPS was $0.51 per share and non-GAAP adjusted SG&A declined $18.1 million year-to-date.

Before I turn to guidance, let me cover the financial treatment of the two actions Cliff described. We expect to incur approximately $4 million of expense in the fourth quarter to return certain rebanner stores to the original layout. Returning stores to the original banners is expected to cost between $2 million and $3 million, which we expect to incur an expense primarily in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The expected layout revert expense is included in our fiscal 2026 GAAP guidance and excluded from our adjusted guidance measures. The anticipated banner expense falls in fiscal 2027 and does not affect fiscal 2026 guidance.

We are lowering our fiscal 2026 guidance to reflect results through the third quarter and current family footwear industry trends. For the fourth quarter, we expect comparable store sales in the range of flat to up 2%. For the full year, we now expect net sales of $1.087 billion to $1.092 billion, representing a decline of approximately 4.3% to 3.8% versus fiscal 2025, a GAAP net loss per share of $0.84 to $0.76 and adjusted EPS of $0.20 to $0.28. Gross profit margin of approximately 31.4% to 31.6%, representing 500 to 520 basis points of compression versus fiscal 2025.

GAAP SG&A up approximately $5.9 million versus fiscal 2025 and a reduction of adjusted SG&A of approximately $11.6 million, inclusive of our fourth quarter advertising investment, and a GAAP tax benefit rate of approximately 11% and adjusted tax rate of approximately 38%. Our adjusted guidance measures exclude the $13.6 million of first quarter charges and the expected $4 million fourth quarter expense to revert our store layouts and adjusted EPS and adjusted tax rate also exclude the $18 million goodwill impairment charge. A reconciliation is included in today's press release. Let me describe the assumptions behind this guidance. We are not assuming the promotional environment improves, and we are not assuming margin recovery in the fourth quarter.

We are assuming a fourth quarter comparable store sales result of flat to up 2%, supported by drivers that are in place today. The boot assortment as a result since the season opened, localized assortments in our stores, intensified holiday advertising, the return of our rebanner stores to a layout customers find easier to shop in a prior year comparison that eased as the quarter progresses. With that, I will turn the call back to Cliff.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Thank you, Kerry. And before we open the line for questions, I want to thank our teams in our stores, our distribution center and our support centers. They have reset assortments, managed inventory with discipline and given us candid feedback on what our customers want. The decisions we announced today come directly from listening to them and to our customers. Our work is not finished. Our focus for the fourth quarter is execution, the right product in the right stores, a store that is easy to shop and a clear message to the customer. Operator, we are ready for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from Mitch Kummetz with Seaport Research Partners.

Mitch Kummetz: I think I'm going to probably break your rule about the one question and one follow-up. Let me start with Shoe Station. So Cliff, I think you said 131 of the stores are rebannered. What's -- remind me, I don't know if you said it in your prepared remarks, what's the total Shoe Station number right now?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Total Shoe Station?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: 163 as of today.

Mitch Kummetz: So 131 of those are rebannered versus like 32 that were either original or were just new stores, right?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: That is correct.

Mitch Kummetz: Okay. And can you speak a little bit to the -- so Shoe Station comp in the quarter was minus 7.6%. Can you speak to the comp performance of the 131 rebannered stores versus the 32 other non-rebannered stores? I assume those performed better.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: I'll give you -- I can tell you directionally that those stores that were rebannered performed worse than the stores that we originally bought. And Mitch, there's reasoning behind that as we -- on the rebannered stores, again, remember we have to remember always that those rebannered stores were in Shoe Carnival Centers or Shoe Carnival cotenancy, Shoe Carnival customers. And when the decision was made to upgrade the product in those stores, we alienated that Shoe Carnival customer that was there for years. She came in, she looked, she couldn't afford. And basically, that was backed up.

That fact was backed up through our focus groups when the customers within our focus groups told us that we rebannered -- we put a new name on the outside of the store and raised the prices. So I believe -- and again, one of the other things I said in my prepared remarks is that we do believe that Shoe Station is the future for our company and that we can grow that banner in markets that we are currently in and in new markets -- but we can't do that if we continue to operate them as Shoe Station Shoe Carnival stores.

If we change the product to the customer that shops those stores today, they essentially become Shoe Carnival stores with a Shoe Station banner on the outside. We can't operate those stores that way and expect to get the growth that we're looking to get out of Shoe Station. It's a dramatic change. -- but it's a change. It has to be made.

Mitch Kummetz: Yes. And then on the return to the original shelving layout on the 74 stores, when exactly -- I know you said you're doing in the fourth quarter, but when exactly in the fourth quarter? I assume you're going to try to get that done before holiday selling really kicks in? And are you doing it in a way that like that's happening when the stores are closed, so there's no sales disruption in the process?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Yes. We'll send teams in after a store closes. We will not disrupt our sales as we move that. And basically, it's a big deal, and I don't want to downplay it because it is. But as the store closes, a team of many will come in and make the change overnight.

Mitch Kummetz: And again, is that going to happen pretty soon?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: That's going to happen after this week. It will begin the first two weeks of December.

Mitch Kummetz: Okay. And then on boots, can you remind us what your boot penetration is in the fourth quarter and kind of what boot comp is assumed for your overall sort of 0% to 2% comp guide?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Boots represent roughly -- and I need Tanya to back me up on this, but I think it represents roughly 25% of our sales during the quarter. It obviously, a higher percentage of that in women's.

Tanya E. Gordon: That's correct. And Mitch, just to follow up on the -- can you hear me? On the comps that we're expecting, so we were down low singles for the quarter, and we really saw a big shift when the warmer weather hit. When it was cooler and they hit, we saw double-digit comp increases, then slid down when it got warmer. And then right when they -- the cool weather hit about a week ago, we saw double-digit increases in the teens again pop back up. So we are expecting double-digit increases through the fourth quarter.

And everything that we have based on style, penetration of short versus tall, for, all of that is lined up and teed up very well as we go through the fourth quarter, which would give me every confidence that as the weather remains cool, we will enjoy those increases through the fourth quarter.

Mitch Kummetz: And then last question for me. W. Kerry Jackson: Well, we're not going to get specific about next year's margin. But you're correct, the inventory liquidation is that on the excess and aged inventory is basically done at this point in time. Mitch Kummetz: Can you at least say how much of the 500 basis point decline this year was due to the inventory liquidation, which is now basically done?

W. Kerry Jackson: That's not as easy as a number to finitely give to the Street. It was significant, but to try to actually pin that down is difficult, and we're not -- I prefer not to do that.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: Can I just follow up on the -- I just want to walk through the stores very specifically, and then I got a couple of other things. There are 131 rebannered stores, of which 31 are Rogan's. Is that correct?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: 27 are Rogan's.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: Okay. And then those 27 are going to go back to Rogan's, correct?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: That is correct. And Sam, can I interject something there? And we'll get to the rest of your question. It's important that we take the station name and separate it from the stores that are going to be highly promotional for our future growth. So it wasn't 100% necessary for us to take the station name away from Rogan's. But if we want a pure brand that we can grow at higher price points and better product, it doesn't need to be associated with a promotional retailer.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: I completely agree. It's -- I mean, what you're doing is localizing everything and letting the customers know who you are. I'm just trying to get the numbers here. So then you have 104 rebannered stores, of which 77 of those are going to be rebannered as Shoe Carnival or rebannered as back to Shoe Carnival.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Yes, we didn't give an exact number, but your calculator is working really well.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: I didn't even use it for that one. And then does that leave us with 20-some-odd stores that are -- that really belong -- are supposed to be -- that they're in the right place to be Shoe Station? Or are those stores that could just say see you later down the road?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: No. Those -- there may be a couple of those stores that will see you later, okay? But for the most part, those stores are performing well under the Shoe Station banner.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: Okay. So then that leaves us with you're not going to -- you're going to remerchandise and reset up the 77 stores over the next few weeks, correct overnight.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: That is correct.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: In those 77 stores. Now how? The traffic is still going to be a problem? How are you going to let the customers know in the short term that these 77 Shoe Station stores are Shoe Carnival stores, and they have better assortments to take advantage of this? Or is this -- is this just counting on the traffic and is why the comps in Q4 are still going to be -- I mean, I guess the for that stuff is going to be challenging and not get positive. I mean, because it still appears to be those stores will -- the traffic issues in those stores will remain, but you're anticipating the conversions to improve because of that.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: We do expect conversions to improve, but the #1 thing is we're not just going to change the banner on the outside of the store and hope for the best. We are going to market it. And it's a we're back kind of a marketing campaign along with -- we won't be.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: But you're not changing signage until spring, correct?

Samuel (Sam) Poser: The signage. So in the meantime, I understand for spring. I get that for spring. I'm really talking about holiday because in holiday, you're going to have the Shoe Station name with the Shoe Carnival layout and the Shoe Carnival assortment in those stores. So how do you bring more customers to the store in holiday when there's the most traffic. I understand the plan for spring, but can't say we're back with Shoe Station stores.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: That's right. And I apologize for that. But the -- for misunderstanding the question. Here's what we're going to do, Sam, is that we have intensified our advertising for the fourth quarter, television, every aspect that we -- every medium that we normally use, we've intensified the marketing to get customers into both our Shoe Station stores and Shoe Carnival stores. And I -- and when they come into a Shoe Station, what they see as a Shoe Station store, but with a Shoe Carnival layout and Spin 'n Win Wheel, they'll see -- they'll experience the fact that Carnival is coming back. And at that point, our people can communicate.

We'll have the mic going again, and our people will communicate to the customers the change in plans.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: And then I mean, on my math, which is always so good, the -- it looks like sort of on the lower end of your gross margin guidance, which would get the higher cost of sales. I mean, your fourth quarter purchases or like sort of receipts, though there's other stuff in it, are really -- are you planning the fourth quarter receipts down in the $20 million range year-over-year to get to the $50 million lower inventory?

Tanya E. Gordon: Hang on, Sam. I am getting that financial report.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: She wants to give you a good number.

Tanya E. Gordon: I want to give you an accurate number. And yes, you are correct. Receipts are down about $20 million. But a lot of that, Sam, just for clarification, last year was not true spring receipts that were received in fourth quarter. A lot of later receipts came in that hit the fourth quarter number. So we will have, based on where our inventory sits today, that is all new spring-driven receipts. So we will be much better positioned in percent of units and lack of aged inventory this year versus last year. So we will be much better positioned in fresh new inventory to start spring '27.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: And then lastly, when we think about that and we think about as you -- it's not really lastly, I have one more, but as you move into spring, I mean, like the -- I assume that the units of that -- the units -- the average selling prices are higher year-over-year just given the inflation within those receipts. So the units are down more than the dollars, like the $20 million...

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: That would be correct. That would be correct.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: Okay. And then, Kerry, if you -- because you're going to lap the $660,000 refunds in third quarter next year. Why not just back that out for clarity? And if we -- and would the tax rate, if we did back it out, still be in that 63% range if we backed -- if we just added back in the $660,000 in the cost of goods because you're not going to lap that next year.

W. Kerry Jackson: That's correct. There's enough noise in our margins right now. We chose not to back that out and show that as adjusted items, but really focused on the strategic changes we're making in our business like the rebanners, the reflows, items like that. But you can make the argument, but it wouldn't change the overall tax rate significantly because a lot of that excess rate is due to more of the permanent items that are being reflected in there and the lower income against them.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: So if all other things are equal, everything is equal as of right now, nothing changes from the world, except for your actions that you're taking. I mean, how should we think about gross margin recovery into '27? I mean, on the stuff you can control and say the macro is exactly the same. I mean...

W. Kerry Jackson: Well, it's a fair question. And obviously, our margins are depressed because of some of the activities we've had to occur this year. We've underestimated the challenge of what we looked at the beginning of the year, and we're making corrective actions such as the reflow, changing the banners back. We'd like to get through this holiday season where we have a significant increase in advertising. We have to localize assortments and see what the promotional cadence that's going to be necessary to drive traffic in our stores again. And that's the key right there, is we have to increase the traffic, which will drive the sales longer term.

We don't want to underestimate the challenge of that in the fourth quarter, and we'll be in a better position to give better information in March after we go through this holiday season and see the benefits of the actions we've taken.

Operator: Your next question comes from Jim Chartier with Monness, Crespi, and Hardt.

James (Jim) Chartier: I just wanted to kind of talk about the fourth quarter comp guidance, flat to up 2%. It's a pretty significant acceleration from where you were in third quarter. Just aside from what seems like a strong start to November, can you just kind of give us some more details as to what's driving your confidence that the business can inflect that way?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: We announced -- Jim, we announced last quarter that we had increased our marketing spend significantly for the fourth quarter. That marketing spend really kicks in around the first part of December. And we've had a little in November, but it really kicks in around our boot assortment -- around our total assortment to the first week of December. And we have confidence that, that is going to reintroduce ourselves to the customers that have not shopped us over the past year because of the changes that were made with our stores. And we believe that the message that we're giving them will drive them into the store or convince them to give us another shot.

So that's the reason we think in December being the largest month of the quarter, the second largest month of the second half, I believe I'm right on that. And the -- we can drive the customers in the store. We have proven time and time again this year that we can convert them. So we're putting a lot of faith and trust in the promotion -- excuse me, in the marketing spend that we put in place for the fourth quarter.

James (Jim) Chartier: Can you quantify how much you've increased the spend for holiday? And then can you kind of compare that to your back-to-school? Was advertising up for back-to-school? And if so, how does that increase compared to what you're doing for holiday?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: It's about a 50% increase in spend, but it is still somewhat lower than what we spend at back-to-school. And the reason for that is back-to-school is really a six- to eight-week time period where you have to market during the entire time, and it's inserts. It's television. It's digital. It's all-encompassing where this is going to be digital and television. So -- but about a 50% more than a year ago.

James (Jim) Chartier: Okay. And then I thought the plan was to leverage the loyalty program during back-to-school and let some of those lapsed customers know that you had improved -- return the assortment closer to what they were expecting. Was that the case? And if so, how did those customers respond to the e-mails that you sent out?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: We did do exactly that. And the response rate was great. Unfortunately, it didn't show up in the total company as the kind of increases that we were expecting, but we did get a good response rate and a good return, especially on those lapsed customers. They did come back at a pretty good rate, just not strong enough to get the business turned around. And so that -- what we've decided to do was continue that marketing campaign to those lapsed customers. Although being very careful because one of the reasons they're lapsed is because we were over marketed to them. So we've adjusted the cadence of how often we reach out to them.

And again, happy with the return rate on that program. It just wasn't enough yet to tell you that, that turned our business.

Operator: There are no more questions at this time. I'll now turn the call back to Cliff Sifford for closing remarks.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Thank you for joining us today. I hope you all have a great holiday season. We look forward to speaking to you again in March.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#2983. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#2982. BW LPG (BWLP) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record freight rates and trading gains fueled a standout quarter for the fleet.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:12PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

BW LPG (BWLP +1.26%) reported its third quarter results, which management described as one of the strongest periods in company history due to high shipping rates and substantial trading gains. Management stated that geopolitical factors and Panama Canal congestion continue to absorb fleet capacity by forcing longer trade routes around the Cape of Good Hope, which has pushed freight rates to record levels. The company reported that U.S. LPG exports reached all-time highs during the quarter, further increasing ton-mile demand. To capitalize on the current market, management is executing a fleet renewal strategy involving the sale of older vessels at record secondhand prices and the addition of eight Panamax VLGC newbuildings. The company indicated that a robust balance sheet and low leverage supported a dividend payout representing 100% of year-to-date shipping net profit after tax.

Aline Anliker: Good morning, afternoon, evening, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. My name is Aline Anliker, and I'm the Head of Corporate Communications at BW LPG. On behalf of the management team, I'd like to extend a warm welcome to our shareholders, investors, analysts and valued stakeholders joining us for our quarterly earnings presentation. We appreciate you taking the time to be with us and for your continued interest and confidence in our company. With me today are our CEO, Kristian Sorensen; CFO, Samantha Xu; as well as our Head of Investor Relations, Kaia Gaarud. In the next 30 minutes, Kristian and Samantha will walk you through the last quarter's performance, key market developments and our strategic priorities moving forward.

Following the presentation, we will open for a Q&A session. [Operator Instructions] Before we begin, I would like to draw your attention to the legal disclaimers shown on the current slide. Please also note that today's presentation is being recorded. And with that, it is my pleasure to hand over to our CEO, Kristian.

Kristian Sørensen: Thanks, Aline, and hi, everyone. Thanks for joining us as we take you through our third quarter financial results with the company and market events from the quarter. Let's turn to Slide 4, please. The third quarter was again shaped by geopolitics and extensive market inefficiencies. Middle Eastern LPG exports remained well below normal levels, while U.S. LPG exports reached all-time highs and longer trade routes, combined with continued congestion in the Panama Canal absorbed substantial fleet capacity. As a result, the combination of our shipping and LPG trading portfolio made the third quarter one of the strongest quarters in our company's history. I will revisit the market developments in more detail in the market section.

Moving on to the Q3 results. We reported a shipping TCE income of $84,100 per available day and $82,200 per calendar day after IFRS 15, FFA and other adjustments. This includes our fixed and index-linked time charter coverage of 51% of our available days at $54,300 per day. The result is below our guidance of $88,000 per day, primarily due to IFRS 15 and FFA adjustments. The Q3 profit after tax was $359 million with profit attributable to equity holders of USD 311 million. This is equivalent to an EPS of $2.05. This corresponds to an annualized return on equity of 66%.

Our trading business, BW Product Services generated a strong realized trading gain of $146 million during the quarter as well as an unrealized mark-to-market gain of $18 million. The gross profit was $163 million, and the profit after tax was $118 million. And as always, it's important to remember that it is the realized result which generates Product Services dividend capacity. Looking ahead for the fourth quarter, we are guiding on about $102,000 per day fixed for 92% of our available days. This includes our fixed time charter coverage of 43% at $44,200 per day and compares with our all-in cash breakeven reported of $24,900 per day.

Please take a note that our TCE guidance excludes potential IFRS 15 and FFA impacts and the full breakdown of our quarterly time charter days and levels are to be found in the appendix in this presentation. The Board of Directors has declared a dividend of $1.30 per share, representing 92% payout of our shipping NPAT for the quarter and bringing the year-to-date dividend payout to 100% of our shipping NPAT. This is well ahead of the 75% set by our dividend policy given our net leverage ratio at 20% and translates into an annualized dividend yield of 24% based on our share price of $21.70 on Thursday, 19 November. Turning to other events.

In September, we issued a 5-year $300 million senior unsecured convertible bond with a 2.25% coupon to partly finance our newbuilding program of 8 Panamax VLGCs. We also continued to capitalize on the strong secondhand market, and we announced the sale of the 2008-built BW Loyalty at a price in the low $80 million scheduled for delivery before the year-end. Two weeks ago, we also announced the sale of the 2015-built BW Mistral, which joined our fleet as part of the 2024 Avance Gas transaction.

This sale is expected to generate a net book gain of about $37 million and net cash proceeds of approximately $104 million with delivery by mid-January 2027 to the new buyers or to the new owners. It's worthwhile to mention that the vessel has generated a chartering revenue result of more than $58 million since she was delivered 2 years ago. Finally, the sale of the BW Birch and BW Levant, which we announced last quarter, the ships were delivered to the buyers in October and November, respectively. And with that, let's move on to the market overview. Next slide, please. Okay. Let's start with the map on the left.

And structural inefficiencies continue to absorb fleet capacity, pushing freight rates to unprecedented levels. Under normal circumstances, the Middle East to the Far East and the U.S. Gulf to the Far East via the Panama Canal are the 2 key benchmark trades for our market. With the Strait of Hormuz still heavily constrained, Middle Eastern and LPG exports remain well below normal levels and Asian importers and India and Southeast Asia, in particular, are relying heavily on LPG from the U.S. instead. In absolute terms, however, China remained the largest destination for U.S. exports, while Japan remained the second largest as of end of Q3. As a result, the U.S. LPG exports are at all-time highs.

With congestion and delays persisting in the Panama Canal during the third quarter, more of these cargoes sailed a much longer route around the Cape of Good Hope to India and the Far East, significantly increasing ton-mile demand. Moving into the fourth quarter, the canal has continued to operate at close to maximum capacity. And with transit availability uncertain, the dynamics have shifted towards more structural rerouting with vessels increasingly avoiding Panama altogether and planning voyages via the Cape of Good Hope. We're also seeing more ship-to-ship transfers in the Indian Ocean, which tie up additional vessels and further reduces the effective shipping capacity available for loading in the U.S. Gulf.

The chart on the right shows how these factors have played out in freight rates this year. Following the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war, rates firmed significantly, reaching close to $200,000 per day in the spot markets. Back in May, when the U.S -Iran ceasefire MOU was signed, the market priced in a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. Far East arbitrage narrowed and the U.S. Gulf freight softened. As the sustained reopening failed to materialize, U.S. Far East rates recovered through the summer and an increased number of attacks on vessels in September have pushed rates even higher.

Lastly, secondhand asset prices are at record levels as the current elevated rate environment and the situation in the Middle East have pushed vessel values to all-time highs. And as you can see on this slide, we are harvesting value from record high secondhand prices while renewing our fleet at competitive newbuilding levels. The chart on the left shows secondhand values translated into newbuilding equivalent value. And for the vintage built 2007 and 2008, the newbuilding equivalent has increased from around $150 million at the start of the year to about $280 million today. For 2015 and '16-built vessels, it has moved from around $135 million to about $200 million.

And over the same period, newbuilding prices have remained relatively flat at around $116 million to $170 million for Korean yards. And in other words, the market is currently valuing our oldest vessels at more than twice the equivalent price of a newbuilding by adjusting for the vessel age. And we've taken advantage of this through disciplined countercyclical asset plays and this year, we sold the 2007-built BW Elm and BW Birch, the 2008-built BW Loyalty and the 2015-built BW Levant and the BW Mistral while ordering 8 Panamax VLGCs back in May. At the same time, with a more uncertain outlook moving into second half 2027, we continue to follow a balanced chartering strategy to protect the downside.

In Q3, 51% of our available days were covered by time charters with 42% on fixed rates averaging $46,300 per day. For Q4, our coverage is 53% with 43% fixed at $44,200 per day. And for 2027, we have already secured 42% fixed rate coverage, averaging $44,000 per day, which is up from 36% fixed rate coverage at the time of our last quarterly presentation. All of these levels are comfortably above our all-in cash breakeven of about $24,900 per day. And further information on our time charter portfolio can be found in the appendix at the end of the earnings presentation. Next slide, please. Turning to the fleet and the order book.

Newbuilding contracting has been considerable with 108 VLGCs ordered so far in 2026, including our own 8 Panamax vessels. The total order book now stands at 177 VLGCs and yards are offering delivery slots in 2029 and well into 2030. As the delivery schedule on the left shows, 41 VLGCs have been delivered so far this year. We expect an elevated pace of deliveries in the coming years, peaking at around 20 vessels in the fourth quarter of 2029. The global fleet now stands at 451 VLGCs on the water, which is up from 437 as per last reported quarter. At the same time, the fleet continues to age.

And today, 8% of the fleet is 25 years or older and another 5% is between 20 and 25 years of age. By the end of 2030, 127 VLGCs will be 20 years or older compared to 68 vessels at the end of this year. As we said before, the LPG exports will continue to grow and how this order book is absorbed will depend on the inefficiencies in the market, including trade patterns, Panama Canal transits and sailing distances as well as the phaseout of older tonnage. Next slide, please. Finally, let's take a look at the LPG export outlook. And our forecast assumes a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz in 2027.

North American VLGC exports are expected to grow by 17% this year to around 70 million tonnes, cushioning the Middle East shortfall with further growth to around 74 million tonnes in 2028. Middle Eastern VLGC exports are expected to fall to around 18 million tonnes this year, which is 27 million tonnes short of the pre-war forecast. Assuming a reopening, we expect a gradual recovery supported by new projects with a shortfall versus the pre-war forecast narrowing to 20 million tonnes in 2027 and 14 million tonnes in 2028. This is because, as we have mentioned before, it will take time to repair production and export infrastructure and recovery time remains uncertain.

Looking at the middle chart, this graph is taken from Enterprise Products Partners' earnings presentation in October and shows the U.S. NGL production forecasted to grow about 34% from 2025 to 2030, roughly 2.4x the growth rate of crude oil. While crude oil production growth is expected to moderate, rising gas-to-oil ratios and richer gas streams continue to support NGL production growth. And turning to export capacity, close to 30 million tonnes of additional North American LPG export capacity is expected to come online from second half 2026 to second half of 2028. And these expansions will be important in allowing continued growth in U.S. NGL production to translate into higher LPG exports and ultimately increased demand for VLGC shipping.

And to sum up, geopolitics and trade patterns continue to create inefficiencies that absorb shipping capacity, while the medium-term outlook is underpinned by growing North American exports and a gradual recovery of Middle Eastern volumes. The timing of a Hormuz reopening and general Panama Canal congestion remain key wildcards, while the growing pace of newbuilding deliveries increases the uncertainty as we move into 2027. And that concludes our market segment. I guess it's over to you, Samantha.

Samantha Xu: Thank you, Kristian. Hello, everyone. Let's dive into what was an incredible quarter. Our shipping business delivered TCE income of $84,100 per available day or $82,200 per calendar day. This includes negative IFRS 15 and FFA adjustments of USD 14.9 million and USD 20.2 million, respectively. Before these accounting effects, which our guidance excluded, our underlying performance was ahead of guidance. The underlying spot performance was very strong. $115,300 per available day, including waiting time and FFA and USD 123,000 per day, excluding both. That shows the earning quality of our platform in a volatile market. Fleet utilization was 97%, reflecting a very strong execution.

Among the uncertainties, we remain prudent, focusing on downside protection through our time charter portfolio and active FFA risk management. In Q3, 51% of our available days were covered by time charter, out of which 42% were fixed rate time charters. Looking ahead for Q4 2026, we have fixed 92% of the available fleet days at an average rate of about USD 102,000 per day. This also includes index-linked time charter contracts, so the final rate may still move with the spot market. Looking at 2027, we have secured 42% of our portfolio through fixed rate time charter at USD 44,000 per day.

This fixed rate time charter portfolio is expected to generate approximately USD 229 million of revenue in 2027, and that gives us a solid earning visibility while keeping our exposure to a strong spot market. Coming to Product Services performance. Product Services delivered an exceptional realized trading gain of USD 146 million in Q3, a great achievement in a turbulent market. The reported result also includes a net realized (sic) [ unrealized ] mark-to-market gain of USD 80 million (sic) [ USD 18 million ], representing USD 82 million increase on cargo positions, partly offset by USD 65 million decrease on paper positions. Gross profit was USD 163 million.

After G&A and tax, profit after tax was USD 118 million with the net asset value arrived at USD 216 million at quarter end. The realized result shows the value of our integrated cargo, paper and shipping platform. The unrealized mark-to-market movements simply reflects valuations at a balance sheet date and can swing in volatile markets until positions are realized. As such, trading gains and losses are realized across different periods and cannot be extrapolated from past performance. It's also worth noting that the reported net asset value excludes the unrealized physical shipping position of USD 170 million at the balance sheet date based on the internal valuation.

In Q3, our average VaR value at risk was USD 18 million, reflecting continued market volatility and the added cargo from our term contracts. We expect the VaR to stay elevated as the market remains volatile and our term contract book builds from late 2026 into 2027. Turning to our financial highlights. We reported net profit after tax of USD 359 million. Profit attributable to equity holder was $311 million or $2.05 per share, representing an annualized earning yield of 33% based on the period-end share price. This includes a one-off gain from the sale of a BW Elm. We reported a net leverage ratio of 20% in Q3, down from the 23.5% at the end of Q2 '26.

The Board declared a dividend of $1.30 per share. That is 92% of shipping NPAT for the quarter and brings the year-to-date payout to 100% of shipping NPAT. Measured against the total profit to equity holders, it is a 63% payout for the quarter. Product Services profit is evaluated for distribution only after the financial year-end. Our dividend policy is 75% payout ratio when leverage ratio is at or above 20%. At 100% of year-to-date shipping NPAT, we are well ahead of that. This reflects our strong performance, solid liquidity position and our confidence in the near-term market.

We continue to take a forward-leaning approach to return earnings to shareholders in this strong market, while strengthening our balance sheet for fleet renewal and growth. At period end, the shareholders' equity was $2.3 billion. Annualized return on equity was 66% and return on capital employed 53%. Q3 OpEx was $8,800 per day. For 2026, we expect operating cash breakeven of about $18,300 per day for the owned fleet and $21,700 per day for the total fleet, including chartering vessels. All-in cash breakeven, including maintenance and dry dock CapEx is about $24,900 per day. In September, we issued USD 300 million of 5-year senior unsecured convertible bond with a 2.25% coupon and a 40% conversion premium.

The proceeds fund predelivery cost of our newbuilding and further strengthens our liquidity. As a result, we maintained a strong liquidity of USD 859 million at the quarter end, consisting of USD 317 million in cash and -- sorry, USD 542 million of undrawn revolving credit facilities. Our repayment profile remains long dated with the bulk of our repayments, including the convertible bonds, fall beyond 2030. In Product Services, trade finance utilization was USD 331 million or 44% of our available credit line, including drawn amounts and letter of credit. This leaves ample headroom for future trading needs. A brief word on the accounting for the convertible bond, which is new for some of us.

Most of the noncash interest is capitalized into the newbuilding while they are under construction. So the effect on earnings is limited. On a fully diluted basis, the bond lowers EPS by about $0.03 per share. Slide 24 sets out the details, and we are happy to take questions on it as well. To sum up, the past quarter has been one of the strongest quarter in our history across both shipping and trading. A strong balance sheet with USD 859 million of liquidity and net leverage of 20%. 100% year-to-date shipping NPAT returned to shareholders while we fund our fleet renewals. And with that, I hope you find the updates satisfactory and informative.

Thank you for listening, and back to you, Aline.

Aline Anliker: [Operator Instructions] Thank you, Samantha. Thank you, Kristian. We would now like to open the call for questions.

Eirik Haavaldsen: So just on the time charter book, you've added a little bit, but not that much. I mean time charter rates have been not necessarily mirroring kind of the spot rate trend as far as at least I've seen. What do you see there? And what will it sort of take for you to add more longer-term coverage, I suppose? I know it's been wrong to do so up until now, but what do you see there?

Kristian Sørensen: Eirik, thanks for the question. We have an aim to protect the downside, as you know, by securing time charters over time. And we -- when we look at the opportunities in the market at the moment, we don't really regard the short-term time charters of 1 year being very lucrative because they are priced, let's say, in the $80,000, maybe $90,000 per day range, which is and the duration is basically 4 round voyages from the U.S. to the Far East. And I think with the relative good visibility we have into 2027, we don't really find the short long-term time charters too attractive.

What we do try to develop is and find attractive is time charters with delivery a little bit further into 2027 and 3-year plus, which we believe is over time, giving us the downside protection that we're looking for and also buffering out the volatility in the market. So you can probably expect us to continue trying to develop time charters of that duration if you find it attractive. And I think we have a history for trying to lock in these time charters when the opportunity arises.

Eirik Haavaldsen: And then the second one, I mean, with the recent -- or the latest vessel sales, I mean, your cash position is exceptional. You have very modest debt levels overall and your trading business continues to do well. So I mean, in recent years, I think you've typically topped up a little bit on your dividend in the fourth quarter with proceeds from trading. Is there any reason not to expect that this year? And can you give any color on how the trading division has done so far in the fourth quarter? I mean, it's a volatile market.

Kristian Sørensen: Well, it's always difficult for the management to make a statement of the future dividends. But like you say, we have a history for topping up the Q4 dividends with some of the profit from Product Services. So I guess it's not unlikely that the same will come up for consideration this time as well. Samantha, anything you'd like to add on that comment?

Samantha Xu: I think it's a very well said, Kristian and I also agree as well. And if you look at our history, we tend to evaluate the dividend capacity after the financial year ends where we will have a better visibility and conclusion of our Product Services realized result performance at which point we will be evaluating for the dividend distribution capacity and amount.

Kristian Sørensen: And on the performance so far in the fourth quarter, I think it's fair to say that we can see that the performance is pretty steady, and we will revert and return with an update as per usual as that would be by mid-January, wouldn't it, Samantha, next time with the trading update.

Eirik Haavaldsen: Okay. Finally, and one on the market. I mean we've seen Asian propane prices are kind of decoupling a little bit from oil prices, and you see U.S. inventories are -- have gone from kind of being much higher than a year ago and now on par with last year, obviously, still at a very elevated level. With the reopening of Hormuz and more volumes through out of the Middle East, would that be a positive or negative for your market now?

Kristian Sørensen: Sorry, a positive or negative in terms of shipping demand from the U.S. Gulf, you mean or the...

Eirik Haavaldsen: Or in general for the market because I guess that would put pressure on Asian prices and then the arb would be pressured. And how do you see this -- I mean, it's the -- is the current -- I mean, obviously, it's hard to argue that the current situation is not a very blue sky scenario. But how do you see this proceeding maybe if you?

Kristian Sørensen: So I believe we could see how the market dynamics unfolded back in May, June when you had the expectations of a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and you could -- like you point to, you can see that the U.S. Far East spread narrowed and slowed down the activity out of the U.S. Gulf, while the Middle Eastern activity and spot rates for shipping also increased on the expectations of more volumes and higher shipping capacity out of the Middle East Gulf. So I think we have seen how the market dynamics most likely will unfold.

And then eventually, in the short term and then eventually, what happened was that the 2 markets will, at one point, balance themselves out, right, and recalibrate. So in the medium term, this will fall back to where we came from before the war where the 2 basins, Middle East and the U.S. Gulf were basically trading around the same TCE level. But I think in the short term, it's not unlikely that we will see activity in the U.S. Gulf coming off, while Middle East activity will pick up significantly. And then it will balance out as we move further out. If it's 1 or 2 quarters, it's hard to say.

One thing which is important to remember, Eirik, is that the U.S. LPG export volumes, they are -- they really need the outlet in Asia to -- because the European and Latin American markets are not big enough to absorb the massive production volumes that Americans are having at the moment. And as the export volumes continue to increase from the U.S. and North America, we believe that there is really no other home for these volumes than the big markets east of Suez. So that will, over time, continue to drive demand for shipping in the U.S. Gulf and North America in general and underpin a long-haul trade, which we are also seeing in the current market.

Aline Anliker: Thank you, Eirik. Do we have any more questions? I don't see any in the chat. No one has raised his or her hand so far.

Kristian Sørensen: I could just add one thing to Eirik's question on the time charter portfolio because we, as before, also want to maintain a significant exposure to the spot market. So it's not like we will increase the time charter coverage dramatically in the future because we believe it's very important for us to maintain the exposure and the upside because the upside potential in the spot market has proven to be quite phenomenal. So just to add to my comment to Eirik's question earlier.

Aline Anliker: Jostein, if you would like to unmute yourself.

Kristian Sørensen: It's a reflection of longer duration time charters in the -- which is in the matrix as that you referred to.

Jostein Aschjem: Yes. And do you have any flavor to add on the '28 coverage? You have announced some longer duration contract before, but any sort of percentage coverage rate on '28, '29 or so you can add?

Kristian Sørensen: Let me say that we can probably revert on that in the next quarterly update. So -- because then we have 2026 behind us, and then we can extend the matrix to also include 2028. I think that's the best way of doing it.

Jostein Aschjem: Yes. Maybe lastly, you used to have this FFA share of coverage in your presentation, and that seems to not be included this time. Are you done with the FFAs for '26? Or do you have more for Q4 and potentially also into '27 as well?

Kristian Sørensen: So '27, we have no FFA coverage. For Q4, we have the same 3%, isn't it? It is equivalent to one ship approximately. Yes. So it's stable from the third quarter into the fourth, I'm as far as I can recall. Yes. But for 2027, we don't have any FFA paper booked.

Aline Anliker: Any more questions? No, it doesn't look like. Well, then this concludes BW LPG's quarter 3 2026 earnings presentation. And a replay of the webcast, together with the call transcript will be made available on our website shortly. Thanks a lot, everyone, for joining us today and for your continued interest in BW LPG. We greatly value the time you've spent with us, and we look forward to seeing you again next quarter. Have a great rest of your day. Thank you.
