#2972. I Rate Buy Now, Pay Later Apps; Here’s My Holiday Advice

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

“Buy now, pay later” can help stretch your holiday budget further, but pick your BNPL app carefully and avoid loan stacking.

Head of Content, Personal & Student Loans

As Americans compile their shopping lists ahead of the holiday season, I’ve been compiling my own kind of list — a list of 25 data points, gathered across six “buy now, pay later” (BNPL) apps, fed into a rubric of five categories and 22 subcategories, to produce a star rating for each app.

It’s a big list. I check it twice (or 10 times).

By the end, I know more about these apps than anyone should, and I’m eager to bestow my knowledge on the next unsuspecting person who utters “Klarna” in my vicinity.

I should have plenty of opportunities this year. Nearly 2 in 5 holiday spenders (38%) plan to use BNPL, according to NerdWallet’s holiday spending report. Concerningly, the same report found that a higher share of BNPL users expect they won’t be able to make their payments in full and on time compared to credit card users.

Using BNPL for holiday shopping isn’t inherently bad, but there are risks, including sneaky fees and the ease of loan stacking across many providers.

Here’s how to minimize those risks and set yourself up for success this holiday season.

Brenton Harrison, a certified financial planner in Nashville, says many of his clients are turning to buy now, pay later in the “messy middle of life,” when everyday expenses are high and budgets are tight. This is especially true during the holidays.

“They have kids they're providing for, or they’re trying to go travel and see family,” Harrison says. “When those expenses pile up, it can be very attractive to be able to spread out payments.”

Since BNPL divides your total purchase into smaller installments, typically due every two weeks, it feels easier on your cash flow than having to pay all at once.

While Harrison is open to his clients using BNPL, he emphasizes how important it is to understand the terms before opting in. BNPL apps only require a soft credit pull and a short application. When you can apply for a loan in just a few clicks, it’s easy to miss when payments are due or whether they’ll include interest.

But if clients understand the terms and are certain they can make the payments, Harrison says BNPL's set repayment schedule can be a better option than more open-ended financing.

“With a credit card, [a holiday purchase] might be something that they buy over and over and over again, because that interest just continues to accrue over time, and they never pay it off,” he says.

Not all BNPL apps are created equal. I measure the top apps across multiple categories, but I weigh affordability the highest. My thinking is if you’re already strapped for cash, it’s a bad idea to pay extra just to break up the payments.

There are providers, like Affirm and PayPal, that don’t charge interest with a common pay-in-four term (your total purchase, divided into four installments). They also charge no fees, including no late fees for missed payments.

Compare that to apps, like Sezzle and Zip, that may charge an automatic service or origination fee with your first installment, as well as late fees.

Long-term BNPL financing, which can stretch months or even years, usually includes interest, expressed as an annual percentage rate or APR. This is a more expensive payment option than a zero-interest pay-in-four.

Pay close attention to your checkout screen to see what you’re offered. Are the installment amounts equal or is the first installment higher than the others? That may mean there’s a fee. Do you see an APR listed? That means you’re paying interest.

Harrison points out that just because a store partners with a BNPL company doesn’t mean that’s your only option. Download a different BNPL app, search for the store and see if you get access to better terms, like a 0% offer.

Taking out multiple loans with different BNPL providers is known as “loan stacking,” and it’s risky.

Because you’re juggling different payment amounts due on different days, it’s hard to keep track of what’s coming out of your bank account. This is especially true if you set up automatic payments, which most BNPL apps require. If you overdraw your checking account, your bank will likely charge a fee.

According to research published in August by the Federal Reserve, 11% percent of BNPL users had a BNPL payment trigger an overdraft or nonsufficient funds fee from their bank in the prior year. People with less savings were even more likely to pay fees.

Before applying for multiple BNPL loans, look at a typical month of expenses and ask if there’s extra room in your budget for those payments, Harrison says.

“If you’re just assuming that because you’re spreading it out that you’ll be able to pay it, that's where I think people can get in trouble,” he says. “They set it and forget it, and they don't realize, ‘Oh, I am in no better position to pay that next month than I am this month, or I have three of these going at the same time, and collectively, it's more than I can manage.’”

Most apps send payment reminders, so you can potentially reschedule the payment or change your payment method.

Still, it’s best to avoid the headache to begin with. If you’re feeling pressured to spend more this holiday season, communicate your limits clearly with loved ones, Harrison says, and avoid any loans you can’t comfortably repay.

“Think about the purchase itself, especially around the holidays,” he says. “There's a big difference between something that I can pay off over three months and something that I should have never been buying in the first place.”

#2971. Eli Lilly vs. Novo Nordisk: Not Every GLP-1 Maker Is Enjoying Booming Sales Trends

Eli Lilly's quarterly sales have outpaced Novo Nordisk's since late 2024, with the gap widening sharply through 2026. Here is how the numbers stack up.

By Brendan Coffey – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Eli Lilly ›

Eli Lilly & Co. (LLY +3.15%) makes medicines for diabetes, obesity, and cancer for a wide range of people.

It won approval for Mounjaro to reduce cardiovascular risk on Aug. 28. It started building an active pharmaceutical ingredient site in Pennsylvania on Nov. 12.

Novo Nordisk (NVO +2.99%) makes treatments for diabetes, obesity, and rare blood disorders.

It raised its full-year guidance for adjusted sales and operating profit on Nov. 4. It filed for Wegovy approval in younger children on Nov. 16.

Revenue here refers to the data provider's standardized income-statement revenue line item. A rise or fall in revenue shows if a business is growing.

Eli Lilly vs. Novo Nordisk Revenue over the last 8 quarters. Figures: Novo Nordisk shown in U.S. dollars, converted from Danish kroner.

The revenue trend is the most obvious metric for investors to examine when considering a stock. The first thing to check for when examining a company's revenue trend is seasonality: some times of the year have stronger buying patterns than others. There usually is some seasonality for every business.

Even in pharmaceuticals, there is seasonality, with the end of the calendar year seeing higher prescription activity as consumers and doctors front-load prescriptions after insurance deductibles have been met, before they reset with the new year.

This chart shows some seasonality, like that for Eli Lilly, with the first quarter of 2025 showing a decline from the last period of 2024. Novo Nordisk shows the same trend, but as we move from left to right on the chart, we see that Lilly's sequential revenue is increasing, while Novo's is choppy. That doesn't necessarily mean Novo Nordisk's business is in trouble, but it does show us Eli Lilly is firing on all cylinders.

Data source: Financial Modeling Prep. Novo Nordisk's figures are converted from Danish kroner to U.S. dollars. Data as of Nov. 20, 2026.

#2970. Etihad’s New Credit Cards Are Primarily for Status Chasers

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

The new cards offer perks like faster paths to status and elevated earning rates when purchasing tickets with partners.

Etihad Guest, the loyalty program of Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways, is expanding its U.S. presence by introducing two new credit cards. Most people won’t get much value from these cards, but they can make sense for Etihad frequent flyers who want elite status.

The two cards are the Etihad Guest Visa Signature® Card ($99 annual fee) and the Etihad Guest Premier Visa Signature® Card ($499 annual fee). Issued by the First National Bank of Omaha, both offer faster pathways to earning and maintaining elite status and the ability to earn extra miles on Etihad purchases.

They also offer extra miles on international transactions (neither has foreign transaction fees) and purchases with Etihad’s partner airlines, which include U.S. carriers like American Airlines and JetBlue Airways.

Here’s what you need to know about the cards.

The Etihad Guest Visa Signature® Card comes with a $99 annual fee, and it earns Etihad Guest miles at the following rates:

3 miles per $1 spent on Etihad purchases.

2 miles per $1 spent on Etihad partner airline purchases.

2 miles per $1 spent on non-U.S. purchases.

1 mile per $1 spent on all other U.S. purchases.

Welcome offer: Through Feb. 3, 2027, the card is offering the following welcome offer for new applicants: Earn up to 40,000 welcome Etihad Guest Miles, including 10,000 miles after the first purchase and an additional 30,000 miles after spending $3,000 within the first three billing cycles after account opening.

Elite status benefits: You’ll also get Etihad Silver status after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days of opening your account. Unlike most airlines, that entry-level status is enough to get you into the business class lounge when traveling through Etihad’s hub at Abu Dhabi’s Zayed International Airport.

You can retain that status by spending $20,000 a year on the card, or $3,000 a year on Etihad purchases.

The Etihad Guest Premier Visa Signature® Card comes with a $499 annual fee, and it earns Etihad Guest miles at the following rates:

5 miles per $1 spent on Etihad purchases.

3 miles per $1 spent on Etihad partner airline purchases.

2 miles per $1 spent on non-U.S. purchases.

1 mile per $1 spent on all other U.S. purchases.

The only differences in rewards between the premium and standard cards are increased earning rates for eligible airline purchases.

Welcome offer: Through Feb. 3, 2027, the premium card offers a higher welcome offer compared to the standard card: Earn up to 60,000 welcome Etihad Guest Miles, including 20,000 miles after the first purchase and 40,000 miles after spending $7,000 within the first three billing cycles after account opening.

Elite status benefits: The premium card offers a faster track to elite status: automatic Silver status upon card approval and Gold status after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days of opening your account.

To maintain Gold status, you’ll need to spend $40,000 a year on the card, or $8,000 on Etihad purchases. Otherwise, you’ll have Silver status.

Wi-Fi benefit: After your first Etihad purchase, you’ll get 3,000 Etihad Guest miles, enough to cover Wi-Fi costs on a long-haul Etihad flight. You’ll then get those miles again after each cardholder anniversary.

Travel benefits: The card offers a statement credit for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck and select travel protections. If you already have a premium travel card, you might already have access to these perks.

The card also includes a Priority Pass lounge access membership. However, an Etihad spokesperson told NerdWallet that it’s the entry-level membership tier, so you’ll need to pay for yourself and guests each time you visit a Priority Pass lounge. Most premium credit cards in the U.S. that offer Priority Pass allow complimentary visits for at least the cardholder.

The Etihad cards make the most sense for Etihad’s frequent flyers who are flying to or connecting through Abu Dhabi several times a year.

That’s because the standard card’s accelerated pathway to Etihad Guest’s Silver status tier can unlock the ability to choose business class lounge access in Abu Dhabi as a status perk.

With the premium card, you get a fast track to Gold. If you select lounge access as a Gold status perk, you can not only bring a guest on the same flight into the lounge, but also access Etihad’s worldwide lounge network. That includes Etihad’s own lounges in New York and Washington, D.C., as well as most partner lounges at other Etihad destinations.

Bear in mind that while Etihad has many partnerships with other airlines, it’s not part of an alliance, so you don’t get lounge benefits when traveling on partners. You’ll need to be flying on an Etihad-operated flight to get into the lounge.

If you primarily fly with other carriers, then Etihad status will have limited upside for you.

However, the Priority Pass lounge membership that comes with the premium card does not have that restriction. You can access Priority Pass lounges while flying on any airline, although you’ll need to pay an additional per-person $35 fee each visit.

The earning rates on the Etihad cards are lackluster for everyday spenders. The bonus categories are for airline purchases with Etihad and its partners, as well as international spending.

That means your day-to-day purchases at home, like groceries, dining out and gas, earn only 1 mile per $1 spent.

Plus, there are more ways to earn Etihad Guest miles than spending on an Etihad credit card. For example, you can transfer points to Etihad Guest from Bilt Rewards, Capital One and Citi ThankYou.

Those programs offer cards that typically have better benefits and bonus categories, and they offer flexibility on how you can use your points and miles. With an Etihad card, you can only earn Etihad Guest miles, which expire after 18 months without qualifying flight activity. (If you’re not traveling on Etihad or its partners at least once every 18 months, then you definitely should not get the cards.)

One of the most interesting perks of the new cards is the bonus category for spending with Etihad partner airlines — 2 miles per $1 for the standard card and 3 miles per $1 for the premium version. Typically, airline credit cards reward customers only for spending on the airline, not partners.

There are better cards available, though. Some offer as many or even more points per $1 on flights purchased directly from airlines.

If you want the card solely to earn more Etihad Guest miles, then the answer for most people is no.

While you can earn more miles for purchases with Etihad and partner airlines, the earning rates aren’t attractive enough to justify the annual fees, especially when compared with existing cards with currencies that transfer to Etihad Guest.

Status chasers could benefit from the fast track to elite status — but you would need to be a fairly frequent Etihad flyer to really take advantage of your elite benefits.

You want a travel credit card that prioritizes what’s important to you. Here are some of the best travel credit cards of 2026:

Flexibility, point transfers and a large bonus: Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card

No annual fee: Wells Fargo Autograph® Card

Flat-rate travel rewards: Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card

Bonus travel rewards and high-end perks: Chase Sapphire Reserve®

Luxury perks: American Express Platinum Card®

Business travelers: Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card

#2969. Conferenza Gattuso: "Taylor vede cose che gli altri non vedono. Supercoppa? Per me è un regalo"

Il mister Gennaro Gattuso ha rilasciato delle dichiarazioni in conferenza stampa poco dopo il fischio finale di Lazio-Lecce

Il mister Gennaro Gattuso ha rilasciato delle dichiarazioni in conferenza stampa poco dopo il fischio finale di Lazio-Lecce

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Mancano otto punti per fare la prima festa. Per il resto ne parleremo quando amncano 8-9 partite. Stupito sì, ma per la mentalità. I primi 15 minuti di oggi non sono andati benissimo, dopo molto meglio, abbiamo sofferto un po' sui nostri calci piazzati a favore. Eravamo un po' piantati sulle seconde palle. Secondo tempo molto orgogliosi della mentalità, della prestazione, non li abbiamo fatti respirare. Era da un po' di tempo che sbagliavamo sempre i secondi tempi, a questo giro siamo stati sul pezzo e li abbiamo messi in grandissima difficoltà.

Gattuso avrà un merito su quel che sta facendo la Lazio? Per come lavorano in allenamento. Ieri ero tranquillo, oggi abbiamo messo in campo Diogo, Pedraza,. La tranquillità me la danno i dati, il senso di appartenenza. Mi prendo questo merito: aver fatto diventare in pochissimo tempo questa squadra una famiglia.

Io ho giocato con otto palloni d'oro nella mia carriera. Taylor vede cose che gli altri non vedono. Gli altri avrebbero tirato di piattone, io sinceramente già lo stavo mandando a quel paese. Nel mio modo di pensare il calcio, quella giocata non m'è passata neanche per l'anticamera del cervello. Dico Rui Costa, dai.

Frattesi? Io non ho salvato la vita a nessuno. Lui è un capoccione, esagera sempre. Ha bisogno d'affetto, come tanti giocatori. Ha bisogno anche di prendere le mazzate nei denti, vuol giocare come dice lui. Il merito su quel che sta facendo è suo. Sono contento che abbia fatto gol di sinistro. Sono contento di tutti, sono felice di allenarli. Oggi mi dispiace che Dele abbia fatto 11 minuti, meriterebbe molto di più. Tanti altri meriterebbero di fare qualche minuto in più, si allenano in un modo incredibile.

Isaksen? Dentro non si passava oggi, dovevamo andare in verticale. L'abbiamo fatto pochissime volte, e quelle poche volte siamo rusciti a mettere pensiero. Anche Noslin oggi a livello tecnico ha sbagliato tanto. Isaksen è un piacere lavorare con lui, ha risolto i suoi problemi. Quest'estate l'abbiamo perso per un po', è un giocatore che riesce a fare delle cose in velocità. Ha la terza marcia con la palla al piede. Ha preso gusto a far gol, e anche a far assist. Ha fatto una partita incredibile anche con la Danimarca.

Supercoppa?  Per me è un regalo, io non c'entro nulla. Non è un impiccio, anzi. È una coppa. Manca un mese, pensa se possiamo pensare alla coppa. Quando arriverà, ci penseremo. Stai lì, provi a giocartela, giochi contro una squadra che sta dettando legge. Adesso recuperiamo due giorni e poi da martedì iniziano a preparare la sfida contro il Torino.

Qual è il segreto di questa Lazio? Noi proponiamo, però chi propone deve avere dall'altra parte gente che ci crede fortemente. Quando il giocatore la pensa in maniera diversa, lì viene il difficile. Bisogna esser bravi a fargli capire perché vogliamo fare determinate cose. Siamo stati bravi noi, sono bravi loro quando facciamo i lavori individuali. Con tutta questa organizzazione che abbiamo messo giù, loro si trovano bene. Noi proponiamo e per il momento tutto sta andando bene. La base di tutto è il lavoro: se vuoi giocare in questo modo qui, la fatica ti deve rimanere nella testa. A parlare è facile, non basta.

#2968. Dollar Tree (DLTR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Traffic-led comps rose as multiprice items gained ground, though tariffs muddied EPS.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:38PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Dollar Tree (DLTR +11.18%) reported third quarter results featuring traffic-led comparable store sales growth and the expansion of its multiprice merchandising strategy. Management stated that the company is experiencing increased frequency from middle and higher-income households as it broadens its assortment of national brands and larger pack sizes. The company indicated it is utilizing five cost mitigation levers to manage ongoing inflationary pressures in freight, fuel, and product costs. For the fourth quarter, management expects momentum to continue through the holiday season despite a cautious consumer spending environment.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the Dollar Tree Q3 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] It's now my pleasure to turn the call over to your host, Daniel Delrosario, Senior Vice President, Investor Relations and Treasurer. Please go ahead, sir.

Daniel Delrosario: Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Dollar Tree's Third quarter Fiscal 2026 Results. With me today are Dollar Tree's CEO, Mike Creedon; and CFO, Stewart F. Glendinning. Before we begin, I would like to remind everyone that some of the remarks that we will make today about the company's expectations, plans and future prospects are considered forward-looking statements under the safe harbor provision of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties, which could cause actual results to differ materially from those contemplated by our forward-looking statements.

Also during this call, we will discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures.

Reconciliations of these non-GAAP items to the most directly comparable GAAP financial measures are provided in today's earnings release available on the IR section of our website. These non-GAAP measures are not intended to be a substitute for GAAP results. Unless otherwise stated, we will refer to our financial results on a non-GAAP basis. Additionally, unless otherwise stated, all discussions today refer to our results from continuing operations and all comparisons discussed today for the third quarter of fiscal 2026 are against the same period a year ago. Please note that a supplemental slide deck outlining selected operating metrics is available on the IR section of our website.

Following our prepared remarks, Mike and Stewart will take your questions. [Operator Instructions] And with that, I'll turn the call over to Mike.

Michael Creedon: Thanks, Daniel, and good morning, everyone. I want to start by recognizing our associates across Dollar Tree and the work they do every day. Their focus on the fundamentals of retail execution and enhancing our customer experience is making a real difference in our stores, and it shows in our results. The third quarter was another strong proof point for Dollar Tree. Total sales grew 6.9%. Comparable store sales increased 4.6%, exceeding our expectations. Traffic grew 3.8%, compared with 0.4% in the second quarter, while average ticket increased 0.8%. The composition of our growth is encouraging. Traffic is accelerating as our assortment, store execution and marketing come together to strengthen our appeal to customers.

A broader assortment helps shoppers meet more of their needs in one trip. Stronger store execution delivers a better and more consistent shopping experience and new marketing expands awareness of the value, convenience and discovery Dollar Tree offers every day. We are also pleased with the underlying profitability of the business. Our results reflect progress on controllable operating drivers as we sharpen merchandise value, manage transportation and other cost pressures and make targeted reinvestments. Stewart will walk through the financial results and the impact of tariff-related items in a moment. In August, we described our focus on a more relevant assortment, improved store execution and stronger customer connections.

Our third quarter performance provides further evidence that this approach is driving results. Our priority now is to drive continued progress. Let me spend a moment on the health of our consumer and how we serve them in all economic environments. As we said in August, consumers are under pressure, and they are increasingly selective about where and how they spend. When under pressure, shoppers prioritize value and buy closer to need. They are also more selective with their purchases. And when customers make those choices, more of them are choosing Dollar Tree. You could see that in our results.

Our consumables comp accelerated to 8.9% as customers look for ways to stretch their budgets, save on everyday essentials and gravitated to our improved overall assortment. We saw broad-based strength with standout performances in snacks, beverages and personal care. Discretionary comp sales increased 0.4% year-over-year despite higher inflation pressuring customer budgets and driving purchases closer to need. While Halloween was modestly below our plan, sell-through was up from last season. Customers bought closer to need and our Dollar Tree associates were ready for the surge in sales throughout the week leading up to the Halloween holiday.

Whether customers are looking to stretch their household budgets with exceptional value on everyday essentials or celebrate special occasions with affordable discretionary and seasonal items, Dollar Tree offers compelling value across a broad range of needs and occasions. That's the power of our model. We strive to balance our $2 or below opening price points with our multi-price points and to balance our consumable and discretionary categories so that we offer multiple ways to meet all customers where they are across all economic cycles. Dollar Tree is built for times like these because when every dollar matters, value matters more. Our job is to earn the trip with unbeatable value, convenience and thrill-of-the-hunt discovery.

Multi-price continues to lead Dollar Tree's evolution. It enables us to broaden our assortment and help customers complete more of their shopping in a single trip. It also gives us more flexibility to delight them with our exciting shopping experience. Our opening price points remain the foundation of our value proposition. Multi-price builds on that foundation by allowing us to offer bigger pack sizes and national brands. It also enables us to offer complementary products and new categories that simply weren't possible under a single price model, and customers continue to respond favorably. Multi-price represented 18% of sales in the third quarter, up about 300 basis points from last year.

But more important is how customers are shopping across price points. Mixed baskets, which combine multi-price and opening price point items, accounted for approximately 25% of the transactions, but nearly half of our sales. These baskets were more than 2.5x the size of an opening price point basket. That tells us something important. Customers continue to rely on our opening price points while adding multi-price items that deliver exceptional value and help them accomplish more in a single trip. So we continue to deliver the entry price point deep value assortment our core customers expect from us while expanding our selection of higher price point items that offer even greater value and make Dollar Tree a more convenient shop.

Let's turn to 2 areas that will play an increasingly important role in driving traffic and frequency: better stores and better customer connection. It starts in the store with shoppability. We are raising our expectations for execution and making it easier for our teams to deliver against them every day. Clean, bright, inviting stores, full shelves, clear prices and strong seasonal execution are fundamental to the customer experience. We are simplifying routines, sharpening accountability and directing investments towards the stores where we see the greatest opportunity. The goal is straightforward: turn every trip we earn into an experience that brings customers back more often. We're also sharpening how we communicate Dollar Tree's value and expanded assortment to our customers.

Our assortment has evolved significantly, and our marketing is bringing that evolution to life, showing customers the value, convenience and discovery that they can find in our stores every day. As you've likely seen, our first national marketing campaign builds on that opportunity, broadening our reach and giving customers more reasons to visit Dollar Tree more often. We see marketing becoming a bigger and more important part of our growth strategy. Over time, we expect to invest more in building awareness, strengthening our connection with customers and driving more frequent visits to Dollar Tree. One year ago, at our Analyst Day, we laid out our strategy for Dollar Tree's new era and the priorities that would guide our execution.

One year in, the report card is encouraging. Now let's take a closer look at the progress we've made against those commitments. First, let's consider merchandising. We committed to using our shelf space more efficiently to deliver a more relevant assortment and stronger sales and margin productivity. We have made tangible progress on that front. Specifically, we've expanded multi-price 300 basis points to 18% of sales, while preserving the opening price point value that defines Dollar Tree. We've built larger baskets across price points, where mixed baskets represented about 25% of transactions, but nearly half our sales in the third quarter.

We've improved sales per foot to $244 from $236 last year as we reallocate shelf space toward more productive categories. And we've increased inventory turns over 12%, supporting a fresher customer-facing assortment and more efficient use of working capital. We have also broadened our marketing capabilities, including the recent launch of our It's All In The Tree national campaign to build awareness of how Dollar Tree is evolving. Second, on operations, we committed to raising store standards and building a more productive and consistent operating model. We've strengthened execution through GOLD with clearer standards, consistent assessments and coaching to improve store conditions and the customer experience. We've reduced shrink, contributing to improved gross margin.

We've improved distribution center throughput and cost efficiency. And we've invested in 3,000 refreshes and renovations across our existing fleet, creating brighter, cleaner and more inviting stores. We are also implementing workforce modernization, which will transform how we manage staffing in our stores. Together, these efforts support comparable sales growth and operating efficiencies. Third, our strategy is driving strong financial performance. We are also generating strong free cash flow and returning capital to shareholders. Over the last 12 months, we've returned over $1.6 billion to shareholders, representing an 8% share count reduction at an average price of $109. That's on top of the 7% last year at an average price of $88.

So one year in, the report card is encouraging. We are delivering against the strategy, building a stronger operating foundation and seeing that progress translate into strong financial performance. There is more opportunity ahead of us, particularly in driving greater consistency across the fleet, continuing to make progress on SG&A and navigating an inflationary cost environment. The path from here is clear: execute with greater consistency, keep raising the bar and build on the progress we've made over the past year. Now let's turn to the tariff refund reinvestments and our outlook.

We have been deliberate about reinvesting tariff refunds in ways that support our customers and growth strategy, $1 price points that deliver value and excitement, marketing that builds awareness and drives higher trip frequency and improved store conditions that deliver the experience our customers deserve every time they shop. As we develop our plans for next year, we are evaluating which initiatives warrant continued support based on customer response and financial returns. Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, we are encouraged by the underlying momentum in the business, particularly the improvement in traffic. At the same time, we recognize the risk from continued inflationary pressure on our customers, higher fuel and freight costs and product cost inflation.

We are using our 5 levers of cost mitigation to address those pressures while protecting customer value. As we think about 2027, we continue to see runway in the initiatives we outlined at Investor Day, a more relevant assortment, more consistent store execution and a more efficient supply chain. Our planning incorporates the evolving cost environment and the actions available to us to manage it, which Stewart will discuss more later. Our teams are earning more customer visits and delivering stronger results while advancing the initiatives needed to sustain that progress. Our say-do ratio is important to us. We remain focused on executing the commitments we have made and building a stronger Dollar Tree for our associates, customers and shareholders.

Stewart F. Glendinning: Thanks, Mike, and good morning, everyone. Third quarter adjusted diluted earnings per share was $1.16 and included $0.42 of cost from the net impact of tariff refunds and reinvestments. Adjusted EPS was above our $0.80 to $0.95 outlook range. Before I review the quarter, you should keep in mind the impact of tariff refunds and reinvestments on the P&L. In order to help you get a full view of the underlying performance, our supplemental investor presentation contains a summary schedule by quarter of the tariff refunds and reinvestments in the line items they are included in. During the third quarter, we received $4 million of tariff refund proceeds, which benefited gross profit.

In the quarter, we reinvested $103 million, including $27 million in cost of sales and $76 million in SG&A. Total tariff refund reinvestments were about $20 million lower than we expected in August. As a reminder, these investments are targeted at discrete customer-facing and operational initiatives, such as our 40th anniversary celebration, marketing and store conditions, all of which are designed to enhance value, convenience and discovery for our customers. Now let's walk through the results and then discuss our updated outlook. Net sales increased 6.9% to $5.1 billion, driven by a 4.6% increase in comparable store sales and a 2.3% contribution from net new store growth.

Comps were driven by a 3.8% increase in traffic as our amplified marketing, broader assortment and compelling values resonated with customers. Ticket increased 0.8% on the back of higher multi-price penetration. By category, consumables delivered a robust 8.9% comp, while discretionary increased 0.4%. Gross margin contracted 10 basis points to 35.7% and included a 45 basis point negative impact related to the net cost of tariff refunds and reinvestments. Lower tariff costs, markdown favorability and an improvement in shrink were gross margin tailwinds. Product cost inflation, higher freight costs and a mix shift to lower-margin consumables were the primary gross margin headwinds. Moving down the P&L.

Total SG&A inclusive of TSA income delevered 110 basis points and included a 150 basis point negative impact from tariff refund reinvestments. The remaining drivers in the total SG&A rate, inclusive of TSA income were favorability in payroll, partially offset by lower TSA income. Adjusted operating margin contracted 120 basis points to 6.1% and included a 195 basis point negative impact related to the net cost of tariff refunds and reinvestments. Below the operating line, net interest expense and the effective tax rate were similar to last year. Turning to the balance sheet. Inventory declined 3.8% versus the prior year, while sales increased 6.9%, resulting in a favorable inventory to sales spread.

We continue to manage inventory tightly, which supports fresher assortments for our customers, working capital efficiency and stronger free cash flow generation. We ended the quarter with $966 million in cash and no commercial paper outstanding. We generated $375 million in cash from operations and invested $254 million in capital expenditures, resulting in free cash flow of $122 million. During the quarter, we repurchased 1.8 million shares for $205 million at an average price of $116 per share. Now I will turn to our outlook for the fourth quarter, full year fiscal 2026 and share preliminary thoughts on fiscal 2027.

For the fourth quarter, we expect net sales in the range of $5.7 billion to $5.8 billion, reflecting comparable store sales growth of 3% to 4%. Adjusted diluted earnings per share are expected to be in the range of $2.46 to $2.66, including a negative impact of approximately $0.25 related to tariff refund reinvestments. Turning to our updated outlook for the year. We expect net sales in the range of $20.6 billion to $20.7 billion, reflecting comparable sales store growth of 3.5% to 4%. We now expect adjusted corporate SG&A inclusive of TSA income in the range of $555 million to $565 million, including our $40 million charitable contribution.

We expect TSA income of $55 million or $10 million lower than we previously assumed. This is primarily the result of the timing of various TSAs rolling off. With respect to net interest expense, we now expect about $55 million. Given the third quarter performance, rising inflation costs, particularly in fuel and updated corporate SG&A expectations, we now expect adjusted diluted earnings per share in the range of $8.05 to $8.25, including an approximate $0.65 benefit related to the net impact of tariff refunds. Finally, as we look forward to fiscal 2027, there are some items to keep in mind. First, the current elevated fuel and freight environment has persisted.

This not only manifests itself as pressure on domestic and direct import transportation costs, but also product cost inflation, all of which we are addressing through our 5 cost mitigation levers. As a reminder, our 5 levers include negotiating with suppliers, reengineering products and pack sizes, diversifying sourcing across countries of origin, discontinuing items that cannot meet margin targets and optimizing pricing. Second, fiscal 2026 benefits from a strong shrink improvement. While we still see opportunity ahead, keep in mind, 2026 has also benefited from a reserve adjustment. Lastly, we expect TSA income to wind down by the end of fiscal year 2026.

In closing, we are pleased with our financial performance since our Investor Day presentation, and I look forward to giving you a more detailed report out during our next quarterly call. We remain focused on delivering against our 3-year growth algorithm. And with that, I'll turn the call back over to Mike. Mike?

Michael Creedon: Thank you, Stewart. We are encouraged by our progress and clear about the work ahead. Our focus remains on earning our customers' loyalty by delivering the value, convenience and discovery they expect on every visit. Thank you to our associates for their commitment and to our shareholders for their continued support. We'll now take your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question today is coming from Matthew Boss from JPMorgan.

Matthew Boss: Congrats on a nice quarter. So first, could you walk through the factors that drove third quarter earnings above the high end of the outlook? And then could you talk to the cadence of comps in the quarter, elaborate on Halloween relative to your expectations? And any color on comp trends that you've seen quarter-to-date in November or any reads early on holiday?

Michael Creedon: Sure, Matt. Let me start. We'll tag team this one. But first of all, I want to start by saying how proud I am of the Dollar Tree team. Our execution continues to improve. And that 4.6% comp was nicely above the 3% to 4% range, and we really liked the acceleration we saw in traffic. The Q3 story was a really great comp sales story. Stewart, do you want to hit some of the margin pieces and then I can circle back to the cadence.

Stewart F. Glendinning: Yes. Thanks, Mike. Matt, let me speak to earnings on an underlying basis. So that means excluding the impact of the tariff reinvestments. If you look at the big factors here, the first thing is that we sold more than we thought, and you can see that in the higher-than-expected comps. That created incremental margin. And of course, it also gave us some leverage on fixed costs like occupancy. The second thing is if you look at relative to our plan for a flattish gross margin, we came in slightly favorable on merch costs and shrink with a little bit of offset from higher distribution costs and negative sales mix, but in total, positive.

On SG&A, the good news there is that the better-than-expected result was driven by SG&A cost leverage and some other cost reductions. It's probably worth pointing out that the TSA income was below our plan. And some of the tariff reinvestments were -- I talked to it on an underlying basis, but tariff reinvestments were a little bit lower than we thought. I know you didn't ask this, but I'm going to make the point anyway that all of that beat has been rolled through into the year. So if you look at the full beat in Q3, we put into the full year forecast.

Michael Creedon: Yes. And then let me just talk about the cadence. Consistency was the theme that I'll point to. It was really a broad-based comp throughout the quarter. We knew at the beginning of the year that the setup was going to be -- the first half of the year would be ticket-driven and the second half of the year would be traffic-driven. I think when we saw it turn -- traffic turned positive in Q2, we were pleased with that. And then it continued to improve. So I think customers are finding a more relevant assortment in better-run stores, and that's driving traffic and frequency. As for Halloween, the sell-through was up versus last year.

But we really saw a customer that shopped closer to need, and we saw a big spike the kind of last 7 to 10 days leading up to the holiday with a really big final day with a Saturday Halloween. So the team was ready to take on that challenge of a late-arriving customer. But that said, sales were still modestly kind of below our plan on Halloween. Quarter-to-date, we're still early, but we're pleased with what we see is this continued momentum. And so I would say we're pleased with where we're at in the quarter.

Operator: Our next question today is coming from Seth Sigman from Barclays.

Seth Sigman: Great quarter. I'm just curious, given all the moving pieces this year, how do we think about the baseline for '27 EPS growth? And if you could share any of the puts and takes for '27, particularly on the gross margin, just given that fuel and input costs, there's so much volatility there, how you're thinking about that? And anything related to the cadence?

Stewart F. Glendinning: Yes. Thanks, Seth. Let me start by saying that 2026 has been a year with enormous volatility. But at the end, it's been a good year for us, and it's demonstrative of the capability of the company to be sort of -- to be able to handle and operate in those kinds of environments. And that's going to be important for 2027. Now I'll have a better picture of '27, of course, when we get to the year-end, but I will give you a few early indicators as you start to think about next year.

The first point is when you want to look at this year versus next year, let's remember to strip out the $0.65 of benefit from tariff refunds and reinvestments. And of course, we've given you a pretty detailed table this quarter, so you know where that's flowing through in the P&L. Mike just mentioned it, but on the top line, we have real momentum with customers. And you can see that in our comp sales this quarter. And if you look forward at the assortment plans we have for next year and the strong progress we're making in store conditions, we're planning to continue that strength into 2027.

But at the same time, as you pointed out, the cost environment has some volatility, particularly around fuel freight and the knock-on to product costs. And in freight, we're seeing pressure from tighter driver market and fuel rates and maybe the watch out for 2027, which I actually called out last year at the same quarter, didn't manifest itself this year, but we always have a watchful eye on what will happen in the freight -- ocean freight rates as we get to the spring contracting season. Shrink. I'll just go to shrink for a second. Forgive me, this is a bit of a long answer, but I want to cover all the pieces.

But on shrink, we've had a very strong performance. And I think if you look at our 2026, we'll benefit by about 50 basis points on shrink for the full year. And about 20 basis points of that was the adjustment to the reserve, which, for obvious reasons, won't repeat next year. So we'll have to lap that 20 basis points in 2027. In 2027, Easter will move earlier. And that, of course, can be a headwind for retailers. But the other side of the equation against all this is that we still have a lot in our control. We have our 5 cost mitigation levers, which, of course, you've seen us deploy against margin pressures.

And in SG&A, we'll be implementing technology this year, which will benefit store labor. And of course, we're looking for other cost opportunities to offset the reduction in TSA revenues. So if I just sort of step back, we feel good about the underlying progress of the business. We feel good about the long-term opportunity, and I'll be back to give you a much more granular look at '27 when we give you the outlook then.

Operator: Our next question is coming from John Heinbockel from Guggenheim Partners.

John Heinbockel: I wonder, Mike, if you can touch on performance of MPP in Halloween. You had a very strong performance last year. So I'm curious, within that -- your discussion of how Halloween went this year, how did MPP do specifically? What does that tell you about holiday, right? And then I guess when you think about the 18% penetration, I mean that's inevitably going to go up. Do you have any thoughts of where the customer takes you on that, say, over the next year or 2 or 3?

Michael Creedon: Yes, sure. Thanks, John. If you look at Halloween, this Halloween, one, Labor Day later, so you get a slow start to Halloween because Labor Day was a week later. And what we saw was that the early parts of Halloween were where we saw the customer pressure and really them being choiceful. And then it accelerated as we got towards the end of the holiday and then certainly the last week and the last day. Multi-price from a unit standpoint was excellent, accelerated over last year. In Halloween, particularly, we had some average unit retails as we introduced these dollar items that put pressure on the sales piece of it.

Remember, we decided as part of tariff refund reinvestment to introduce these dollar price points at a time when you can't really buy for them. It was a late add with the refunds. We like what we did in terms of driving some perception, not a big mover of the P&L and certainly impacted the comp of Halloween. But multi-price continues to be early innings. You look back, it's 18% now. Where do I see it going? I certainly believe that we'll follow our customer. As we continue to delight our customer with thrill-of-the-hunt discovery with the value that we can bring to them in everyday essentials via multi-price, that will dictate how we grow.

But I look at it and say we're still early in multi-price, and we've got a lot of runway ahead of us in terms of growing this business.

Operator: Next question is coming from Michael Lasser from UBS.

Michael Lasser: Your comp in the third quarter was concurrent with all of the investments that you've made from the tariff refunds that you received. So a, how much do you think your comps benefited from those investments? B, would it make economic sense to further the investments even in the absence of the tariff refunds in 2027? And c, if you don't make investments next year, should we be calibrated for modestly slower comps for Dollar Tree in the year ahead?

Michael Creedon: Yes, Michael, I'll start -- it's really not the driver. Actually, and I was kind of alluding to this in answering John's question on Halloween. You look at these dollar items, they were pressure on the comp. What's driving our performance and our traffic is what we laid out at Investor Day. It's a better assortment in better-run stores, inspired by talking to our customers in ways we never have before. And that one, the last one, that better customer engagement is super early. And I don't think you really see the benefits of that yet. I think that takes time. So really, I look at it and say, we wanted to take the tariff refunds, invest in our customers.

That was really price was the big driver of that. We invested back in price. That was not a big driver of the P&L at all. And in fact, it hurt our comp. Stewart, anything you want to...

Stewart F. Glendinning: I think you covered it, Mike. I mean, Michael, as Mike said, look, there's pricing store conditions and engagement. And on the pricing, we had the real-time feedback from that. Obviously, we did see negative elasticity on that, although it attracted customers. On store conditions, that's a slower burn. I mean customers don't come rushing in because you repainted the walls or fixed some shelves, but it creates a much better shopping environment. I think that gives us the kind of setup that I spoke about for 2027. And then on the customer engagement side, the nature of that marketing was sort of top-of-the-funnel brand building kind of marketing.

That's also the kind of marketing that requires a little bit of repeat to build a head of steam. So I mean this is a good news story is that our comp wasn't dependent on that. And -- but the items, as we said before, the requirement for these investments was that they were onetime investments with the potential for long-term benefit. And that is how we set it up, and that's how we think it will play out.

Operator: Next question is coming from Rupesh Parikh from Oppenheimer.

Rupesh Parikh: Can you give us the state of the union on freight costs? Remind us how much you contracted versus spot and the breakdown between multiyear and 1-year contracts? It also would be helpful how we should think about the elevated fuel costs. And then since we're getting a lot of questions on the topic, is there maybe a rule of thumb in terms of how we can understand the cost headwind and just overall plans to mitigate some of the higher energy prices?

Michael Creedon: Yes. Thanks, Rupesh. Well, look, I'll build on some of my comments that I made in the earlier question against 2027. But look, I'll start by saying we've seen this movie before. Dollar Tree has navigated these kind of headwinds on freight and other costs for 40 years. And for most of that time, we were a single price point retailer. And for a long time, we bought and managed the margin. So I just want people to understand that as I give you these comments on freight because freight is an area of pressure, particularly as we cycle last year's favorable freight environment. And I just break it into 2 pieces.

You've got direct imports and you've got domestic transportation. On imports, we've got good visibility into the ocean freight costs. And I'd say the majority of our volume is under 1-year contracts with a smaller amount on multiyear contracts. And so that -- those 1 years are going to renew, of course, every year. The spot rates, the spot loads are sort of mid-single digits. So they're a relatively small part of our portfolio. And that import group, just to help you dimensionalize this, is about 1/3 overall of our freight, our overall transportation costs.

We've taken benefit this year from favorable ocean rates generally as against history and lower spot usage, but we've seen higher fuel costs offsetting that, and those come in surcharges. And I said last quarter, those surcharges, of course, will move up and down with the price of fuel. So I think over the long haul, that's probably a positive. On the domestic side, we contract those rates by lane with carriers. And the challenge right now is that there's a very tight driver market. And when those carriers don't have enough drivers, we have to rely more on the higher cost surge drivers.

So domestically, we're dealing with higher fuel costs and a tight driver market and on imports, that pressure is coming from fuel. With respect to your sort of rule of thumb, the best way I could describe that is that on the 2/3, which is the domestic transportation, about $1 in diesel price is worth somewhere around $40 million of annual cost to us. So meaningful but manageable. On the direct -- on the import side, it's much more complicated because of shifting countries, contract rates, surcharges and therefore, I'm hesitant to sort of give you a rule of thumb on that. But the good news is, look, we've got a well-established playbook on this.

And I just want to remind everybody on this call the sort of 5 levers that we use in managing these kinds of costs. Supplier. We've got supplier renegotiation to push back on the cost, reengineering products and pack sizes to accommodate the price point, discontinuing items that cannot meet the margin targets. We have seen shift in countries of origin to accommodate lowest cost product. And finally, the last point for us is optimizing pricing. And we view that as a last step. So hopefully, that gives you a full picture of freight and how we manage it.

Operator: Our next question today is coming from Bobby Griffin from Raymond James.

Robert (Bobby) Griffin: Congrats on a good quarter. I guess, Mike, I just want to see if you could give us a little bit more color on the consumable strength versus the discretionary deceleration in the quarter. Anything besides Halloween to call out department-wise there? And then kind of how is the team thinking about that interplay given the consumer backdrop, but as we go into a very important kind of discretionary quarter around holiday?

Michael Creedon: Yes. Thanks, Bobby. First of all, I want to say really happy with the strength of the comp and the health of the comp. If you took that discretionary on a 2-year basis, 5.2% 2-year stack on that. So the positive comp in discretionary was on top of a very strong comp last year. I think the mix is reflective of a consumer right now that is really buying for need, looking to stretch their budget. And the broad-based strength we saw in consumables is exactly what that consumer needs. I mentioned Halloween.

I think we had with our dollar items, with a later Labor Day, we certainly saw some pressure in Halloween, but what a comeback in terms of how it finished the last 7 to 10 days and certainly the last day for us to just have a modest -- miss below our plan. So I really look at it and say Halloween was a factor, but I think that was more specific to Halloween and some of the things we did in terms of the dollar items and other multi price investment. Party is the other one that we continue to watch. Helium was about a $5 million impact in the quarter. That hurts your balloon business.

But party was probably the laggard we saw there, a little bit of the softness we talked about in Halloween. But as I look forward, I don't have that average unit retail pressure as I look forward to like a Christmas holiday that I had from Halloween. I think we have a good setup there. And I really look and expect the customer to do similar things. I think they'll buy for need, they'll buy closer to need, but they're still going to celebrate. They're choiceful and they're going to choose Dollar Tree. That's the way I look at it.

Operator: Our next question is coming from Edward Kelly from Wells Fargo.

Edward Kelly: I wanted to ask you about next year and the potential for pricing as a mitigating factor of all the cost pressure that you've mentioned here. And I'm just kind of curious, you have the levers. Is pricing a lever that you intend to use? To some extent, Mike, right, like maybe this needs to become more muscle memory for Dollar Tree, but at the same time, there's been friction in the past on pricing. So I'm curious as to how you're thinking about that.

And then Stewart, as it pertains to all of this, are the levers and the communication that you're talking about for next year, is your intention to really tell us that you are going to manage the business to sort of protect the gross margin around what your long-term goals are?

Michael Creedon: Yes. Ed, thanks for the question. I want to be very clear. This is -- we just celebrated our 40th year a couple of weeks ago. We've taken price at scale twice in our history, break the dollar and then the inflationary cost environment of last year. When we talk about 5 levers, price is last for a reason. Our merchants do a phenomenal job working with our supplier partners, vendor partners to really get the right costs. They engineer the pack sizes to get the right fit. We have a new muscle in country of origin that we simply didn't have even 3 years ago.

So we look at it -- and then Dollar Tree doesn't have to sell anything. If we have an item that doesn't fit, we take it out. Price is last for a reason. It has been used very sparingly. And when you are looking to a customer that is cherishing value right now, the last thing we want to do is mess with that value equation for them. They're finding Dollar Tree. Our traffic is growing. We believe she will continue to come to Dollar Tree for the value. And so we'll use our 5 levers and prices last for a reason. Stewart, anything you want to add to that?

Stewart F. Glendinning: Yes. Just relative to the question about next year, I'm not giving the outlook at this point in time simply because there's a lot of moving pieces, and we're better off getting to the end of the year and me giving you a really well-informed point of view on next year. The point I wanted to make today is that there are some margin pressures. There are cost pressures. But I wanted to give you the reassurance also that this is a management team that has handled significant volatility in these last 2 years that has a game plan for addressing volatility. Of course, we're deploying those kinds of measures against the pressure.

And ultimately, we're working to achieve the 3-year growth algorithm that we shared with you when we met at our Investor Day last year. So give us the space. We'll give you more color when we see you in March.

Operator: Our next question is coming from Scot Ciccarelli from Truist Securities.

Unknown Analyst: This is [ Kate ] on for Scot. I was wondering if you can give us an update on where you are on store standards? And if you're getting the sales results you've previously suggested when a store moves up into the GOLD star rating bracket?

Michael Creedon: Yes. Thanks, Kate. When I look at the big 3 of what's driving this traffic acceleration, the performance of the business, the above guide comp, it is really a better assortment in better-run stores with a better customer engagement. And so those -- the GOLD scores, there's 2 things at play there. Yes, stores are improving. They're "moving to the right in terms of what we call the Himalayas performing better. And what Jocelyn Konrad and our store teams are doing, they're also raising the bar on themselves. So you get a double benefit. One, you have overall stores improving and the bar they have to jump over to be GOLD and to move to the right is getting higher.

So I look at it as real progress and something that will continue to be a benefit because we will continue to raise the bar on ourselves.

Operator: Our next question is coming from Simeon Gutman from Morgan Stanley.

Simeon Gutman: I have a question. So look, the traffic was excellent. You've gone through a lot of multi-price changes over the last few years. I know it's hard to say if everything is in the past, but do you think now the business has sort of rebased, the consumer understands some of the changes that have happened and understands potential future changes and now the traffic just builds going forward? It's kind of like a turning point here with traffic that you can keep making changes to multi-price and now the consumer understands your value prop really well.

Michael Creedon: Yes, Simeon, I think that's well said. I mean I look at it, there's a number of things I can point to. We track sentiment. I see the sentiment improving. We track price mentions in scrapes of whether it's Reddit or Google or we're doing this customer connection where we want to hear what they have to say. And what we're hearing is that they are kind of moving on. I mean, look, I will still get that. I can't believe everything is not a dollar. We still will get that. I think we will get that forever. But the reality is our customer is now coming.

And if you look, so much of our growth is this trade-in customer, too. It's -- our business is still the lower income customer, but we're seeing a lot of growth in the middle and higher income customer. And they're finding a Dollar Tree and finding an assortment because of multi-price that is just far more relevant to them. And that drives the repeat visits. That is a huge factor as we look to this run of traffic that we can go on and ticket. I mentioned we're now seeing mixed baskets that have both opening price point and multi-price in it. It's 25% of the baskets.

It's half the sales because that basket comes so much bigger with a 2.5x the size of the basket. So I think that's another good proof point of this customer acceptance. And then the one thing I want to add, and I do, I think you said it well. The one thing I want to add is that some people believe that the value is the opening price point, the thrill-of-the-hunt discovery is in the multi-price. I will tell you, there's thrill-of-the-hunt and opening price point, and there's unrivaled value in multi-price.

Operator: Our next question is coming from Michael Montani from Stifel.

Michael Montani: I was going to ask for some additional color, if you could, to help us understand the trade-in dynamics that might be happening. And then also if you could unpack some of the incrementality from multi-price as well as how to think about the journey from here for upgraded GOLD stores and what those could add to the comp?

Michael Creedon: Yes. Thanks, Michael. Yes, we -- we're seeing growth. Obviously, we're growing. We're growing households. We are, as I mentioned, whether I look at a lower-income store or a middle-income store or a high-income store, they're all growing. The more than half of our growth is coming from that trade-in customer. And we really believe what we call it our passionates which are largely our lower-income shopper. I mean, these folks shop us 70-plus times a year. We had that slide at Investor Day, whereas you have a new customer finding us, they might be 4 to 6 times a year, and they really come for seasons and holidays.

What we're seeing with multi-price is the ability to get more frequent trips out of that customer that's finding us. Maybe they come in because of a party or a celebration. And they see everyday wow, that they know they just have to keep coming back for. So I believe the trade-in dynamics are -- they came 4 to 6x. They're increasing their frequency, which helps us with traffic. And then in terms of the multi-price journey, I said it earlier, we will follow our customer. The third thing we have is that better customer engagement, that's marketing, that's serving, that's listening to our customer.

We're going to follow their lead, do a lot of test and learn to see what resonates with them. You look at this dollar Halloween item we put in, like I said, it wasn't a big mover of the P&L. It actually hurt the comp a little. But what do we learn in terms of what our customer wants and that we can look towards the future where we can buy to a margin and maybe bring dollar items in that we've prepared for. That's all part of this multi-price journey.

Stewart F. Glendinning: Mike, if you don't mind, I'd just throw one extra thing in here because I think I'd just like to underscore a point that Mike made about the frequency of visits. The most difficult thing for most businesses is actually attracting new customers. And in fact, one of the big assets for our business is the fact that we have enormous penetration. Think about it, more than 100 million out of 130 million households in the United States. The challenge is not so much for us to add customers. It is just simply to get existing customers to come and visit us more frequently. And that is at the very heart of the benefit that multi-price offers.

You've got a big group of customers who find your store much more interesting because they've got more money and they'd like to come to your store more frequently because there's a greater assortment on offer.

Operator: Our next question is coming from Chuck Grom from Gordon Haskett.

Charles (Chuck) Grom: I just wanted to follow up on that on the unpacking the traffic between new and repeat. So can you give us a little bit of a sense there? And then on marketing, maybe double-click on the opportunity. There's a handful of retailers that have had tremendous success. Can you talk about how much spend you currently do on marketing and the opportunity there? And my last question is just if we strip out the $0.65 of tariff benefit net, you get roughly EPS of $7.50. Do you think you can algo earnings next year of 8% to 10% that you guys outlined at Investor Day last year?

Michael Creedon: I'll jump in on the first 2, Chuck, and ask Stewart to handle the last one. In terms of the traffic dynamics, I really believe our biggest opportunity is in getting this middle and higher income customer that may visit us 4 to 6 times a year to increase. You get one more trip. I think we said at Investor Day, you get one more trip, it's like $1 billion. That's a huge opportunity. All the while, multi-price exists for all of our shoppers. I said it earlier in an answer, sometimes people say, oh, your value is in the opening price point and the thrill-of-the-hunt is in the multi-price.

And the reality is there's value and thrill-of-the-hunt and convenience, by the way, in both opening price point and multi-price. And I think you see that as I unpack these mixed baskets that 25% of the baskets now, half of our sales are coming from someone that comes in and is finding both opening price point and multi-price. And when they build that basket, it's 2.5x the size of a traditional basket. So these new customers, I mean, they're showing real growth. They're above our traffic growth is these new customers coming in. But at the same time, we love this core customer that we know multi-price exists for them as well. Marketing, Dollar Tree never did it.

And I still stay in close touch with our founders. And we were a build it and they will come. Doug Perry would always say, just get the best real estate, you don't have to worry about marketing. And we still do that. We still have great stores, great locations. We just opened our 9,500th store right here in Hampton Roads. But the reality is while we have unbelievable awareness of Dollar Tree, multi-price has changed what's in the store. And that's what we want to scream about. That's where we want to connect with our customer and let them know, yes, greeting cards, you come to Dollar Tree. You want to celebrate, you come to Dollar Tree.

Guess what, there's more in the Tree for you than you knew before. In fact, it's all in the Tree. And so that's why we're focused on that and getting that messaging out to our customer. It is so early, Chuck. We'll continue to kind of talk about this. I'm excited about it. And by the way, the response has been great to it, but it's just so early, and I agree with you. I think others have done this really well. We'll continue to do it. Stewart, do you want to just handle the last part of Chuck's question.

Stewart F. Glendinning: So first, Chuck, on the number of marketing, we haven't given a number to that, but I'll tell you that our average sort of the benchmark, right, if you look at the marketing as a percentage of sales, much lower than most businesses. So this is not a cost that is sort of expanding dramatically. But for us, it has increased meaningfully in our own P&L. As it relates to next year, look, I'm going to give you a picture of that when we get to March. I said that earlier that I don't really want to comment on the specific outlook for next year.

But I'd just ask you to go back to the Investor Day we had last year, take our starting point, run that forward the way you would have seen it and ask yourself, do you think we can hit that algo? And I would just run that EPS forward. And I think so far over this last year or so, we've done a nice job of advancing it. We feel good about how we're moving the strategy forward. And when I come to March, I'll give you a lot more on that. But understand, our focus is in doing what we tell you we're going to do.

Operator: Our final question today is coming from Greg Melich from Evercore ISI.

Gregory (Greg) Melich: I'd love to follow up on just 2 things. One, just maybe describe the competitive environment and how you're seeing it out there. Other people have increasing costs into next year and they have IEEPA rebates, et cetera. How do you see the competition reinvesting that.

Michael Creedon: Yes. Thanks, Greg. It's interesting. I mentioned earlier, 40 years in business, we've taken price at scale twice. The competition is changing their pricing all the time. When we have to take price, which we did last year in the inflationary cost environment that we were in, the worst day for us is the day we take price. Every day after that, we get better. And so when I look at it, and we watch this every week, you can see reports on it. We feel that value is king for Dollar Tree. We think we are the value solution as shoppers look to stretch their budget and hopefully celebrate for less.

And so we like the position we're in, zeroed in on that value convenience and still providing kind of guilt-free thrill-of-the-hunt pleasure and discovery. So we like where we sit. Like I said, the worst day for us is the day we have to take price, and we just keep getting better from there. So I think that we see a good environment for Dollar Tree.

Operator: I just want to turn it over to you for any further closing comments.

Michael Creedon: All right. Thank you so much. First of all, I just want to thank everyone for joining us this morning, for your continued interest in Dollar Tree. It's not lost on us. This is -- sorry, Thanksgiving week. So please, everyone, have a blessed Thanksgiving. And we look forward to talking to you soon. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. That does conclude today's teleconference and webcast. You may disconnect your line at this time, and have a wonderful day. We thank you for your participation today.

#2967. What Is a Reconditioning Fee on a Used Car?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. Used-car dealers may charge you a reconditioning fee to cover their costs of getting cars ready for sale.

A reconditioning fee is an added dealer charge you might find when buying a used car. It’s intended to cover any costs the dealer incurs to make sure a used car is showroom-ready, from mechanical inspections to detailing.

The reconditioning process varies between dealerships, but typically includes these steps:

A visual exterior inspection. An auto tech does a quick walk-around the vehicle and notes any corrosion, damage or wear.

An interior inspection. The engine and auto interior are examined and tested, and any issues are documented.

A test drive. The car is taken out for a drive to check that it runs well and that the radio, brakes, A/C and other components are all functioning properly.

Service and repair. Any interior or exterior mechanical, functional or cosmetic issues that were found are repaired, including paint, dents, oil changes and major engine work.

Inspection. Once repairs are completed, the car is inspected again to make sure everything looks and functions as it should.

Detailing. This includes deep interior, engine and exterior cleaning as well as any necessary leather refurbishing, bumper repair or wheel restoration.

Reconditioning fees are legal, but that doesn’t mean you have to pay them. Dealers can charge whatever they want for a reconditioning fee, and it’s not uncommon to find them ranging from around $500 to over $2,000.

The good news: Reconditioning fees, like most dealer extras, can be negotiable. Ask the dealer for a breakdown of the reconditioning fee to see what kind of work was done to prepare the car for sale. If the work was minor but the fee is high — for example, if they’re asking for $1,995 but replaced the floor mats only — that’s a good sign it’s a bogus charge.

However, when it comes time for negotiation, don’t just haggle over the reconditioning fee or other individual fees. The best way to negotiate is to focus on the out-the-door price, or the total amount you’re paying for the car. This simplifies the negotiation process and keeps you focused on the true price of your car.

All dealers invest some amount in reconditioning, but those costs are often built into the dealer’s asking price for a vehicle, rather than as a separate charge.

Some dealers opt to add a reconditioning fee to the bill because it allows them to advertise a lower asking price online, which doesn’t include fees. It’s a tactic to get you into their dealership, since the asking price is lower than that of other dealerships.

However, once you arrive, you may find that the out-the-door price is the same — or more — compared with what other dealers are asking.

Some car-buying experts recommend avoiding dealerships that charge reconditioning fees altogether. But remember that the out-the-door price is what matters at the end of the day, so it’s worth comparing prices at multiple dealerships to find the best deal.

Reddit is an online forum where users share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like car buying, so we sifted through Reddit threads to get a sense of how users feel about reconditioning fees. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

Reddit users are generally skeptical toward reconditioning fees. Many users view these fees as a bait-and-switch tactic: dealers advertise an attractive price online and then tack on the fee at the dealership, inflating the actual out-the-door cost well above what was listed. Car buyers frequently share stories of being hit with reconditioning fees ranging from a few hundred dollars up to $2,000 or more, often with little or no evidence of what work was actually done.

Car-buying experts on Reddit point out that most dealerships already build reconditioning costs into the sticker price, so if the fee is listed separately, the dealership may be double-dipping. Several users suggest that car buyers ask their dealer for an itemized breakdown of the work done, but most users recommend negotiating the total out-the-door price rather than individual fees.
