#2966. Tesla and SpaceX Just Assembled Deal Teams for a $3.2 Trillion Merger. Here's What Investors Need to Know.

Two of the market's most high-profile companies have taken the next step toward joining forces.

By Danny Vena, CPA – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:39PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

Elon Musk has made no secret of the fact that he would like to have many (if not all) of the companies he runs under one roof. And the enigmatic CEO has already taken several steps to accomplish that goal. Artificial intelligence (AI) start-up xAI merged with Twitter (now called X) before the combined company was folded into Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -5.65%) aka SpaceX.

However, Musk's biggest coup would be to bring together SpaceX and Tesla (TSLA -0.20%). The long-rumored combination just took another step closer to reality. Reports emerged on Tuesday that the electric vehicle (EV) maker and rocket launch company had appointed a handful of directors to oversee the largest merger in corporate history.

Bringing together two companies of this size will be a daunting task. SpaceX has a market cap of roughly $1.7 trillion, while Tesla's clocks in at $1.5 trillion, making the combined entity worth $3.2 trillion and placing it among the world's five most valuable companies (as of this writing).

SpaceX and Tesla have chosen five of the companies' directors to conduct merger negotiations, according to a report that first appeared in The Financial Times. The quintet of executives -- two from SpaceX and three from Tesla -- have been charged with hashing out the details for the all-stock merger, according to the report.

The diversity and wealth of experience among this group should give it the tools needed to complete the job -- though it won't be an easy one.

The job at hand is extraordinarily complex and will face a number of challenges in combining two companies of this size. One such hurdle will be determining a fair "exchange ratio" between Tesla and SpaceX shares. If the exchange is seen as favoring one company over another, it might not get the shareholder votes needed to succeed. Even if it's ultimately approved, an appearance of inequity could lead to shareholder lawsuits that could drag on for years. Any deal must also pass regulatory muster, considering the potential antitrust and national security implications.

To get it right, the special committees from both companies have hired independent financial advisors to help develop and refine the financial models that will form the foundation for the merger discussions. The principals will also be charged with developing a governance framework and deciding who will lead the newly formed entity.

While Musk is barred from the proceedings -- due to his inherent conflict of interest -- the special committees are permitted to "consult" with senior executives during their negotiations -- and no one is more senior than Musk. He has described the process as an "odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can't be in the conversation."

At this juncture, we simply don't have enough information to make informed decisions about the implications for shareholders of either company.

That said, there's a strong case to be made for the joining of SpaceX and Tesla. Both companies are investing heavily in AI, with Tesla's Full Self-Driving (FSD) and SpaceX's Grok at the heart of those efforts. The companies are already inextricably intertwined, with Tesla supplying Megapack battery systems, vehicles, engineering support, and various parts and accessories to SpaceX. The pair are also joined at the hip regarding Terafab, the joint semiconductor manufacturing project. If combined, SpaceX and Tesla could integrate their efforts in AI, robotics, and connectivity.

The success or failure of the deal will likely hinge on the valuations assigned to each company and any resulting shareholder dilution. It will then have to run the regulatory gauntlet.

#2965. Did Nvidia Make a Big Mistake by Reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO so Quickly?

It took less than two weeks after resigning for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO.

By David Jagielski, CPA – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:45PM EST

Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%) made a big announcement yesterday: Jensen Huang was returning as CEO. It was a sharp and seemingly sudden turnaround from recent days when it looked as though the company's board was ready to move on with Colette Kress as its Interim CEO while it took a long look at the situation and considered a permanent replacement.

While many investors were likely bracing for a potentially long, drawn-out process, that didn't end up happening. Instead, on Monday morning, news came out that Huang was back. Will that prove to be a big mistake?

Nvidia's board was clearly swayed by the U.S. president, who said he was behind the deal to bring Huang back as CEO. While he provided assurances that there weren't national security risks, the fact that an investigation remains ongoing raises questions about whether that assessment might ultimately change.

It also calls into question how the president convinced the board so quickly to reinstate Huang, especially since it recently said it wasn't considering making the move at all. To do a complete 180 so quickly is definitely surprising. It certainly looked as though the board had moved on from Huang.

Although the tech stock was sinking amid news of Huang's resignation, the move to reinstate Huang seemed rushed, calling into question the board's overall governance. It did, however, state in its decision to reinstate Huang that the investigation "will proceed to conclusion." But given that Huang has already been reinstated, it would be an even worse look for the board to change its mind yet again.

Meanwhile, Huang is still scheduled to meet with Congress relating to his involvement with a possible Chinese spy. The issues related to Huang are by no means resolved, and the board's quick and sudden move to reinstate him could end up backfiring if more serious issues are indeed uncovered.

Nvidia's board effectively caved. Even before the president stepped in, it appeared that with the massive decline in Nvidia's share price, the market had spoken -- it wanted Huang back. I believe even without the president's push, Huang would have returned as CEO; it may have just taken a bit longer.

While it is disappointing to see the board not diligently and thoroughly investigate the matter first before making a decision, I don't believe it'll prove to have any lasting or serious effects on the stock. For the time being, it didn't appear to have much of a choice given the stock's massive sell-off.

Nvidia remains a top tech stock to own, and any issues relating to Huang likely aren't going to be enough to weigh on its future. In fact, now can be a good time to buy the stock, as its valuation has taken a beating in recent weeks.

#2963. What Are Repositioning Cruises?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Repositioning cruises move ships between seasonal destinations, often with longer sailings, fewer port stops and lower fares.

A repositioning cruise is a one-way sailing that moves a ship from one region to another. For example, many ships sail in the Mediterranean Sea during the summer and move to the Caribbean Sea for the winter, and that trip between the two is a repositioning cruise.

Repositioning cruises are most common in spring (roughly March to May) and fall (roughly September to November), though they can occur at other times of year.

Because ships are crossing oceans, these trips often include many days at sea. For some travelers, that’s a chance to relax and enjoy the ship’s onboard amenities. Sometimes, these sailings can also be cheaper than traditional cruises.

One key consideration for a repositioning cruise is that the embarkation and disembarkation ports will be different. This means you generally can’t buy a standard round-trip flight to and from the same city. Instead, you’ll need transportation to where the cruise starts and another way home from where it ends, which usually means two one-way flights (or one open-jaw ticket) unless you live near one of the ports. While these one-way sailings may be more affordable than traditional cruises, airfare costs may be higher.

This could be a great opportunity to redeem miles for your flight.

Another feature that sets these cruises apart is that stops along the way tend to include ports that aren’t traditionally part of regular itineraries. These might include islands like Bermuda, the Azores or the Canary Islands, and on some northern routes, Greenland.

Just keep in mind that the main purpose of these sailings is to get to a new region for the next season’s itineraries rather than make daily port stops. So if you’re someone who wants to visit as many places as possible on a cruise, a repositioning sailing may not be the ideal choice.

Repositioning cruises are often longer than standard cruises, commonly running two to three weeks compared with about a week for a typical sailing, which may appeal to travelers looking for an extended vacation. The experience is often more relaxed, with many days at sea and less of a rush to book shore excursions or visit important sites when off the ship.

If there are particular ships with certain amenities — like tattoo parlors or massive waterparks — that you really want to experience, keep in mind that not all ships reposition between regions. Some stay in certain regions year-round.

For ships that do change locations for the season, there are plenty of onboard activities to fill the time. You can enjoy shows, food and wine tastings, organized activities and time at the spa, pool or casino.

Many repositioning crossings are relatively smooth, and modern ships use stabilizers to reduce movement. But since these itineraries cross open ocean rather than staying closer to land, there can be more motion, especially on North Atlantic crossings in fall and winter.

If you tend to get seasick, this could be a dealbreaker. Even if a repositioning sailing is smooth, temperatures can be chilly on the open ocean, especially on northerly or spring and fall transatlantic routes, with strong winds that may make suntanning by the pool less appealing.

You can book one of these sailings in the same way you would book a traditional cruise. But if you’re searching for dates and itineraries on a cruise line’s website, they may be listed as transatlantic, transpacific or Panama Canal sailings rather than repositioning cruises, though some lines do use the term "repositioning." There’s even a website that specializes in rounding up these cruises: RepoCruises.com.

Keep an eye out for themed sailings that focus on topics like wine, theater or music, where fellow guests on the ship may share similar interests. Cruise lines often schedule them on repositioning cruises to spur demand.

Here are some repositioning cruises for 2027. They often take place during shoulder seasons, between the most popular cruising times in places like the Mediterranean or Caribbean.

This journey repositions the ship from Miami, where it sails on Caribbean itineraries, to Seattle, where it will visit ports in Alaska during the spring and summer months. Departing April 8, 2027, the 18-night cruise includes stops at various ports in Colombia, Panama and Mexico, as well as San Diego and Los Angeles, before arriving in Seattle on April 26.

Regent Seven Seas Cruises' all-suite luxury ship Seven Seas Mariner will sail between New York and Lisbon, making stops in Canada, Morocco and the Portuguese islands of Madeira and the Azores.

Departing April 29, 2027, the 16-night journey ends in Lisbon, Portugal, as the ship repositions to Europe, where it will sail various itineraries, including Mediterranean sailings later in the summer season.

Departing Seattle on Sept. 28, 2027, Norwegian Jade will sail to Yokohama, Japan, with stops in Alaska and northern Japan. This is a way to travel across the Pacific with less jet lag, since the journey takes place over several days, with ship clocks typically adjusted gradually (often an hour at a time) during the sailing. Note that the voyage also crosses the International Date Line.

If Greenland has been on your bucket list, this 16-night sailing is a way to get up close and personal with its natural scenery. Departing Reykjavik on Aug. 25, 2027, Azamara Quest will sail from Iceland to the U.S. It will make stops in Greenland, Canada and New England before reaching the Big Apple.

Departing Bergen, Norway, on June 11, 2027, this 28-night sailing aboard Viking Vela sails around Iceland's coast, makes two stops in Greenland and crosses the Atlantic before reaching New York.

Subscription growth carried record results, but a customer bankruptcy trimmed the U.S. base.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Kenny Green: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for standing by. My name is Kenny Green, and I am part of the investor relations team at Ituran. I would like to welcome all of you to Ituran's results Zoom webinar, and I would like to thank Ituran's management for hosting this conference call. All participants other than the presenters are currently muted. Following the formal presentation, I will provide some instructions for participating in the live question-and-answer session. I would like to remind everyone that this conference call is being recorded, and the recording will be available from the link in the earnings press release and on Ituran's website from tomorrow. With me today on the call are Mr. Eyal Sheratzky, CEO, Mr.

Udi Mizrahi, Deputy CEO and VP Finance, and Mr. Eli Kamer, CFO of Ituran. Eyal will begin with a summary of the quarter's results, followed by Eli with a summary of the financials. We will then open the call for the question-and-answer session. You should have all received by now the company's press release. If not, please view it on the company's website. I would like to remind everyone that the safe harbor statement in today's press release also covers the contents of this conference call and the associated presentation. Now, Eyal, would you like to begin, please?

Eyal Sheratzky: Thank you, Kenny. I would like to welcome all of you to our third quarter 2026 results call, and thank you for joining us today. We are very pleased to report a strong third quarter for Ituran, with record revenue, operating income, and EBITDA. For the quarter, overall revenue grew 15% year-over-year to a record of $107 million, and our recurring subscription revenue grew by 19% to $81 million, over 75% of our overall revenue. Beyond that, the results show the clear operating leverage inherent to our business model. All our profitability metrics, operating income, EBITDA, and net income are growing faster than our revenue.

Our Big Data capabilities have significant long-term potential to support governments, transport authorities, commercial centers, OEMs, and other customers, enabling them to make better decisions based on vast amount of transportation data while creating revenue opportunities that can grow beyond our traditional subscription model. Beyond this contract, we are continuing in advanced discussions with a number of potential customers, and we remain active on a number of pilot projects. We would hope to be able to announce a further Big Data agreement with one of these in the near terms. Ituran continued to be a strongly cash-generating business, and during the quarter, we generated a very high level of cash flow from operations of $25.3 million.

Our growth engines and the opportunities to monetize our Big Data assets are all examples of this. We remain confident in our ability to continue delivering revenue growth and increase profitability for the quarters ahead, and in our long-term strategy to transform Ituran into a significantly larger company. With that, I hand over to Eli. Eli, please go ahead.

EBITDA for the quarter was $29.9 million, or 28% of revenues, an increase of 21% compared with EBITDA of $24.6 million, or 26.7% of revenues in the third quarter of last year. Finance expenses in the third quarter were $0.5 million, compared with finance expenses of $0.3 million in the third quarter of last year. Net income for the third quarter was $18 million, or 16.9% of revenues, or diluted earning per share of $0.91, an increase of 23% compared with $14.6 million, or 15.9% of revenues, or diluted earning per share of $0.74 in the third quarter of last year. Cash flow from operations for the third quarter of 2026 was $25.3 million.

As of September 30th, 2026, the company had net cash, including marketable securities of $107.6 million, which includes no debt. This is compared with a net cash, including marketable securities of $103.7 million as of June 30th, 2026, and $107.6 million as of the year end 2025. The Board of Directors declared a dividend of $10 million for the quarter, or $0.50 per share. The current dividend take into account the company's continuing strong profitability, ongoing positive cash flow, and strong balance sheet. During the quarter, $1.9 million in share were purchased under our existing buyback program. The total remaining authorization is $8.1 million. Share buybacks are funded by available cash and are made in accordance with SEC Rule 10b-18.

With that, I'd like to open the call for a question-and-answer session. Operator?

Kenny Green: Thank you. Okay, we will now open the call for the question-and-answer session. If you have a question, please raise your hand on the platform, and we will call for questions. Our first question is from Sergey Glinyanov of Freedom. Sergey, go ahead.

I do not have to say that cars of 10 years and 20 years are irrelevant. We are talking about secondhand cars from the last years. We signed, as you know, two major contracts with two major OEM providers, which is Yamaha and BMW. I must say that we talk with others, and we also now started to offer it also to the secondhand market.

Sergey Glinyanov: Got it. Thank you, guys.

Kenny Green: Okay. Thanks, Sergey. Unless you have another question, we'll move on. Okay. We'll move now on to Derek Greenberg of Maxim. Derek, please go ahead.

Derek Greenberg: Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my questions. First one for me, I was wondering if you could just tell us what the FX impact was for the quarter.

Udi Mizrahi: If we're talking about the top line compared to last year, the FX is around $5 million-$6 million benefit. If we're talking comparing to the previous quarter, then we are talking about roughly -$1 million.

Derek Greenberg: Okay. Great. On some of the newer initiatives, you had talked about signing up the Big Data customer and having a strong pipeline there and active discussions. I was wondering if you could maybe touch on the other two initiatives as well in terms of the carbon credits and the IturanMob rideshare product. I was wondering just how those are progressing.

Eyal Sheratzky: Both initiatives that you mentioned, which is the Credit Carbon business as well as the remote rental cars, which we just launched in the United States market, are ongoing. Of course, it's not yet materialized, and it's not yet something that we providing, let's say, material information. In the carbon, in the Credit Carbon issue, as I said in the past, it's much longer term initiate because there is a lot of regulatory steps. We also cross some of them or even the major of them, but it's something that it's taking time before we will do the first or two contract.

I must say that we already have the relationship and the, let's say, potential pilot project with customers and big customers also in Latin America and in Europe, but all of us are still waiting for some regulation and regulatory confirmation, which we hope will arrive during 2027. We still don't have revenues from this part. From the remote rental solution that we offer, which we already have in Israel and Brazil, and we just started to launch it in the United States, we already have 10s of customers, which each one of them has 10s of cars, small and mid rental companies in a few countries in the United States.

But the number is still not material that it's contribute to our results. Based on the traction and based on these tens of customers, we really continue to believe that the U.S. market has a huge potential, and we also believe that we will lead this specific application and need.

Derek Greenberg: Yeah. Great. That's super helpful. Just last one from me. I was wondering if maybe you could give any color in terms of how your pipeline looks for potential new OEM partnerships just over the next year or so.

Eyal Sheratzky: When we talk about four-wheel cars, we covered many during the last three years. So our main focus is to expand geographies with the same OEMs, such as General Motors, Nissan, Renault, Stellantis, which has, by the way, many brands. So we are continuing to try to expand it to other countries. Of course, we talk with other. We have to understand that such is in the rest of the world as is Israel, the Chinese brand are now penetrating also to Latin America. We have discussion also with local manufacturers or dealers of Chinese brands. But as it always was, this is a long cycle.

It's not happen in a week or in a quarter, and we expect again to have at least one during next year. But more important to mention is that we realized a lot of interest in the motorcycle OEMs. We already did two OEM deals, and we continue to discuss with few more to go in OEM deals, which will include hardware and services, whether it is in the OEM product lines, whether it is internally in PDIs or dealers houses. This something that I have a strong confident that it will be faster than new car OEMs, and we will report, I hope, during 2027 at least also one more deal with motorcycle brand.

Derek Greenberg: Yeah. Great. No, that is super helpful. Well, thanks for taking my questions, guys, and congrats on the quarter.

Kenny Green: Okay. Thanks for that, Derek. I think that comes to the end of our Q&A session. Before I hand back to Eyal, I just want to mention that we will post the recording on the Ituran website, and you can see it from the Zoom link within the next day or two. With that, I would like to hand the call back to Eyal. Eyal, go ahead.

Eyal Sheratzky: On behalf of the management of Ituran, I would like to thank you, our shareholders, for your continued interest and long-term support of our business. We look forward to continuing our success over the coming years. If you are interested in meeting or speaking with us, please feel free to reach out to our investor relation team. With that, we end our call. Have a good day.

#2961. Mortgage Rates Today, Tuesday, November 24: Lower, But …

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates are down this morning, but could seesaw back up tomorrow.

Another day, another substantial swing. This one's lower, but don't count on it starting a trend: We keep seeing mortgage rates move back and forth, but no one's expecting rates to take a dive. If you're watching this space because you're waiting to refinance, it's unlikely your wait is about to end.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.13% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 25 basis points lower than yesterday and unchanged from a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

The amount of day-to-day discrepancy we've been seeing prompted me to take a little cruise around the web this morning to see what 30-year rates lenders are advertising. Mortgage lenders' rates are never identical, but when we're seeing rapid change, the gaps between lenders tend to widen — and that's for sure what I saw. I looked at six different lenders, and saw a nearly 70-basis-point difference between the highest and lowest APRs. (And yes, that was looking for the same loan amount, location and so on.)

My point is, whether you're looking to buy or refinance, make sure to shop multiple lenders. You're the same candidate bringing the same financials to each one, but you could end up with extremely different rate quotes. And it pays to compare. Freddie Mac estimates that comparing at least two lenders could save you up to $600 per year in interest. Compare four or more, and that savings is over $1,200 annually.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context. For more, keep reading below the charts.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Mortgage rates may be lower today, but like I mentioned above, it's been more of a seesaw than a ski slope — and we may be about to hit the high side again. The latest Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index is due out tomorrow morning. Recently, when rates have moved higher, inflation's been in the mix.

Strong inflation's generally bad for borrowing, including to buy a home, because higher interest rates are the remedy. Raising the federal funds rate (the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers of the Federal Reserve actually set) is the Fed's main tactic for managing inflation. While the Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, its decisions influence the entire economy. That includes mortgage lenders, who tend to adjust rates ahead of its decisions.

We already know how PCE's likely to go, since it's the last of the three big inflation measures to be released. We've already gotten last month's Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index. October's CPI came in worse than predicted, showing widespread price increases. (When most of the increase is driven by one area, it's easier to be optimistic that inflation can be contained.) And October’s PPI showed wholesale inflation climbed at its fastest pace in almost four years. PPI measures the price businesses pay for things, so it's often a preview of what consumers could face once those costs get passed along.

Predictions for October PCE aren't great, so at this point the hope is that the numbers aren't even worse than expected. And again, PCE's out tomorrow morning. We'll know whether we're getting seconds (actually, thirds) of bad October inflation news well before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

Markets are currently anticipating a quarter-point hike at the Fed's December meeting. Even though that'll remain the most likely outcome, a poor showing from PCE could spark speculation about a half-point hike. That probably won't be good for mortgage rates.

But back to the upcoming holiday: Markets will be closed on Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, so we'll all have a bit of a break this week. Mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.63% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

#2960. UP Fintech (TIGR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record client assets arrived as commissions slipped and Hong Kong inflows surged.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:54PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

UP Fintech (TIGR +2.33%) reported total revenues of $172.6 million for the third quarter, noting that a diversified revenue mix provided stability as user trading activity moderated. Management stated that the company remains on track to reach its full-year target of 150,000 new funded clients, having already added 110,000 through the first nine months of the year. The company reported that growth was driven primarily by the Singapore and Hong Kong markets, which together contributed more than 80% of new funded accounts. Management noted that the mainland Chinese retail client contribution to both revenue and assets continued to decline, in compliance with regulatory adjustments implemented since May 2022. Strategic focus has transitioned toward expanding wealth management services and extending 24/5 trading capabilities to global markets.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for standing by and welcome to the UP Fintech Holding Limited third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. There will be a presentation followed by a question-and-answer session. I must advise you that this conference is being recorded today, November 24, 2026. I would now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker today, Mr. Aron Lee, the Head of Investor Relations. Thank you. Please go ahead.

Aron Lee: Thank you, operator. Hello, everyone, and thank you for joining us for the call today. UP Fintech Holding Limited third quarter 2026 earnings release was distributed earlier today and is available on our website at ir.itigerup.com as well as global news wire services. On the call today from UP Fintech are Mr. Tianhua Wu, Chairman and CEO, Mr. Qing Fei (John) Zeng, our CFO, Mr. Huang Lei, CEO of U.S. Tiger Securities. Mr. Wu will give an overview of our business operations and discuss corporate highlights. Mr. Zeng will then discuss our financial results. They will both be available to answer your questions during the Q&A session that follows their remarks. Now let me cover the Safe Harbor.

The statements we are about to make contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the U.S. Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. A number of factors could cause actual results to differ materially from those contained in any forward-looking statement. For more information, please refer to our Form 6-K furnished today and our annual report on Form 20-F filed on April 24, 2026. We undertake no obligation to update any forward-looking statement except as required under applicable law. It is my pleasure to now introduce our Chairman and CEO, Mr. Wu. Mr. Wu will make remarks in Chinese, which will be followed by English translation. Mr. Wu, please go ahead with your remarks.

Speaker 3: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining the UP Fintech Holding Limited third quarter 2026 earnings conference call.

Speaker 3: In the third quarter, we remained focused on strengthening our products, services, and operating capabilities. By optimizing our revenue mix, maintaining disciplined expense management, and improving operating efficiency, we continue to strengthen our fundamental organic growth. Total revenue for the third quarter was $173 million, broadly stable compared with the same period last year. Market volatility increased during the quarter, and both client trading activity and commission income declined. However, our diversified revenue mix continued to support our overall performance. Interest income reached $82.7 million, increasing 12.9% year-over-year and 3.6% quarter-over-quarter, mainly driven by higher securities lending activity. Other revenue increased 14.7% sequentially to $24 million, as wealth management products, including fixed coupon notes, continued to gain traction with clients.

For the first nine months of 2026, total revenue increased 16.8% year-over-year to $510 million. On profitability, we continued to manage expense carefully and improve operating efficiency. Net income and non-GAAP net income attributable to UP Fintech were $46.4 million and $49.9 million, increasing 17.9% and 16.4% quarter-over-quarter respectively. Both reached the second highest quarterly level in our history, demonstrating the resilience of our profitability across different market conditions.

Speaker 3: Turning to client growth, we added 48,500 new funded clients in the third quarter, up 48.9% quarter-over-quarter and 54.1% year-over-year. Singapore and Hong Kong remain the two largest contributing markets. We focus not only on the number of new clients, but also on client quality and long-term asset contribution. In the third quarter, strong net asset inflow and positive market movements supported continued growth in client assets. Net asset inflow came mainly from retail clients. Although parts of the market, including certain AI-related stocks, pulled back during the quarter, client portfolios still saw positive market gains overall. Together, these factors led total client assets up 6.7% quarter-over-quarter to a new record of $64.8 billion. Hong Kong was particularly strong.

Net asset inflow from the market approached $1 billion in the third quarter, the highest quarterly level since we entered the market, driving client assets in Hong Kong up more than 20% sequentially. At the same time, client assets increased quarter-over-quarter across all of our overseas markets, reflecting the continued trust global clients place in Tiger Brokers' platform.

Speaker 3: We continue to refine local app features, improve the client experience, and invest in branding awareness. Recently, TradeUP, our U.S. platform, launched Hong Kong equity trading, giving U.S. clients a more complete cross-market investing experience and broader access to Asian markets. We also continue to expand market access and extend trading hours, giving investors around the world greater flexibility in accessing the U.S. market. in November, building on our existing 24/5 U.S. stock trading service, Tiger Brokers became one of the first online brokers globally to support extended-hour trading in eligible U.S. equity options. Orders are routed directly to U.S. options exchanges, allowing clients to adjust their positions and manage risk more efficiently outside regular market hours.

In December, we plan to support the new overnight sessions for U.S. stocks and ETFs from the time they are launched by the exchanges. As the number of execution venues increase and the market structure becomes more diversified, we will build on our established 24/5 trading infrastructure, continue product enhancement, and improve market liquidity to better serve clients who want to manage their U.S. investments around the clock. Apart from adding online products and trading features, localization is also about engaging directly with clients. In October and November, we launched flagship offline events in Hong Kong, Tiger Investment Festival.

This event extended the Tiger Brokers platform experience into an in-person setting, helping more local investors learn about and experience Tiger Brokers while strengthening our connection with the local community. #2959. Before Automating A Role, Audit What It Does

Dan Haiem is the founder and CEO of AppMakers USA, helping business leaders design, build and scale apps that deliver real-world impact.

Every time someone says, “We can automate that,” I think of “the doorman fallacy” that marketer Rory Sutherland shared in his book Alchemy.

It goes like this: A manager looks at the doorman and sees one job: opening the door. An automatic door does that for less money, so the doorman is let go. Then the hotel slowly learns the other tasks the doorman did: greeting guests, noticing who walked in and finding a taxi when it rained.

In May, AI was cited as the leading cause of U.S. job cuts for the third month in a row, with 38,579 cuts, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. I’m not here to debate those decisions, but it’s important that someone at least understands what a role actually does before deciding which ones are necessary.

In evaluating roles, many leaders only look at their most visible task. A technical support answers tickets, a QA finds bugs and a project manager sends updates.

Those verbs are often easy to automate, but they also miss the judgment, relationships, small catches and in-betweens. In my experience, a good QA engineer knows which bug a client will actually notice. A good support rep knows which customer is about to leave.​

Trust me, I’m not against automation. My team automates plenty, but I’ve learned that the most important question is: Which part of a role is the door, and which part is the doorman?

We’ve automated a few things on my team, and client onboarding is where we learned this lesson the hard way. In our onboarding process, a prospect would fill out the contact form on our site and get an email with an NDA and a link to a questionnaire. Once they submitted it, an automation tool read their answers and decided whether we were a fit.

It looked efficient but we had a hard time closing clients. It took us a while to connect that to the form. You see, people often fill out a questionnaire just to finish it. I know because I do the same sometimes, especially when I’m busy. You pick whatever gets you to the next screen.

A real project, though, with its half-formed ideas and open questions, rarely fits in a dropdown. Short answers and ticked boxes told us very little about what they actually needed. I now believe that was one of the reasons. We had automated a judgment call, not a door.

Now, we get on a call first and have a real conversation, with follow-up questions about what they’re trying to solve. A form can only ask the questions you thought of in advance. A conversation can follow the answer that surprises you.

Only once we agree it’s a good fit does the NDA, contract and other paperwork run on automation. Based on what I’ve seen, prospects appreciate that conversation more than any form.

If you’re under pressure to show AI savings, here’s what I’d do before touching a role. Write down everything the role does, including things that go beyond its stated description. Ask the person doing it, because they know what they catch.

Based on those insights, sort each item as mechanical, judgment or relationship. Mechanical work is repeatable and rule-based. Judgment is deciding when the rules don’t fit. Relationship is anywhere the other person cares that you’re human.

Automate the mechanical bucket first, and only that one. In our case, the paperwork that follows a yes was the right thing to automate. Our onboarding form went wrong because we let a tool make a judgment call that looked like a form field.

If a step needs follow-up questions to get to the truth, it belongs in the judgment bucket. In that case, keep at least one human touchpoint to build that trust. For us, that’s the discovery call.

In my experience, none of this takes long. It’s an afternoon with the person who does the job and a whiteboard.​

AI is going to automate a lot of doors, and plenty of them deserve it. Before you do, find out who’s standing there and what they actually do all day. Creating savings on the spreadsheet is easy. The value you can’t see is the part you only notice after it’s gone.​​

#2954. Booking vs. Chewy: Booking Has Higher Revenue, But Chewy Sales Are More Stable

Booking's revenue swung widely from quarter to quarter while Chewy's stayed steadier, and the recent pattern raises questions about what comes next.

By Brendan Coffey – Nov 24, 2026 at 4:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Booking Holdings ›

Booking Holdings (BKNG +1.17%) runs online travel and dining reservation platforms for individual consumers.

It launched an artificial intelligence travel agent named Vayo on Oct. 14. It announced it will appeal a European ruling blocking an acquisition on Nov. 18.

Chewy (CHWY -0.96%) sells pet food, supplies, and medications online to animal owners.

It launched its fifth annual holiday charity and adoption campaign on Nov. 2. A federal judge paused a sales tax lawsuit against Chewy on Sept. 28.

Revenue here refers to the data provider's standardized income-statement revenue line item. Rising revenue shows the business is generating more money.

Booking vs. Chewy Revenue over the last 8 quarters.

Normally, the first thing to note when examining a company's revenue trend is seasonality: some times of the year have stronger buying patterns than others. For most stocks, compare revenue year over year, by quarter. In normal times, seasonality holds true for consumer stocks like these as well.

Booking Holdings gets exceptional volume for summer months in the Northern Hemisphere, which translates into seasonally high revenue being registered in the third quarter.

Chewy has less seasonality, generally around Christmas, like most retailers. The strength of its autoship program mitigates seasonality; however, one would expect its growing focus on veterinary services to further smooth it out.

This chart shows the decision investors face: is it better to have higher revenue that is volatile from quarter to quarter, as with Booking, or to have stable, sequentially stable sales, like Chewy?

Ultimately, such a decision comes down to risk tolerance: the more steady revenue a business has, the less volatile its stock price will be, but the higher-sales, more volatile company will probably see greater rewards from the market over time.

#2953. When AI Finds Data It Shouldn’t: Why Relevance Isn't Permission

Vibhor Kumar is a technology executive and author focused on enterprise data and AI platforms, modern architecture, and technology strategy.

​In one enterprise search project I advised on at a large financial services organization, data from a governed operational system was copied into a separate search layer to improve retrieval speed. The source system had established access rules. The search copy did not carry them all forward.

We discovered this when an analyst searched for information and received a client record that the original application would not have allowed that person to see. The search system had not been compromised. It was doing exactly what it had been built to do: finding information in the data available to it.

We had moved the data without fully moving the authorization that belonged with it. I have thought about that incident again as enterprises connect more of their data to AI systems, and it shaped three practices I now recommend.

A lot of the discussion about AI data risk starts with the model: whether it could memorize sensitive information, expose something through a prompt or be tricked into returning data someone should not see. Those are valid concerns. But there is another problem that happens earlier. The AI may not need to get around a security control at all. We may already have put the data somewhere it can reach.

Data gets copied into vector stores, search indexes, analytical systems and training datasets, usually for understandable reasons. The source database may have years of work behind its access model: roles, tenant boundaries, retention policies, audit history and application-specific authorization. But the new retrieval layer may reproduce only part of that logic. Authentication does not fix that problem. The system still has to determine whether that user is allowed to retrieve this particular information, in this context, at this time.

The immediate fix in that project was to stop relying on the search copy as if it carried the same authorization model as the source system. The team tightened the retrieval path so that access was checked against the user’s actual permissions before a record became eligible to appear in search results. That experience is one reason I now use the phrase “filter first, search second.” Relevance should be evaluated only within the set of information the user is entitled to retrieve.

Semantic search is very good at answering, “What information is most related to this request?” It should not be responsible for answering, “Is this user allowed to receive it?” Before records become eligible for retrieval, the system needs deterministic controls around tenant, role, geography, entitlement or data sensitivity. If the system retrieves broadly and tries to apply authorization afterward, sensitive information may already have crossed the boundary you were trying to protect.

The more important change was architectural. We stopped treating security on the source system as sufficient protection for downstream copies. Any new search or analytical layer had to account explicitly for how source permissions would be preserved, synchronized or enforced at retrieval time.

That does not mean enterprises should stop copying data. Sometimes, a separate index is the right way to meet latency requirements, and analytical replicas can isolate expensive workloads from transactional systems. The distinction I care about is whether the duplication is intentional. When a team can explain why the copy exists, who owns it, who can reach it, how permissions stay aligned with the source and when the copy should disappear, the trade-off is reasonable. Problems start when the copy survives longer than the thinking that created it. At that point, it becomes architectural debt.

A simple test: When a customer, employee or document loses access in the source system, can the organization show that the same information is no longer retrievable from every derived copy? If that answer is unclear, the access model is probably unclear, too.

If a CIO asked me where to begin, I would not start with a large governance program. I would first map where sensitive data has been copied for AI, search and analytics, and then compare those copies with the systems they came from. For each one, I would want to know who owns it, how access is enforced, how permissions change, how deletion works and whether anyone can prove that those controls are still aligned with the source.

AI is making enterprise information much easier to find. But finding the right information is only half the job. The other half is ensuring that it reaches someone who was actually allowed to receive it.​

#2952. ​How Much Autonomy Is Too Much For An AI Agent?

Alexey Spas is the founder and CEO of Instinctools, a software engineering company focused on AI-powered digital solutions.

​What happens when an AI agent you trust breaks its limits of autonomy and won’t take no for an answer?​​

Neither the Australian nor the Canadian government was prepared for this kind of trespassing, yet it happened to their websites. An OpenAI model gained unauthorized access to Australia’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service while researching public medical spending, while an unidentified AI agent attempted to hack Canada’s Library and Archives website. Neither incident resulted in a confirmed compromise of individual records or government systems, but both involved AI agents taking actions beyond their intended research tasks. The activity occurred in May and June 2026 but wasn’t publicly disclosed until September, when OpenAI and the research lab Transluce independently reported their findings.​​​

What this signals to me is that AI agents are forcing both public and private sectors to raise the drawbridge against a threat they didn’t even know was coming. For companies deploying agents at scale, the governance challenge extends beyond choosing a theoretical level of autonomy to ensuring that abnormal behavior can be detected, contained, reconstructed and assigned to a responsible owner.​

MIT recognizes five levels of AI agent autonomy. Starting from level 3, as the human gradually steps back to give the agent more room to act, a handoff problem arises. The system needs to recognize where its authority ends and when escalation to a human is required. The harder failure mode appears when an agent continues pursuing a legitimate goal after crossing that boundary, despite signals telling it to stop.​

This suggests a useful operating principle: the autonomy granted to AI agents can’t safely outpace the maturity of the company’s incident response and AI governance policies. Policies on paper are not enough; they need to be enacted. That maturity rests on four capabilities:

1. Detection: Identifying unusual actions as they happen

2. Investigation: Tracing back the agent’s actions

3. Response: Stopping agent activity and rolling back or mitigating the consequences

4. Accountability: Establishing clear responsibility when an agent’s actions affect a person or a company

A weakness in any one of those capabilities raises the cost of failure: unusual behavior may go unnoticed, incidents may be harder to reconstruct, containment may come too late or responsibility may remain unclear when an agent’s actions affect people or business operations.

Not every scenario can be rehearsed in advance. So the decision to give an agent any degree of autonomy depends on answering a few questions first:​

Every consequential output should have a way to be checked—a second system, a source link or a human-created reference—before the agent is allowed to act on it.​

The Medicare case above illustrates what can happen when an agent treats a block as something to overcome rather than a boundary to respect. A block should stop an agent in its tracks and trigger escalation to a human. It shouldn’t become an obstacle to work around.​

Impact should be classified by severity and blast radius. An agent accessing a public webpage poses a different level of risk than one accessing an internal server or sensitive business systems. The more sensitive the data and consequential the actions an agent can access, the tighter its permissions, oversight and safeguards should be.​

When several vendors are involved, incident ownership can’t fall through the cracks. From where I stand, someone on the customer side needs to be ultimately accountable, even if detection, investigation or remediation depends on external providers. That means defining from the get-go who detects an incident, who notifies whom and who can switch the agent off.

The autonomy ladder can only be climbed when the evidence is there. Autonomy should be earned, with each traceable and reviewable log supporting more trust in the agent. The ladder also runs downward. When the environment, model, tools or performance indicators change, the autonomy limits narrow again until the evidence rebuilds.​

Anthropic found an interesting pattern: new Claude Code users enable auto-approve about 20% of the time. Past 750 sessions, this rate rises to 40%. Yet experienced users also interrupted their agents more often. Anthropic reinforces that effective oversight is not about approving each action but being able to intervene when necessary.​

Enterprise deployments can follow the same principle: greater trust should lead to more selective oversight, not less accountability. Rather than relying on subjective confidence in an agent, organizations can use operational metrics to determine whether its autonomy is justified and where additional controls may be needed. NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework Playbook similarly emphasizes incident tracking, response planning and human oversight. Some useful indicators include:​

• How often humans intervene or override an agent​

• The frequency of rejected or blocked actions​

• How often actions require rollback or remediation​

• Actions that fall outside expected behavioral patterns​

• Incidents categorized by action type and severity​

For a professional services group’s AI operational platform developed at Instinctools, the autonomy was phased in: the low-risk employee assistant agent was deployed before higher-risk quoting and advisory agents. The email triage agent only reached all the business units after its accuracy was raised from 74% to 87%, past the client’s 85% target.

Following MIT’s definition of five autonomy levels mentioned above, I keep returning to this distinction between agents’ autonomy and humans’ authority. Freedom to act within defined boundaries belongs to agents. But authority stays with humans who answer for what agents do and decide if and when their scope is ready to grow.​

The test is simple: deploy only those agents that stop when told no and only when you have a framework in place to watch and contain them, investigate what happened and take responsibility if needed. If an agent can reason its way around a limit, it’s not a limit.​​

#2951. Prediction: A $10,000 Investment in Nvidia Stock Will Be Worth This Much by Year-End 2027

Nvidia faces several risks, but it has solid upside despite potential headwinds.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 24, 2026 at 4:02PM EST

A lot has changed for Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%) in a very short period of time, and this will ultimately have a big impact on where the semiconductor stock trades by the end of 2027. Given the stock's strong performance over the years, it tends to be widely held by retail investors. With a lot on the line, let's see where the stock could be headed over the next year.

The biggest change for Nvidia comes at the top. In a shocking turn of events, co-founder Jensen Huang, who had been the only CEO in the company's history, resigned earlier this month only to be welcomed back by the board less than two weeks later. Huang stepped down after he admitted marital infidelity as reports of multiple affairs bubbled to the surface. Investors focused on his relationship with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no relation), who has been accused of being a Chinese spy.

Singapore-based Megaspeed has been a significant Nvidia customer, buying nearly $5 billion worth of its chips over the past few years. However, there are now allegations that many of these chips were illegally being directed to China.

The return of Jensen Huang as CEO for Nvidia is huge. Huang was a visionary who seemingly knew where the market was headed before anyone else. There are multiple examples of the company taking action based on his foresight, including:

These have all helped the company transform from a simple chipmaker into a complete AI infrastructure company that has been getting an increasingly larger percentage of spending per gigawatt of compute capacity.

However, there is still a question of what happens with China. The U.S. has further cracked down on export controls of AI chips. The risk is that there is a lot more indirect Nvidia revenue coming from China, which could disappear.

The Huang situation is not the only news Nvidia has endured this month, though. The midterm elections saw a sweeping victory for Democrats and candidates that ran on anti-data-center campaigns. These candidates have widely called for a data center build-out moratorium, and it is expected that the regulatory environment for building new data centers will get a lot tougher in the coming years. Neoclouds are expected to face the brunt of this, which could be bad news for Nvidia, which saw about 44% of its data center revenue last quarter coming from neoclouds and businesses.

On top of this, Anthropic (ANT -6.54%) revealed that its Claude Mythos model was able to switch models running on Nvidia's GPUs to run on Advanced Micro Devices' (AMD -8.86%) GPUs with little human intervention in just a few days. This process used to take six to 12 months and a dozen engineers. This could be a serious blow to Nvidia's CUDA moat and eventually lead to lower prices and serious gross margin compression.

That said, Nvidia is still well positioned in the medium term, as it has significant supply chain advantages. It has locked up a substantial amount of the supply-constrained high bandwidth memory (HBM) required by AI chips, as well as capacity at foundries. In addition, with its Vera Rubin platform, it is now getting $40 billion per gigawatt of compute capacity compared to the $25 billion per gigawatt it is capturing with Grace Blackwell, which is a significant revenue lift. This will help support the 75% growth the company projected for fiscal 2028 (ending January 2028) and beyond.

The issues Nvidia faces are likely to keep a cap on its forward P/E multiple, but it should still see solid growth in the medium term. I think it should be able to maintain a forward multiple of at least 12, which would value the stock at around $261 at the end of 2027 based on the fiscal 2029 analyst consensus of $21.75. As such, a $10,000 investment today — getting you 61 shares as I write this — would be worth over $15,900. That’s my prediction.

There is some decent upside to the AI stock from its current beaten-down levels, despite potential risks.

#2949. A SpaceX-Tesla Deal Could Come in December. Here's Why 1 Group of Investors Should Be Worried.

A merger is likely to make Tesla's robotaxi more competitive in the future, spelling trouble for its rivals.

By Lee Samaha – Nov 24, 2026 at 4:07PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

A merger between Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -5.65%) and Tesla (TSLA -0.20%) would have far-reaching consequences, not least by combining a leader in physical artificial intelligence (AI) -- Tesla's electric vehicles, robotaxi, and Optimus robots -- with a company that has a rapidly growing AI infrastructure services business (SpaceX).

That combination could have profound consequences for the major near-term catalyst for both companies, namely robotaxi, and that should be considered a threat to Uber Technologies (UBER +0.98%). Here's why.

To be clear and consistent, I don't think aggressively pursuing a merger is in the best interest of Tesla shareholders right now. In truth, we don't know if a bid will occur and what the terms will be. However, it strikes me that Tesla shareholders have waited for years and endured plenty of missed robotaxi timelines, the disappointments of Cybertruck, and industrywide downward revisions to electric vehicle sales, only to sell out just as Tesla is set to scale up its robotaxi rollout.

That's an issue for Tesla shareholders, as they could end up with a larger share of the new company than the 47% ownership stake Bank of America analysts estimated in an all-stock deal. Still, I think there's another group of shareholders who should be more worried: Uber shareholders.

A merger would create even better conditions for Tesla to realize its ambition to become a transportation-as-a-service (TaaS) company running a fleet of low-cost-per-mile Cybercabs. That's a direct threat to Uber's marketplace, at least in the areas where Cybercab has regulatory clearance. The threat has not gone unnoticed, and there's a reason Uber already has multi-partner autonomous robotaxi arrangements with companies like Waymo, Zoox, and Wayve.

When Tesla CEO Elon Musk says the "vast majority" of Cybercab will be "Tesla-owned and Transport-as-a-Service," this is highly unlikely to encompass a partnership with Uber.

In addition, merging with SpaceX would bring many benefits for Tesla's robotaxi.

All told, everything points to a merger making it easier for Tesla to ramp robotaxi and drive Cybercab's total cost of ownership (TCO) per mile lower. The latter is the key metric to follow, as it would facilitate a virtuous cycle in which low ride fares encourage further Cybercab fleet expansion. That's a real risk for Uber, because if its robotaxi partners can't achieve a comparable TCO, then Tesla's robotaxi could make significant inroads into some of its most profitable geographies.

#2947. B2B Companies Should Stop Letting B2C Set Their Digital Commerce Roadmap

Jary Carter is CEO and Co-Founder of Oro Inc., the company behind OroCommerce, a B2B eCommerce platform for manufacturers and distributors.

​For years, B2B companies have taken their cues on digital progress from consumer commerce. Amazon was treated as the model that B2B would eventually have to follow, with every buying experience starting to look more like Amazon.

As the CEO of an e-commerce platform who works closely with B2B partners, I can tell you that never happened. Amazon became another channel, not the blueprint for B2B commerce.​

Now agentic purchasing is getting similar treatment. B2B companies have seen this pattern before: A consumer trend gets treated as the future of commerce before anyone asks how well it fits B2B.

So what happens when that thinking starts setting the digital commerce roadmap?

Consumer commerce tends to treat less human involvement as progress. Search, buy, check out, done.​

B2B buyers want plenty of independence, too. But taking the seller out of the experience can take valuable context out with them. ​

For many B2B companies, the seller’s knowledge of the customer is part of the competitive advantage. Digital commerce should build on that advantage, not erase it.​

One specialty distributor we work with learned this the hard way. Its first e-commerce launch struggled so badly that leadership questioned whether digital selling made sense for the business at all. The team later described the experience as “anonymous e-commerce” because it separated buyers from their account context and the people who knew them.​

On its second attempt, the company brought account management straight into the digital experience. Customers could see their dedicated rep inside the portal, while sales and service staff used impersonation to handle onboarding, guide first orders and troubleshoot on the fly.​

Buyers still get the independence they wanted. The difference is that going digital no longer cuts them off from the people who know their account.​

A retail-style roadmap can make the seller look like friction to remove. In B2B, digital commerce should do the opposite: Give the buyer-seller relationship a place to continue online.

The same problem shows up in how commerce teams define flexibility. The conversation often stays at the experience layer: change the storefront faster, launch a new journey, test a different way to buy.​

Useful. But B2B companies usually discover the limits of their technology somewhere else.​

Can you bring an acquired business onto the same setup when it has a different ERP? Add a region with its own catalog and pricing rules? Change an approval process or introduce a new sales model without rebuilding half the system?​

A company can have a highly flexible front end and still struggle with changes like these. Being able to redesign the buying experience quickly doesn’t mean the commerce setup can adapt quickly to the business behind it.​​

For B2B, flexibility is tested when the business changes, not when the homepage does. The roadmap has to account for that.

AI is the newest version of the same pattern. Retail attention has centered on shopping agents, conversational discovery and AI that can research or complete a purchase.

Those ideas may have a place in B2B, too. They just aren’t automatically the best place to start.​

In B2B, AI can play a different role: help sellers know their buyers better, surface customer and deal information faster and take repetitive work out of the sales process.​

While my company’s platform offers AI features, which certainly shapes my view on this topic, the shift I’m pointing to is about identifying where AI makes the most sense in B2B rather than which tools to adopt. ​

More than 75% of B2B orders still arrive through email, PDFs, spreadsheets, voicemail or handwritten notes, according to Distribution Strategy Group. Their research found that AI-based order processing can deliver productivity gains of 20% to 30%. Gartner also found that AI is already saving sellers an average of 4.8 hours per week.​

Some of the highest-value AI in B2B may sit far from the storefront. That is why copying the retail roadmap can send investment toward the most visible use cases instead of the most valuable ones.

Watch what B2C does with search, usability and convenience. But it should not decide what progress looks like for your B2B business. ​

The next priority should come from the processes your company needs to improve, the relationships it needs to strengthen and the markets it plans to enter. Use retail for inspiration. But don’t adopt its story. B2B has a more interesting one to tell. ​

Our robust customer pipeline is more than a leading indicator of future revenue, however. We believe it reflects the growing criticality of our solutions in the AI era, as rapid technological evolution creates ever more complex challenges across numerous and different markets. Customers are increasingly turning to ADI's higher-value offerings to help lower their total cost of ownership, accelerate their time to market, and, of course, enhance system performance. We are benefiting from the intensely demanding test requirements of modern AI compute, memory, networking, and power systems, where complexity is increasing at an extraordinary rate. In industrial automation, customers continue to digitalize, automate, and deploy robots across semiconductor fabs, biopharma, data centers, and other manufacturing environments to accelerate productivity and address evolving geopolitical and labor dynamics. As a result, our automation revenue and design-ins across industrial control, connectivity, and robotics segments accelerated significantly in fiscal 2026, with the fastest growth coming from robotics.

We expect the next evolution of robotics from automation to autonomy will unlock tasks that historically required human intervention and create opportunity for higher-value ADI content and subsystems that can reduce latency and increase system accuracy. Autonomous robotic modalities, including humanoids, which can require up to 10x more ADI content compared to traditional robots, will steadily increase our opportunity over time. In aerospace and defense, systems are evolving rapidly to sense threats earlier, communicate securely in contested environments, and make mission-critical decisions much, much faster. These requirements are driving increasingly complex radar, communications, and autonomous machines, where ADI's ability to combine RF, signal processing, IMUs, and power management into higher-value solutions is differentiated.

In this sector, we almost doubled growth in our design pipeline this past year across both established and emerging defense customers, which we believe positions us for continued growth in 2027 and beyond. In healthcare, our revenue growth accelerated in 2026 as innovation across the industry increasingly converged around continuous glucose monitoring, AI-assisted imaging, and surgical robotics. Our precision sensing, signal processing, algorithms, and ultra-low-power technologies are helping customers to deliver innovative solutions designed to better manage chronic disease, help clinicians detect and diagnose conditions earlier, and make complex procedures more precise and less invasive. Our growing design and pipeline across myriad applications there positions ADI for continued growth in fiscal 2027 and reinforces the potential of our longer-term opportunity.

In energy, rapidly rising electricity demand is magnifying one of the world's most fundamental engineering challenges: how to generate, manage, store, and deliver significantly more power while improving efficiency and reliability. ADI sits at several key points across that system. For example, our precision sensing enables greater visibility and control of the grid, while our battery management technologies enable more efficient storage and local distribution. Energy was one of our strongest areas of pipeline growth through fiscal 2026, reinforcing our long-term outlook for this business. Turning now to automotive, we delivered a second consecutive year of record revenue, despite lower vehicle production, due to our strong and expanding position in next-generation ADAS and infotainment systems.

As vehicles move toward greater autonomy, they must process dramatically more sensor information, move more data, and reliably power many interconnected subsystems, all the while meeting demanding requirements for signal integrity, energy efficiency, and safety. These challenges play to ADI's strengths in high-speed connectivity and power solutions designed to support functional safety requirements. L2+ autonomous driving systems remain relatively early in their global adoption, and as the industry progresses toward higher levels of autonomy, we expect content opportunities for ADI to continue to increase. In the past year, design and growth across our GMSL, A2B, and functionally safe power solutions underscores our substantial role in enabling the vehicle of tomorrow.

We saw a strong increase in designs for battery management solutions, which we expect to grow in the coming year and beyond as EV adoption increases. Not surprisingly, our data center business was our fastest-growing market in fiscal 2026, both from a revenue and design-in perspective. Robust investments in AI infrastructure are creating enormous challenges around two of the physical bottlenecks to scaling AI: moving exponentially more data and efficiently delivering unprecedented power loads. ADI is well-positioned to address both. In the networking domain, our optical control technology keeps electro-optical systems precisely tuned across everything from pluggables to OCS, so that every packet of light is accurate, stable, and efficient.

As you know, data center power has become one of the most significant constraints to AI advancement, as increasing rack and processor densities are fundamentally changing how power is converted, controlled, protected, and delivered. Customers are choosing ADI to help ensure that every watt used in the data center is available for computation and maximum impact. As the resulting thermodynamic challenges grow with increasing power density, liquid cooling is shifting from an option to a requirement. Customers are turning to ADI to translate physical signals, such as temperature, flow, leakage, and coolant health, into actionable intelligence, which is creating a new differentiated content opportunity.

Overall, we believe our data center revenues will continue to be one of the faster-growing businesses in 2027 and beyond. Finally, continued demand at the premium end of the consumer market overcame memory headwinds to drive double-digit growth in revenue and design activity across premium handsets, wearables, hearables, and gaming segments, which positions ADI for continued diversified growth in this sector in 2027 and beyond. In closing, FY 2026 demonstrated what makes ADI different. We are built to define and capture new waves of opportunity as we compound the businesses underpinning our resilience through cycles.

We leverage a six-decade culture of curiosity and cutting-edge innovation to continuously advance the state of the art at the electrophysical interface, a boundary that is increasingly central to the advance of technology's most valuable applications. Our customers increasingly choose ADI as a strategic partner for our applications, domain expertise, scope of high-performance analog software and AI capabilities, and differentiated hybrid manufacturing strategy. As we enter 2027, we continue to invest with discipline to further enhance and extend the value we can deliver to our customers and shareholders alike in the years ahead. With that, I'll turn it over to Rich.

Il ritorno in campionato, poi una rete cancellata dal fuorigioco. Albert Gudmundsson ritrova il campo in Serie A nella vittoria della Lazio contro il Lecce e nel recupero arriva anche a superare Falcone. Un’azione che avrebbe completato il suo pomeriggio all’Olimpico, ma che non modifica il risultato: finisce 3-0, con la doppietta di Noslin e il pallonetto di Frattesi. Per l’islandese resta il ritorno a disposizione di Gennaro Gattuso anche in una partita ufficiale. Dopo il percorso di recupero e il passaggio nell’amichevole durante la sosta, contro i salentini arriva uno spezzone nel finale.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Gattuso manda in campo Gudmundsson all’88’ al posto di Andrea Pinamonti, con la Lazio avanti di due reti.

Poco dopo Frattesi firma il terzo gol, mettendo definitivamente al sicuro il successo biancoceleste. Il minuto della sostituzione è confermato dal tabellino ufficiale della società. Nel recupero l’islandese trova lo spazio alle spalle della difesa, evita Falcone e deposita il pallone in rete. La partenza in posizione di fuorigioco rende però vano il suo tentativo. Prima del Lecce, Gudmundsson aveva già ritrovato minuti nell’amichevole del 14 novembre contro il Mgarr United.
