#2942. DICK'S (DKS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management raised its core guidance, yet promotional footwear pressure and Foot Locker losses remain in focus.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 4:08PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

DICK'S (DKS +14.59%) reported third quarter results that included a raise to the full year operating income guidance for its core business segment. Management indicated that the company gained market share during the period and is continuing the integration of the Foot Locker acquisition. The company issued $1 billion in senior notes and repurchased 6.7 million shares of common stock during the quarter. President and Chief Executive Officer Lauren Hobart stated that the company is investing in long-term growth through experiential retail concepts and the expansion of the GameChanger youth sports platform.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the DICK'S Sporting Goods, Incorporated Q3 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Nate Gilch, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Nathaniel A. (Nate) Gilch: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us to discuss our third quarter 2026 results. On today's call will be Ed Stack, our Executive Chairman; Lauren R. Hobart, our President and Chief Executive Officer; and Navdeep Gupta, our Chief Financial Officer. A playback of today's call will be archived on our Investor Relations website located at investors.dicks.com for approximately 12 months. As a reminder, we will be making forward-looking statements, which are subject to various risks and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ materially from these statements.

Any such statements should be considered in conjunction with cautionary statements in our earnings release and risk factor discussions in our filings with the SEC, including our last annual report on Form 10-K as well as cautionary statements made during this call. We assume no obligation to update any of these forward-looking statements or information. Please refer to our Investor Relations website to find the reconciliation of our non-GAAP financial measures referenced in today's call. I also want to note a couple of admin items. First, a quick reminder on our comparable sales reporting.

Foot Locker will be included in our quarterly comp calculations beginning in Q4 of 2026, which will mark the start of their 14th full month of operations post acquisition. And finally, for future scheduling purposes, we are tentatively planning to publish our fourth quarter 2026 earnings results on March 9, 2027. With that, I'll turn the call over to Ed.

Edward W. Stack: Thanks, Nate. Good morning, everyone. Our third quarter performance was driven by another strong quarter in the DICK'S business with comps up 2.6%. We had a very strong back-to-school season. Our team continued to execute at an extremely high level, and we're gaining market share. We're very confident in our competitive position. We also made solid progress at Foot Locker, despite the athletic footwear market continuing to be challenging. Global Foot Locker comps increased 0.5% for the quarter with the U.S. Foot Locker banner, where we focused our efforts first, comped over 4%. One of the great advantages of the company we've built is the breadth and flexibility of our portfolio.

If the consumer moves between brands or categories, we move with them. We've also built multiple pillars for profitable and sustained growth. Many of you invested in DICK'S, because you believed in the opportunity House of Sport and Field House create for us. Today, we can tell you very clearly, they're working. The economics are compelling. For House of Sport in year 1, we continue to expect approximately $35 million omnichannel sales and very strong profitability with EBITDA margins of approximately 20%. Our athletes love the experience and our brand partners and landlords want to be a part of it.

GameChanger is another important part of our growth story, continuing to create a unique connection to millions of youth athletes and their families. Lauren will take you through the progress we're seeing across House of Sport, Field House and GameChanger, and we've included additional detail in our investor presentation. Moving to Foot Locker. We've often said that Foot Locker is the -- that footwear is the engine that pulls the chain. It's a critical part of the DICK'S business, and one of the reasons we acquired Foot Locker was our belief that it would make DICK'S even stronger over time. Our brand partners will continue to evolve their marketplace strategies.

At different points, they may lean into sport or they may lean into sneaker specialty. We believe owning DICK'S and Foot Locker gives us the flexibility to serve the consumer and partner with brands across the entire marketplace. We participate in the full life cycle of footwear. We can help brands launch innovation through atmos, our Tier 0 athletic specialty retailer, create heat and demand through Foot Locker and our House of Sport locations, scale winning products across DICK'S, Foot Locker and Champs Sports and ultimately help manage end-of-life inventory through Going, Going, Gone. We don't believe there's another retailer that can do all of this at our scale.

Our reach makes us an important partner to the brands, gives us access to differentiated and high-demand product. We believe that we have a unique competitive position in the marketplace. This position gives us the opportunity to accelerate the growth of House of Sport, Field House and the overall company. At Foot Locker, we continue to address the fundamentals, the assortment, the stores, the customer experience and the economics of the business. We've learned a lot about the Foot Locker consumer. And one thing is very clear, newness matters. We're shifting the assortment toward what the consumer is responding to with more in-demand product, and we are moving quickly to reassort brands, franchises and silhouettes as preferences change.

As we indicated last quarter, the athletic footwear marketplace remains promotional as there's too much legacy product in the channel. As a result, the level of promotional activity in Q3 was generally in line with our expectations. However, we do continue to see strong consumer response to newness and innovation. The launch business also improved this quarter with consumers responding favorably to key Jordan Retro launches and the Caitlin 1 shoe. This demand for compelling new product is showing up across our business. In fact, footwear outperformed the overall DICK'S business. And as I mentioned earlier, Foot Locker delivered slightly positive comps for the quarter. We're also making progress in our stores.

During Q3, we expanded Fast Break by approximately 75 stores, bringing the total to approximately 390 across the globe. They continue to outperform the balance of the Foot Locker fleet, and we remain very confident in the opportunity that Fast Break presents. Additionally, we've developed a menu of options to strengthen the Foot Locker business and focus our resources on the biggest opportunities. We're actively evaluating those options, and we'll take action where we believe it can improve the health and profitability of the business. That includes taking a close look at stores that aren't meeting our profitability expectations and determining the right path. Moving to capital allocation.

We've always said it would -- we've always said we would be opportunistic with share repurchases when we believe the valuation created an attractive opportunity. This past quarter, we believe the market had overreacted to short-term challenges and our share price did not reflect the long-term strength of our company. We accessed the bond market, completing a $1 billion senior note offering and in the third quarter, repurchased 6.7 million shares of stock for over $900 million. We remain very disciplined in how we will deploy capital. Our priorities are clear. We'll continue to invest in the DICK'S omnichannel centered around House of Sport, Field House and GameChanger, while improving Foot Locker's performance.

We'll continue returning capital to shareholders through dividends, while remaining opportunistic with share buybacks. When we step back and take a look at the company today, we believe our strategic position has never been stronger. We've built something that's difficult to replicate. We have the leading sports retailer -- we have the leading sports retail business in the country. House of Sport and Field House continue to be our primary growth vehicles. We have a global position in sneaker culture through Foot Locker and DICK'S. And we believe through DICK'S and Golf Galaxy, we're the largest partner to the golf brands. GameChanger diversifies our revenue stream and enables us a unique connection to youth sports and their families.

We have deep relationships with the most important brands across the industry. All of this puts us at the center of sport and culture and gives us more ways to serve the athletes wherever and however they engage. We are focused on continuing to gain market share and increase long-term shareholder value. Before I turn it over to Lauren, I'd like to thank our teammates across the globe. They've done a great job this quarter, and we all really appreciate everything they continue to do for our athletes and our business. I'd also like to particularly recognize our WSS teammates. The team delivered positive comps and a profitable quarter. We're very proud of their performance.

With that, I'd like to turn it over to Lauren.

Lauren R. Hobart: Thank you, Ed, and good morning, everyone. As Ed mentioned, we delivered another strong quarter in the DICK'S business. We continue to gain market share and execute against the strategic pillars that have driven our sustained growth. In Q3, we delivered total sales growth of 3.1% and comp sales growth of 2.6% for the DICK'S business. Our comps were driven by broad-based growth, including a very strong back-to-school season. Footwear was particularly strong, outperforming the overall DICK'S comp. We also saw continued strength in team sports, including increased demand in soccer following this summer's FIFA World Cup as well as continued momentum in license and trading cards.

More broadly, we continue to benefit from strong sports participation trends and our active athlete database continues to grow. Given the continued strength we're seeing across the DICK'S business, we are raising the low end of our full year comp sales outlook and increasing our operating income expectations. Navdeep will provide more detail on our updated outlook later in the call. Athletes are responding to newness and innovation and our increasingly differentiated assortment gives them more reasons to choose DICK'S. House of Sport is a big part of that. We've talked with you quite a bit about the concept over the last several years.

As we continue to scale House of Sport across the country, we want to be very clear, we are extremely pleased with the sales, profitability and returns we've seen, and our conviction in the opportunity continues to grow. As Ed mentioned, we continue to expect House of Sport to have approximately $35 million in year 1 omnichannel sales and EBITDA margins of approximately 20%, with cash-on-cash returns well above our cost of capital. House of Sport is also informing how we're evolving the broader DICK'S fleet, most notably through Field House. As we apply key learnings from House of Sport, we're seeing stronger Field House productivity than we initially expected.

We now expect our Field House locations to generate approximately $17 million in first year omnichannel sales and approximately 20% year 1 EBITDA margins. And now that we have several years of performance across a growing base of House of Sport locations, we're seeing the strength of the model extend beyond year 1. These stores have consistently driven positive comps in subsequent years with profitability continuing to improve as they have matured. Those strong economics make continued investment in House of Sport and Field House, a terrific use of our capital. In Q3, we opened 6 new House of Sport locations and 3 new Field House locations, bringing us to 47 House of Sport and 55 Field House locations nationwide.

But the value of House of Sport goes well beyond the economics of the individual stores. House of Sport is creating more opportunities for unique collaborations and access to differentiated products, while serving as an increasingly important platform for our brand partners. It allows us to bring brands and products to life in ways that aren't possible in a traditional format. And for newer brands, it provides a powerful platform to launch and build their business with us before expanding across our broader portfolio. We've seen that with brands like HOKA, On, and FP Movement, and we're excited about newer relationships with brands, including Gymshark, Vuori and Arc'teryx.

Beyond these advantages, House of Sport is helping us elevate the entire DICK'S ecosystem. It gives us a platform to test new ideas, learn what works and scale the best of those ideas across Field House stores and the broader DICK'S fleet. We've done that with concepts like House of Cleats and Collectors Clubhouse as well as enhanced storytelling experiences powered by the DICK'S Media Network. The success of House of Sport is also opening up new real estate opportunities for us. Landlords want House of Sport because of the traffic it generates and the positive impact it can have on their properties.

As a result, we now have access to some of the best real estate in the country, including locations like Tysons Corner, Palm Beach Gardens, and Topanga in L.A., opportunities that simply were not available to us 5 years ago. So when we think about the return of House of Sport, we think about much more than the individual store P&L. Moving on to GameChanger. GameChanger is another great example of how we are deepening our relationship with athletes. This November marks 10 years since DICK'S acquired GameChanger. And over that time, the team has built a highly profitable, high-growth subscription business and one of the most trusted platforms in youth sports used by millions of families across America.

The growth has been significant. GameChanger's annual revenue has grown from approximately $8 million when we acquired the business to nearly $150 million in fiscal 2025, a compound annual growth rate of nearly 40%. For fiscal 2026, we expect GameChanger's revenue to approach $200 million, and we see a lot of opportunity ahead. While we remain excited about continued growth in diamond sports, basketball is our next significant opportunity. More than 13 million kids between the ages of 6 and 17 play basketball in the U.S. We're bringing the technology and reach that we've built in diamond sports to basketball, while tailoring the experience to the unique needs of basketball clubs and athletes.

We're seeing strong momentum in other parts of the DICK'S business as well. Our highly profitable e-commerce business continues to grow faster than the DICK'S business overall, while DICK'S Media Network is creating new opportunities for our brand partners to connect with our highly engaged athlete base. We're also finding new ways to connect with athletes where sport and culture come together. Just a few weeks ago, we were thrilled to announce a multiyear partnership with Caitlin Clark, making her the first-ever brand partner across both DICK'S and Foot Locker. Caitlin's relevance extends well beyond basketball.

Her passion for sport broadly makes her a great fit for both businesses and creates exciting opportunities for us to connect with athletes in new ways. In closing, we have tremendous confidence in the DICK'S business and the opportunities we have to extend our leadership position and drive long-term growth. At Foot Locker, we're encouraged by the progress we're seeing, while remaining focused on the work required to build a healthier, more productive business over time. Before I turn it over to Navdeep, I want to thank all of our teammates. Your hard work and dedication to our athletes every day are what make our success possible.

As we head into Thanksgiving and the busy holiday season, we are all especially grateful for everything you continue to do. With that, I'll turn it over to Navdeep to share more detail on our financial results and 2026 outlook. Navdeep, over to you.

Navdeep Gupta: Thank you, Lauren, and good morning, everyone. Let's begin with a review of our third quarter results. As a reminder, the current quarter includes the full 13-week of Foot Locker results compared to approximately 8 weeks in the prior year period following the acquisition close on September 8, 2025. Consolidated net sales increased 23.2% to $5.13 billion. Within this, the sales of the Foot Locker business increased $866 million due primarily to the additional 5 weeks of Foot Locker ownership. Comp sales for the DICK'S business increased 2.6%, driven by a 3.7% increase in average ticket, partially offset by a 1.1% decline in transactions.

We delivered a very strong back-to-school season and saw broad-based growth across footwear, team sports, license and trading cards. Warmer weather in October pressured our cold weather categories and contributed to lower transactions, partially offsetting the strength we saw earlier in the quarter. Importantly, the 2.6% comp was on top of a strong 5.7% comp increase from last year. Pro forma comps for the Foot Locker business increased 0.5% for the quarter, driven by a 1.3% increase in North America. Notably, the U.S. Foot Locker banner delivered comp growth of 4.1%. From a margin perspective, consolidated non-GAAP gross profit was $1.66 billion or 32.4% of net sales, down 73 basis points from last year.

The year-over-year decline was primarily driven by the mix impact from the Foot Locker business from the additional ownership period. For the DICK'S business, gross margin declined 26 basis points from last year. This decline was driven by higher occupancy and supply chain-related costs, including higher fuel costs as well as product mix and pricing investment in athletic footwear. These pressures were partially offset by strong growth from DICK'S Media Network and GameChanger. Turning to expenses. On a non-GAAP basis, consolidated SG&A expenses increased 25.1% or $278.4 million to $1.39 billion and deleveraged 42 basis points compared to last year's non-GAAP results. For the DICK'S business, SG&A expenses deleveraged 10 basis points.

Consolidated non-GAAP operating income was $249.7 million or 4.86% of net sales compared to $242.2 million or 5.81% of net sales last year. This includes operating income of $290.6 million or 8.71% of net sales for the DICK'S business and operating loss of $40.9 million for the Foot Locker business. Moving down the P&L. Consolidated non-GAAP income tax expense was $67.2 million or a rate of 28.6%. Our effective tax rate for the quarter was shaped by the mix of our earnings in foreign jurisdictions. In total, we delivered consolidated non-GAAP earnings per diluted share of $1.94 for the quarter. This compares to non-GAAP earnings per diluted share of $2.07 last year.

On a GAAP basis, our earnings per diluted share were $1.87. For additional details, you can refer to the non-GAAP reconciliation tables of our press release that we issued this morning. Now looking to our balance sheet. We ended the quarter with approximately $464 million of cash and cash equivalents and no borrowings on our $2 billion unsecured credit facility. Inventory was $6.1 billion at the end of the quarter, an increase of 9% versus last year. Within this, inventory for the DICK'S business increased 5.7%, while inventory for Foot Locker business increased 15.8%.

At Foot Locker, the inventory growth reflects a combination of planned investments in new and differentiated brands and styles as well as higher-than-desired inventory in certain legacy franchises following the shift in consumer demand we discussed last quarter. We are taking appropriate action to address this through markdowns, returns and cancellation of the product on order. Turning to capital allocation for the quarter. We remain committed to maintaining a strong balance sheet, while investing in the business and returning capital to shareholders. During the quarter, net capital expenditures were $335 million, and we returned $110 million to shareholders through dividends. As Ed discussed, we took advantage of the dislocation in our stock price during the quarter.

We completed a $1 billion senior notes offering and repurchased 6.7 million shares of our stock for $903 million at an average price of $134.21. Year-to-date, we have repurchased 7.4 million shares for $1.04 billion. Before moving to our outlook, I would like to provide a brief update on expectations surrounding Foot Locker. First, as part of our cleanout of the garage action and broader merger and integration work, we continue to expect total pretax charges of up to $750 million. To date, we have recognized $520 million of these charges. The remaining pretax charges will be incurred through 2026 and over the medium term as we complete this work.

Specifically, for 2026, we continue to expect approximately $200 million from these acquisition-related charges, which have been excluded from today's non-GAAP EPS outlook. Second, we remain confident in achieving our previously announced $100 million to $125 million of cost synergies over the medium term, primarily from procurement and direct sourcing efficiencies. A portion of these synergy benefits are expected in 2026 and are reflected in our outlook. Now moving to our outlook for 2026. Our updated guidance reflects the continued strength of the DICK'S business and the progress we are making at Foot Locker, all within the context of dynamic geopolitical and macroeconomic environment.

Within athletic footwear specifically, the marketplace remains promotional as the industry continues to work through elevated levels of legacy product. Against that backdrop, we are raising our full year expectation for DICK'S business, while maintaining our outlook for the Foot Locker business. Beginning with the DICK'S business, we now expect full year comp sales growth in the range of 3.3% to 4% compared to our prior comp growth expectation of 2.5% to 4%. We now expect full year operating income for DICK'S business in the range of $1.56 billion to $1.61 billion compared to our prior expectation of $1.54 billion to $1.6 billion. Turning to the Foot Locker business.

We continue to expect full year pro forma comp sales in the range of negative 2% to flat. We continue to expect full year operating loss for the Foot Locker business in the range of $80 million to $40 million. At the consolidated company level, we now expect full year non-GAAP earnings per diluted share in the range of $11.45 to $12.30 compared to our prior expectation of $11 to $12. Our earnings guidance is based on approximately 87.5 million average diluted shares outstanding compared to our prior expectation of approximately 90 million average diluted shares outstanding. We continue to anticipate a consolidated effective income tax rate of approximately 29% for the full year.

For Q4, our earnings guidance assumes approximately 83 million average diluted shares outstanding and a net interest expense of approximately $30 million. Finally, from a capital allocation standpoint, we continue to invest in the business to strengthen our leadership position, drive profitable organic growth across the DICK'S business and support the turnaround at Foot Locker. And we now expect full year net capital expenditures of approximately $1.3 billion compared to our prior expectation of approximately $1.4 billion. The reduction reflects efficiencies we have identified across our capital program, while preserving the investment we believe are the most important to our long-term growth.

In closing, we are pleased with the continued strength of the DICK'S business and encouraged by the progress we are making at Foot Locker. Our updated outlook reflects confidence in the opportunities ahead, while maintaining appropriate measured view of the work still underway. We remain focused on strong execution as we close out the year. This concludes our prepared remarks. Thank you for your interest in DICK'S Sporting Goods. Operator, you may now open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Simeon Gutman from Morgan Stanley.

Simeon Gutman: I'd like to start with the DICK'S business maybe to Lauren. So you delivered another positive comp in Q3, and you mentioned a strong back-to-school season and market share gains. At the same time, the comp moderated a bit from Q2. So if you can walk us, please, through the puts and the takes behind the quarter.

Lauren R. Hobart: Yes. Thanks, Simeon. We were really pleased with the 2.6% comp we had in Q3 on top of a 5.7% comp, and we continue to gain market share. The quarter had a lot of significant wins in it. And I would point to the back-to-school season where we really did deliver broad-based growth with footwear outpacing the overall comp. That actually was the case for the entire quarter, really strong footwear growth, but also strong performance in team sports and license and trading cards and apparel through the back-to-school season. Our consumer is remaining really strong. And so as we've talked about for many quarters now, we are seeing growth in our overall database.

We're actually having increased ScoreCard penetration and our athlete database is getting younger each year, which is just, I think, a testimony to the fact that we're bringing in so much newness and excitement. This quarter, we did also see all income demographics grow, and we didn't see trade down from best to better or better to good. So again, the consumer is going through a lot right now, but they are still prioritizing health and wellness, and they're certainly gravitating toward performance and newness and authenticity, and that's true across the entire portfolio. In October, as we all know, it was a very unseasonably warm October.

And for us at DICK'S that's a time when the cold weather apparel categories are very heavy in our mix. So fleece is a big driver in October. That warm weather certainly affected our comps for the quarter and our transactions for the quarter. But the base business is doing really, really well. And as we look to the holiday, we're very excited about the areas of newness and giftable items throughout the entire assortment. So we feel really, really terrific about the business.

Simeon Gutman: Okay. The second part, maybe just for Ed. So last quarter, we spoke about a pretty tough athletic footwear and apparel marketplace, especially around the legacy footwear silhouettes. Can you talk about what has -- how the conditions evolved since then? How are you thinking about the duration of the promotional pressure? And looking further ahead, how should we think about Nike's planned Jordan reset and the potential impact on DICK'S and Foot Locker?

Edward W. Stack: Thanks, Simeon. We indicated that our footwear business last year was -- or last quarter was very good, but just under margin pressure due to too much inventory in the marketplace. And we feel that's still the same way. It's been primarily caused, as we've talked about, by too many legacy franchises and silhouettes, and that hasn't changed. Our team has really done a great job bringing new styles and new materials and embellishments into some of the legacy models, which have now started to do relatively well with those new materials and embellishments.

We brought in new styles and broadened out some brands that are really doing extremely well in the marketplace, whether it's On, HOKA, Birkenstock, UGG and brands like that. So our footwear business, as we said, comped better than the company as a whole. So it's going to continue to be promotional through the balance of the quarter and maybe into -- a little bit into next year as we -- as everybody kind of cleans through that inventory. As far as the Jordan piece goes, I think it should be known that the Nike business at Foot Locker is really doing quite well. It's the Jordan business that's been difficult.

The decision Nike has made is, although a bit painful right now, is really the right decision for the Jordan brand for Nike and for Nike's partners. It's going to be really good for us going forward, but we're going to experience a little bit of pain here in the short term as they reset this business. So we're going to be a big beneficiary of the Jordan change longer term, but it is going to be a little bit painful and more so for Foot Locker than for DICK'S going forward into next year.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Kate McShane from Goldman Sachs.

Katharine (Kate) McShane: It does seem like with regards to margins, you came in a little bit better than originally guided. So could you maybe walk through the dynamics of that? Did you not have to promote necessarily as much as you thought? Are you getting more vendor support than maybe you originally guided for? And how should we think about that dynamic through the end of the year?

Edward W. Stack: I think there's a number of different things that we did. So was there some vendor support that we worked through? Yes. Did we have to promote quite as much? The silhouettes that needed to be promoted, that didn't change. But the team did a great job working the mix of bringing in some of these more in-demand products. The brands were helpful supporting us to get us that product. So we worked the mix a little bit there also. So it was -- it wasn't any one thing. It was a number of small things that our team really did a terrific job working through to help that margin rate.

Katharine (Kate) McShane: And then a follow-up question is, could you maybe update us on how you're thinking about any kind of underperforming assets within the Foot Locker portfolio? Are there stores that are under active consideration for closures either in Europe or at other branches? And how should we think about the possibility of change there?

Edward W. Stack: Yes, there are -- we are definitely looking at stores that, as I said in the script, are not meeting our profitability expectations. And there will be some stores that will close, and we're looking at those stores, and there'll be some across the globe, as you would imagine. There's stores in North America, in Europe, in Australia and New Zealand that aren't meeting our profitability expectations. And we don't see a path by which we could get them there. So they'll be closed, and we're starting to have these conversations with landlords about how we're going to go about that.

We want to try to be fair to our landlords, but we also need to make sure that we do what's right for our business. So we're in active discussions today.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Brian Nagel from Oppenheimer.

Brian Nagel: So first question I want to ask, this may be more for Ed, but on the more qualitative side, if you take the tone of the commentary today versus what we heard 3 months ago when you reported Q2 and some of the numbers, it seems like there's more confidence, right? So the question I want to ask is, I mean, a, am I hearing that correctly? But then maybe more importantly, if that's the case, is it more is DICK'S managing better than expected, a still tough environment? Or did the environment actually get better for DICK'S?

Edward W. Stack: Brian, I'd like to -- I don't know exactly how to say this, but I'm going to just try to say it. We didn't -- we never lost confidence. I think the Street kind of overreacted for whatever reason, and we understand that happens at times. But we were confident last time, we weren't happy about some of the promotional -- the promotional environment that we had to participate in. But as I said in the last call, we really felt that participating in that promotional environment was really a great investment and the right investment to make in our business, but we had never really lost confidence. So we're extremely confident in our business.

And I think you know us, we're somewhat conservative. There's got to be a lot of confidence for us to go out and buy 6.7 million shares of stock. And for the year, we're now up over 7 million shares of stock that we've repurchased. I think there's going to be a bumpy road with Foot Locker. It's going to be a bit bumpier than we had originally thought with what's going on with Jordan isn't helpful.

A couple of other brands have been a little bit more difficult, but there's brands that's really working, and we're in the process of working through those brands, bringing in more of the product that maybe Foot Locker hadn't had before from an On standpoint, HOKA standpoint, and adding those brands into Foot Locker and into different banners inside Foot Locker. So we remain very confident. It's just going to be a little bit bumpier road. As far as DICK'S goes, we're extremely confident about the DICK'S business with what we're doing with House of Sport, Field House, what's going on with GameChanger.

And I've often said GameChanger is our secret weapon of the data that we have with the youth sports and youth families. As we push into basketball with GameChanger, we couldn't be more excited about GameChanger. So on the DICK'S side, we're extremely confident, always have been. The Foot Locker side, we can kind of manage Foot Locker, and we've still got some work to do. We've got to work through some of the brands, and we've got to work through the Jordan issue. But we will work through that. And Nike is absolutely making the right decision of what they're doing with Jordan for the long term.

And I applaud them for having the courage to make that long-term decision and look at the business over the long term as opposed to trying to -- for a quarter or 2. They're making the right -- we couldn't be happier with what they're doing.

Brian Nagel: That's very helpful. And my follow-up question is on Foot Locker. We talked before about the remodeling, the Fast Break locations. Maybe I missed it, but any update there either how far you push into that remodeling of the performance of those units?

Edward W. Stack: When you say how far we push it, what do you mean? Are we going to do more of them or...

Brian Nagel: Like how many. Sorry, how many stores have now been remodeled?

Edward W. Stack: There's been -- we're up about 370 of them across the globe. I'd say we'll get close to 400 in the not-too-distant future.

Brian Nagel: And how are they performing now?

Edward W. Stack: They're outperforming the balance of the chain. We're pretty enthusiastic about it, especially as we reassort these stores with different product.

I guess how much was that -- would you attribute to the success of some of the Jordan launches and the Caitlin versus unit performance and AUR recovery? And then more broadly, how significant is the potential headwind from the model count reduction in terms of Foot Locker's mix? I think there's -- as you look back over the past 6 years, Foot Locker merchandise margin is down like 600 basis points, clearly, probably selling some units, but at a very heavy discount.

Edward W. Stack: Well, I think of the 4% comp in North America, we're not going to -- the Jordan piece was an important part of that. As we talked about in our call last quarter, we said that we felt that the launches in Q3 were going to be better than the launches in Q2. So that happened. Caitlin was important. Caitlin was probably more important for DICK'S than it was for Foot Locker, to be honest with you. And as we take a look at the headwinds with Jordan, we're still working through all of this with Nike. And Nike understands this. We're working through where we can get offsets in other styles and categories of product.

And our team is also working with other brands to take a look at how that we can offset what's going to happen from a Jordan standpoint. But we'll figure that. That's our job is to go figure these things out. And we're working through how to offset as much of the Jordan drop as we possibly can.

Christopher Horvers: I guess as you look back at Foot Locker's business prior to the acquisition, I mean, do you have a sense of what, I don't know, percentage full price selling or how much the AUR came off full price to try to drive some of those units and how just better in-stocks in key sizes and styles and high heat product can create an AUR tailwind that can provide a strong offset to what could be some unit headwinds?

Edward W. Stack: We think -- so I think you're looking at it the right way that there's going to be better in-stocks. There's going to be some -- we think more full price selling. You have to remember what happened with Foot Locker with Nike's modification to their go-to-market strategy when they went primarily DTC, a big part of that was taking product away from Foot Locker. And they were taking product away from Foot Locker that was the high heat product. They were taking product away from Foot Locker that was -- that the retro side of the business didn't get access to some other parts of the Nike business.

And that was because they really didn't feel Foot Locker had invested in their business. They have not invested from a marketing standpoint. They were -- as Nike said, they were an undifferentiated retailer. We're in the process of changing all of that. We've got Nike's full support along with the full support of other brands as we're doing this, and it's just going to take a little bit of time. But I would expect that there will be -- we are seeing more full price selling, and we will continue to see more full price selling going forward. And some of the AURs are picking up.

I mean, -- so I think you're looking at it the right way, and it's just going to take a little bit of time to do that.

Adrienne Yih-Tennant: Great. Edward W. Stack: Adrienne, before Navdeep answers that, I apologize. I just got called on to a vendor call that we've been trying to get taken care of. So I apologize, I've got to jump off, but Navdeep and Lauren can take it from here. I wish everybody a great Thanksgiving.

Navdeep Gupta: Actually, we'll share -- I would say some of the factors that you mentioned, the freight, the fuel as well as looking at some of the newness that you talked about are all the factors that we are considering in addition to what Ed mentioned around the Jordan allocation changes. On the DICK'S side, we continue to be extremely confident about the House of Sport and the Field House and the GameChanger growth opportunity. #2941. Why Connectivity Needs To Become Programmable

Mobile networks were designed with a person at the end of every connection. A contract carries a name, and a plan is sized for one phone. When something breaks, someone calls support or walks into a store.

That design fits a shrinking share of the people and things now using networks. Delivery robots, connected cars, smart meters and medical wearables are among the fastest-growing users, and none of them has a name on a contract. At the same time, AI assistants handle more everyday tasks for people, but connectivity is still largely out of their reach.

After years of building connectivity for travelers and distributed teams, I see these as one problem. Whether the user is a person or a device, the connection should be set up and managed through software. In other words, connectivity has to become programmable.

But machines don’t sign contracts, so someone has to own the relationship on their behalf. They also move: A sensor shipped from a factory in Poland may spend its working life in Brazil. Their usage looks nothing like a person’s. A smart meter sends a few kilobytes a day for 10 years, while a robotaxi can move gigabytes in an afternoon, and a consumer-style plan suits neither.

People run into the same friction, though it’s less visible. In our support conversations, the hardest questions are usually about status rather than speed: Is my plan active? Why did data stop at the border? Which line am I paying for? A well-designed system should answer those without requiring a support ticket.

Ericsson counted around 4.5 billion cellular IoT connections at the end of 2025 and expects that number to approach 8 billion by 2031. Its June 2026 Mobility Report also notes that uplink traffic is growing faster than downlink for most operators, and that additional AI traffic could push uplink to three times its 2025 level by 2031.

Software is also starting to act for people. Gartner predicted that 40% of enterprise applications would include task-specific AI agents by 2026, up from less than 5% in 2025. If an assistant can book your hotel, people will reasonably expect it to get them online at the destination as well. Today, that step usually leads to a QR code or a carrier portal designed for manual clicks.

Put these trends together, and more connectivity decisions will be made by software acting on someone’s behalf.

A SIM in every device connects the device, but it doesn’t make the connection manageable. Programmable connectivity means the connection itself can be requested, switched, limited and retired through APIs, much as cloud platforms let teams manage servers. I think that requires four capabilities.

• Delegated Identity: Every connection should be traceable to an accountable owner such as a company or a fleet operator, even when software manages it. Otherwise, fraud and misuse are very hard to attribute.

• Programmatic Provisioning: Devices without screens can’t scan QR codes. The GSMA’s SGP.32 specification already allows eSIM profiles on IoT devices to be downloaded, switched and retired remotely. The next step is exposing that capability through APIs, so a fleet platform, an app or an AI assistant can arrange connectivity on demand.

• Policy And Spend Controls: Software should manage connectivity within set limits: which networks, which regions, how much data and what maximum cost. Finance teams already set budgets for cloud usage, and connectivity should work the same way.

• Life Cycle Portability: A connected car or medical device may outlive three generations of network technology and several carrier contracts. Its connectivity has to move with it, across borders and providers, without anyone opening the casing.

Our enterprise customers rarely struggle with the first activation. Problems tend to come months later, when an employee relocates or a device changes hands. Those are the moments where programmable connectivity saves the most time.

A fair objection is that operators will build this themselves, and some already are. Network slicing reserves guaranteed performance for specific use cases, and Ericsson counted 84 commercial offerings built on it in June 2026, up from 65 seven months earlier.

I see the roles as complementary. An operator runs its own network. A platform layer works across networks: countries, operators, device types and budgets. A car built in Germany, sold in Brazil and driven across borders needs both.

I learned this from travel. Travelers plan around destinations, such as Lisbon on Monday and Madrid on Thursday, rather than around operators. The platform’s job is to match that plan with the right network at the right price, without asking anyone to understand roaming agreements. eSIM is what makes this workable: Because the SIM profile is software, a a network identity can be switched or retired remotely, whether on a phone or on a sensor bolted to a shipping container.

Imagine booking a trip through an assistant that, with your permission, also arranges a local data plan within a budget you’ve set. You land, turn off airplane mode and you’re online.

For the person at the center, programmable connectivity should mean fewer decisions. People don’t want to have to compare roaming rates, scan QR codes or follow up on support tickets. Connectivity works best when people don’t have to think about it, and making it programmable is a practical way to get there.​

#2935. ​Building A Data Foundation That Makes Enterprise AI Work

Niraj Nagrani is Chief Data and AI Officer at Altimetrik.

After more than 30 years as an enterprise leader, I’ve been through many transformation journeys, from building hyperscale systems and training data for machine learning to migrating from legacy architectures to modern data platforms. Today, I see many organizations struggle to move from a successful AI pilot to a reliable production system​.

The problem is not with foundation models, which have improved exponentially over the past few years. In my experience, the problem almost always comes back to the underlying data architecture.

Many organizations are still working with data that isn’t ready for AI. Data quality and lineage may be governed inconsistently or not governed at all. And governance is often bolted on at the end rather than built in from the start.

I’ve worked with companies running over 100 siloed systems. When information is scattered that widely, it can be almost impossible to establish a consistent view of the business. Unstructured data like contracts, emails and support tickets can disappear into blind spots because they don’t fit neatly into traditional data structures. Another problem is the lack of a shared definition of business entities like revenue, customers or other important measures across systems. ​

Earlier machine learning learned patterns from a curated, labeled dataset to do one narrow task. Agents reason and act in real time across systems. At the moment of action, an agent has to know what a “customer” means, which policy applies, whether the data is current and what it is allowed to see. Without that context, you get a confident wrong action. Earlier machine learning needed clean training data; agents need living context.

The key first step of data modernization is what I call “business rule archaeology.” Over time, organizations accumulate business logic in stored procedures, SQL queries and their dependencies. Some of that logic is documented, but a lot of it isn’t, which makes it difficult to understand how the existing business processes actually work. Companies often underestimate the effort required to untangle these dependencies.​

Before planning for​ modernization, understand how the business uses its data and how its processes operate. From there, organizations can build an incremental migration plan rather than trying to move everything at once.​

​I think about modernization as four steps, and each one becomes a layer of the platform you end up with. First, unify the isolated systems in an open lakehouse built on object storage and open table formats such as Iceberg or Delta, holding one governed copy of structured and unstructured data. Feed it through streaming and change data capture, because agents need current information, not last night’s batch.

Second, define shared business definitions in a semantic layer, so “revenue” or “customer” means the same thing in every system. Third, capture how those entities relate in an ontology and knowledge graph. This is what gives an agent the context for its decisions. Fourth, put governed retrieval across structured and unstructured data, with governance as code providing access management, lineage and a replayable audit trail. Agents also need their own identities with least-privilege access, and cost controls belong in the design from the start, because the cost of running models decides what is affordable at scale.​

Data trust is crucial, but it’s especially challenging when different teams have different standards for what good data looks like. Trust is an interface problem you engineer: one definition, enforced in the pipeline.

One useful mechanism is a data contract, a machine-readable agreement covering schema, quality requirements and service-level expectations between producer and consumer. It functions like a stable API, making the relationship between those parties more predictable.

Many current operating systems and data warehouses were built to answer yesterday’s question for a human. An agent-ready platform has to serve decisions to a machine in real time, with context, semantics and governance built into its design. That is what matters most as we design the next generation of data platform architecture.​

Store traffic and proprietary brands drove a return to growth, while digital lagged.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 4:08PM EST

Kohl's (KSS +19.48%) reported a return to comparable sales growth in the third quarter, supported by positive performance across all major merchandise categories. Management stated that strategic investments in store experience and inventory depth contributed to a 2% increase in store-based comparable sales. The company raised its full-year 2026 guidance for sales and earnings, reflecting progress in its proprietary brand portfolio and marketplace expansion. To prepare for the holiday season, the company is scaling its gifting assortment and expanding same-day delivery through partnerships with DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Instacart.

Second, our priority brands continue to resonate with our customers and delivered a positive 3.4% comparable sales performance in the quarter. Next, let me provide details on our three key initiatives and the progress we are making to deliver a better customer experience.

Beginning with our first initiative, offering a curated and more balanced assortment that fulfills the needs of all customers. This initiative focuses on addressing customer demand by clarifying assortments, elevating product relevance, and offering the key items and categories shoppers want. While there is still more work ahead in this initiative, our work is resonating with customers in the third quarter. Every line of business improved sequentially versus prior quarter and delivered a positive comp. Starting with the women's business, we returned to growth in the third quarter with a 0.5% comparable sales increase. Strength continues to be led by our juniors business, which delivered its fourth straight quarter of high-single-digit comparable sales increases.

We saw outperformance in our transition to cool weather goods with fleece and long-sleeve tees up low teens, and we expect this momentum to continue in the fourth quarter. Our intimates and sleepwear businesses were pressured in the quarter, and we continue to make progress with our reduced choice counts and improved depth, which is especially important to these categories. Moving to our men's business, which delivered a +1.5% comparable sales performance. Within active, we've also experienced strength from Tek Gear and Nike apparel. Our dress category also delivered strong performance in the quarter, up 11%, highlighted by Haggar. Softness in the men's business was driven by sportswear, which is still in the process of editing through assortments to provide improved clarity. Within kids apparel, we're seeing solid results from our fall seasonal merchandise with key brands like FLX Kids and SO. Although early, we are pleased with the initial results we saw within our baby and infant category, where we recently reintroduced the offering of our opening price point proprietary brand, Jumping Beans. Additionally, our Babies“R”Us initiative delivered another quarter of positive growth.

This September, we completed 56 additional Babies“R”Us shop build-outs and recently rolled out accessories towers in nearly all stores offering our highest velocity gifts and accessories. As we anticipated, our footwear business returned to growth in the third quarter, generating a 4% positive comp. This marks over a 700 basis point improvement from just the second quarter. Highlights include improved newness and depth in key brands like Nike, adidas, and Skechers, all delivering positive comparable sales. Additionally, we're excited about the performance we saw within our boots business, which was heavily impacted by tariffs last fall. Our accessories business improved and delivered a +0.7% comparable sales performance. Through this initiative, we are able to offer frequent newness and great value to our customers, featuring everyday essentials and small gifting items. Our Sephora at Kohl's business ran down 1.9% versus prior year. Although this continues to underperform the company, the Q3 results mark a 200 basis point improvement from Q2. This includes expanded gifting and value sets, new travel-sized assortments, exciting brand launches, and unlocking same-day delivery for Sephora customers by leveraging our DoorDash and Instacart partnerships.

Looking deeper, fragrance remained a bright spot in the third quarter with outperformance in key brands like YSL, KAYALI, and Valentino. We saw additional strength from prestige brands such as Charlotte Tilbury and Merit. Skincare continues to be the biggest challenge as we lap expanded distribution headwinds. This fall, we have introduced a lot of newness in the skincare business with exciting brands like Beauty of Joseon in the K-beauty category and Salt & Stone in the body category, both of which are off to strong starts.

Home continued to improve their business in the third quarter, delivering a 1% comp increase. This performance was driven by strength in electronics and bath categories. In small electrics, we continue to see newness and innovation resonate with customers, with key national brands Shark, Ninja, and KitchenAid posting strong double-digit comparable sales increases. Within our seasonal décor business, we were able to right-size our depth and invest more into choice counts. We are pleased with the customer response in our harvest and holiday décor businesses. Next, let me move to our second initiative, re-establishing Kohl's as a leader in value and quality.

In today's environment, it is evident that our customers have become increasingly choiceful with their discretionary spending as their budgets remain under pressure. Customers are looking to stretch every dollar, and we know how important it is to meet their needs, especially this upcoming holiday season. Our goal is to firmly position Kohl's as a trusted destination where families can consistently find excellent quality and relevant styles at compelling price points. We are delivering value through several avenues in order to deepen customer engagement while also attracting new shoppers. This work begins with elevating our proprietary brand portfolio, which, as I mentioned before, delivered over 3% sales growth in the third quarter.

These brands match affordability with modern style and continue to play an essential role in our assortment. In Q3, we made further progress enhancing these brands by increasing inventory depth while also investing into the in-store experience and scaling our marketing efforts to effectively build awareness for new and existing customers. Brands like SO, FLX, and LC Lauren Conrad continue to lead our apparel assortment, while brands like Miryana and Mingle & Co. drove strong performances in home. Additionally, we continue to discover new ways to enhance our ability to connect with customers throughout their shopping journey.

This includes leveraging targeted offers to deepen our engagement with our savvy Kohl's Card customers, who love the additional discounts they receive as Kohl's most loyal shoppers. Lastly, we saw a strong response from customers during our Kohl's Deal Days event in early October. This event highlighted broader and more simplified value messaging across key brands and categories to showcase the value we are offering. We are building on this success to provide exceptional value throughout our shopping experience. Our gifting and impulse business continues to become more impactful and serves to drive incremental units in our customers' baskets.

Our toy towers and deal bars are driving momentum by providing a compelling assortment of toys and home décor at price points under $10. Finally, our back-to-school offerings included thousands of back-to-school items priced under $25 to fit all budgets, all of which delivered strong results in the third quarter. Turning to our third initiative, building a frictionless omnichannel experience. Our teams made measurable progress in the third quarter across our inventory, store experience, and digital capabilities. Starting with our inventory management and allocation, disciplined merchandise planning remains foundational to our operating model. By establishing more timely, targeted inventory flows, we drove stronger full-price sell-through across key seasonal categories, reflected in our fall seasonal business increasing low single digits.

A core component of this inventory management and allocation is tailored to deliver trip assurance. We are intentionally simplifying the shopping experience by increasing our apparel inventory depth by mid-teens while trimming total choice counts by high teens. This deliberate shift delivers improved clarity and ensures our core high-demand items are reliably in stock. In addition, we are refining our allocation algorithms to better support lower-volume stores, ensuring a more consistent shopping experience across our store fleet. While still early in this work, we are already seeing the payoff as stores delivered positive comparable sales in the quarter. Another way to support our stores is through a more elevated experience.

Our store fleet serves as a competitive advantage for Kohl's, as we are investing in an enhanced in-store environment to drive engagement and conversion. This September, we rolled out this elevated experience to nearly all of our stores, highlighting our By Kohl's brands. These dedicated areas feature upgraded outfitting mannequins, clear navigation signage, and find your fit guides that make styling and self-service easier. Additionally, we are testing a strengthened brand and storytelling presentation with key brands like Nike and Levi's. Finally, on digital modernization, we are evolving our digital ecosystem to give customers inspiration and flexibility in how they shop. We continue to be encouraged by the initial results from our Ask Kohl's agentic shopping assistant.

Customers who engaged with Ask Kohl's are finding a more personalized experience, driving higher conversion and revenue per visit. In today's retail environment, customers are prioritizing speed and convenience. To capitalize on this, we recently launched same-day delivery offerings through partnerships at DoorDash and Uber Eats to complement our Instacart partnership. We are pleased with the start of this strategy and believe there is further opportunity to leverage our large and conveniently located store base to reach our customers. Additionally, we launched Klarna earlier this month, which provides a flexible payment option for our customers. Now, I would like to provide a brief update on how we are positioned for the important holiday season.

Our focus is on solidifying Kohl's as the go-to destination for value, gifting, and convenience. Consumers remaining highly choiceful with their spending, how we show up will be even more important. Knowing this, we identified three primary areas of focus this holiday. First, offering a sharpened value in our assortment. We are meeting budget-conscious shoppers with clear, compelling value, featuring $5-$20 opening price point gifts and impulse stocking stuffers. Freshness will be front and center, with nearly half of our holiday gift shop assortment being completely new this year, with the vast majority priced under $15. At the same time, we have scaled gifting across our destination categories.

This includes expanding our fine jewelry presence, dedicated in-store toy towers featuring items under $10, and curating over 2,000 Sephora prestige beauty gifts under $30. The Sephora partnership continues to be an incredible traffic driver, bolstered this season by exciting new brand arrivals and gift sets. Second, an engaging marketing campaign. Our holiday campaign, The North Kohl's, bridges inspiring brand storytelling with purposeful basket building. In our stores, we have simplified the shopping journey by creating curated discovery hubs such as the Cozy Corner, Style Square, and Hosting Headquarters, designed to drive cross-category conversion.

Across all media channels, we are leaning into broader, simplified promotional messaging to ensure our value proposition cuts through the holiday noise, particularly during peak volume moments, including Black Friday, Cyber Week, and the post-Christmas clearance window. Third, enabling frictionless omnichannel execution. Winning the holiday season requires exceptional operational agility, and we are meeting our customers however they choose to shop by launching our new AI-powered digital shopping assistant, integrating flexible payment options at checkout, and significantly expanding same-day delivery. Furthermore, for shoppers prioritizing speed and convenience right down to the wire, most of our buy online, pick up in store orders will be fulfilled and ready within two hours straight through Christmas Eve.

We are excited about the plan we have underway, and we are ready to serve our customers this holiday season. With that, I would like to hand the call over to Jill.

Jill Timm: Thank you, Michael. In the third quarter, we realized a tax benefit of $137 million from the release of a tax reserve following a positive outcome on a prior period tax position. This benefited our earnings per share by $1.16 in the third quarter and $1.17 year-to-date. Our underlying effective tax rate is estimated to be 23% for the year. Year-to-date, our net income was $391 million, or $3.33 of earnings per diluted share. This includes one-time benefits of $1.17 per share from the tax reserve release, $0.93 from tariff refunds, and $0.39 from real estate gains. Moving on to the balance sheet and cash flow statement.

We continue to operate in a significantly better cash position compared to last year, finishing the quarter with $723 million of cash and cash equivalents. We continue to invest in increased apparel depth up mid-teens while reducing choice counts by high teens in Q3 to restore trip assurance for our customers.

Looking ahead, we are planning receipts up high-single-digits in the fourth quarter to support depth of our fall seasonal assortment, invest in low-volume stores, and transition goods stronger into spring. We now expect capital expenditures to total approximately $365 million-$375 million for the year. Second, we will continue to return capital to shareholders through our dividend. We returned approximately $14 million to shareholders through our dividend in the third quarter. Year-to-date, we've returned approximately $42 million. Fourth, we will return excess capital to shareholders through our share repurchase program.
