So from a gross margin perspective, the inherent guide was always to be negative in Q4, and that hasn't changed. I think when you pull apart the tariff benefit that we tried to outline for you'll see that our gross margin will be negative in Q4 because we know it's a promotional time of year, value's critically important to the customer, and we wanted to be set up to be able to compete well in that space.

I think so far, that's afforded us a lot of opportunity, obviously with the progressive improvement you've seen from the top-line perspective. SG&A will be a little bit elevated in Q4 as well. We've seen great returns off of the store payroll investments that we've made. We've talked to you about the fact that we tested that store payroll for well over a year, and we saw when we gave them customer-facing payroll, it heightened the engagement, and we saw a sales lift. We were able to put a lot of that in place in Q3, which you saw payback with the 2% comp in our stores.

So we're going to continue to lean into that into Q4, as well as we're going to see media. We outlined, we have a great marketing campaign that continues to drive that newness and excitement into Kohl's. Then, of course, there is the fuel pressure with transportation, which does heighten in the fourth quarter, just given the fact that cost of shipping is impacted by that, as well as we have much more frequency of trips going to our stores, given just the volume that we do through the fourth quarter. Then into 2027, obviously haven't given a guide yet, but continue to expect that we can leverage off of a one comp.

So really, anything off of a one comp and above, you know that this model works quite efficiently. That's where our variable cost model kicks in. So we should be able to definitely, with positive comps, drive an expansion from a margin perspective. But obviously, we'll have more conversation with that at the end of the year.

Mark R. Altschwager: That's great. Thank you. Michael, bigger picture, the two-year stack improved by more than 400 basis points this quarter. What do you think has changed in how the customer sees Kohl's, and where are you winning share back? What gives you confidence in a lasting return to growth here? Thank you.

Michael J. Bender: Yeah. Thanks for the question, Mark. I would say that a lot of our emphasis, as you've seen over the last year, has been on curating this balance of proprietary brands and national brands in portfolio, complete with Nike, Levi's, et cetera, and the strong group of proprietary brands that we have. I think that's one of the things that's certainly resonating with the customer base that we're working off of. The team has been really zeroed in on that effort over the last year or so to bring that back.

We've been supremely focused on value and making sure that the combination of what we offer in value, not being defined just by price, but by price, quality, convenience, style, and making sure that the combination of those elements bring forward an inspiring experience for the customer. We've mentioned also in our release that we've been focusing on making sure that the in-store customer experience is something that we'll see improvements in. I think the customer's starting to notice that as well. So when you add all those things up, I think the combination of value, convenience, the trip assurance that our customers ask for, and that inspiring experience is really what's helping the customer come back to us.

Maybe lastly, this focus that we also mentioned around the Kohl's Card customer and the focus that we've had there in making sure that we're bringing back the elements that really focus them in on our business has been a big positive for us going forward. I think we're all really excited about how quickly that has snapped back. If you recall, this time last year, we were talking about that particular cohort of our customers performing not the way we wanted to. The fact that they are now up and positive is a really big testament to the work that we are doing to excite that customer about Kohl's again.

Mark R. Altschwager: Great. Congrats on the return to positive comps, and best of luck over holiday.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Robert (Bob) Drbul with BTIG. Your line is open. Please go ahead.

Robert (Bob) Drbul: Hi. Good morning. Just two questions from me. First, on the footwear business. Can you talk a bit more around the trends that you are seeing with the key brands that you mentioned, and I guess sort of more as you are seeing fourth quarter and into 2027 around the footwear business? Then second question is, can you expand a bit just on the performance of the digital business, as well as the digital modernization that is underway and what you are seeing within that piece of the business? Thanks.

Michael J. Bender: Yeah. I will take a shot maybe at the first question around footwear, and Jill, please chime in as well. Footwear has been an exciting turnaround category story for us, Bob, and it is 700 basis point improvement from the prior quarter and a big, big change. We had said that we would start to see that business turn around the back-to-school timeframe, and the merchant that leads that business has been spot on in terms of her expectation of that happening, and that is what we are seeing.

Obviously, we had some challenges last year with tariffs that prevented us from having a full assortment that is focused in that footwear category, but the team has worked very hard in bringing that back to life for us that is showing up in the business. Boots is a big bright spot for us going forward in that category, and we have every expectation that will continue to go forward. So, we feel good about that. As far as the digital business is concerned, we have some opportunity, we know, to continue to make that business one that contributes more to the business for us.

We are not pleased with the slowdown, but we have got a number of initiatives underway inside the business to continue to make that piece of the business continue to perform for us better. Jill, anything else you would—

Jill Timm: Yeah, I think you asked about kind of what modernization means, and I think there is a couple things. First, it is going to be a long-term play for us, Bob. This is not going to happen overnight. We brought in Arianne Parisi, and she has made a lot of quick changes. Obviously, our marketplace growth, bringing in different payment options, speed for convenience with having DoorDash, Uber Eats, Instacart. We have Ask Kohl's on the agentic commerce side, which although still small, we are meeting the customer where they want to be, and we do see that when we have them engage with Ask Kohl's, we have a higher revenue per visit.

So those are all leading indicators, I think, of why we think this business will get back to growth. But there are things like the site enhancements for just faster performance, better product experiences, improved discovery and navigation, that is going to take a longer term for us to really get back out to parity with competitors. I think in the short run, we feel great with some of the initiatives that we have in flight, but we know over the long term, we have to compete stronger here and definitely not pleased with the slowdown we saw, but feel very confident in the work and efforts we have ahead.

Robert (Bob) Drbul: Great. Thank you very much.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Dana Telsey with Telsey Advisory Group. Your line is open. Please go ahead.

Dana Telsey: Hi. Good morning, everyone, and so nice to see the progress. As you think about the Kohl's Card customer, one of the benefits has been the increased coupon eligibility. Where are you on that path? Are the brands you want all on there? Is there more to come? Then when you think about not just Q4, but even a framework for 2027, on the margin structure, Jill, how do you think about puts and takes, and where does freight and fuel costs land? Thank you.

Michael J. Bender: Yeah, Dana, thanks for the question. I would say on the Kohl's credit card customer, you're exactly right. The coupon eligibility has been a big driver of our ability to continue to improve that performance. We made those changes last year in two different tranches, one in April, one in August of last year. I would say we're about where we need to be at this point. As we continue to bring different brands on, we'll make that evaluation.

But we feel very good about that and the response that you're seeing in terms of that customer cohort being positive now, I think is a big testament to the fact that we listened to the customer and we built the story around making sure that we were able to bring the products that they are interested in buying from us, whether it's petites or jewelry or some of the others that are coupon-eligible brands back into the mix, and that's what's showing up.

Jill Timm: Then I think from a margin structure perspective, I definitely think, as we mentioned, when we get to a 1% comp, that's our sweet spot and when we can start leveraging and expanding our operating margin. Clearly, this is where we got to from this quarter. There will be pressures, like you mentioned, freight and fuel, but I think this company does an amazing job. They step up to the plate when we have some of these pressures. I think last year, tariffs was a specific example. You saw the sourcing team, the merchant team really come together to find a way to offset the tariff pressure, and we really didn't have that conversation last year.

Then this year, as you can see, we're letting the tariff benefit flow through. So, I would say definitely going to see it as a continued pressure, but feel good with the work the team is doing to find ways to offset some of that pressure. So, as long as it maintains where it is at, obviously it is ever-moving, I feel like we have a good plan forward, and we will obviously be able to speak more to that in detail as we give our 2027 guidance.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Michael Binetti with Evercore ISI. Your line is open. Please go ahead.

Michael Binetti: Guys, congrats on a great quarter. Nice to chat with you today. I guess, on Sephora for a minute, nice to see the sequential improvement there. How do you think about how the merchandise changes that you guys laid out today help with recruiting that incremental beauty customer via the assortment versus servicing existing customers that are coming in at a lower price point today? Are you seeing any changes in those dynamics as you start to see the sequential improvement in trends in 3Q? And then, to your comments about October being the best month of the quarter, I do not think we have heard that elsewhere in retail.

Can you just help us think about the better trends you saw in the South and how those categories or initiatives are starting to translate into the rest of the fleet or the other markets as we get into fourth quarter?

Michael J. Bender: Yeah, sure. On your first question about Sephora and the category alignment there, we made changes a little while ago in terms of the positioning of juniors across from Sephora, as an example. That category, as we had mentioned, has shown four straight quarters of high-single-digit improvement over the past year or so. We think that's a direct reflection of the fact that we've situated that positioning of our business across from Sephora, and we'll continue to do that. That will continue to drive the business going forward with the Sephora customer. We have seen the conversion of that customer continue to improve going forward as well, and that's something that we'll curate as we go.

Jill, I'll turn it over to you for the second question.

Jill Timm: Yeah. I love that we can be an outlier on the positive side, Michael, in terms of where October is. Definitely ending with strength and leading into November feels good. I would say a couple things there. One is we talked about our Deal Days resonated incredibly well, and that helped drive some momentum into October, which to me is always a good sentiment of what's to come, right? That's our first step into really from a holiday perspective, showing great value, and it resonated with the customer. We also had a really good pricing event.

I know our Kohl's Charge customer, we talked about the coupon eligibility had an effect on them, but just showing up with great prices also continues to benefit from a customer perspective. I said the third thing is we had some opportunities to really reinvest into depth. We've edited out choice and restored trip assurance with that customer, and that doesn't happen overnight, obviously, with inventory coming in, and I think we really showed up great throughout the quarter. We were able to build on that momentum. Particularly in those southern markets, I would say that we had opportunity to fill those in with more inventory, really when we talk about some of the small store strategies we've had.

Being able to bring them in inventory, they were actually able to really be productive with that investment and show strength, particularly in October, as that inventory was setting, all which sets us up, in my opinion, with good momentum as we lead into the fourth quarter. Clearly still had some weather headwinds in those cold weather categories, like Michael mentioned, where specifically in the North, you had outerwear and some fleece and sweaters that did see a slowdown as the weather warmed up. What I would say now is we're kind of seeing that cold weather come into play. We're definitely seeing a pickup in that business as well.

I would say that we were able to take advantage of the value orientation that we had centered around all year, the inventory depth that we had talked about restoring that trip assurance for the customer, and really that played through well into October and should build momentum into Q4.

Michael Binetti: Can I follow on that? Can we read that as you were able to deliver comps in third quarter that are within the range that you are guiding us to for fourth quarter without the benefit of weather? Can we interpret that as we are in the range today that you guided to for fourth quarter, or would weather turning be a source of upside? What can we read from your comments there? Thank you.

Jill Timm: Sure. I mean, my implied guide for Q4 was flat to up 2%, and right now, that means the midpoint is what we just finished on. So, I kind of feel like the low end is you have headwinds, whether that be macro or uncertainty or weather, and the high end continues to say that the momentum that we have talked about and the progress that we have put up this year continues, and the midpoint is right where we are at. So, that is how I would look at the guidance. Obviously, we have huge days ahead of us, Michael, which are going to be a big factor in the outcome of Q4.

But I believe, based on the strategy that we have employed, the momentum that we have seen, we are set up well to take advantage of those.

Michael Binetti: That is great. Thank you so much, Jill.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Blake Anderson with Jefferies. Your line is open. Please go ahead.

Blake Anderson: Hey, guys. Appreciate the question, and congrats on the great results and positive comp. Wanted to start with the commentary regarding trade-down. Curious if you can provide any color. Are these new customers? I believe you mentioned some higher income. Are they shopping more in-store or online? How are you ensuring you can maintain their spend over time as well, kind of on that trade-down dynamic? Then, Jill, I believe you mentioned the comp was more transaction-driven. Can you just talk about traffic conversion AUR, what you expect for Q4, and how should we think about the ability to drive higher AUR as well over time?

Jill Timm: Well, I would say in terms of the customer, when you're in a macro environment that we're navigating, we see a trade-down out of a higher income into our stores, and we need to take advantage of that. We can do that through the power of our national brands, like I mentioned. Nike, adidas, Levi's, all doing quite well for us in the quarter. That's an opportunity we have to introduce them into Kohl's. I think the elevation of our proprietary brands, showing them that we actually do have fashion and style in our stores, Sephora serves as a great anchor for that as well, are all opportunities for us to keep that customer in.

I think from a keeping that customer, we also see trade-offs in the middle, and that's where we're benefiting off of our proprietary brands right now. People have to make choices. They are definitely struggling in terms of where they're going to make payments with pressure and fuel and inflation. So, if we can give them a great product at a little bit lesser price point, that's where we see people making trade-offs, and that's where the power of the proprietary portfolio comes into play. Clearly, up 3.4% in the quarter, we saw that play out. In terms of the comp, we saw definitely it was driven both by transactions, which for us is an exciting pivot point.

We haven't been able to talk about transactions being positive in a while, so I think that's a big sentiment of positive growth. But also, we saw it in ATV, and that was more about the trade-offs that we just spoke about. Our units per transaction were up, offset with the lower AUR. I think this just goes to the fact that value is going to be incredibly important to this customer as we play out the rest of this holiday season. For us right now, we're focused on driving value, not so much expanding higher AURs.

I do believe when we're in a cycle that AURs are expanding, we have the right to play there, and we can do that through our national brands, like we talked about Nike, Sephora, and adidas. We can play in both spaces. Right now, I think for the customer, the most important thing is to deliver them value, and that's how we guided our Q4. I think that's what we would anticipate we will continue to do into 2027, unless we see a difference from an inflationary perspective. Obviously, we have opportunity to sharpen our pencils on 2027 and give you that guidance at the end of the year.

Michael J. Bender: Blake, the only other thing I would add, in addition to what Jill shared, is just the fact that from a consumer perspective, the importance of speed and convenience. You heard us talk about these initiated opportunities with DoorDash, Instacart, Klarna from a payment standpoint. Those are all pieces that factor into this value equation that our customer is working their way through as they're deciding where to shop, and the ability to get an item as quickly as possible, order it the way they want, have it show up quickly, and in some cases, pay for it over time with the support like Klarna.

Those are all things that we're adding into the mix to make sure that we're listening to what our customer is asking for from us to create that value equation that resonates most notably with them.

Blake Anderson: That's very helpful. Thanks so much.

Operator: We have reached the end of the Q&A session. This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#2926. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2921. 19 Signs Your Company’s Technology Is Creating More Work

Technology should simplify workflows and improve productivity. However, when systems are difficult to navigate, unreliable or disconnected, employees may develop alternative solutions just to get their jobs done.

These workarounds can reveal deeper problems with technology adoption, system design and organizational processes. Below, Forbes Technology Council members share warning signs that employees are spending too much time working around their company’s technology rather than benefiting from it, along with insights on addressing the underlying issues.

The biggest tell for me is hearing, “Here’s how we actually do it.” If that follows with some description that combines spreadsheets, duplicate data entry, manual handoffs or clever ways around the system, that’s a pretty clear sign the technology is creating work rather than removing it. - Abhijit Singh, Jefferson

If employees constantly ask coworkers for help with the same system tasks or there’s an unofficial cheat sheet, chat thread or go-to “expert” everyone relies on to navigate a tool, the technology is not intuitive enough to be used on its own. Low adoption of mandatory tools or new hires taking too long to be productive with a tool are indicators that people are spending too much time figuring out the technology instead of using it. - Austin Berglas, Nardello & Co.

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Working around a system can increase your cognitive load—the mental effort placed on your working memory. A recent survey found that since AI was introduced, enterprise workers spend longer searching for information, parse through more alerts, and juggle more tabs and applications. Symptoms like these can indicate employees are working harder to manage the technology than realizing its benefits. - Mazy Dar, HERE Enterprise (here.io)

Jumping across multiple tools and screens to complete one workflow is a clear sign that people are just becoming workers for the tools rather than using those tools to deliver their work better and faster. This is more relevant in the AI era. - Raja Shanmugam, TATA Consultancy Services

When employees rely on personal texts, phone calls or spreadsheets to compensate for enterprise systems, there’s a workflow problem. These workarounds often emerge because existing tools are too slow, fragmented or unreliable. Leaders should investigate where employees bypass technology and address the underlying friction before it creates operational risks. - Judit Sharon, OnPage Corporation

Watch for employees delaying decisions because they don’t trust how current the information is. If a sales or marketing team has to wait for an overnight update before responding to a customer or adjusting a campaign, the technology is setting the pace instead of supporting the work. Teams should be able to act on what is happening now, not yesterday’s picture. - Vibhor Kapoor, AdRoll

One sign is that unofficial spreadsheets become essential to completing everyday work. In capital markets, employees may repeatedly export trade data, reconcile it manually, and re-enter the results across systems. When these workarounds become routine, the technology is shifting effort onto employees rather than removing it. Those spreadsheets reveal where workflows need fixing. - Lakshmanan Alagappan, Genpact UK

Shadow documentation is a sign that the official documentation is lacking or so generic that it is hard to adapt to use cases that are fairly common. The more guides that are built to explain how to use a piece of software, the more it should be evaluated for improvement. Simplify the interface with role-based views, and rename custom fields and data so they’re clearer. Just don’t forget to clean up the shadow documentation too. - Luke Wallace, Bottle Rocket

One sign is that the know-how lives in people, not the system. When a tool doesn’t do exactly what’s needed, rather than asking for changes to the tool, work becomes manual, and one person ends up as the only one who knows how it really runs. Sometimes that’s accidental and sometimes it’s job security; either way, it’s a bottleneck. - Anila Siraj, OpsBridge Advisory

One sign is employees building integrations the vendor never intended. Not plugins. Not configurations. Custom code written at midnight by someone who needed two systems to talk to each other and could not wait six months for a roadmap update. That unauthorized integration is not ingenuity. It is your architecture silently fracturing one undocumented API call at a time. When engineers route around the system, the system has already failed. - Mukul Arora

People clicking straight through warnings is a sign. Track override rates and fix the friction behind them. If employees routinely hit “proceed anyway” on a blocked link or a security prompt, the tool is getting in the way of real work, and they have stopped reading it. That is a workaround too, albeit a quiet one, and it trains them to ignore warnings—maybe even those that matter. - Flavius Plesu, OutThink

One clear sign is when employees spend more time figuring out how to make a tool work than doing their actual jobs. If everyone knows which buttons to avoid, which errors to ignore and when to restart the system, your technology isn’t saving time. It’s wasting it. - Margarita Simonova, ILoveMyQA

Check the expense reports, not the help desk tickets. When employees start reimbursing themselves for $30 SaaS subscriptions, they’ve already given up on the official tools and bought their way around them. Finance sees it first. IT sees it months later. The line items are small enough to approve without question, which is exactly why they keep adding up. - Nidhi Jain, CloudEagle.ai

Map the value stream from user intent to task outcome. If employees are required to navigate more than three non-value-added steps to complete a task, I’d question the process before adding more steps. Workarounds add effort yet little to no customer value. Even worse is when teams automate workarounds when they should be eliminating the reason it exists in the first place. - April Ho-Nishimura, Infineon Technologies AG

When I ask a client team how their leadership report is produced, a common answer is that someone builds a spreadsheet by hand before every meeting. That tells me the official systems are being worked around. The hours are the visible cost. The bigger one is that leaders start questioning the numbers in the room instead of making decisions. - Dimitar Dimitrov, Accedia

Count the decisions the technology changed last week. Many companies hand managers a data platform and announce that every number is in there, ready for any table they want. Almost nobody opens it because it asks them to become analysts. They keep deciding using their gut and old reports. A tool that shows each manager their own score and the next move gets checked daily. If a system doesn’t trigger decisions, it is overhead. - Vivek Thomas, AISensum

You must watch how often employees double-check a tool’s output before acting on it. If a manager has to pull the original records to verify every report, the system may be saving time on preparation while adding it back in review. So, ask what people still check by hand and why. That extra checking is part of the cost of the tool, too. - Elton Chan, Second Talent

Take a construction site where the real system is WhatsApp. A delivery gets redirected to another site in a group chat; nobody updates the records, materials arrive at the wrong site, and machinery stands idle. When orders change in chats and handwritten logs, the ERP is just a reporting duty. Count how many changes never reach your system of record. - Andrew Babkin, Azati

One sign is when employees lower the quality of their work because company technology cannot support enough detail. Engineers may simplify technical assessments, while customer service teams may give incomplete responses because systems restrict what they can record or process. Leaders should check whether technology limitations influence the quality of business outcomes. Technology should support professional judgment, not force employees to compromise it. - Salice Thomas, Wipro Limited
